stem: Carol is a 15 year old who presents in the emergency department because of vomiting over a 24 hour period. She appears dehydrated and weak but her Glasgow Coma Scale is normal. Her parents describe to you a 3-week history with symptoms consistent with hyperglycemia. Over the past 24 hours, Carol has vomited 3-4 times and has been feeling weaker. You suspect that Carol has diabetes and wonder if she is in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Which initial investigations would you order to determine if Janet is in DKA?

options.html: Fasting blood glucose, blood gas, serum electrolytes
Random blood glucose, blood gas, urine ketones
Random blood glucose, hemoglobin A1C, blood gas
Fasting blood glucose, urinalysis, serum electrolytes
Oral glucose tolerance test, blood gas, hemoglobin A1C

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. B. She is symptomatic, so one random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L already establishes diabetes. The only question is DKA, which needs the other two legs of the definition: acidosis (blood gas) and ketosis (urine or serum ketones). That is exactly the lecture's workup: random glucose, urine dipstick for glucose and ketones, and a blood gas if DKA is suspected.

  • A and D ask for a fasting glucose, which a vomiting, dehydrated child cannot wait for and which adds nothing in a symptomatic patient. D also omits the blood gas.
  • C and E add A1c or an OGTT. The lecture says FPG and A1c are usually unnecessary in new-onset T1DM, an OGTT in a vomiting child is inappropriate, and neither identifies ketoacidosis.

stem: Loki is a 14 year old boy who has had Type 1 diabetes for 8 years. He is currently receiving NPH at breakfast and at bedtime, and Novorapid at breakfast and suppertime. His insulin is injected into his legs and abdomen. He checks his blood glucose levels four times daily. He is seen regularly in a pediatric diabetes clinic and his most recent hemogloblin A1C is 8.4%. Which of the following is true with regards to Loki’s glycemic control?

options.html: Loki’s target blood glucose should be 6-12 mmol/L at bedtime to decrease his risk of overnight hypoglycemia
Loki’s daytime blood glucose should be 4-10 mmol/L in order to optimize his glycemic control
It is acceptable for Loki to be having hypoglycemic events once daily
Loki’s hemoglobin A1C should be monitored on an annual basis
Loki’s hemoglobin A1C should be less than 7.5% in order to decrease his risk of long-term complications

answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. E. The lecture's target for a patient under 18 with T1DM is A1c < 7.5%, with FPG 4-8 and post-prandial 5-10 mmol/L. The DCCT is why the target exists: lower A1c means fewer long-term microvascular complications. Loki's 8.4% is above it.

  • A and B quote ranges that are not the lecture's targets (4-8 pre-meal, 5-10 post-prandial). The notes give no separate bedtime target, so A's exact numbers cannot be checked against the notes.
  • C: daily hypoglycemia is never acceptable. Frequent lows mean the regimen needs adjusting.
  • D: A1c reflects about 3 months of glycemia and is checked roughly every 3 months, not annually (frequency reasoned from general principles).

preamble.title: The case - Loki
preamble.html: The case. Loki is a 14 year old boy who has had Type 1 diabetes for 8 years. He is currently receiving NPH at breakfast and at bedtime, and Novorapid at breakfast and suppertime. His insulin is injected into his legs and abdomen. He checks his blood glucose levels four times daily. He is seen regularly in a pediatric diabetes clinic and his most recent hemogloblin A1C is 8.4%.

stem: What recommendations, if any, would you make to improve Loki’s glycemic control?

options.html: Loki should inject his insulin after meals so that he can give insulin to suit the amount of carbohydrates he has eaten
Loki should switch to a more intensive insulin regimen or on to an insulin pump in order to optimize his glycemic control
Loki should be eating small meals frequently throughout the day to decrease his glycemic excursion
Loki should only inject insulin in his abdomen in order to achieve consistent insulin absorption
No changes need to be made to Luke’s diabetes regimen

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. B. Loki is on twice-daily NPH plus rapid-acting insulin with an A1c of 8.4%. The DCCT showed that more intensive insulin therapy (basal-bolus or 4-injection schedules) lowers A1c and microvascular complications, and insulin pumps add better control, more reliable absorption, precise dosing and a lower hypoglycemia risk. Intensifying is the lever.

  • A: bolus insulin is dosed before meals on a sliding scale for the planned carbohydrate. Injecting afterwards lets the post-prandial spike run ahead of the insulin (timing reasoned from general principles).
  • C: the dietary pillar is carbohydrate counting matched to bolus dosing, not grazing.
  • D: absorption differs between sites, but restricting to one site does not fix an under-intensive regimen and invites lipohypertrophy (general principles).
  • E: his A1c is above the < 7.5% pediatric target, so something must change.

stem:
Wanda also has Type 1 diabetes. She comes to your office with blood glucose levels that have become very variable. Her insulin doses are as follows: Before breakfast: humalog (lispro) 6 units Before lunch: humalog (lispro) 8 units Before supper: humalog (lispro) 10 units Bedtime: Levemir 30 units Based on these blood glucose values, which of the following would you recommend to Wanda at this time? (select all that apply)

AC BreakfastAC LunchAC SupperBedtime
Monday16.3 mmol/L8.3 mmol/L3.6 mmol/L9.3 mmol/L
Tuesday18.9 mmol/L6.9 mmol/L3.2 mmol/L5.9 mmol/L
Wednesday14.7 mmol/L4.2 mmol/L6.1 mmol/L7.1 mmol/L

options.html: Decrease the Levemir dose to 27 units
Increase the Levemir dose to 33 units
Increase the Humalog at breakfast by 1 unit
Increase the supper Humalog by 2 units
Decrease the supper Humalog by 1 unit
Decrease the lunch Humalog by 1 unit

answer:
The correct answers are B and F.

From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. Fix the insulin given before the abnormal reading. Read the table by column, not by day.

  • AC breakfast is high every day (14.7-18.9). The insulin covering the night is the bedtime basal, Levemir, so B: increase Levemir. A (decrease it) goes the wrong way.
  • AC supper is low (3.6, 3.2). The insulin covering the afternoon is the lunch Humalog, so F: decrease lunch Humalog.
  • C: breakfast Humalog governs the AC lunch reading, which is acceptable to low-normal (4.2-8.3). The high breakfast value is a basal problem, not a breakfast-bolus problem.
  • D and E: supper Humalog governs the bedtime reading (5.9-9.3), which needs no change either way.

stem: A 52-year-old overweight woman presents to the clinic for a diabetes management. She had not been doing well controlling her blood sugars with metformin. Her last hemoglobin A1C was 13.4%, despite her taking her medication every day. The physician decides to start her on a long-acting insulin that is injected only once a day for better glucose control. Also, he wants the insulin to have a minimal risk of hypoglycemia. What is the most likely medication given to this patient?

options.html: Insulin aspart
Insulin lispro
Insulin glargine
NPH insulin
Regular insulin

answer: The correct answer is C. The only long-acting insulins in this list are glargine and NPH. Compared to NPH, insulin glargine presents lower risk of hypoglycemia.

stem: You are asked to see a 22-year-old man who comes in with severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. In the ER his initial investigations showed the following: ​ Sodium 130 (N 134-145), Potassium 3.2 (N 3.5-5), Bicarbonate 10 (N 22 – 32), random blood glucose of 25 mmol/L​ Which of the following test would be most helpful to confirm your diagnosis :

options.html: Venous blood glass and serum ketones (beta hydroxybutyrate)
Liver enzymes (ALT, ALP, AST and total bilirubin)
CBC
Urine electrolytes and osmolality

answer:
The correct answer is A, venous blood gas and serum ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate).

The lecture keys this A and gives its own rationale: "This a young patient with no history of diabetes presenting with hyperglycemia, hyponatremia and hypokalemia - likely new presentation of Type 1 DM with DKA - Venous blood gas and ketones will help arrive at the diagnosis." It is also the only option that matches the stem's anion-gap picture.

stem: You are seeing a patient with Type 1 Diabetes for a routine follow up visit. He tells you that he has been experiencing tingling and numbness in his feet. Two months ago, he developed a small ulcer that took 1.5 months to heal. On his recent eye exam, he was told that he had ”leaky blood vessels”. You review the report from the optometrist which states that he has non-proliferative retinopathy. He has no chest pain or shortness of breath. He has no calf cramping/pain when walking. No stroke/TIA symptoms. ​ Which category of complications does this patient have?

options.html: Microvascular
Macrovascular
Microvascular and macrovascular
None of the above

answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes. A. Every finding is a small-vessel complication.

  • Tingling and numbness in the feet: peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy (glove and stocking, feet before hands because of nerve length).
  • The slow-healing foot ulcer: a consequence of that neuropathy (loss of protective sensation).
  • "Leaky blood vessels": non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, the most common microvascular complication.
  • B and C need a macrovascular finding (MI or angina, stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease), and the stem deliberately denies chest pain, dyspnea, claudication and stroke/TIA symptoms.
  • D: he clearly has complications.

stem: A patient presents to the ER with polydipsia and polyuria that have been going on for several days. Blood glucose is 30 mmol. pH is 7.4. Creatinine is elevated and the patient is looking very sick. The patient’s mother has a history of T2DM. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: DKA
Septic shock
HHS
None of the above

answer: The correct answer is C. Given the patient’s symptoms, very high BG, normal pH and their family history of T2DM, HHS is the most likely diagnosis. There is nothing in the question that supports a diagnosis of a septic shock.

No further action is needed

stem:
A 22-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for the past 12 hours. She reports missing her last two insulin doses because of a viral illness. On examination, she appears dehydrated and tachypneic, with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min and fruity-smelling breath.

Based on the above findings, which of the following best explains the laboratory abnormalities confirming a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?

options.html: Severe hyperglycemia with a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
Hyperglycemia with elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis and ketosis
Hypoglycemia with non–anion gap metabolic acidosis
Hyperglycemia with respiratory alkalosis and ketonuria

answer:
The correct answer is B. The deck's next slide lists the T1D high-yield points (diagnostic criteria, DKA presentation and treatment, monitoring K, lowering BG slowly) but gives no written rationale, so the reasoning here is ours, checked against Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes.

DKA is hyperglycemia (often > 15 mmol/L) + an elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis (low pH, low bicarbonate) + serum and urine ketones. Her labs fit exactly: glucose 26, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12, anion gap 22, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8. The gap is raised because the unmeasured anions are ketoacids, so A and C (normal or non-gap acidosis) are wrong; she is tachypneic from Kussmaul compensation for a metabolic acidosis, not a primary respiratory alkalosis (D).

stem: Which of the following is most suggestive of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic syndrome (HHS)?

options.html: An anion-gap metabolic acidosis and Kussmaul breathing
Reduced mental status and effective serum osmolality over 320 mosm/kg
A blood glucose level of 38 mmol/L and pH 7.15
A history of type 2 diabetes and a serum creatinine over 250 umol/L
Elevated serum beta-OH-butyrate level and low serum sodium level

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes.

From the review session. HHS is severe hyperosmolality with an altered sensorium and little ketosis: glucose usually over 33 mmol/L, effective osmolality over 320 and pH over 7.3. The other options fit DKA better.

HHS is enough insulin to stop ketogenesis but not hyperglycemia, so the defining features are very high glucose, serum osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg and depressed consciousness, with pH > 7.3 and no significant ketones or anion gap. A gap acidosis with Kussmaul breathing (A), a pH of 7.15 (C) and raised beta-hydroxybutyrate (E) all point to DKA. T2DM and renal impairment (D) are common in HHS but do not define it.

stem:
A 57-year-old homeless man is found comatose in the community and is brought to the emergency department. On physical examination he is unresponsive. His temperature is 37.5 degrees, blood pressure 105/60, pulse 125, and respirations 18 and unlaboured. Laboratory studies include a blood glucose of 54.9 mM, serum sodium 129 mM, and serum HCO3 21.6 . Urinalysis reveals no ketones but there is 4+ glucosuria.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: SIADH
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Cushing’s syndrome
Sepsis
Type 1 diabetes mellitus

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes.

From the review session. Type 1 diabetes would show ketones. A glucose of 54.9 with no ketones is HHS, which belongs to type 2.

Glucose 54.9, no ketones, near-normal bicarbonate and unlaboured breathing in an older man is HHS, the hyperglycemic crisis of type 2 diabetes: enough insulin to stop ketogenesis but not hyperglycemia. The low sodium is dilutional from the glucose. T1DM (E) would present in DKA, with ketones and a gap acidosis.

stem:
A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes is admitted in DKA. Her initial serum potassium is 4.6 mmol/L. She is started on IV normal saline and an insulin infusion.

Over the next few hours, which change in her electrolytes is the most important to anticipate?

options.html: Potassium rising as the acidosis corrects
Potassium falling as insulin moves it into cells
Sodium rising sharply from the saline load
Calcium falling from the fluid resuscitation
Glucose rising again from counter-regulatory hormones

answer: The correct answer is B. In DKA total body potassium is depleted even when the serum level looks normal, because insulin lack has shifted K⁺ out of cells. Insulin drives it back in, so serum K⁺ falls with treatment, and the fall can cause arrhythmias and death. That is why the SR slide says to monitor K very closely and why replacement is often needed during treatment.

stem:
A 24-year-old man with DKA has been on an insulin infusion and IV saline for six hours. His glucose is now 13 mmol/L, but his anion gap is still 19 and his pH 7.24.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.html: Stop the insulin infusion until the glucose rises again
Switch to subcutaneous basal insulin and stop the drip
Add dextrose to the fluids and keep the insulin running
Give an IV bolus of sodium bicarbonate
Halve the fluid rate and recheck the glucose in four hours

answer: The correct answer is C. The glucose falls before the ketoacidosis clears. The lecture's rule is to add dextrose (D5W with NS) once glucose reaches 12-14 mmol/L, so the insulin can keep running until the anion gap normalises without causing hypoglycaemia. Stopping or switching the insulin (A, B) lets ketogenesis restart; the endpoint is the anion gap, not the glucose.

stem: A 45-year old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your office with poorly controlled plasma glucose levels. He was initially prescribed metformin but due to GI intolerance, he was switched to gliclazide six months ago. Which of the following may be related to the decreased efficacy of gliclazide in reducing hyperglycemia in this patient? Select all that apply.

options.html: Renal dysfunction
Desensitization of the ATP-sensitive receptors
Decreased ability of the adipose cells to reduce free fatty acids
Decreased ability of the pancreatic beta cells to secrete insulin

answer: The correct answers are B and D. Gliclazide, a sulfonylurea, increases the secretion of insulin by acting on the ATP-sensitive potassium channels. It has been observed that over time, patients develop tolerance to the SU drugs. This may be explained by desensitization of the receptors and loss of functionality by the pancreatic beta cells. The decreased ability of the adipose cells to reduce circulating fatty acids would affect the efficacy of the TZDs more than the SUs - that being said, accumulation of fat in the body could contribute to poor control of blood glucose (energy balance). Renal dysfunction would affect the elimination of gliclazide but not its ability to reduce glycemia.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (9 questions).
stem: A 43-year-old woman with Type-2 diabetes has been taking insulin with meals as well as metformin. Her blood glucose remains poorly controlled. Her doctor prescribes an additional drug, which is an analog of an endogenous peptide that inhibits glucagon secretion. What is the most likely medication this patient is taking?

options.html: Pioglitazone
Repaglinide
Sitagliptin
Gliclazide
Liraglutide

answer: The correct answer is E. Pioglitazone is a TZD that activates PPAR. Repaglinide is a meglitinide that inhibits the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in the beta cells. Sitagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor that targets the DPP-4 enzyme. Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea that also inhibits the ATP-sensitive potassium channel. Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that is an analog of the endogenous GLP-1 peptide and inhibits the secretion of glucagon.

stem: A 45 year old man comes to your clinic for management of his hypertension. You note that he now also has pre-diabetes. You would like to discuss weight management. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.html: Weigh him right away and calculate his BMI and waist circumference
Advise him to lose 10% of his body weight through diet and exercise
Ask permission to discuss his weight and listen to his experiences
Prescribe a GLP-1 receptor agonist to support his weight loss

answer: The correct answer is C. The first step of the 5A's approach is to Ask permission to discuss weight while listening openly to the patient's experiences.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (5 questions).
stem: Sophie has been taking semaglutide at the maximally tolerated dose for 12 weeks and has lost only 2% of their initial body weight. What is your most appropriate next step?

options.html: Continue semaglutide indefinitely.
Encourage increased activity to achieve further weight loss.
Consider switching to tirzepatide because the treatment goal has not been achieved.
Refer immediately for bariatric surgery regardless of eligibility.

answer: The correct answer is C. The goal of pharmacotherapy is to achieve at least 5% weight loss after 12 weeks at the maximally tolerated dose. If this is not achieved, it is important to consider changing medications. While increased activity is important, the 5% weight loss target with pharmacotherapy is an important threshold for considering efficacy, as some patients may not achieve weight loss with a particular agent.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (5 questions).
stem: Raul presents two months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with persistent nausea, poor oral intake, and confusion. His vitals reveal a BP of 90/56 mmHg, HR 120 bpm. You have started him on Ringer's lactate IV fluids. What else should be done immediately?

options.html: Give D50W push.
Give thiamine.
Given calcium gluconate.
Nothing else needs to be done at this time.

answer: The correct answer is B. Thiamine deficiency can occur within 1-3 months after surgery, particularly with poor oral intake and nausea. Recognizing thiamine deficiency is critical as there are serious neurologic sequelae - importantly, thiamine should always be given immediately before any glucose to prevent onset of Wernicke's encephalopathy.

stem: A 30-year-old patient presents to your family medicine office with concerns regarding their weight. The patient meets the criteria for pharmacotherapy. As part of your general assessment, you run a patient health questionnaire (PHQ-9) and suspect that the patient might be suffering from depression. Which medication would you not prescribe to this patient?

options.html: Orlistat
Semaglutide
Liraglutide
Bupropion/Naltrexone

answer:
The correct answer is D. Bupropion/Naltrexone may worsen depression initially

From naltrexone-bupropion and 09 - Introduction to Obesity. The obesity lecture ranks the agents tirzepatide > semaglutide > naltrexone-bupropion > orlistat. The drug note for Contrave lists one serious adverse effect: ↑ risk of suicidal thoughts in patients with depression. Its bupropion component acts centrally on noradrenergic/dopaminergic POMC circuits. A positive PHQ-9 therefore makes it the agent to avoid until the depression is assessed and managed.

  • A Orlistat blocks gut lipase and acts peripherally. Its problems are GI and limited efficacy, not mood.
  • B, C semaglutide and liraglutide are GLP-1 agonists whose limiting effects in the notes are GI upset and pancreatitis, with no psychiatric warning.

"But bupropion is an antidepressant." It is, on its own, and that is the fair objection. The question is about the obesity combination: naltrexone-bupropion carries a warning for suicidal thoughts in patients with depression, and the other three options carry no psychiatric warning at all. With a positive PHQ-9 and the depression not yet assessed, it is the one to hold off on, not a drug that can never be used.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman with class III obesity (BMI 37 kg/m²) presents for evaluation for bariatric surgery. She has tried multiple diets and exercise programs without significant long-term weight loss. She currently smokes half a pack per day and has a history of T2D, and depression that is partially controlled with sertraline.

Based on criteria for bariatric surgery, which of the following statements is most appropriate?

options.html: She is not eligible for surgery due to current smoking and mental health concerns; surgery should be denied.
She qualifies for surgery, but she requires pre-op optimization of smoking cessation and mental health stabilization.
She is eligible for surgery immediately; preoperative counseling is optional since risks are minimal.
She is not eligible because only patients with BMI ≥ 45 kg/m² qualify for bariatric surgery.
She should start insulin therapy before surgery due to obesity-related insulin resistance.

answer:
The correct answer is B. The deck's next slide lists the criteria to meet before surgery, "including smoking cessation"; the rest is ours, checked against Introduction to Obesity.

Bariatric surgery is indicated at BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with complications, or ≥ 30 with poorly controlled T2DM, so a BMI of 37 with T2D qualifies (not D). The lecture makes smoking cessation mandatory, and maintained after surgery, and requires mental health conditions to be treated and managed first. Only unstable psychiatric illness makes someone an inappropriate candidate, so partially controlled depression means optimise, not deny (A). Counselling is not optional (C), and insulin has nothing to do with eligibility (E).

lectureMeta: Source: Schulich Reviews - Endo Review Questions (Rhidita & Hana), high-yield slide, slide 14.
stem:
A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department three months after a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She has had persistent vomiting and poor intake for two weeks and is now confused, with nystagmus and an unsteady gait. Her capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L.

What should be given first?

options.html: An IV dextrose bolus
IV thiamine
Oral vitamin B12
An IV iron infusion
Oral calcium with vitamin D

answer: The correct answer is B. After bariatric surgery the most serious deficiency is thiamine, because of Wernicke's encephalopathy; it can appear 1-3 months post-op, especially with poor intake and vomiting. The lecture's rule: always give thiamine immediately, before any glucose, since glucose first can precipitate it. B12, iron and calcium/vitamin D deficiencies are also common after Roux-en-Y, but they are not the emergency.

stem: 29-year-old G1 woman currently at 24 weeks gestation age was asked to go for GDM screening. She had the 50 g oral glucose tolerance test. Her 1hr post ingestion blood glucose was 8.8 mmol/L. What is the next best step?

options.html: She has a diagnosis of GDM and therefore no further testing is required. Refer to the Endocrine Pregnancy clinic for GDM management.
She does not have GDM. She does not need to worry about her blood sugars.
She needs to have her HbA1c checked for confirmation of GDM.
She needs to have the 75g OGTT next to determine if she has GDM.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes. D. The Canadian two-step screen at 24-28 weeks starts with a non-fasting 1-h 50 g challenge: < 7.8 normal, ≥ 11.1 diagnoses GDM, and 7.8-11.0 goes on to a fasting 75 g OGTT. Her 8.8 is in the middle band. On the 75 g test, any one value at or above fasting 5.3, 1 h 10.6 or 2 h 9.0 makes the diagnosis.

  • A: 8.8 is below the ≥ 11.1 that would diagnose on the 50 g test alone.
  • B: 8.8 is above the < 7.8 normal cut-off, so she cannot be cleared.
  • C: A1c is not used in GDM; the lecture says not to check it.

stem:
You are seeing a 25-year-old woman with GDM in your Endocrine Pregnancy Clinic. She is managing her GDM with metformin. She is also following the GDM diet with 45 g meals 3x/day and 20g snacks 3x/day. In the last few days, she feels that her sugars are increasing despite walking 10 min after each meal. What would you recommend based on her on log:

DateacB1h pcB1h pcL1h pcS
Aug 55.37.79.08.8
Aug 65.47.88.88.8
Aug 75.48.27.87.9
Aug 85.57.78.97.8
Aug 95.88.08.87.7

options.html: Stop metformin as her blood sugars are well below target.
Do nothing as her sugars are well controlled.
Recommend she decreases her carbohydrate intake by 50% and increase the intensity of her exercise.
Recommend adding insulin as all her blood glucose readings are well above target..

answer:
The correct answer is D. Read the log against the pregnancy targets - fasting < 5.3 and 1 hour post-meal < 7.8 mmol/L - and every column fails:

  • acB runs 5.3 → 5.8, at or above the fasting target every day, and trending upward.
  • 1h pcB, pcL and pcS run 7.7 → 9.0, at or above the post-meal target on almost every reading.

She is already on metformin, already on the GDM diet, and already walking after meals, so the non-pharmacological levers are spent - A and B misread a failing log as a good one, and C asks more of the two things that have not worked. Insulin is the next step, and it is the only agent that can be titrated to bring both fasting and post-prandial numbers to target in pregnancy.

stem: Which of the following antibodies are indicative of Type 1 Diabetes mellitus (T1DM) ?

options.html: Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase (GAD)
Zinc transporter (ZnT8)
Anti-M antibodies
A and B
All of the above

answer:
The correct answer is D. Both GAD and Zn18 are antibodies associated with T1DM

From 01 - Intro to Diabetes. T1DM is autoimmune beta-cell destruction, and the lecture's autoantibody panel is insulin/proinsulin, GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8 ("Zn18" in the key is a typo for ZnT8). GAD is the most specific marker (positive in ~70%). Remember too that the number of antibodies carries the risk, not their presence: one alone does not raise risk above baseline, three means ~40% in 5 years.

  • A, B alone are each true but incomplete, since both belong to the panel.
  • C (anti-M) is not part of the T1DM panel. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies point to primary biliary cholangitis, not the beta cell.
  • E fails because C is wrong.

stem: You recently diagnosed Mark, an 18-year-old patient with T1DM. He works shifts in a factory and frequently skips meals because of his work schedule. What would be the best MDI insulin regimen for him considering the nature of his work?

options.html: 3-injections per day (1 long-acting + 2 fast-acting)
4 injections per day (3 fast-acting + 1 long-acting)
4 injections per day (2 long-acting + 2 fast-acting)
None of the above

answer: The correct answer is B. A 4-dose MDI consisting of 3 fast-acting insulin doses before meals and a single long-acting would be best for reducing the risk of hypoglycemia in this patient. For example, if they have to skip a meal because of work, they can skip the insulin dose associated with that meal

stem: Which of the following is FALSE regarding the diagnosis of T1DM

options.html: Polyuria and polydipsia are classic symptoms of T1DM
A random blood glucose of > 11.1 is sufficient for the diagnosis of T1DM in a symptomatic patient
You must do a fasting plasma glucose and/or HbA1c to confirm the diagnosis of T1DM in a symptomatic patient
None of the above

answer:
The correct answer is C. The question asks which statement is FALSE. With symptoms of diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss), a single random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L is enough to diagnose diabetes, so no fasting glucose or HbA1c is needed to confirm it. HbA1c is not one of the type 1 diagnostic criteria at all. C claims a confirmatory test is required, which is false.

B is the true statement the old key picked. A is true: polyuria and polydipsia are the classic symptoms. Symptoms alone do not make the diagnosis; they make one abnormal glucose sufficient. (A used to say they were "diagnostic", which readers rightly found ambiguous.)

stem:
A 15-year-old with type 1 diabetes is found by his mother at home, sweaty and too drowsy to swallow safely. His meter reads 2.1 mmol/L.

What is the best treatment his mother can give?

options.html: Orange juice poured into his mouth
Two glucose tablets to chew
Glucagon, IM, SC or intranasal
An extra dose of rapid-acting insulin
Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes first

answer: The correct answer is C. He has severe hypoglycaemia (neuroglycopenic, needing assistance), and nothing should go by mouth if he cannot swallow safely (A, B). The SR slide's emergency treatment is glucagon (IM/SC) or IV dextrose, and the lecture adds intranasal glucagon; glucagon is the one a family member can give at home.

stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding T1DM and T2DM?

options.html: T1DM and T2DM are both caused by absolute insulin deficiency
T2DM often presents as an acute condition
Patients with T2DM are more likely to have other manifestations of metabolic syndrome
None of the above is true

stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding the risk of T2DM

options.html: A child born to a parent with T2DM has a higher risk of developing T2DM
If a twin develops T2DM, their monozygotic twin has a 90% risk of developing T2DM
The risk of developing T2DM is the same for monozygotic and non-monozygotic twins
A and B are both true
None of the above

answer: The correct answer is D. Both A and B are true. Having a first-degree relative with T2DM increases the risk of T2DM, and monozygotic twin concordance for T2DM is about 90%. C is false: concordance is far higher in monozygotic than in non-identical twins, which is the evidence for T2DM's strong genetic component.

stem:
A 52-year-old man presents for a routine check-up. He has a BMI of 31 kg/m² and reports increased thirst and urination for the past few months. He has no significant past medical history and is not taking any medications. His blood work shows the following:

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient’s management?

options.html: Repeat HbA1c in 3 months before making a diagnosis
Start insulin therapy immediately
Diagnose type 2 diabetes and initiate lifestyle modifications plus metformin
Diagnose prediabetes and advise lifestyle changes only
Begin dual oral therapy with metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor

answer:
The correct answer is C. The deck's following slide gives the T2D criteria (FPG ≥ 7.0, 2-h OGTT ≥ 11.1, A1c ≥ 6.5%, random ≥ 11.1 with symptoms; with symptoms one test is enough, without them repeat on another day). The rest of the reasoning is ours, checked against Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology and Prevention of Complications of Diabetes.

He is symptomatic (thirst, polyuria) and all three tests are in the diabetic range (FPG 8.2, A1c 7.2%, 2-h 12.0), so there is nothing to repeat (A) and this is not prediabetes (D). Metformin is first line for T2DM without many symptoms and no liver or renal concern; insulin first (B) is for the very symptomatic, and nothing here calls for dual therapy up front (E).

stem:
A 34-year-old man has had type 1 diabetes since age 16. He has no known coronary disease, his blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, and his LDL is 2.6 mmol/L.

Should he start a statin?

options.html: Yes: he is over 30 and has had diabetes over 15 years
No, because statins are only indicated from age 40 in diabetes
No, because he has no known coronary artery disease
Only if his LDL rises above 3.5 mmol/L on repeat testing
Only once he develops microalbuminuria or retinopathy

answer: The correct answer is A. In diabetes without known CAD, a statin is indicated at age ≥ 40, or at age ≥ 30 with diabetes for more than 15 years. He is 34 with 18 years of diabetes, so he qualifies. The duration clause is exactly the one people forget (B).

stem: Which of the following is a benefit of SMBG (self-monitoring of blood glucose) ?

options.html: Allows patients to determine if they’re hitting their glycemic control target
SMBG is needed to prevent hypoglycemia
It can guide decisions by clinicians
Only A and B are true
A, B and C are true

answer:
The correct answer is E. Refer to the lecture on targets for glycemic control

From 08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes. The lecture's point is that HbA1c is the target and SMBG is how you get there. The notes list what SMBG does:

  • it gives real-time feedback on whether the patient is at target (A)
  • it is needed to prevent hypoglycemia in anyone on insulin or a secretagogue, and to confirm and treat an episode (B)
  • it guides medication decisions, including pre-meal bolus doses (C)

SMBG is also the only way to assess control when the A1c is unreliable.

  • D fails because it drops C: clinician dose titration is one of the listed uses.
  • A, B or C alone would each be incomplete, and none is offered on its own anyway.

stem: A pregnant patient presents to your family medicine office at 25 weeks gestation for a routine visit. The patient’s random blood glucose is 12 mM after drinking 50g of glucose. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.html: Order a confirmatory HbA1c
Ask the patient to fast and then repeat the test with 75g of oral glucose instead of 50g
The patient has gestational diabetes (GDM). You should refer them to diabetes education and a dietitian.
None of the above

answer:
The correct answer is C. The 1-hour 50 g screen is diagnostic of GDM at ≥ 11.1 mmol/L, and 12 is above that. No fasting 75 g oral glucose tolerance test is needed.

The thresholds from Pregnancy and Diabetes: under 7.8 is normal and needs nothing further; 7.8 to 11.0 is the grey band that goes on to a fasting 75 g OGTT (B would be right there); ≥ 11.1 is GDM. HbA1c (A) is not used to diagnose GDM.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman, G2P1, at 26 weeks gestation, presents for routine prenatal care. She has no significant past medical history. Her BMI is 27 kg/m². She undergoes standard gestational diabetes screening.

The 50 g oral glucose challenge test (non-fasting) result shows a 1-hour plasma glucose of 8.5 mmol/L.

What is the most appropriate next step, and if she is diagnosed with gestational diabetes, what is the correct counselling?

options.html: No further testing is required; this result is normal. Reassure her that gestational diabetes would only occur if glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L.
Repeat the 50 g glucose challenge test in two weeks; if still elevated, begin metformin therapy and reassure that it resolves completely with no future risks.

Perform a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) for diagnostic confirmation; if GDM is diagnosed, counsel that it usually resolves after delivery but increases future risk of type 2 diabetes and fetal macrosomia.
Start insulin therapy immediately and counsel that gestational diabetes will persist after delivery and cause congenital malformations if untreated.
Perform a fasting plasma glucose test only; if >7.0 mmol/L, diagnose GDM and reassure that the condition has no effect on the baby.

answer:
The correct answer is C. From the deck's next slide: on the 50 g challenge, < 7.8 is normal, ≥ 11.1 diagnoses GDM, and 7.8-11.0 goes to a 75 g OGTT (fasting < 5.3, 1 h < 10.6, 2 h < 9.0; any one exceeded is diagnostic). GDM carries no risk of congenital malformation, because organogenesis is done, but does bring macrosomia, C-section, stillbirth and neonatal hypoglycemia. Pregnancy and Diabetes adds that it is transient after delivery and that up to 60% later develop T2DM, so she is re-screened with a 75 g OGTT at 6 weeks to 6 months postpartum.

8.5 mmol/L is in the 7.8-11.0 band, so she needs the 75 g OGTT, not reassurance (A), a repeat challenge (B), insulin (D), or a fasting glucose alone (E).

stem:
Two women attend the same diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic. One has type 1 diabetes with an A1c of 9% at conception. The other was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks.

Which risk to the baby applies to the first woman but not the second?

options.html: Macrosomia
Neonatal hypoglycemia
Caesarean delivery
Congenital malformations
Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia

answer: The correct answer is D. The difference is timing. Pre-existing diabetes is present during organogenesis, so hyperglycaemia at conception raises the risk of malformations (neural tube, cardiac, GI, GU). GDM is diagnosed at 24-28 weeks, after organogenesis, so it causes no congenital malformations. Macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, caesarean delivery and hyperbilirubinaemia (A, B, C, E) occur in both.

stem:
A woman with type 1 diabetes is 9 weeks pregnant and reports several hypoglycaemic episodes on her usual insulin doses. She asks how her insulin needs will change.

Which pattern should you describe?

options.html: Fall in trimester 1, rise sharply in trimester 3, drop after birth
Rise steadily from conception onwards, and fall only after the delivery
Stay the same until the third trimester, then fall slowly
Fall throughout pregnancy, then rise sharply after delivery
Rise in trimester 1, level off, then rise again after delivery

answer: The correct answer is A. Trimester 1: needs fall, so hypoglycaemia is a risk (not explained by nausea). Trimester 2: needs start to rise as placental hormones increase. Trimester 3: needs rise a great deal. Postpartum: needs fall remarkably, because the placenta is gone, and glucose can drop especially while breastfeeding.

stem:
A 24 year old woman is brought to the hospital following a seizure. On arrival she is found to be confused. A fingerstick glucose level is 2.7 mM. A blood sample is taken for glucose, insulin, and c-peptide levels and she is resuscitated with intravenous glucose. The results of the lab tests are as follows:

  • Random plasma glucose 2.3 mM
  • Serum C-peptide level 0.05 nM (normal 0.26 – 1.03 nM)
  • Plasma insulin level 345 pM (fasting normal < 175 pM)

The most likely diagnosis is:

options.html: An insulinoma
Post-prandial hypoglycemia
Exogeneous insulin administration
A tumour producing IGF-2

answer:
The correct answer is C. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Pharmacology of Insulin.

From the review session. C-peptide is the marker of endogenous insulin production. Hers is low while her insulin is high, so she is taking insulin surreptitiously.

The beta cell cleaves proinsulin into insulin plus C-peptide in equal amounts, so endogenous insulin always brings C-peptide with it. High insulin with a suppressed C-peptide means the insulin came from outside. An insulinoma (A) is endogenous, so it raises insulin and C-peptide together.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a history of PCOS and a mother with type 2 diabetes. She conceived her first pregnancy by fertility intervention and is now at 25 weeks. Her weight is 100 kg and her BP is 135/95 on three measurements. Which feature of this presentation is not a recognised risk factor for gestational diabetes? (originally a narrative case; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A history of PCOS
A first-degree relative with type 2 diabetes
Age 35 and obesity
None - all of these are recognised risk factors

answer:
The correct answer is D - every feature listed is a risk factor, which is exactly why the case stacks them.

  • PCOS is an insulin-resistant state in its own right, and is independently associated with GDM.
  • A mother with T2DM gives a strong family history.
  • Age ≥35 and obesity (100 kg) are both standard risk factors.
  • Conception by fertility intervention travels with PCOS and with older maternal age.

Two details in the case are not GDM risk factors but still matter: BP 135/95 on three occasions puts her diastolic at or above 90, so she needs assessment for hypertension in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia alongside the diabetes; and her 12-hour physically demanding job and drug plan shape what treatment is actually feasible (see Q51).

stem: She has a 50 g screening test of 8.5 mmol/L, and proceeds to a 75 g OGTT which returns 6.5 / 10.9 / 10.6 mmol/L (fasting / 1h / 2h). How should this be interpreted? (originally a narrative case; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Normal - no further testing
GDM is diagnosed; all three values are above target
Only the fasting value is diagnostic; repeat the test
The 50 g screen was normal, so the 75 g test should not have been done

answer:
The correct answer is B. The 50 g screen of 8.5 sits in the 7.8-11.0 grey band, which is precisely the band that sends her for the 75 g OGTT - so D is wrong.

On the 75 g test, all three values clear their thresholds (fasting ≥ 5.3, 1h ≥ 10.6, 2h ≥ 9.0):

Her valueThreshold
Fasting6.5≥ 5.3
1 hour10.9≥ 10.6
2 hours10.6≥ 9.0

One value at or above threshold is enough to diagnose GDM; she has three.

options.html: Start insulin at once, before any diet change or glucose monitoring
Dietitian referral for diet, and a nurse to teach glucose testing
Start metformin and review her glucose log in one month
Repeat the 75 g OGTT in two weeks to confirm the diagnosis first

answer:
The correct answer is B. The case's next steps are an interview with the RD for diet and an interview with the RN to learn how to test blood glucoses.

Management of GDM starts non-pharmacologically - diet and activity - with glucose monitoring put in place first, because the monitoring is what tells you whether diet alone is going to be enough. Starting insulin before there is any log to read (A) has nothing to titrate against. D is wrong because the diagnosis is already made.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman has a history of PCOS and a mother with type 2 diabetes. She conceived her first pregnancy by fertility intervention and is now at 25 weeks. Her weight is 100 kg and her BP is 135/95 on three measurements. She has a 50 g screening test of 8.5 mmol/L, and proceeds to a 75 g OGTT which returns 6.5 / 10.9 / 10.6 mmol/L (fasting / 1h / 2h).

stem: After one week on diet and walking after meals, her log shows high fasting (acB) and post-breakfast (pcB) values, with no real trend after lunch or supper. The team suggests insulin aspart 4 units before breakfast and insulin detemir 6 units at bedtime. What is the logic of that particular regimen? (originally a narrative case; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Each insulin is aimed at the interval that is actually out of range
Both are started at full replacement doses to normalise every reading
Rapid-acting insulin is given at every meal regardless of the log
Basal insulin alone would be sufficient for both abnormalities

answer:
The correct answer is A. This is the same principle as the small-group insulin cases (Q42-44): treat the interval that is out of range, with the insulin that acts over it.

  • The high fasting (acB) value is an overnight problem → detemir at bedtime.
  • The high post-breakfast (pcB) value is a prandial problem at one specific meal → aspart before breakfast only.
  • Lunch and supper show no trend, so they get no insulin - which is why C is wrong.

The notes point out that high fasting and post-breakfast values are a common pattern in GDM. Note also how small the starting doses are (4 and 6 units): you start low and titrate, rather than aiming to normalise everything immediately (B).

Her drug plan and her 12-hour physically demanding job are in the case for a reason - the drug plan makes analogue insulins affordable, and the long physical shifts raise the stakes on hypoglycemia, which is an argument for the cautious dosing and for not covering meals that do not need it.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman has a history of PCOS and a mother with type 2 diabetes. She conceived her first pregnancy by fertility intervention and is now at 25 weeks. Her weight is 100 kg and her BP is 135/95 on three measurements. She has a 50 g screening test of 8.5 mmol/L, and proceeds to a 75 g OGTT which returns 6.5 / 10.9 / 10.6 mmol/L (fasting / 1h / 2h).

stem: By 37 weeks her insulin requirements are aspart 40 units at breakfast, 10 at lunch, 10 at supper, and detemir 60 units at bedtime - up from 4 and 6 units. What best explains this escalation? (originally a narrative case; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: She has developed type 1 diabetes during the pregnancy
Placental hormones drive progressively increasing insulin resistance as pregnancy advances
The original doses were calculated incorrectly
Insulin requirements fall in the third trimester, so this represents a dosing error

answer:
The correct answer is B. Insulin requirements rise steeply through the second and third trimesters because the placenta produces hormones that antagonise insulin - the case names prolactin among the pregnancy hormones behind the higher insulin needs. A tenfold rise in the breakfast dose is a normal trajectory in GDM, not a failure of treatment.

D has the direction backwards for late pregnancy. It is worth holding the contrast: insulin requirements fall in the first trimester (which is the module's own knowledge check, Q48) and then climb for the rest of the pregnancy.

preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman has a history of PCOS and a mother with type 2 diabetes. She conceived her first pregnancy by fertility intervention and is now at 25 weeks. Her weight is 100 kg and her BP is 135/95 on three measurements. She has a 50 g screening test of 8.5 mmol/L, and proceeds to a 75 g OGTT which returns 6.5 / 10.9 / 10.6 mmol/L (fasting / 1h / 2h).

stem: Her obstetrician books induction at 38 weeks because the baby is judged to be at the 97th percentile. The baby is delivered vaginally with a small tear, weighs 4.5 kg, and spends two days in the NICU with low blood glucoses and under UV light. Which explanation of the newborn's low blood glucose is correct? (originally a narrative case; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: The newborn's pancreas was damaged by the maternal hyperglycemia
Fetal hyperinsulinemia outlasted the maternal glucose supply at delivery
Insulin crossed the placenta from the mother and lowered his glucose
It was caused by the induction rather than by the diabetes itself

answer:
The correct answer is B. Glucose crosses the placenta; maternal insulin does not - which is what makes C wrong. Chronic maternal hyperglycemia therefore drives the fetal pancreas to oversecrete insulin. That fetal hyperinsulinemia is responsible for both findings here:

  • macrosomia - 4.5 kg and the 97th percentile, insulin being a growth factor. This is what prompted the induction at 38 weeks, and what put her at risk of shoulder dystocia and of the perineal tear she sustained.
  • Neonatal hypoglycemia - at delivery the glucose supply is cut but the high insulin level persists for a time, so the newborn goes low.

The UV light is phototherapy for neonatal jaundice, also more common in infants of diabetic mothers.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman has a history of PCOS and a mother with type 2 diabetes. She conceived her first pregnancy by fertility intervention and is now at 25 weeks. Her weight is 100 kg and her BP is 135/95 on three measurements. She has a 50 g screening test of 8.5 mmol/L, and proceeds to a 75 g OGTT which returns 6.5 / 10.9 / 10.6 mmol/L (fasting / 1h / 2h).

stem: By six months postpartum she has lost 40 pounds (BMI now 28), is active daily, follows a low-fat, high-fibre diet and is still breastfeeding. Her 75 g OGTT shows fasting 5.0 mmol/L and 2-hour 7.5 mmol/L. What does this result mean? (originally a narrative case; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: The result is normal, and it confirms her GDM has resolved - but she remains at long-term risk of type 2 diabetes
The result is normal, so she carries no further risk and needs no further screening
The result is diagnostic of type 2 diabetes
The result is diagnostic of impaired glucose tolerance

answer:
The correct answer is A. Fasting 5.0 and 2-hour 7.5 mmol/L are both normal, so the GDM has resolved as expected - and the case has you congratulate her on the diabetes prevention she has done, because the weight loss, daily activity, diet and continued breastfeeding are all working in her favour.

B is the trap. GDM identifies a woman whose beta cells could not meet the demand of pregnancy, and the lecture puts the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes at up to 60%, depending on length of follow-up and ethnic background. A normal postpartum OGTT resets the clock; it does not remove the risk, and she needs ongoing periodic screening.

stem:
She is six weeks post-partum after a pregnancy managed as gestational diabetes. Why might "gestational diabetes" have been the wrong label for some women, and what finding would show it?

(originally a narrative case; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Some are pre-existing type 2 - the glucose never returns to normal
Some never had diabetes, and the OGTT is unreliable in pregnancy
GDM cannot be distinguished from type 2 diabetes at any point
They should be re-tested during the pregnancy rather than after it

answer:
The correct answer is A. Because glucose is first tested at 24-28 weeks, a woman with undiagnosed pre-existing type 2 - or, less often, early type 1 - diabetes will be picked up then and labelled "GDM", since that is simply when the test happens.

Two things give it away:

  • During the pregnancy, the glucoses and the medication needed to control them are quite high - a hint that there is more going on than GDM.
  • After delivery, in true diabetes the blood glucoses do not return to normal - which is the definitive discriminator, and the reason the postpartum OGTT in Q54 is not optional.

stem: A 35-year-old man has a history of type 2 diabetes of 2 years. He also has hypertension. He is on metformin monotherapy for his diabetes and amlodipine for his hypertension. He has no structural complication of diabetes (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy). What should be his target A1c?

options.html: No specific target; treat symptoms only

answer:
The correct answer is A, ≤ 6.5%. The case's own factors to consider:

  • Young and otherwise healthy, so a longer life expectancy in which to accrue benefit
  • Short duration of diabetes
  • ⭐ No structural complications yet - they can still be prevented
  • Low risk of hypoglycemia: he is on monotherapy, and not on any medication that can cause hypoglycemia

This is the ≤ 6.5% tier: ⭐ T2DM at low risk of hypoglycemia, tightened to further reduce CVD, CKD and retinopathy. metformin alone does not cause hypoglycemia, which is what makes the tighter target safe to chase. Everything that would argue for loosening is absent.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has longstanding type 1 diabetes (30 years) managed with insulin on multiple daily injections. Her past medical history includes coronary artery disease, hypertension and dyslipidemia. She has no history of severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia unawareness. She has neuropathy but no nephropathy or retinopathy. She works as an administrator and maintains an active lifestyle. What should be her target A1c?

options.html: No specific target; treat symptoms only

answer:
The correct answer is B, ≤ 7.0%. The case's own factors to consider:

  • Prolonged history of diabetes
  • ⚠ Is on medications that can cause hypoglycemia (insulin)
  • Has both macrovascular and microvascular complications
  • ⭐ No indications of frailty, functional decline, or limited life expectancy

This is the validated default tier - most patients with T1DM or T2DM sit here.

She is the instructive middle case. The insulin and the established complications rule out tightening to 6.5%, because the hypoglycemia risk is real and the complications she has are no longer preventable. But she is active, working and not frail, which rules out loosening as well. ⭐ Being complicated is not the same as being frail, and that is the discrimination this case exists to test.

stem: An 85-year-old woman has type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease with severe dementia. She is dependent for all her ADLs and IADLs. She is managed with an oral regimen of metformin, gliclazide and canagliflozin, plus weekly semaglutide. Her daughter administers all her medications. What should her target A1c be?

options.html: No specific target; treat symptoms only

answer:
The correct answer is C, 7.1 - 8.5%. The case's own factors to consider:

  • Dementia
  • Functionally dependent
  • ⚠ On a medication that can cause hypoglycemia (gliclazide)

⭐ In the frail elderly, hypoglycemia is more dangerous than hyperglycemia - it causes falls, and severe hypoglycemia carries increased mortality. A patient with severe dementia cannot reliably report or self-treat a low, which is what makes the sulfonylurea the dangerous drug in her regimen.

D is the trap. Loosening the target is not the same as abandoning it: the minimum goal of care is still that she be free of clinically significant symptoms of hypo- and hyperglycemia, so a target range is still set, just a higher one.

Sulfonyureas
SGLT2 inhibitors
GLP1-RAs
Both A and C

answer: The correct answer is B. Of the drugs listed here, SU’s have the highest risk of hypoglycemia

stem:
A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has taken metformin for eight years. His eGFR has fallen to 24 mL/min.

Why should the metformin be stopped?

options.html: It causes hypoglycaemia once the kidneys fail
It causes fluid retention and precipitates heart failure
It raises the risk of genital and urinary infections
It stops lowering glucose at all below this eGFR
It accumulates and can cause lactic acidosis

answer: The correct answer is E. Metformin is renally excreted, so in kidney failure it accumulates, and the pharmacokinetic consequence is lactic acidosis. That is why it is not used below an eGFR of 30 mL/min. It does not cause hypoglycaemia as monotherapy (A); fluid retention and heart failure belong to the TZDs (B); genital infections to the SGLT2 inhibitors (C).

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes had a second agent added to her metformin three months ago. She now has her second vulvovaginal yeast infection and feels light-headed when she stands up. Her weight has fallen by 2 kg.

Which agent was most likely added?

options.html: Gliclazide
Sitagliptin
Pioglitazone
Insulin glargine
Dapagliflozin

answer: The correct answer is E. SGLT2 inhibitors increase urinary glucose excretion, and the SR slide's adverse effects follow from that: glucose in the urogenital tract → UTI and genital infections, and ECF contraction → hypovolaemia and dehydration (hence the postural symptoms; stop them when ill). Weight loss fits too. Gliclazide (A) is a secretagogue that causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia; pioglitazone (C) causes weight gain and oedema; insulin (D) causes weight gain.

stem:
A 44-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 36 wants a drug that will also help her lose weight. She carries a RET mutation, and her father had medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Which agent should be avoided?

options.html: Empagliflozin
Sitagliptin
Metformin
Semaglutide
Acarbose

answer: The correct answer is D. GLP-1 receptor agonists (and tirzepatide) are contraindicated in patients with medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2, as well as pancreatic cancer. A RET carrier with a family history of MTC has MEN2 until proven otherwise. An SGLT2 inhibitor (A) would also help her weight without that contraindication.

stem:
An 84-year-old widow who lives alone has type 2 diabetes with an A1c of 8.1% on metformin. She sometimes skips meals.

Which add-on is least appropriate for her?

options.html: Sitagliptin
Linagliptin
Glyburide
Empagliflozin
Semaglutide

answer: The correct answer is C. Sulfonylureas are insulin secretagogues that release insulin independent of glucose, so they carry a real risk of hypoglycaemia (and weight gain). The lecture says not to prescribe them to the elderly, people living alone, or people who drive for a living, and glyburide is the one avoided earliest as kidney function falls. The DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitor and GLP-1 receptor agonist have a low hypoglycaemia risk.

stem: Which pancreatic cell type produces glucagon?

options.html: α-cell
β-cell
δ-cell
D1 cell
PP cell

answer:
The correct answer is A.

  • α-cells → glucagon
  • β-cells → insulin and amyloid
  • δ-cells → somatostatin
  • D1 cells → Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP)
  • PP cells → Pancreatic Polypeptide (PP)

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a fate of excess serum glucose?

options.html: Increased filtration and excretion by kidneys
Conversion of glucose to sorbitol
Increased protein glycosylation
De novo synthesis of diacylglycerol (DAG) leading to increased protein kinase C activity
Increased hemoglobin production

answer:
The correct answer is E. These are the mechanisms by which high glucose damages the body:

  • A true: elevated glucose raises serum osmolality, so the kidneys may filter it out.
  • B true: excess glucose is shunted from normal metabolic pathways into others - notably the sorbitol pathway, which also consumes NADPH, causing oxidative stress.
  • C true: all normal glucose activities are increased to handle the influx, so protein glycosylation rises - this is the basis of the HbA1c measurement.
  • D true: for similar reasons, DAG and PKC activity increase.
  • E false: glucose has no noticeable effect on hemoglobin production.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following are NOT chronic complications of poor serum glucose control? Select all that apply.

options.html: dehydration
retinopathy
vasculopathy
nephropathy
hypotension

answer:
The correct answer is A, E. 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes separates the acute crises from the chronic damage of years of hyperglycemia. Retinopathy, vasculopathy and nephropathy are chronic. Dehydration and hypotension belong to the acute crises: the lecture lists dehydration and hypotension with tachycardia (shock) on the exam in DKA and HHS.

  • A (acute): increased glucose filtration drags water out too (filtered glucose raises urine osmolality) → dehydration.
  • B: accumulated sorbitol-pathway products damage cells, most commonly retinal cells; microvasculopathy also contributes → retinopathy.
  • C: Advanced Glycation Endproducts (AGEs) make serum "sticky" and produce dysfunctional proteins that drive inflammation and oxidative damage, most commonly in blood vessel walls.
  • D: upregulated DAG/PKC activity is thought to drive excessive extracellular matrix production → renal fibrosis → nephropathy; vasculopathy contributes.
  • E (acute): hypotension comes from volume loss in DKA or HHS. Over the long term, diabetes leads to hypertension instead.

flags.title: The workbook's question had no right answer
flags.html: The workbook asked which is NOT a complication and keyed E, but the lecture lists hypotension in DKA and HHS, so every option was a complication. It now asks about chronic complications, using the lecture's own split. Readers reported this.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Regarding the various forms (short vs. Long acting) of insulin; which of the following is true?

options.html: Modifiers are added to formulations only as preservatives, and not to affect the pharmacokinetics.
Hexameric insulins are more soluble than monomeric insulins and therefore have a more rapid response.
Human insulin never forms dimeric molecules.
Many of the different forms of insulin have been modified by changes in its amino acid sequence.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Insulin formulations range from ultra-short-acting (~5-8 h) to long-acting (up to 24 h), allowing tighter glycemic control. These formulations are made both by modifying the amino acid sequence of human insulin and by adding modifiers - so A is incorrect and D is correct.

Those modifications alter solubility: insulin that forms large hexameric (6-molecule) structures is less soluble than small monomeric insulin, and therefore slower acting - so B is backwards. Human insulin often forms dimers, so C is wrong.

See 03 - Pharmacology of Insulin.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: An 18-year-old patient presents with 2-month history of worsening polydipsia, fatigue and polyuria. Being the smart medical student you are, type I diabetes is on your differential. His random blood glucose comes back at 10.9mmol/L. What would you tell him?

options.html: You have type I diabetes due to high sugars and your symptoms. You will have to begin insulin therapy immediately.
You do not have type I diabetes because your sugars are <11.1mmol/L. Diabetes is not the cause of your symptoms.
We suspect you may have diabetes but are not yet certain. We would like to do further testing.
A random blood glucose cannot diagnose type I diabetes. We will have to test your fasting sugars in the morning.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Diagnostic criteria for diabetes:

  • Symptoms of diabetes plus a random plasma glucose > 11.1 mmol/L; or
  • A fasting plasma glucose (FPG) > 7.0 mmol/L with hyperglycemic symptoms; or
  • A 2-hour plasma glucose (2hPG) on OGTT > 11.1 mmol/L
  • CDA guidelines add an HbA1c > 6.5% in adults

At 10.9 mmol/L he does not yet meet criteria, but his sugars are trending high and he has diabetic symptoms (polydipsia, polyuria) - so diabetes is not off the differential either. C is the appropriate answer. "Further testing" could be a 75 g OGTT, a fasting plasma glucose, or an HbA1c.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: True or false: Both insulin and oral hypoglycaemic agents can be used in combination to control type 1 diabetes by lowering blood sugars.

options.html: True
False

answer: False. Insulin is the ONLY therapy to control type 1 diabetes. In contrast, type 2 diabetes has a multitude of available medications, because T2DM has an overarching problem of insulin resistance that drugs can target and the beta cells still produce some insulin. In type 1 the beta cells have been destroyed and cannot produce insulin, so it must be replaced exogenously.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following is a difference between diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)?

options.html: DKA presents with much higher plasma glucose values than HHS.
DKA usually presents with a lower pH than HHS.
DKA is far more likely to present with neurological symptoms.
HHS causes many symptoms but is rarely lethal.

answer:
The correct answer is B. DKA and HHS are the most important acute complications of diabetes.

  • A false: both present with high plasma glucose, but HHS often equals or exceeds DKA.
  • B true: DKA is defined by acidosis; HHS is not.
  • C false: the hallmark of HHS is neurological symptoms. DKA can produce them, but the first problem to appear - and the first to threaten life - is the metabolic acidosis. DKA always presents with the expected findings of metabolic acidosis but not necessarily with neurological findings; those signal severe or prolonged DKA. HHS's main clinical findings are neurological impairment and hypotension.
  • D false: HHS is very serious and can certainly be lethal.

See 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: \* Which lab level(s) during DKA emergency treatment should you closely monitor?

options.html: Sodium
Bicarbonate
Potassium
Glucose
A & C

answer:
The correct answer is E (sodium and potassium). All of these matter initially, while establishing the DKA diagnosis - but during treatment the critical two are sodium and potassium:

  • If sodium drops too drastically → rapid brain swelling → coma or death.
  • Potassium below 3 or above 6 mmol/L → arrhythmias.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: As a part of a regular screening, a 60 year old female is found to have a random blood glucose of 10.8mmol/L. She does not have any symptoms. On further testing, she is found to have a fasting blood glucose of 6.5mmol/L. Other investigations are unremarkable. Based on this information, what would you tell her?

options.html: She has developed type 2 diabetes and should be started on hypoglycaemic therapy.
She has impaired glucose tolerance and is at risk of developing diabetes in the future.
She has impaired fasting glucose and may develop diabetes in the future.
Because she is asymptomatic, we are not yet concerned about her blood sugars.
She has developed high blood sugars due to a poor diet, lack of exercise, and other lifestyle factors.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Recall the criteria (see Q53). Lab values should be repeated once to confirm a diagnosis of diabetes - exception: OGTT requires only 1 test. Two prediabetic states:

  • Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) - 2-hour BG during OGTT 7.8-11.1 mmol/L
  • Impaired fasting glucose (IFG) - FBG 5.6-7.0 mmol/L

Her FBG of 6.5 puts her in IFG only. IGT is defined only by the 2-hour value of a 75 g OGTT; her 10.8 was a random glucose, which below 11.1 diagnoses nothing, so IGT cannot be claimed. E is wrong both because we have no lifestyle information and because it is not the first thing to communicate to her.

The key adds a general exam tip: questions often ask what you would say to the patient, and options that do not seem appropriate to say to a patient can often be eliminated even when not strictly incorrect.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes?

options.html: Type 2 diabetes is strongly tied with insulin resistance in body tissues.
There is a sharp decline in insulin secretion during the early stages of type 2 diabetes.
Fetuses exposed to high sugars in utero develop protective factors that reduce their risk of diabetes later in life.
Obesity decreases the risk of developing insulin resistance.

answer:
The correct answer is A. The central concept in T2DM is insulin resistance: cells across the body become less responsive to insulin over time and the pancreas cannot keep up, so blood glucose rises.

B is wrong: while relative insulin deficiency can occur early, the disease begins with the pancreas trying to overcome the resistance - insulin levels do not fall immediately. C is wrong and backwards: fetal exposure to uncontrolled gestational diabetes increases the child's later diabetes risk. D is wrong: obesity increases insulin resistance and diabetes risk.
