lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following does insulin NOT stimulate?

options.html: Lipogenesis
Glycogenesis
Glucose uptake by cells
Protein synthesis
Insulin stimulates all of the above.

answer: The correct answer is E. The general concept: insulin promotes energy storage, so it builds things up - fat, protein and glycogen - and lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular uptake. All of the above are correct.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following is FALSE regarding insulin resistance?

options.html: Insulin resistance is influenced by genetics.
The in-utero environment influences the development of diabetes.
Insulin resistance is mostly caused by a relative increase in insulin receptor activity.
Glucose transport function of the GLUT4 transporter is decreased in insulin resistance.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Insulin resistance is caused by a number of factors including a decrease in insulin receptor activity - which makes logical sense, since it means MORE insulin is required for the same effect. C states the opposite.

A is true - shown by concordance rates in identical twins. B is true - both hypo- and hyperglycemia in pregnancy affect the child's later glucose metabolism. D is true - glucose transport is required for glucose to enter cells, an action of insulin, so it follows that this transport is less active in insulin resistance.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Mr. X has been recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at age 75. He has had a 10-year history of heart failure that has slowly progressed since his first heart attack. Which of the following medications would you certainly want to avoid?

options.html: Biguanides (ie: Metformin)
Insulin
Thiazolidinediones (ie: pioglitazone)
Acarbose
Sulfonylureas (ie: glyburide)

answer:
The correct answer is C. Thiazolidinediones such as pioglitazone and especially rosiglitazone are contraindicated in heart failure, as they may worsen it (fluid retention). The other options may not all be first-line, but none is contraindicated on the information given.

The key notes that pharmacology questions often hinge on what looks like a single side-effect tidbit - but these are exactly what gets stressed in lecture and on slides.

flags.title: Workbook error
flags.html: The key writes "rosiglitazone (Vioxx)". Vioxx is rofecoxib, a withdrawn COX-2 inhibitor; rosiglitazone's brand name is Avandia. The claim that rosiglitazone "is no longer even available" is also outdated - its REMS restrictions were lifted in 2013 - though it is effectively unused. The letter answer stands. See 07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following medications are not known for causing hypoglycemia?

options.html: Insulin
Sulfonylureas (glyburide)
Biguanides (metformin)
Meglitinides (repaglinide)

answer: The correct answer is C. Insulin, sulfonylureas and meglitinides all have the potential to cause hypoglycemia. Metformin does not, which is part of why it is such a popular first-line medication.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: What is the major mechanism of action of sulfonylureas?

options.html: Inhibition of DPP-IV and increases GLP-1 to increase insulin secretion and inhibit glucagon release.
Improving peripheral insulin sensitivity.
Targets adipocytes to bind to PPARy which leads to enhanced glucose uptake
Target the B cells in the pancreas and increases insulin secretion.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Sulfonylureas are "insulin secretagogues" - the name gives away the mechanism: they act on pancreatic β-cells to increase insulin secretion.

A describes DPP-4 inhibitors (e.g. Januvia). B describes metformin, the only available biguanide. C describes thiazolidinediones such as pioglitazone (PPARγ).

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: A 35-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes comes into your family practice office. She strongly expresses that she is interested in starting a family with her partner, but is concerned about her diabetes harming her child. What would you tell her?

options.html: With good blood glucose control before and during the pregnancy, we can minimize the risks to her and the developing fetus.
She should try to avoid having children because there is an increased risk of congenital malformations.
The risk of harming her child in utero is minimally increased, but she should avoid having children due to a high risk of maternal death and morbidity
Due to her insulin resistance, she likely has PCOS and will first require treatment for fertility.

answer:
The correct answer is A. There are genuinely increased risks in diabetic pregnancies - congenital malformations across multiple organ systems and infant mortality - but these risks are relatively low with good diabetic control.

B and C both advise her not to have children, which would not be appropriate even given an increased risk; C is additionally untrue because maternal death and morbidity risks remain low even if increased. D is wrong - she may have PCOS, but nothing in the case suggests it. See 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: True or false: Gestational diabetes, just like type 1 and 2 diabetes, can increase the risk of congenital malformations.

options.html: True
False

answer: False. Congenital malformations must occur in the first trimester. Gestational diabetes develops in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, so the vulnerable period has already passed. The child is still at risk of macrosomia and delivery complications.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: A 24-year-old mother has developed gestational diabetes in the 2nd trimester of her pregnancy. Which of the following statements about her risks would NOT be true?

options.html: Without treatment she will likely begin feeling symptoms of diabetes such as polyuria and polydipsia.
Without treatment her baby is at higher risk of being born large (macrosomic and be preterm.
Without treatment her baby has a higher risk of developing obesity and diabetes in the future.
Her baby is not at increased risk of being born with congenital malformations.

answer:
The correct answer is A. In most cases the mother with gestational diabetes is entirely asymptomatic and simply has elevated blood sugars - the immediate risks are to the fetus and the delivery. So A is not true; she will likely feel nothing.

B is true - macrosomia is a major risk because the fetus is exposed to excess sugar. C is true - a major concern is the child's long-term risk of obesity and diabetes. D is true, per Q69.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Mr. P, a 57-year-old man, has been recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. His HbA1c is 7.5 and his fasting sugar is approximately 8mmol/L. He has no other medical conditions and is on no other medications. He has heard some medicines can cause weight gain and he makes it very clear he does not want that side effect. Which of the following would be an appropriate option to treat his diabetes?

options.html: Starting insulin therapy
Metformin
Pioglitazone
Glyburide

answer: The correct answer is B. Many options could be argued as first-line in a newly diagnosed patient, and all of these may be correct in different circumstances - but this question turns on weight gain. All of these carry weight-gain potential except metformin, which is also (per Q66) unable to cause hypoglycemia on its own. Another weight-neutral option not listed would be DPP-4 inhibitors.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT an important aspect of treating and monitoring diabetes and its complications?

options.html: Reinforcement of diet and exercise
Blood pressure control
Daily aspirin
Yearly hearing assessment
Lipid control

answer: The correct answer is D. Diabetes is one aspect of metabolic syndrome, and all its risks must be managed - blood pressure, lipids and hypercoagulability - with diet and exercise helping all of them. Chronic complications require ongoing monitoring: foot care to prevent diabetic foot, and yearly eye assessments for retinopathy. A yearly hearing assessment is not part of diabetes monitoring. C (daily aspirin) is not routine either: the lecture gives acetylsalicylic acid 81 mg only for secondary prevention, in known coronary artery disease, and no antiplatelet for primary prevention. D is still the best answer, because aspirin is part of care for many patients with diabetes while hearing assessment is part of it for none. See 10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following cannot help prevent diabetes?

options.html: Metformin
Thiazolidinediones
Exercise
Low fat diet
Sulfonylureas

answer:
The correct answer is E. Know the studies discussed in lecture that showed a reduction in the development of diabetes.

  • Exercise and low-fat diet - effective in multiple studies (often quite strict regimens).
  • Metformin - effective in the Diabetes Prevention Program and others.
  • TZDs - supported by the DREAM study. Rosiglitazone is gone but pioglitazone remains.
  • Sulfonylureas - some evidence that they hasten progression by "burning out" the pancreas. They do not prevent diabetes.

Reasoning route if you forget the trials: low-fat diet and exercise moderate sugar and insulin levels, and biguanides/TZDs improve insulin action in a glucose-dependent way, whereas sulfonylureas force insulin secretion glucose-independently - which is why they would be expected to accelerate progression. See 12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following does NOT increase the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in childhood?

options.html: Caucasian ancestry
Family history of type 2 diabetes
Obesity, especially BMI in the 85th%
Excessive daily screen watching.
Lack of activity

answer:
The correct answer is A. Certain ethnic groups are at higher risk - First Nations, African, Asian and Hispanic ancestries. Caucasian ancestry is not itself a risk factor, though that does not mean Caucasians are not at risk.

B is true - family history increases risk and shifts onset earlier in life. C, D and E are true; obesity and inactivity are the modifiable factors driving the rising incidence, and screen time is associated with both.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: How much % total body weight loss are the Roux-en-Y and sleeve gastrectomy associated with?

options.html: 3-5%, which is roughly the same as with current obesity-approved medications in Canada
40% in most cases
25-30% in most cases
10% in most cases

answer: The correct answer is C. They typically produce 25-30% total body weight loss - much more than pharmacological treatment. This is particularly relevant to fatty liver disease, which requires a near-40% weight reduction, unlike most other metabolic conditions where only a 5-7% reduction demonstrates risk reduction. See bariatric surgery.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which gastric bypass (bariatric surgery) method is absolutely NOT indicated for a 38-year-old female patient with a BMI of 55 kg/m2, coronary artery disease (CAD), and is failing to lose weight on pharmacotherapy but is still motivated to lose weight.

options.html: Sleeve gastrectomy
Roux-en-Y
Lap gastric band
Biliopancreatic diversion (BPD)

answer:
The correct answer is C. Lap gastric banding is absolutely not recommended because patients control the level of restriction on the gastric opening themselves, which produces poorer weight-loss outcomes.

  • A Sleeve gastrectomy - tends to be safest, ~25% total body weight loss.
  • B Roux-en-Y - up to 30% total body weight loss, but risks malabsorption and is restrictive.
  • D BPD - significant malabsorption risk and perioperative morbidity/mortality, but 70-80% total body weight loss; reserved for patients with high BMIs - which this patient has.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a microvascular complication of diabetes?

options.html: Retinopathy
Nephropathy
Peripheral vascular disease
Neuropathy

answer:
The correct answer is C. Chronic cardiovascular complications of diabetes split into:

  • Microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy
  • Macrovascular: myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral vascular disease

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: What is characteristic of proliferative retinopathy?

options.html: Capillary dilatations
Dot haemorrhages
Retinal infarct (cotton wool spots)
Macular edema
Neovascularization of the optic disc

answer: The correct answer is E. Proliferative retinopathy is defined by the growth of new vessels in the retina, which may lead to retinal detachment and visual distortion - what makes it an especially worrying complication. The other options may be present in proliferative retinopathy but are characteristic of background/non-proliferative retinopathy.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: What is the best intervention to prevent neuropathy in type 2 diabetics?

options.html: Controlling blood pressure to <=130/80.
Daily aspirin
Controlling lipids
Controlling blood sugars to target of <=7.0% HbA1C
Using ACE inhibitors

answer: The correct answer is D. The only proven intervention for reducing the risk of neuropathy in type 2 diabetes is controlling blood glucose. The other interventions may benefit other complications, but not neuropathy. See 08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes.
noteTerms: 08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following medications can create an anion gap metabolic acidosis?

options.html: Metformin
Insulin
Pioglitazone
Acarbose
Gliclazide

answer: The correct answer is A. Metformin is first-line in T2DM for convenience, effectiveness and safety, but its serious potential adverse event is lactic acidosis - a type of anion gap metabolic acidosis, like DKA. Remember that one of metformin's effects is increased hepatic lactic acid production.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which is the BEST marker for long term glucose control in diabetes?

options.html: Fasting blood glucose
2-hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)
HbA1C
Random blood glucose
Urine glucose

answer:
The correct answer is C. HbA1c reflects glucose control over the last 3 months: it measures the percentage of glycosylated hemoglobin, and since hemoglobin turns over every 90-120 days, its glycosylation state integrates the glucose load over roughly that window.

A is an important test but only a point value. B is a great test of glucose tolerance but also a point value. D is a point value additionally distorted by everything eaten in the past few hours. E is no longer usually performed - blood glucose is far more accurate, ideally there is no glucose in urine at all, and renal glucose clearance is highly sensitive to factors unrelated to diabetes, making it unreliable for monitoring.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT consistent with endogenous overproduction of insulin?

options.html: Low blood glucose
Low glycogen
High insulin
High c-peptide
Low β-OH-butyrate

answer:
The correct answer is B. Overproduction of insulin drives excessive glucose into cells, giving low serum glucose (A consistent). But insulin increases glucose storage, so insulin overproduction is unlikely to leave a glycogen deficiency - B is inconsistent.

C and D are consistent for obvious reasons. E is consistent: β-OH-butyrate is a by-product of fatty acid catabolism, synthesized from acetyl-CoA during fasting states like ketone bodies - but in hyperinsulinemic states the body does not synthesize it, because it is fooled into thinking it is not fasting even when it is.

See insulinoma.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following features can differentiate between exogenous vs endogenous insulin administration?

options.html: Low blood glucose
Low glycogen
High insulin
Low c-peptide
Low β-OH-butyrate

answer:
The correct answer is D. C-peptide distinguishes endogenous from exogenous insulin: it is cleaved from pro-insulin during processing in the Golgi, so it is not generated if the circulating insulin came from outside the body.

A, C and E are all features of hyperinsulinemia from either source. B (low glycogen), per Q84, is not indicative of a hyperinsulinemic state at all.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: A 35 year old woman with DM-I for 20 years has persistent microalbuminuria and does not wish to conceive. Which of the following medications to prevent DM complications would you suggest to her?

options.html: ASA 81mg
Metformin
Rosuvastatin
ACE inhibitor
C & D

answer:
The correct answer is E (C & D).

  • Statin is indicated after age 30 with DM1 for >15 years.
  • ACEI is indicated for microalbuminuria, to prevent further renal impairment - and note she does not wish to conceive, so the fetal contraindication does not apply.
  • ASA is not recommended for primary prevention in this group.
  • Metformin is not indicated in DM-1.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q59. Tests [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT part of metabolic syndrome in women?

options.html: Hyperglycemia
PCOS
Hypertension
Abdominal Obesity
Dyslipidemia

answer:
The correct answer is B. Metabolic syndrome is defined as at least 3 of:

  • Abdominal obesity (men ≥ 102 cm; women ≥ 88 cm)
  • BP ≥ 130/80
  • Triglycerides ≥ 1.7 mM
  • BG 5.6-7.0 mM
  • HDL < 1.0 mM (men), < 1.3 mM (women)

Women with metabolic syndrome may also present with PCOS due to overlapping risk factors, but PCOS is its own separate syndrome and does not directly contribute to metabolic syndrome.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2. Tests [[04 - Clinically Useful Endocrine Principles]].
stem: With regards to endocrine physiology, which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: Paracrine chemical mediators act on an adjacent cell while autocrine chemical mediators act on the same cell
Hormones can be classified as a peptide/polypeptide, steroid, or amino acid.
IGF-1 is a growth factor that is released from the pancreas in response to GH secretion from the anterior pituitary.
Growth hormone displays both a diurnal and ultradian pattern of secretion

answer: The correct answer is C. IGF-1 is released in response to GH secretion. However, it is released from the liver, and not the pancreas.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q1-Q2. Tests [[04 - Clinically Useful Endocrine Principles]].
stem: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: Vasopressin (ADH), and Prolactin are secreted by the posterior pituitary gland.
Steroid hormones like estrogen or testosterone must be bound to travel through the bloodstream.
Hypothalamic release of SRIF (Somatostatin) inhibits the release of GH from the anterior pituitary.
Hypothalamic release of Dopamine inhibits the release of Prolactin from the anterior pituitary.

answer: The correct answer is A. Vasopressin (ADH) and oxytocin are the two hormones secreted by the posterior pituitary, not vasopressin and prolactin. Prolactin is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q14. Tests [[09 - Introduction to Obesity]].
stem: Andy is a 56 year old male. He has a BMI of 32.2 kg/m2. His medical history is not significant. He has a family history of epilepsy. Which of the following weight loss interventions would you recommend? Choose up to two answers.

options.html: Lifestyle management (diet and exercise)
Pharmacotherapy - orlistat
Pharmacotherapy - naltrexone/bupropion
Pharmacotherapy - metformin
Surgery

answer:
The correct answers are A & B. Although the patient's BMI is above 30 and he meets criteria for pharmacotherapy, his family history of epilepsy is a contraindication to naltrexone/bupropion (bupropion lowers the seizure threshold). Metformin is not approved for weight loss.

Surgery is recommended for BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with comorbidities, or ≥ 30 with type 2 diabetes or insufficient weight-loss effect. See 09 - Introduction to Obesity.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6, Q14. Tests [[09 - Introduction to Obesity]].
stem: Match the food type with the calories per gram.
answer:
The pairings:

Food typeCalories per gram
Carbohydrate4 Calories per gram
Protein4 Calories per gram
Fat9 Calories per gram
Alcohol7 Calories per gram

Carbohydrate and protein both have 4 Calories per gram. Fat has 9 Calories per gram, while alcohol has 7 Calories per gram.

flags.title: Off-curriculum
flags.html: This year's lectures do not teach this. Checked against 09 - Introduction to Obesity, the nearest lecture, which says: “Obesity is much more complicated than a simple imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure.”.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q48-Q58. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]], [[05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology]], [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the action of insulin in the body:

options.html: Insulin stimulates glucose production and inhibits glucose uptake in the liver.
Insulin inhibits glucose uptake in muscles.
Insulin's action is primarily mediated through tyrosine kinase receptors.
Excess insulin can quickly cause hyperglycemia in predisposed patients.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Insulin acts to store glucose, lowering blood glucose, and opposes glucagon (which mobilizes glucose and raises it). Insulin therefore inhibits glucose production and stimulates glucose uptake - A and B state the opposite.

At the molecular level insulin acts through tyrosine kinase receptors at the cell surface, meaning it does not need to enter the cell to act. D is wrong because excess insulin causes hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia.

flags.title: Off-curriculum
flags.html: This year's lectures do not teach this. Checked against 03 - Pharmacology of Insulin, the nearest lecture, which says: “Mechanism of action: activation of the insulin receptor ↑ translocation of the GLUT-4 transporter”.

review.t: Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: A 30-year-old woman in her 2nd trimester has been diagnosed with gestational diabetes. What would be the first line option for treatment to control her blood glucose?

options.html: Newer insulins (glargine) that can be dosed once a day for convenience.
Older insulin such as NPH.
Metformin
Glyburide
Only diet and exercise, medications are unsafe.

answer:
The correct answer is B. Insulin is first-line for gestational diabetes - and specifically the older insulins (NPH, regular), because there is very little safety data for diabetic medications in pregnancy for obvious ethical reasons, and these are known to be both safe and effective. Newer insulins may work well in other forms of diabetes but lack pregnancy safety data.

Metformin and glyburide were both still under investigation at the time of writing. Diet and activity are vital but rarely sufficient alone - only patients able to sustain extremely stringent compliance avoid medication, and the majority of GDM patients will use insulin at some point in the pregnancy.

flags.title: Off-curriculum
flags.html: This year's lecture teaches this differently, so the key here may not match what you are examined on. Checked against 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes, which says: “Insulin is the gold standard and is safe; case: Start insulin aspart 4 units before breakfast, and insulin detemir 6 units at bedtime”.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q63-Q87. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]], [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]], [[11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes]], [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: True or false: Both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia are potential complications of daytime fasting. Patients with type 2 diabetes will fast regardless of our recommendations. Many diabetics can safely fast, but there are many complications to look for.

options.html: True
False

answer:
True. Hypoglycemia makes intuitive sense; hyperglycemia occurs because of increased food intake at night, which can even cause weight gain in some patients.

Even without the extra intake, fasting at any time of day can produce rebound hyperglycemia via the Somogyi effect: in response to hypoglycemia the body releases, in order, glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines and growth hormone to liberate stored glucose.

stem: What are the three components of Whipple's triad?

options.html: Neurogenic/neuroglycopenic, laboratory hypoglycaemia documented during symptoms, symptom reversal with glucose
Neurogenic/neuroglycopenic, laboratory hyperglycaemia documented during symptoms, symptom exacerbation with glucose
Neurogenic/neuroglycopenic, triggered by hyperglycaemia, symptom reversal with insulin
Neurogenic/neuroglycopenic, triggered by hypoglycaemia, symptom reversal with insulin

answer:
The correct answer is A. Whipple's triad signifies insulin-induced hypoglycemia:

  1. (early) neurogenic and/or (late) neuroglycopenic symptoms
  2. Lab-documented low blood sugar during symptoms
  3. Symptom reversal with glucose administration

B describes the opposite of insulin-mediated hypoglycemia. C and D are wrong because glucose - not insulin - reverses the symptoms; giving insulin would deepen the hypoglycemia and worsen symptoms.

stem: Which of the following complications of pregnancy does NOT result from gestational diabetes mellitus?

options.html: Fetal macrosomia
Caesarean section
Shoulder dystocia
Neonatal hypoglycemia
Increased fetal mortality

answer:
The correct answer is E. All the others are possible complications of GDM — but although there are statistically significant differences in morbidity, there is no statistical difference in fetal mortality.

Fetal macrosomia → shoulder dystocia → cesarean section is the causal chain behind A-C. Neonatal hypoglycemia occurs because the infant has been abruptly cut off from the high blood-sugar supply it was accustomed to.

stem: Which of the following pregnant women does not need to be screened for GDM?

options.html: 24 y.o. with a previous pregnancy history of 1 miscarriage
19 y.o. with BMI a of 31, no previous pregnancies
35 y.o. with previous pregnancy history of 2 large babies
23 y.o. with a family history of type 2 diabetes, no previous pregnancies
40 y.o. woman with high blood pressure, no previous pregnancies

answer:
The correct answer is A. Only women deemed "low risk" may skip screening for GDM. The low-risk group is:

  • age < 25
  • ethnic group not predisposed to diabetes
  • no past history of large-for-dates babies
  • normal body weight
  • no family history of diabetes

A previous miscarriage is not on that list of risk factors, so patient A remains low risk. All other patients should be screened at 24-28 weeks with a 50 g OGTT.

stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding bariatric surgery for obesity management?

options.html: Sleeve gastrectomy reduces the stomach to 25% of its original size
Sleeve gastrectomy is often recommended for patients with a high preoperative risk
Lapgastric band is not routinely recommended
All of the above are true

answer:
The correct answer is D. Refer to the Intro to Obesity lecture

From 09 - Introduction to Obesity and sleeve gastrectomy. All three statements match the notes:

  • A: sleeve gastrectomy removes 75-85% of the stomach, leaving a banana-sized tube of roughly 15-25%. It is a purely restrictive procedure.
  • B: because it has no bypass or anastomosis, it is "more often considered for those at high operative risk".
  • C: the lecture states that laparoscopic gastric banding is no longer performed and is explicitly not recommended. Sleeve and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass are the two most common operations.

Since A, B and C are all true, D is the only complete answer.

lectureMeta: 46-year-old woman, longitudinal case adapted from NEJM Case 10-2024. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: A 46-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is maintained on insulin glargine 30 units daily, insulin lispro 10 units three times daily with meals, and glimepiride. Her fasting glucose has been running 5.5-7.0 mmol/L but her 2-hour post-prandial readings are consistently 15-18 mmol/L, and her A1C is 11.0%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next change to her regimen?

options.html: Increase insulin glargine to 40 units daily
Increase the pre-meal insulin lispro dose
Replace insulin glargine with NPH insulin twice daily
Add a second sulfonylurea
Add a bedtime dose of insulin lispro

answer:
B. The decision here is which defect is uncontrolled, not how much insulin to give. Her fasting glucose is at target, so the basal component is doing its job - escalating glargine (A) would push her toward overnight hypoglycemia without touching the problem. The abnormality is confined to the post-prandial window, which is the prandial insulin's territory.

  • C swaps one basal for another; NPH's peak would add hypoglycemia risk, not prandial coverage.
  • D stimulates insulin secretion in a glucose-independent way and would compound the hypoglycemia risk she already carries on a secretagogue plus insulin.
  • E puts rapid-acting insulin where there is no meal, which is how nocturnal hypoglycemia is caused.

Principle: match the agent's time-action profile to the interval that is out of range. Fasting out of range → basal; post-prandial out of range → prandial.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 46-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is maintained on insulin glargine 30 units daily, insulin lispro 10 units three times daily with meals, and glimepiride. Her fasting glucose has been running 5.5-7.0 mmol/L but her 2-hour post-prandial readings are consistently 15-18 mmol/L, and her A1C is 11.0%.

stem: The same patient is now taking glimepiride, pioglitazone, insulin glargine and insulin lispro. Which adverse effect should you counsel her about as the most likely consequence of this particular combination?

options.html: Lactic acidosis
Hypoglycemia and weight gain
Genital mycotic infection
Flatulence and bloating
Acute pancreatitis

answer:
B. Three agents that lower glucose by three different routes are stacked - a secretagogue, a sensitizer, and exogenous insulin - so the additive hypoglycemia risk is the immediate safety issue. Separately, all three of SUs, TZDs and insulin drive weight gain, and pioglitazone adds fluid retention on top.

  • A belongs to metformin, which she is no longer taking.
  • C belongs to the SGLT2 inhibitors - relevant to her earlier empagliflozin, not this regimen.
  • D belongs to the AGIs.
  • E is a concern for the incretin-based agents, none of which she is on.

Principle: when a regimen stacks agents, ask what the shared toxicity is. Here two mechanisms converge on hypoglycemia and three converge on weight.

stem: Two years earlier, empagliflozin had been added to her regimen. Two months later she presented with dysuria and urinary frequency; urine culture grew E. coli. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.html: Treat the infection, counsel on hygiene and fluid intake, and continue empagliflozin
Discontinue empagliflozin permanently and treat the infection
Treat the infection and add prophylactic daily antibiotics
Discontinue empagliflozin and substitute an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor
Withhold antibiotics and increase fluid intake alone

answer:
A. A single uncomplicated urinary tract infection is an expected, mechanism-predictable event on an SGLT2 inhibitor - glucose delivered into the urinary tract is a bacterial substrate - and it is not by itself a reason to abandon a drug that is working. Treat the infection and keep the agent, with counselling.

  • B is the right call only for recurrent or severe genitourinary infection, or urosepsis. Discarding the class after one event costs her the glycemic, weight and cardiorenal benefit.
  • C commits her to antibiotic exposure and resistance risk after a first uncomplicated episode.
  • D substitutes a weaker agent and does not follow from a UTI.
  • E undertreats a culture-positive infection in a patient with diabetes.

Principle: distinguish an anticipated, manageable adverse effect from one that mandates stopping the drug. Frequency and severity decide, not the first occurrence.

stem: Six months before presentation she was admitted with abdominal pain; endoscopy showed erosive gastritis and duodenitis due to H. pylori, and she was started on amoxicillin, clarithromycin, bismuth subsalicylate and pantoprazole. She remains on glimepiride, pioglitazone and insulin. Two days later she has repeated morning capillary glucose readings of 2.8-3.3 mmol/L. Which of the following best explains this?

options.html: Amoxicillin displaces glimepiride from plasma protein binding sites
Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, raising glimepiride and pioglitazone levels
Pantoprazole reduces the subcutaneous absorption of insulin glargine
Bismuth subsalicylate increases the renal clearance of insulin
Eradication of H. pylori abruptly increases insulin sensitivity

answer:
B. This is the pharmacokinetic trap in the case. Clarithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; both glimepiride (a sulfonylurea) and pioglitazone undergo extensive hepatic metabolism, so inhibiting their clearance raises drug levels and converts a stable regimen into a hypoglycemic one. Bismuth subsalicylate may contribute a hypoglycemic effect of its own, which the lecture noted alongside the interaction.

  • A - protein-binding displacement is the reflex exam answer, but it is the wrong mechanism for amoxicillin here.
  • C - acid suppression is irrelevant to a parenteral drug.
  • D - insulin is not renally cleared in a way bismuth alters.
  • E - plausible-sounding, but far too slow and too small to produce hypoglycemia within 48 hours.

Principle: whenever glycemic control changes abruptly and the diabetes regimen did not, look at what was added for something else.

preamble.title: The case

stem: Over the following 21 months her BMI falls from 45.6 to 17.0 (weight 42 kg) despite escalating insulin. She is cachectic with diffuse loss of fat and muscle, and has developed acromegaly-like facial features, extensive acanthosis nigricans, skin tags and vitiligo. Her A1C remains 11.0-14.0% and her total insulin requirement now exceeds 50 units/kg/day. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

options.html: Covert non-adherence to her insulin regimen
A growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma
Autoantibodies directed against the insulin receptor
Congenital generalized lipodystrophy
Endogenous hypercortisolism

answer:
C. Type B insulin resistance. Three features converge: an insulin requirement an order of magnitude above ordinary resistance (>50 units/kg/day against a typical 0.5-1), severe acanthosis nigricans and skin tags as the cutaneous signature of extreme insulin-receptor signalling failure, and vitiligo marking a broader autoimmune diathesis. The catabolic wasting despite massive insulin doses is the giveaway that insulin is being delivered but not acting.

  • A cannot explain hyperglycemia that persisted through supervised inpatient IV insulin infusions across six admissions.
  • B - acromegaly causes insulin resistance and coarse features, but not vitiligo, and not resistance of this magnitude.
  • D is congenital; she had a BMI of 45.6 five years earlier, so a lifelong lipodystrophy is excluded by her own history.
  • E would give central obesity with proximal myopathy, not diffuse cachexia.

Principle: insulin resistance severe enough to defeat IV insulin is a receptor or post-receptor problem, not a dosing problem. The skin is where you read it.

stem: Which single investigation would best confirm the diagnosis in the patient above?

options.html: Serum IGF-1
Anti-insulin antibodies
Antibodies to the insulin receptor
Anti-GAD65 antibodies
24-hour urinary free cortisol

answer:
C. The target of the autoantibody is the diagnosis, so the assay must be directed at the receptor.

  • B is the trap. Anti-insulin antibodies and anti-insulin receptor antibodies are different tests answering different questions. The former bind the hormone and are largely a consequence of exogenous insulin exposure; only the latter establish type B insulin resistance.
  • A would test for acromegaly - reasonable to send given the facial features, but it explains neither the vitiligo nor receptor-level resistance.
  • D tests β-cell autoimmunity, which speaks to type 1 diabetes and does not cause resistance of this magnitude.
  • E screens for hypercortisolism, already argued against by the body habitus.

Principle: when the mechanism is antibody-mediated, name the antigen before you order the test.

stem:
A 47-year-old man with type 2 diabetes diagnosed 2 years ago takes metformin BID and presents with fatigue and headache. He works as a consultant engineer, travels several days most weeks, struggles to maintain diet and exercise, and often forgets his second daily dose. He has gained 12 lb in the past year. He has a history of IBS.

ParameterResultFlag
fasting glucose178 mg/dLhigh
creatinine1.0 mg/dL
A1C8.3%high
total cholesterol250 mg/dLhigh
LDL150 mg/dLhigh
triglycerides220 mg/dLhigh

Which of the following is the most appropriate second agent?

options.html: Glimepiride daily
Pioglitazone daily
A once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist
Acarbose with each meal
Repaglinide three times daily with meals

answer:
C. Every one of his problems points the same way. Weight gain of 12 lb and dyslipidemia call for an agent that produces weight loss; his normal creatinine leaves the class available; and the decisive practical factor is that he already fails a twice-daily schedule, so a once-weekly injection is the dosing interval most likely to actually be taken.

  • A and B both cause weight gain in a patient whose weight is already the problem, and the SU adds hypoglycemia risk to an irregular travelling schedule.
  • D requires dosing with every meal - the worst fit for his adherence - and his IBS rules it out on tolerability grounds anyway (Q8).
  • E is three times daily, is a secretagogue with hypoglycemia risk, and causes weight gain.

Principle: when efficacy is comparable across several classes, the tie is broken by weight, hypoglycemia risk, and a dosing frequency the patient will keep to.

stem: For the same patient, which drug class is contraindicated by his medical history?

options.html: SGLT2 inhibitors, taken with the first meal
DPP-4 inhibitors, taken once daily
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors
Thiazolidinediones, taken once daily
Metformin, taken with meals

answer:
C. The lecture's caution-and-contraindication table lists chronic intestinal disorders and obstruction as contraindications to the AGIs - and his IBS is exactly that. The mechanism makes it obvious: undigested carbohydrate delivered to the colon and fermented there produces flatulence, bloating and cramping, which is to say it reproduces and worsens his existing symptoms.

  • A, B and D carry cautions in renal and hepatic dysfunction, which he does not have (creatinine 1.0).
  • E he already takes uneventfully.

Principle: an adverse-effect profile that overlaps a patient's existing symptoms is a contraindication, not merely a caution.

stem: Before starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist in this patient, which element of the history would most strongly contraindicate it?

options.html: Cholelithiasis on a previous ultrasound
A family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma
Irritable bowel syndrome, diarrhoea-predominant
Dyslipidaemia on a moderate-intensity statin
A body mass index of 31 kg/m²

answer:
B. Medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 are listed contraindications to the GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, so a family history is the item here that stops the prescription.

  • A and C are cautions worth noting - gallbladder disease, and delayed gastric emptying or gastroparesis, appear in the caution column - but neither is an absolute bar.
  • D and E are indications to prefer the class, not reasons to avoid it.

Principle: read a drug table in two columns. Caution changes your monitoring; contraindication changes your choice.

lecture: Case 3 - Nancy (Secondary Failure and Hypoglycemia Fear)
lectureMeta: 62-year-old woman on maximum-dose dual oral therapy. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes of 5 years takes maximum-dose metformin; gliclazide was added last year, which brought her A1C from 7.8% to 7.1%. Today her A1C is 7.9% on maximum doses of both, and she has gained 5 lb since starting gliclazide (BMI 26). She reports taking both medications reliably. Which of the following best explains her loss of glycemic control?

options.html: Progressive β-cell failure with secondary sulfonylurea failure
Tachyphylaxis at metformin's AMPK target
Evolving type 1 diabetes
Undisclosed non-adherence
A drug interaction reducing gliclazide absorption

answer:
A. The pattern is diagnostic: a real but temporary response to a secretagogue (7.8% → 7.1%), followed by drift back up on an unchanged maximum dose. A sulfonylurea works only through β-cells that can still secrete; as β-cell mass and function decline, and as the K⁺/ATP channel target desensitizes, the drug runs out of substrate to act on.

The follow-on the case asks: would glyburide or repaglinide have been better? No - both act on the same K⁺/ATP channel in the same failing β-cell. Switching within the secretagogue mechanism cannot recover a mechanism that is exhausted. She needs a class that does not depend on β-cell secretory reserve.

  • B is not a recognised phenomenon at this target.
  • C would bring weight loss, ketosis-prone decompensation and a far steeper deterioration, not a 0.8% drift.
  • D is contradicted by the history, and would not have produced the initial clean response.
  • E would be an abrupt change traceable to a new medication; she takes none.

Principle: initial response then progressive failure on an unchanged dose is the signature of secondary failure, and it tells you to change mechanism, not dose.

lecture: Case 3 - Nancy (Secondary Failure and Hypoglycemia Fear)
lectureMeta: 62-year-old woman on maximum-dose dual oral therapy. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes of 5 years takes maximum-dose metformin; gliclazide was added last year, which brought her A1C from 7.8% to 7.1%. Today her A1C is 7.9% on maximum doses of both, and she has gained 5 lb since starting gliclazide (BMI 26). She reports taking both medications reliably.

stem: The same patient's stated goals are to control her glycemia, lose weight, avoid hypoglycemia, and stay on affordable oral therapy. She refuses insulin because she dislikes needles and fears hypoglycemia, since her eating is inconsistent. She is unemployed and cares for her mother, who has dementia. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition?

options.html: Substitute glyburide for gliclazide
Add an SGLT2 inhibitor
Add pioglitazone
Start basal insulin at bedtime
Add repaglinide with each meal

answer:
B. It is the only option that satisfies the constraints she has actually set: oral, weight loss rather than gain, low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk because its action is insulin-independent, and cardiorenal benefit as a bonus. Crucially it does not depend on the β-cell reserve that has already failed her (Q10).

The honest tension: cost. She is unemployed and paying out of pocket, and an SGLT2 inhibitor is not cheap - so coverage has to be checked, and it is the one goal this choice may not meet. A DPP-4 inhibitor is the reasonable alternative if cost is prohibitive: oral, very low hypoglycemia risk, but weight neutral rather than weight-reducing, and more modest efficacy.

  • A stays inside the mechanism that is failing, and picks the worst SU for hypoglycemia (Q12).
  • C gives weight gain, fracture risk in a 62-year-old woman, and higher cost - three of her four goals violated.
  • D is explicitly refused, and her irregular eating makes her fear of hypoglycemia legitimate rather than irrational.
  • E requires dosing with every meal in someone who eats inconsistently, and is again a secretagogue.

Principle: patient-stated goals are selection criteria. Score each candidate class against all of them and the answer usually declares itself.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes of 5 years takes maximum-dose metformin; gliclazide was added last year, which brought her A1C from 7.8% to 7.1%. Today her A1C is 7.9% on maximum doses of both, and she has gained 5 lb since starting gliclazide (BMI 26). She reports taking both medications reliably. She refuses insulin because she dislikes needles and fears hypoglycemia, since her eating is inconsistent. She is unemployed and cares for her mother, who has dementia.

stem: Given her inconsistent eating pattern and her role as sole caregiver, which agent would carry the greatest risk of hypoglycemia for this patient?

options.html: Glyburide
Gliclazide
Linagliptin
Metformin
Acarbose

answer:
A. Among the sulfonylureas, glyburide carries the highest hypoglycemia risk - longest effective duration of action, active metabolites, and the least forgiving profile when a meal is missed. It is also the SU avoided earliest as renal function declines. In a patient who eats irregularly and is responsible for someone with dementia, a prolonged unrecognised hypoglycemic episode is the specific harm to avoid.

  • B is a sulfonylurea and carries real risk, but less than glyburide - which is why gliclazide, glimepiride and repaglinide tolerate moderate impairment better.
  • C acts in a nutrient-dependent way, so it does not drive insulin secretion in the absence of a meal.
  • D and E carry no hypoglycemia risk as monotherapy; neither increases insulin secretion.

Principle: hypoglycemia risk tracks with glucose-independent insulin secretion and with duration of action. Ask what the drug does when the patient skips a meal.

lecture: Case 4 - Albert (SGLT2 Inhibitor, AKI and Shock)
lectureMeta: 72-year-old man admitted to ICU. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].
stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted to the ICU with acute kidney injury and severe shock. For 3 days he has felt unwell with foot swelling, decreased urine output, nausea and shortness of breath. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and GERD. Medications: valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, canagliflozin, sitagliptin, metformin, insulin degludec, insulin aspart and pantoprazole. His capillary glucose is 9.1 mmol/L. Which investigation is most important to obtain now?

options.html: Serum β-hydroxybutyrate
HbA1c
Serum insulin and C-peptide
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Urine culture

answer:
A. He is acutely unwell on an SGLT2 inhibitor, which puts euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis at the top of the list - and the glucose of 9.1 mmol/L is precisely why it gets missed. Urinary glucose loss blunts the hyperglycemia you would ordinarily use as the trigger to test for DKA, so a near-normal glucose does not exclude it. Measure ketones regardless of the glucose reading.

A serum lactate is the strong second call: he is on metformin with an acute drop in renal clearance and tissue hypoperfusion from shock, which is the exact setting for lactic acidosis.

  • B describes the last three months and changes nothing today.
  • C has no role in established type 2 diabetes in an emergency.
  • D does not explain this presentation.
  • E is reasonable in a shock workup, but it is not the test uniquely likely to be overlooked here.

Principle: when a drug removes the sign you normally screen on, screen on something else. Ketones in any unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor.

lecture: Case 4 - Albert (SGLT2 Inhibitor, AKI and Shock)
lectureMeta: 72-year-old man admitted to ICU. See [[13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)]].

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 72-year-old man is admitted to the ICU with acute kidney injury and severe shock. For 3 days he has felt unwell with foot swelling, decreased urine output, nausea and shortness of breath. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and GERD. Medications: valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, canagliflozin, sitagliptin, metformin, insulin degludec, insulin aspart and pantoprazole. His capillary glucose is 9.1 mmol/L.

stem: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of this patient's AKI and shock?

options.html: Osmotic diuresis from canagliflozin, compounded by his diuretic and ARB
Metformin accumulation causing lactic acidosis as the primary event
Sitagliptin-induced acute interstitial nephritis
Excess insulin degludec causing hypoglycemic collapse
Pantoprazole-induced acute interstitial nephritis

answer:
A. Three drugs pull in the same direction on his intravascular volume: canagliflozin produces glucosuria and osmotic diuresis, hydrochlorothiazide adds natriuretic volume loss, and valsartan removes the angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar tone that would otherwise defend glomerular filtration pressure as volume falls. Layer an acute illness with poor intake on top and you get severe dehydration, hypotension, reduced renal perfusion and prerenal AKI.

  • B inverts cause and effect. Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is a consequence of the AKI and hypoperfusion here, not the initiating event - though it is a reason to hold metformin now.
  • C and E are genuine drug causes of AKI, but neither fits: no eosinophilia, rash or fever is described, no new drug was started, and neither explains shock.
  • D is excluded by the glucose of 9.1 mmol/L.

Principle: in polypharmacy, look for drugs whose effects converge on one physiological axis. Three volume-depleting agents is not three small risks; it is one large one.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 72-year-old man is admitted to the ICU with acute kidney injury and severe shock. For 3 days he has felt unwell with foot swelling, decreased urine output, nausea and shortness of breath. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and GERD. Medications: valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, canagliflozin, sitagliptin, metformin, insulin degludec, insulin aspart and pantoprazole. His capillary glucose is 9.1 mmol/L.

stem: Reviewing his records, which feature of the preceding 18 months should have prompted reassessment of his regimen?

options.html: Recurrent falls attributed to postural hypotension
A stable A1C
GERD requiring pantoprazole
No medication changes in 2 years
The foot swelling of the last 3 days

answer:
A. canagliflozin was started roughly 18 months earlier, and over that same period he had several falls due to postural hypotension. That is the clinical readout of established volume depletion, and it was a standing invitation to review an SGLT2 inhibitor plus a thiazide plus an ARB in a 72-year-old. The ICU admission was the endpoint of a process that had been signalling for a year and a half.

  • B is reassuring on glycemia and says nothing about volume status - which is the trap: his diabetes looked well managed.
  • C is unrelated.
  • D is the absence of a trigger for review, not a warning sign.
  • E is part of the acute presentation, not the preceding window the question asks about.

Principle: postural symptoms and falls in an older patient on volume-depleting drugs are a medication review trigger, not an incidental geriatric finding.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 72-year-old man is admitted to the ICU with acute kidney injury and severe shock. For 3 days he has felt unwell with foot swelling, decreased urine output, nausea and shortness of breath. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and GERD. Medications: valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, canagliflozin, sitagliptin, metformin, insulin degludec, insulin aspart and pantoprazole. His capillary glucose is 9.1 mmol/L.

stem: He recovers with fluid resuscitation. At discharge his eGFR has stabilised at approximately 28 mL/min. Which of the following best describes the correct approach to his canagliflozin?

options.html: Restart it at full dose immediately for glycemic control
It is permanently contraindicated at this eGFR and must be stopped
Not newly initiated at this eGFR, but continued once he is euvolemic
Replace it with glyburide at an equivalent dose
Replace it with maximum-dose metformin

answer:
C. The SGLT2 inhibitors sit in a "do not initiate, but may continue" band below an eGFR threshold, and the reason is the key idea from this session: cardiorenal benefit is preserved even where glucose-lowering efficacy falls off. The drug stops being much of a glucose-lowering agent at this eGFR while remaining worth taking for the kidney and the heart. What must be fixed is the volume context - restart only once he is euvolemic, and revisit the thiazide and the ARB alongside it.

  • A ignores the volume depletion that put him in the ICU.
  • B overcorrects and discards the cardiorenal indication.
  • D picks the sulfonylurea most likely to cause hypoglycemia and the one avoided earliest in renal impairment - the wrong drug for a 72-year-old with an eGFR of 28.
  • E goes the wrong way: metformin requires stepwise reduction as eGFR falls, not maximisation.

Principle: an agent's indication can outlive its original purpose. Ask what you are now prescribing it for.

stem: A 68-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 12 mL/min. His A1C is 8.4% and his oral agents are being reviewed. Which of the following glucose-lowering options can still be prescribed?

options.html: Metformin
Saxagliptin
A sulfonylurea
Insulin

answer:
The correct answer is D, insulin. Graded in-class poll key: 14 of 15 responses chose insulin, marked "Is correct".

Insulin has no renal cut-off - it is titrated to effect, which is exactly what lets it survive to the lowest eGFR. Everything else here is limited by renal clearance:

  • A requires stepwise dose reduction as eGFR falls and is then avoided outright at the lowest ranges; an eGFR of 12 is well past that.
  • B is renally cleared and needs dose reduction. Note the discriminator: linagliptin is the DPP-4 inhibitor requiring no adjustment, because its clearance is non-renal.
  • C accumulates, and the resulting hypoglycemia is prolonged and dangerous.

Principle: at the extremes of renal function, ask which agent's dose is set by titration rather than by clearance.

lectureMeta: The two graded in-class polls from the same session. **These are the only questions in this note with an official key.
stem: An 84-year-old woman lives alone with mild cognitive impairment. Her eGFR is 45 mL/min and her A1C is 8.0% on metformin alone. Avoiding hypoglycemia is the dominant priority. Which drug class is among the safest options for her?

options.html: DPP-4 inhibitors
SGLT2 inhibitors
Sulfonylureas
Thiazolidinediones

answer:
The correct answer is A, the DPP-4 inhibitors. Graded in-class poll key: 15 of 16 responses chose DPP-4 inhibitors, marked "Is correct".

They are well tolerated, weight neutral, and carry minimal hypoglycemia risk because they act in a nutrient-dependent way - amplifying incretin-driven insulin secretion only when a meal has been eaten. That is the property that protects a frail patient living alone who may skip meals. Linagliptin needs no renal dose adjustment.

  • B brings volume depletion, postural hypotension and fall risk in exactly this demographic - see Q13-16.
  • C is the worst choice here: glucose-independent secretion, plus prolonged action, plus living alone, plus cognitive impairment is the recipe for unrecognised severe hypoglycemia.
  • D brings fluid retention, HF risk and fracture risk in an 84-year-old.

Principle: in the frail elderly the target shifts from tight control to avoiding harm; pick the class whose mechanism is self-limiting.

stem: Molly Flanders is a 26-year-old woman with 5 cycles in the past year, acne and excess facial hair. She has had no period for 4 months, and in the last two months has been up at least once a night with nocturia and has had three yeast infections. She and her partner would like to have a baby. Exam: height 1.50 m, weight 81 kg (BMI ~36 kg/m²), BP 135/85, mild facial hirsutism, acanthosis and skin tags on the neck, no Cushingoid stigmata. Labs: A1c 6.7%, fasting plasma glucose 7.4 mmol/L. Which pair of diagnoses best fits this presentation? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Type 1 diabetes and Cushing's syndrome
Type 2 diabetes and PCOS/PMOS
gestational diabetes and primary hypothyroidism
Impaired glucose tolerance and a prolactinoma

answer:
The correct answer is B, type 2 diabetes and PCOS/PMOS.

Why T2D fits: she is symptomatic (polydipsia, nocturia) with a fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L and an A1c ≥6.5% - either one is diagnostic in a symptomatic patient. BMI ~36 kg/m², acanthosis and skin tags all point to insulin resistance. The absence of wide purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, thin skin over the dorsum of the hand and spontaneous bruising argues against Cushing's and so against secondary diabetes. PCOS/PMOS is itself a T2DM risk factor. T1DM is not completely impossible.

Why PCOS/PMOS fits: she meets the Rotterdam criteria - clinical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne) plus ovulatory dysfunction (oligomenorrhea) - which is 2 of 3 after exclusions.

stem: Molly is symptomatic. According to the Diabetes Canada criteria used in this session, how many abnormal tests are required to diagnose diabetes in a symptomatic patient, and how many in an asymptomatic one? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: One abnormal test if symptomatic; two abnormal tests on different days if asymptomatic
Two abnormal tests if symptomatic; one abnormal test if asymptomatic
Two abnormal tests on different days in both cases
One abnormal test in both cases, provided it is an A1c

answer:
The correct answer is A. Diabetes Canada 2018: a symptomatic patient (polydipsia, polyuria/nocturia, weight loss) needs ONE of - fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, A1c ≥6.5%, 2-hour OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L, or random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L. An asymptomatic patient needs TWO abnormal tests on different days.

The OGTT is rarely used now outside GDM screening, and should be avoided where there is already symptomatic hyperglycemia.

stem: In adults, which criteria does the 2023 International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline use to diagnose PCOS, and what did that update change?

options.html: Rotterdam criteria - 2 of 3; the 2023 update allows AMH to replace ultrasound in defining polycystic ovarian morphology
Rotterdam criteria - all 3 required; the 2023 update added fasting insulin as a fourth criterion
NIH criteria - hyperandrogenism alone; the 2023 update added obesity as a requirement
Rotterdam criteria - 2 of 3; the 2023 update removed hyperandrogenism from the criteria

answer:
The correct answer is A. The Rotterdam criteria require 2 of 3, after exclusions:

  • clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism
  • ovulatory dysfunction (e.g. irregular cycles)
  • polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) on ultrasound

2023 update: AMH may replace ultrasound to define PCOM. AMH reflects the antral follicle count, so it reduces the need for transvaginal ultrasound. Use it only where it is needed to complete the criteria.

flags.title: The PMOS lecture counts differently
flags.html: 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) teaches a triad with all three needed: hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction (oligomenorrhea or cystic ovaries), and exclusion. Cystic ovaries and irregular cycles are one criterion there, so ovulatory dysfunction alone never makes the diagnosis.

stem: Molly and her partner are trying to conceive. Which single test is the most important to obtain before deciding on her management? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test
A serum beta-hCG
A transvaginal ultrasound for ovarian morphology
An overnight dexamethasone suppression test

answer:
The correct answer is B, a serum beta-hCG - she could be pregnant, and the entire management plan forks on the result.

The rest of the workup in a newly diagnosed patient with T2DM who is contemplating pregnancy: serum creatinine and urine ACR, lipids, an optometry exam to screen for diabetic eye disease, and a foot exam including monofilament to screen for peripheral sensory neuropathy. A CBC is reasonable to confirm the A1c is reliable. For PCOS/PMOS, a total testosterone level.

  • A should be avoided where there is already symptomatic hyperglycemia.
  • D is not indicated - she has no Cushingoid stigmata.

stem: Molly's pregnancy test is negative. Which management plan best fits the session's approach? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Start insulin now, target A1c <5.0% before conception, and recheck A1c in one month
Refer to the DEC; low threshold for metformin; pre-conception A1c <6.5%; recheck 3-4 months
Start a sulfonylurea, begin home glucose monitoring now, and recheck the A1c in 3 months
Lifestyle change alone, with no drug therapy until A1c exceeds 8.0%; recheck in 6 months

answer:
The correct answer is B. Refer to the DEC for education, diet and activity, with a long-term weight-control goal. Have a low threshold for metformin - it is the safest oral agent in pregnancy and it also helps induce ovulation in PCOS, which matters because she is trying to conceive. The pre-conception A1c target is <6.5%. Recheck the A1c in 3-4 months.

Home glucose monitoring only if starting a drug that can cause hypoglycemia - which metformin does not.

options.html: True
False

PregnancyGeneral adult
A1c≤6.5% (≤6.1% if possible)≤7.0% without unacceptable hypoglycemia

lecture: Case 2 - Steve Dedalus (Longstanding Type 1 Diabetes, A1c 11.0%)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases" and its facilitator deck. Q26-29. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]] and [[08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes]].
stem: Steve Dedalus is 37 and has had type 1 diabetes for 27 years. His most recent A1c is 11.0%. What does the A1c measure, and over what period? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Glucose irreversibly bound to hemoglobin over the preceding ~90 days
Fasting plasma glucose averaged over the preceding 7 days
Glycated serum albumin and other proteins over the preceding ~14 days
Peak post-prandial glucose averaged over the preceding ~30 days

answer:
The correct answer is A. The A1c measures glucose irreversibly attached to hemoglobin (glycosylation), and reflects ambient plasma glucose over the preceding ~90 days in a patient with normal hemoglobin dynamics.

It is the best-validated measure of long-term structural-complication risk: clinical trials show clinically important reductions in the onset and progression of diabetic eye disease, neuropathy and nephropathy when the A1c is lowered.

preamble.html: The case. Steve Dedalus is 37 and has had type 1 diabetes for 27 years. His most recent A1c is 11.0%.

stem: Steve's A1c is 11.0%. Roughly half of patients with type 1 diabetes of 10 years or more will not reach an A1c below 7.0%. Which statement best captures his glycemic goal of care? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Target A1c ≤7.0% without unacceptable hypoglycemia; any improvement still lowers risk
Target A1c ≤7.0%; if it cannot be reached, partial improvement gives no added benefit
Target A1c <6.0%, accepting frequent hypoglycemia as the cost of tighter control
No A1c target is appropriate after 10 or more years of type 1 diabetes

answer:
The correct answer is A. The target is A1c ≤7.0% without unacceptable hypoglycemia, and "unacceptable" is patient-specific - for example severe (assist-requiring) lows, or frequent (daily) self-treated lows.

The key point: at least half of patients with T1D for ≥10 years will not reach an A1c <7.0%, but because risk falls continuously with A1c, any improvement still lowers complication risk - going from 11.0% to 9.5% is worth having even though it misses the target.

To reach ≤7.0%: fasting / ac-meal glucose ~4.0-7.0 mmol/L, and 2-hour post-prandial ~5.0-10.0 mmol/L.

preamble.html: The case. Steve Dedalus is 37 and has had type 1 diabetes for 27 years. His most recent A1c is 11.0%.

stem: Steve's fingerstick values over two weeks range from 2 to 20 mmol/L. Before escalating his regimen, which step does the session put first? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Immediately switch him to an insulin pump
Identify the sources of his glycemic variability
Add a sulfonylurea to his existing insulin regimen
Increase every one of his insulin doses by 20%

answer:
The correct answer is B. A range of 2 to 20 mmol/L is a variability problem, and you cannot fix variability by adding insulin. Look first for:

  • injection-site problems - is there lipohypertrophy?
  • timing of the NovoRapid relative to meals (~15 minutes before)
  • over-correcting lows
  • whether he has a system for pre-meal bolus dosing based on the glucose level plus expected carbohydrate intake
  • possible gastroparesis

Then offer referral to the Diabetes Education Centre, especially if it has been a while.

C is wrong outright - a secretagogue does nothing in T1DM, where there are no functioning beta cells to stimulate.

NPH insulin at bedtime only
An insulin pump
Adding metformin

answer:
The correct answer is C, an insulin pump - stated in the session as preferred for all individuals with T1DM.

The full escalation pathway: address variability → DEC → full basal-bolus MDI, with rapid-acting insulin before breakfast, lunch and supper dosed on a correction factor plus carbohydrate intake, and a longer-acting basal (glargine, degludec) instead of Levemir/detemir → CGM, subject to coverage → insulin pump.

stem: A family doctor calls you at 4:30 pm on the Friday before the May long weekend about Fitzwilliam Darcy, a 55-year-old man with a random plasma glucose of 55 mmol/L. He has no history of diabetes but has had two weeks of increased thirst, blurred vision and polyuria every half hour. Which type of diabetes is most likely? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Type 1 diabetes, because of the severity of the hyperglycemia
Type 2 diabetes, the most common form overall
Gestational diabetes, given her age and presentation
Drug-induced diabetes from a recent prescription

answer: The correct answer is B. Type 2 diabetes is most likely and it is the most common form of diabetes overall. Severity of hyperglycemia alone does not classify the diabetes - a glucose of 55 mmol/L is entirely compatible with T2DM presenting as HHS.

Primary adrenal insufficiency
Diabetes insipidus

answer:
The correct answer is A. Both are potentially lethal and both need to be excluded before anything is deferred over a long weekend.

  • HHS - suggested by impaired mental status plus an effective serum osmolality ≥ ~320 mosm/kg.
  • DKA - suggested by an anion-gap metabolic acidosis, which is why the bicarbonate and anion gap were requested.

stem: How is the effective serum osmolality calculated in this context? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: (2 × [Na⁺]) + [glucose]
(2 × [Na⁺]) + [urea] + [glucose]
[Na⁺] + [K⁺] + [glucose]
(2 × [glucose]) + [Na⁺]

answer:
The correct answer is A. Effective serum osmolality = (2 × [Na⁺]) + [glucose], and a value ≥ ~320 mosm/kg together with impaired mental status is the concern for HHS.

Urea is excluded because it crosses cell membranes freely and so is not an effective osmole - it does not drive the water shift that produces the neurological findings.

Calculated vs effective osmolality. The calculated serum osmolality, 2 × [Na⁺] + [glucose] + [urea], does include urea. The question asks for the effective osmolality (tonicity), the one used for HHS, and that leaves urea out. If a source puts urea in, it is giving the calculated value, which is a different measure.

flags.title: Urea and the formula
flags.html: A reader reported that urea (BUN) should be in the formula and that the small-group case was in error. Urea belongs in the calculated osmolality; the question asks for the effective one, which excludes it, so the key stands.

preamble.title: The case - Mr. Darcy
preamble.html: The case. A family doctor calls you at 4:30 pm on the Friday before the May long weekend about Fitzwilliam Darcy, a 55-year-old man with a random plasma glucose of 55 mmol/L. He has no history of diabetes but has had two weeks of increased thirst, blurred vision and polyuria every half hour.

stem: What advice should you give the family doctor at 4:30 pm on the Friday of a long weekend? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Send him to the Emergency Department now
Book him into your clinic on Tuesday and start metformin in the meantime
Advise oral rehydration with fruit juice and review after the weekend
Arrange outpatient labs for the following week

answer:
The correct answer is A. If he has not had the tests needed to rule out HHS and DKA, or he has had them and the results are consistent with either, the safe thing is the Emergency Department now. Both are potentially lethal if not treated quickly, so leaving it over the long weekend is not a good idea.

He should also stop drinking anything except water and diet juices - which is why C is actively harmful.

stem: Why is insulin the drug of choice for Mr. Darcy's severe new hyperglycemia, even though he most likely has type 2 diabetes? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: It is the only agent licensed in new-onset diabetes
It controls severe hyperglycemia fastest, and may not be needed long term
All oral agents are contraindicated in type 2 diabetes at diagnosis
It is the only agent that does not require renal dose adjustment

answer: The correct answer is B. Because there is concern about acute decompensation, the threshold to start insulin ahead of all other anti-hyperglycemic drugs is very low. It is the most effective option for quickly controlling severe uncontrolled hyperglycemia. He may not need insulin long term - the choice is driven by the acuity, not by the eventual classification.

He has no history of diabetes but has had two weeks of increased thirst, blurred vision and polyuria every half hour.

stem: At the Diabetes Education Centre, Mr. Darcy is seen by a nurse and a dietician. Which best describes what the nurse will cover? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Survival skills - safe insulin use, hypoglycemia and sick-day rules
A calorie-reduced, balanced diet plan and carbohydrate counting teaching
Screening for retinopathy and nephropathy at this visit
Titration of his statin and his antihypertensive medication

answer:
The correct answer is A. The nurse concentrates on survival skills:

  • safe use of insulin - dose setting, how to inject, injection timing, storage
  • hypoglycemia - detection, prevention, treatment
  • glucose monitoring
  • driving guidelines
  • sick-day management

B is the dietician's role - assess his current diet, then build a plan on the Diabetes Canada 2018 guidelines: nutritionally balanced and, if he is overweight, calorie-reduced for weight loss. He also learns about carbohydrates generally, and may later be taught carbohydrate counting, especially if he ends up on MDI.

stem: Mr. Darcy's father died in his early 60s of kidney failure after a leg amputation. Which statement about protecting his kidneys is correct? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Use an ACE inhibitor or an ARB, but never both together
Use an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together for additive renal protection
Neither class has a role once diabetes is diagnosed
An ARB is only indicated once dialysis has begun

answer:
The correct answer is A. For prevention of renal failure: screening urine ACR annually, blood glucose control, blood pressure control, and an ACE inhibitor or an ARB - but not both.

Dual RAAS blockade adds hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without an offsetting benefit, which is why the "or" in that sentence is the examinable part.

stem: Is ASA used for primary or secondary cardiovascular prevention in diabetes? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Primary prevention in all patients with diabetes over 40
Secondary prevention only
Both, at equal doses
Neither - ASA has no role in diabetes

answer:
The correct answer is B, secondary prevention only. Meta-analyses and RCTs show that in primary prevention the benefit does not clearly exceed the harm, so ASA is not used for that indication in diabetes.

The rest of the macrovascular prevention package for coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke and peripheral vascular disease: blood pressure control, LDL-C control with a statin, smoking cessation, and anti-hyperglycemic drugs proven to prevent MACE in the cardiovascular outcome trials.

stem: Which set of interventions is used to prevent vision loss from diabetic eye disease? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Eye exam, glucose and BP control, smoking cessation, fenofibrate
An annual screening eye exam and nothing further
Blood glucose control and nothing further
Laser photocoagulation for every patient at diagnosis

answer:
The correct answer is A. For diabetic eye disease: a screening eye exam roughly annually, blood glucose control, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, and fenofibrate.

Set against the other structural complications from the same notes:

  • Renal failure - screening urine ACR annually, BG control, BP control, an ACE inhibitor or an ARB.
  • Peripheral sensory neuropathy - BG control.
  • Foot ulcers / amputation - everything that prevents neuropathy and peripheral vascular disease, plus regular foot exams and patient education, especially in high-risk feet.

stem: Agnes Wickfield is a 32-year-old Air Canada pilot with polyuria and polydipsia. She is not pregnant, her random blood glucose is 25.4 mmol/L, and urinalysis shows 3+ glucosuria but is negative for ketones. Which pairing of clinical features with the diabetes type they favour is correct? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: acanthosis favours type 1; DKA at presentation favours type 2
DKA at presentation favours type 1; acanthosis favours type 2
Both DKA and acanthosis favour type 1
Neither feature has any discriminating value

answer:
The correct answer is B. DKA at presentation favours T1D; acanthosis favours T2D.

The other features available from history and exam: ethnicity (T2D more common in First Nations, African American, Asian and Hispanic populations), family history (stronger in T2D - identical-twin concordance ~100%, and ≥half of T2D patients have a close relative with diabetes, versus only ~15% of new-onset T1D having a first- or second-degree relative with T1D), past GDM (favours T2D), older age (favours T2D), and obesity (favours T2D).

flags.title: No single factor is decisive
flags.html: T1D has been described in patients in their 80s, being overweight does not protect against immune-mediated beta-cell loss, and DKA can occur in T2D. The features are combined, not applied individually.
