preamble.title: The case - Agnes
preamble.html: The case. Agnes Wickfield is a 32-year-old Air Canada pilot with polyuria and polydipsia. She is not pregnant, her random blood glucose is 25.4 mmol/L, and urinalysis shows 3+ glucosuria but is negative for ketones.

stem: Which investigations would specifically support a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes in Agnes? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Pancreatic autoantibodies and a low serum C-peptide
A high serum C-peptide and a fasting insulin level
An OGTT and a fructosamine level
A A1c above 10% alone

answer:
The correct answer is A.

  • Pancreatic autoantibodies - GADA, IAA, ZnT8A, IA-2A, ICA - marking immune-mediated beta-cell loss.
  • A low serum C-peptide - favours T1D, because C-peptide is co-secreted with endogenous insulin and so falls as beta-cell function is lost.
  • HLA typing - T1D is associated with DR3, DR4, DQ8.

stem: Why does it matter whether Agnes has type 1 or type 2 diabetes? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Only because the long-term complication risk differs
Type 1 means insulin, which has occupational implications for a pilot
It does not change management at this glucose level
Only because type 1 requires a different A1c target

answer:
The correct answer is B. Two reasons are given:

  • If she has type 1 diabetes, insulin is the required treatment - not an option among others.
  • She is a commercial pilot, so the diagnosis and the need for insulin carry direct occupational and regulatory implications.

lecture: Cases 5-7 - Adjusting Insulin from the Glucose Record
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases" and its facilitator deck. Q42-47. Three patients on insulin: read the record, decide whether to change the regimen and what to change. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]] and [[08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes]].
stem:
Patient 5 is a 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and an A1c of 8.4%, on rapid-acting NovoRapid before each meal and glargine 16 units at bedtime. His week of readings (mmol/L):

DayBreakfastLunchSupperBedtime
Mon4.26.812.316.7
Tue3.912.514.618.2
Wed6.88.59.212.6
Thu3.26.98.54.7
Fri4.15.211.916.5
Sat2.811.413.48.4
Sun3.99.414.315.9

Which description of his pattern is correct? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Morning hypoglycemia, with hyperglycemia at supper and at bedtime
Morning hyperglycemia, with hypoglycemia at supper and at bedtime
Hypoglycemia at every reading
A flat, well-controlled profile

answer:
The correct answer is A. Reading down the columns: the breakfast values run low (2.8, 3.2, 3.9, 3.9, 4.1) - morning hypoglycemia; the supper values run high (up to 14.6) - hyperglycemia at supper; and the bedtime values run high (up to 18.2) - hyperglycemia at bedtime.

Reading the record by time of day rather than by day is the whole technique here - the pattern is in the columns, not the rows.

preamble.html:
The case. Patient 5 is a 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and an A1c of 8.4%, on rapid-acting NovoRapid before each meal and glargine 16 units at bedtime. His week of readings (mmol/L):

DayBreakfastLunchSupperBedtime

stem: Which set of insulin adjustments does the session recommend for Patient 5? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Decrease bedtime glargine; increase lunch and supper NovoRapid
Increase bedtime glargine; decrease lunch and supper NovoRapid
Decrease every one of her doses by 20%
Make no change and repeat the A1c in three months

answer:
The correct answer is A.

  • Decrease bedtime Lantus/glargine by 10-20% - it is the insulin acting overnight, and he is waking low.
  • Increase lunch NovoRapid by 10% - it covers the interval ending at the pre-supper reading, which is high.
  • Increase supper NovoRapid by 10% - it covers the interval ending at bedtime, which is high.

lecture: Cases 5-7 - Adjusting Insulin from the Glucose Record
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases" and its facilitator deck. Q42-47. Three patients on insulin: read the record, decide whether to change the regimen and what to change. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]] and [[08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes]].
stem: What is the general principle for adjusting a basal-bolus regimen from a glucose record? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Adjust the insulin acting before the abnormal glucose, typically by 10-20%
Adjust the insulin given after the abnormal glucose
Adjust the basal insulin only, whatever the pattern
Change all components simultaneously to reach target faster

answer:
The correct answer is A. Adjust the insulin acting before the abnormal glucose, typically by 10-20%:

  • morning low → decrease the bedtime basal
  • high pre-supper → increase the lunch rapid-acting
  • high bedtime → increase the supper rapid-acting

The reading tells you which insulin was responsible for the interval that just ended.

lecture: Cases 5-7 - Adjusting Insulin from the Glucose Record
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases" and its facilitator deck. Q42-47. Three patients on insulin: read the record, decide whether to change the regimen and what to change. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]] and [[08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes]].
stem: Patient 6 is a 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a seizure disorder. Her A1c is 6.9%, and her record shows many single-digit readings with occasional highs. What is the concern, and what should be done? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Too tight for her seizure disorder - reduce degludec, loosen the target
Too loose for her age - increase the degludec dose by 20%
Her A1c is ideal, so make no change to her regimen
Stop the insulin entirely and start a sulfonylurea

answer:
The correct answer is A. An A1c of 6.9% is probably too tight given her seizure disorder - hypoglycemia can provoke seizures, and she is already running lots of single-digit values. The occasional high readings are likely corrections or over-corrections of a previous low, not true loss of control.

  • Reduce the Tresiba/degludec by 10-20%.
  • Consider a higher A1c target (e.g. 7.5%), especially if she has no glycemic-responsive (eye, kidney, nerve) complications.

The notes qualify this by whether her seizures are controlled and whether she has eye, renal or neuropathic complications.

stem: Patient 7 is an 81-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, advanced dementia, living in a nursing home with caregiver-administered insulin. His A1c is 9.1% and most readings sit above the 4.0-7.0 mmol/L ac-meal target. What insulin adjustment is recommended? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Increase the basal insulin by 20%
Add rapid-acting insulin at every meal
None
Stop insulin altogether

answer:
The correct answer is C, none. His glucoses are high relative to the ac-meal targets needed to reach an A1c of ~7.0% - but given his dementia, older age and limited life expectancy, the glycemic goals of care shift away from preventing structural complications through a lower A1c and toward keeping him free of symptomatic hypo- and hyperglycemia.

This is the case that makes the point: the right answer to "would you change the regimen?" is sometimes no, and tightening control here would buy complication prevention he will not live to benefit from at the cost of hypoglycemia he cannot reliably report.

lecture: Cases 5-7 - Adjusting Insulin from the Glucose Record
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases" and its facilitator deck. Q42-47. Three patients on insulin: read the record, decide whether to change the regimen and what to change. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]] and [[08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes]].
stem: What determines the glycemic target in an older adult? (originally an open-ended discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Chronological age alone
Functional status and life expectancy
Duration of diabetes alone
Body mass index

answer:
The correct answer is B, functional status and life expectancy - not age. As frailty increases, targets loosen to reduce hypoglycemia risk.

StatusA1c targetIdea
Functionally independent≤7.0%treat like a younger adult
Functionally dependent<8.0%some relaxation of target
Frail / dementia<8.5%prioritise avoiding hypoglycemia
End of lifeno A1c targetavoid symptomatic hyper- and any hypoglycemia

The exact numbers are not the point - the concept is that the frailer or more dependent the patient, the looser the target, because the harm of hypoglycemia starts to outweigh the benefit of tight control. This is exactly why no adjustment was recommended for Patient 7.

lectureMeta: Q59, the case posed in the `Diabetes Pathophysiology T1DM` slide deck. **Keyed** - the deck reveals the answer by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded, but gives no written rationale, so the explanation is reasoned from [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]]. Previously banked as a module concept check; moved here because it is a patient case.
stem: You are seeing a 10 year old with a sibling with T1DM. He has anti-GAD and anti-insulin antibody positivity. His fasting glucose is 6.5 mmol/L. He is at which stage of developing T1DM?

options.html: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4

answer:
The correct answer is B. Every stage of T1DM is defined by beta-cell autoimmunity already being present; what separates the stages is the glucose and the symptoms.

  • Stage 1 - autoantibodies with normoglycemia, pre-symptomatic
  • Stage 2 - autoantibodies with dysglycemia, still pre-symptomatic
  • Stage 3 - symptomatic diabetes

His fasting glucose of 6.5 mmol/L sits in the impaired fasting glucose band (6.1-6.9 mmol/L), so he is dysglycemic but not yet diabetic, and he has no symptoms. That is Stage 2. D is a pure distractor - there is no Stage 4.

Worth noticing separately: he carries two antibodies (GAD and insulin). Antibody count, not mere presence, is what carries risk - one antibody leaves him at the ~0.4% background risk, two confers ~25% within 5 years, three ~40%.

lecture: Case - Clarifying the Type of Diabetes (Case Illustration)
lectureMeta: Q60-62, the "Case Illustration" from the `T2DMellitus` deck (Objective 2). **Keyed** - the deck lists five candidate next steps and the lecturer's own commentary on each appears on the following slide, transcribed into the answers below.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 28-year-old, previously well, is found to have a blood glucose of 12 mmol/L. The only symptom is fatigue, and he is on no medications. His mother has type 1 diabetes (DKA at age 6) and his grandfather has type 2 diabetes (diagnosed at 70, on metformin alone).

stem: Why does this patient need a repeat or confirmatory test before the diagnosis is made?

options.html: Because his only symptom is fatigue, so he is effectively asymptomatic
Because a single glucose of 12 mmol/L is below the diagnostic threshold
Because his family history makes the result unreliable
Because A1c must always be measured before a diagnosis can be made

answer:
The correct answer is A. The notes' own comment is "absolutely, get a confirmatory test as he has negligible symptoms of high BGs."

⭐ The rule turns on symptoms, not on the size of the number. A single abnormal glucose is diagnostic only when the patient is symptomatic with polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss. Fatigue alone does not count, so he needs a second abnormal result on a separate day.

B is factually wrong - 12 mmol/L is well above the random threshold of 11.1 mmol/L; it is the absence of symptoms, not the value, that forces the repeat. C confuses risk assessment with diagnosis. D is too absolute: a repeat fasting glucose or an OGTT would serve equally well.

lecture: Case - Clarifying the Type of Diabetes (Case Illustration)
lectureMeta: Q60-62, the "Case Illustration" from the `T2DMellitus` deck (Objective 2). **Keyed** - the deck lists five candidate next steps and the lecturer's own commentary on each appears on the following slide, transcribed into the answers below.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 28-year-old, previously well, is found to have a blood glucose of 12 mmol/L. The only symptom is fatigue, and he is on no medications. His mother has type 1 diabetes (DKA at age 6) and his grandfather has type 2 diabetes (diagnosed at 70, on metformin alone).

stem: You are clarifying which type of diabetes he has. Which of these next steps is not done routinely?

options.html: Ask about his activity level
Ask about recent weight change
Abdominal ultrasound
Repeat the blood glucose, OGTT or A1c

answer:
The correct answer is C. The case's comment: "theoretically he could have pancreatic insufficiency from islet cell destruction from pancreatic Ca. However, that would be quite odd at his age, and with no other symptoms of illness would be unlikely. So, we don't tend to do imaging routinely."

The other three are all endorsed, and each is a discriminating question rather than a general one:

  • Activity level - if he was very active and then stopped, the lost muscle work alone could tip him into the diabetic range, which argues for type 2
  • Recent weight change - gain points to type 2; ⚠ a sudden dramatic loss should raise concern for severe hyperglycemia and incipient type 1
  • Repeat testing - needed to confirm the diagnosis at all, as in Q60

Principle: imaging is not part of working out which type of diabetes someone has.

lecture: Case - Clarifying the Type of Diabetes (Case Illustration)
lectureMeta: Q60-62, the "Case Illustration" from the `T2DMellitus` deck (Objective 2). **Keyed** - the deck lists five candidate next steps and the lecturer's own commentary on each appears on the following slide, transcribed into the answers below.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 28-year-old, previously well, is found to have a blood glucose of 12 mmol/L. The only symptom is fatigue, and he is on no medications. His mother has type 1 diabetes (DKA at age 6) and his grandfather has type 2 diabetes (diagnosed at 70, on metformin alone).

stem: If this patient does have type 2 diabetes, what would his C-peptide and anti-GAD antibodies be expected to show?

options.html: C-peptide high, anti-GAD low
C-peptide low, anti-GAD high
Both high
Both low

answer:
The correct answer is A. The case states it directly: "C-peptide would be high and anti-GAD Ab would be low if type 2 DM."

C-peptide is released with insulin in equal amounts, so it measures endogenous insulin production. In T2DM the pancreas is still secreting - the problem is resistance - so C-peptide is preserved or high. In T1DM the beta cells are destroyed, so C-peptide is low and anti-GAD, the most specific marker, is positive. That makes B the T1DM pattern.

flags.title: Why they are often not ordered
flags.html: The case is candid that this is optional: "sometimes we do these, but usually we just let time and response to medications indicate which type of DM he has… not often necessary, and might incur a cost at the lab as not all tests are covered by OHIP." ⭐ The response to treatment over time is itself a diagnostic test, and a cheaper one.

lecture: Case - Inherited and Intrauterine Risk (Alertness Check)
lectureMeta: Q63-64, the "Alertness Check" scenario from the `T2DMellitus` deck (Objective 4). **Keyed** - the deck poses both questions and prints its own answer under each.

preamble.title: The scenario
preamble.html: The scenario. Your patient's mother had type 1 diabetes during the pregnancy with her, and she was born at 34 weeks following premature rupture of membranes, unrelated to the diabetes.

stem: Is she at increased risk for type 2 diabetes?

options.html: Yes - both the intrauterine glucose exposure and the prematurity raise her risk
Yes, but only because of the prematurity
No - maternal type 1 diabetes carries no type 2 risk for the child
No, provided maternal glycemic control was excellent

answer:
The correct answer is A. The notes: "Yes, technically; she had exposure to higher glucose in the womb (even with excellent maternal control), and premature birth is itself a risk factor for later metabolic dysfunction."

Two independent mechanisms stack here, which is why B is incomplete and D is the trap: ⭐ good maternal control reduces but does not abolish the intrauterine exposure.

This sits inside the notes' wider point that birth weight extremes at both ends - underweight and overweight infants alike - show increased metabolic risk decades later. The intrauterine environment is a T2DM risk factor in its own right, alongside inheritance, lifestyle, obesogenic diet and lower socio-economic status.

preamble.title: The scenario
preamble.html: The scenario. Your patient's mother had type 1 diabetes during the pregnancy with her, and she was born at 34 weeks following premature rupture of membranes, unrelated to the diabetes.

stem: Is she at increased risk for type 1 diabetes?

options.html: Yes - about 3% lifetime risk
Yes - about 25% lifetime risk
Yes - about 50% lifetime risk
No, maternal type 1 diabetes confers no inherited risk

answer:
The correct answer is A. The case: "Yes, slightly, but only about 3% lifetime risk. The inherited risk for Type 1 DM is much lower than for Type 2 DM."

⭐ This is the counterintuitive pairing worth holding. T1DM feels like "the genetic one" because it presents in childhood, but the inherited risk is far lower than for T2DM - monozygotic twin concordance is 50% in T1DM versus 90% in T2DM, and 40% of people with T2DM have an affected parent.

B is roughly the figure for two autoantibodies within 5 years, a different question entirely (see Q59). C is the monozygotic twin concordance, not the offspring risk.

lectureMeta: Q65, the third "POP QUIZ" in the `PreventionofDMComplications 2024` deck. **Keyed** - the deck shows no answer slide but draws a **green highlight box** around the correct options in place. Previously banked as a module concept check; moved here because it is a patient case.
stem: A 31-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes for 20 years presents to your clinic. She has persistent microalbuminuria and does not wish to conceive. Which of the following medications to prevent diabetes complications would you suggest to her? (originally a check-all-that-apply poll over four drugs; rewritten as an MCQ over complete sets)

options.html: An ACE inhibitor only
Rosuvastatin only
Rosuvastatin and an ACE inhibitor
ASA 81 mg and an ACE inhibitor

answer:
The correct answer is C. ⭐ The case highlights both option 3 and option 4 - she needs a statin and an ACE inhibitor, and picking either alone is a half-answer.

Why the ACEi: persistent microalbuminuria is diabetic nephropathy, and ACEi (or an ARB) is given for nephropathy even in a normotensive patient - the indication is renal protection, not blood pressure. The detail that she does not wish to conceive is not scene-setting: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic, so the stem is clearing the one contraindication that would otherwise block it.

Why the statin: the lecture's own criteria are age ≥ 30 AND diabetes > 15 years. She is 31 with 20 years of diabetes, so she qualifies on both counts.

A is wrong on type - metformin is not a T1DM drug and does nothing for microalbuminuria - and ASA is not given for primary prevention in a 31-year-old without established cardiovascular disease, which rules out D.

lectureMeta: Q66-68, the worked "Mr. X" case that closes the `PreventionofDMComplications 2024` deck. **Keyed** - the deck poses no question but walks the case through three slides (at diagnosis, first-line medication, and follow-up over the years), and the answers are taken from those. **Originally a worked case with no posed question**; each slide is rewritten as an MCQ.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Mr. X is a 30-year-old man just diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. BMI 35, blood glucose 15 mmol/L, A1c 14%, normal creatinine, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 10 mmol/L.

stem: Mr. X has just been diagnosed. Which set of referrals and actions should follow at diagnosis?

options.html: Dietitian, diabetes nurse and optometry, with bloodwork every 3 months
A dietitian referral only, with annual bloodwork thereafter
Immediate referral to both nephrology and cardiology
Nothing until the diagnosis is confirmed on a second sample

answer:
The correct answer is A. The case's at-diagnosis bundle:

  • Dietitian - low fat, high fibre, portion control
  • Diabetes education nurse - what diabetes is, how to test, how to manage a low, how to manage sick days
  • Optometrist - and note the patient can self-refer
  • Aim for very good glucose control in the next few months
  • A1c every ~3 months, with lipids and renal function
  • Check BP, and if not < 130/80, get him monitoring at the pharmacy or at home

⭐ Prevention starts at diagnosis, not at the first complication, and most of it is education and allied health rather than drugs. C inverts that - he has normal creatinine and no cardiac disease, so specialist referral is not indicated. D misapplies the confirmation rule: with a glucose of 15 and an A1c of 14%, the diagnosis is not in doubt.

lecture: Case - Preventing Complications from Diagnosis (Mr. X)
lectureMeta: Q66-68, the worked "Mr. X" case that closes the `PreventionofDMComplications 2024` deck. **Keyed** - the deck poses no question but walks the case through three slides (at diagnosis, first-line medication, and follow-up over the years), and the answers are taken from those. **Originally a worked case with no posed question**; each slide is rewritten as an MCQ.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Mr. X is a 30-year-old man just diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. BMI 35, blood glucose 15 mmol/L, A1c 14%, normal creatinine, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 10 mmol/L.

stem: What determines whether Mr. X starts on insulin rather than metformin?

options.html: Whether he is very symptomatic - thirst, polyuria, weight loss
His body mass index and waist circumference at diagnosis
His A1c value considered entirely on its own
Whether he has already failed a trial of lifestyle measures

answer:
The correct answer is A. The case is explicit: insulin if very symptomatic (very thirsty, polyuria, yeast infections, weight loss, malaise); if not very symptomatic, and with no concern about liver or renal impairment, metformin is the usual first medication.

⭐ The trigger is the symptom burden, not the number. An A1c of 14% is alarming, but it is how he feels that decides whether he needs insulin now, which is why C is wrong.

The reassurance worth knowing: patients ask whether insulin can ever be stopped, and ⭐ the answer is potentially yes, depending on the glucose response. Starting insulin is not a life sentence in T2DM.

lectureMeta: Q66-68, the worked "Mr. X" case that closes the `PreventionofDMComplications 2024` deck. **Keyed** - the deck poses no question but walks the case through three slides (at diagnosis, first-line medication, and follow-up over the years), and the answers are taken from those. **Originally a worked case with no posed question**; each slide is rewritten as an MCQ.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Mr. X is a 30-year-old man just diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. BMI 35, blood glucose 15 mmol/L, A1c 14%, normal creatinine, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 10 mmol/L.

stem: Mr. X is now some years into treatment and attending regular visits. What should you both expect over that time?

options.html: That his medication needs will likely increase over time
That once at target, he can be reviewed once a year
That medication can be steadily withdrawn as his weight falls
That his A1c target should be tightened with each year

answer:
The correct answer is A. Every 3-4 months: a weight check with encouragement of any weight loss, and a review of his home glucose record to reinforce the goals. And explicitly: ⭐ "he and you would not be surprised if BG control medication needs to be increased with time."

This is the progressive-disease point. T2DM involves ongoing beta-cell decline, so needing more medication is the expected course, not a failure - by the patient or by you. Framing it that way in advance is what stops escalation being heard as blame.

C is the mirror-image error; weight loss can genuinely reduce requirements, but it is not the expectation to set. D contradicts individualised targets, which loosen rather than tighten as complexity and frailty accumulate.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Gurdeep Sidhu is a 55 year old female new to your family practice, presenting with blurry vision. She has not seen a doctor in over a decade. Social history - born and raised in India, came to Canada in her teens; divorced three years, under much stress; finds it difficult to discuss her weight, as her husband would often make fun of her size; a history of bullying and obesity in childhood; lives with her two daughters; a former hairdresser, on ODSP since a back injury eight years ago; high school education, speaks English and Punjabi; does not smoke or drink. Medical history - two C-sections, both infants large for gestational age (daughters now 11 and 15), chronic lower back pain, cholecystectomy at 42, remote tonsillectomy. HPI - three months of blurry vision, no eye exam in decades, straining to read, intermittently worse, both eyes equally, no diplopia; occasional throbbing headaches at the vertex relieved by acetaminophen. On review of systems - thirsty and drinking more, urinating more frequency, no dysuria, intermittent vaginal itching and white discharge; last period at 54, still some hot flashes, menarche 13 with lifelong irregular periods, maybe three a year; a year of fatigue; no chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, presyncope or syncope; burning at the bottom of both feet, worse at night; poor diet, usually fast food, sedentary. Medications - curcumin and niacin supplements. Family history - both parents with high blood pressure and high cholesterol; father had an MI at 64.

stem: Based on the limited information you have, what issues have you identified?

options.html: An isolated ophthalmological problem, given that her vision is the complaint
Undiagnosed hyperglycemia, with symptoms suggesting complications already
Perimenopausal symptoms accounting for the fatigue, sweats and the thirst
A primary anxiety disorder, given the stress, fatigue and somatic symptoms

answer:
B. ⭐ Three separate threads in the history all converge on one diagnosis, which is what makes this a problem list rather than a complaint:

ThreadWhat she reportsPoints to
⭐ Osmotic symptomsthirst, drinking more, urinating morehyperglycemia
⭐ Already-complicated disease3 months of blurry vision, ⭐ burning feet worse at night⚠ retinopathy and neuropathy BEFORE diagnosis
Permissive infectionintermittent vaginal itching and white dischargeglycosuria

⭐ Her risk profile was in place long before today. The lecture names South Asian populations and ⭐ women with previous GDM as at particular risk - and ⚠ two infants large for gestational age is a GDM history she was never told she had. Add obesity, a sedentary lifestyle, poor diet and a family history.

⚠ The social history is a clinical finding, not background. ODSP, stress, a decade without a physician, weight discussed with shame and a language other than English at home are each barriers to the follow-up this diagnosis is about to require.

A takes the presenting complaint as the whole problem. C is real - she is post-menopausal - but ⚠ hot flashes do not cause polyuria, burning feet or blurry vision. D explains nothing on the list.

Social history - born and raised in India, came to Canada in her teens; divorced three years, under much stress; finds it difficult to discuss her weight, as her husband would often make fun of her size; a history of bullying and obesity in childhood; lives with her two daughters; a former hairdresser, on ODSP since a back injury eight years ago; high school education, speaks English and Punjabi; does not smoke or drink. Medical history - two C-sections, both infants large for gestational age (daughters now 11 and 15), chronic lower back pain, cholecystectomy at 42, remote tonsillectomy. Medications - curcumin and niacin supplements. Family history - both parents with high blood pressure and high cholesterol; father had an MI at 64.

stem: What differential diagnosis (DDx) are you considering?

options.html: Type 2 diabetes foremost, with other causes of polyuria and polydipsia
Diabetes insipidus foremost, since polyuria and polydipsia dominate here
Primary polydipsia foremost, driven by the stress she describes at home
A pituitary macroadenoma foremost, given the headaches and the vision

answer:
A. ⭐ The question asks what you are considering, not what you have concluded - so the answer is a ranked list, with T2DM at the top on probability:

Cause of polyuria + polydipsiaAgainst it here
⭐ T2DM⭐ nothing - every risk factor and symptom fits
DI⚠ does not cause vaginal candidiasis or burning feet
hypercalcemiapossible; needs a calcium
hyperthyroidism⚠ thyroid exam is pending; no tremor or palpitations reported
UTIno dysuria
Primary polydipsiaa diagnosis of exclusion

⭐ Blurry vision has its own short differential, and they are not the same answer: osmotic refractive change from hyperglycemia (which reverses as glucose falls), ⭐ diabetic retinopathy with macular edema, cataracts, and uncorrected presbyopia at 55 - and ⚠ the last of these is genuinely likely in a woman who has not had an eye exam in decades.

⭐ Keeping presbyopia on the list matters - it is the one cause here that a pair of reading glasses fixes, and missing it is as much an error as missing the retinopathy.

B, C and D each promote one possibility over the one the whole history points at.

lectureMeta: Q125-127, continuing the same case. Stems verbatim. ⚠ **Reasoned, not keyed.** Q126 is a written exercise rather than a multiple-choice question, and is banked in that form.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Examination findings. Temperature 37.5 °C, pulse 83 regular, ⭐ blood pressure 170/89, SaO₂ 100% on room air, in no acute distress. ⭐ BMI 35, waist circumference 89 cm. Head and neck - moist mucous membranes; thyroid not enlarged, soft, mobile, non-tender, no palpable nodules; no cervical lymphadenopathy. ⭐ Fundoscopy - no papilledema, the macula is poorly visualized, and several cotton wool spots are seen. CVS - normal S1 and S2, no murmurs or rubs, JVP 4 cm above the sternal angle, peripheral pulses palpable. Resp - chest clear. Abdomen - obese, soft, non-tender, normal bowel sounds, no organomegaly. Extremities unremarkable; skin dry, no rashes/esions, no nail changes. Neuro - cranial nerves unremarkable except ⭐ visual acuity 20/30 bilaterally; full extraocular movements without diplopia; normal power and tone; ⭐ reflexes 2+ throughout EXCEPT zero at both ankles; ⭐ vibration absent at the great toes, present at the MTP joints.

stem: Does the above information expand or refine your DDx?

options.html: It expands it, since cotton wool spots point away from a diabetic cause
Neither, since the examination findings are essentially unremarkable here
It refines it, confirming complications and adding untreated hypertension
It refines it toward a pituitary lesion, given the visual acuity reduction

answer:
C. ⭐ It refines rather than expands - the exam removes alternatives and stages the disease rather than opening new possibilities:

FindingWhat it settles
⭐ Cotton wool spots⭐ retinal infarcts = PRE-PROLIFERATIVE diabetic retinopathy - the lecture's stage ②
Macula poorly visualized, VA 20/30possible macular edema, which ⭐ is what changes vision
⭐ Absent ankle reflexes, absent vibration at the toes⭐ peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy, ⚠ glove and stocking, feet before hands because longer nerves conduct proportionally slower
⭐ BP 170/89⚠ a NEW diagnosis of hypertension
BMI 35obesity confirmed
Thyroid normal, no dysuriahyperthyroidism and UTI drop off the list

⚠ The one genuine expansion is the blood pressure, and it matters more than it looks: ⭐ in T2DM it is blood pressure control, not glycemic control, that buys the macrovascular benefit. Glycemic control moves the microvascular complications only.

⚠ A is worth reasoning through rather than dismissing. ⭐ Cotton wool spots are not specific to diabetes - they appear in hypertensive retinopathy too, and she has a BP of 170/89. But they are a recognised feature of pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, so they confirm a diabetic cause rather than pointing away from one; the honest reading is that both of her new diagnoses can produce them, and ⚠ that is a question worth raising in the session.

B overlooks a blood pressure of 170/89 and two absent reflexes. D - ⚠ her acuity is 20/30 with full eye movements and no field defect described, which does not describe a chiasmal lesion.

Neuro - cranial nerves unremarkable except ⭐ visual acuity 20/30 bilaterally; full extraocular movements without diplopia; normal power and tone; ⭐ reflexes 2+ throughout EXCEPT zero at both ankles; ⭐ vibration absent at the great toes, present at the MTP joints.

stem: What investigations would you like to order and why?

options.html: An oral glucose tolerance test alone, as the most definitive single test
A1c and glucose to diagnose, then lipids, renal function and an ACR
A CT head and formal visual fields, given the headaches and the vision
A random glucose alone, which is sufficient if it is clearly elevated

answer:
B. ⭐ The investigations split into three jobs, and the "why" in the stem is asking you to say which is which:

① Establish the diagnosis. ⭐ Any ONE of these makes it, confirmed on a second occasion unless she is symptomatic with unequivocal hyperglycemia:

TestDiabetes
⭐ FPG⭐ ≥ 7.0 mmol/L
2h 75 g OGTT or RPG≥ 11.1 mmol/L
⭐ HbA1c⭐ ≥ 6.5%

② Stage the complications she already appears to have - ⭐ and she is the reason this cannot wait: creatinine and eGFR, an ⭐ albumin-to-creatinine ratio (⚠ diabetic nephropathy is preceded by microalbuminuria at 30-299 mg/24 h, and ⭐ ACE inhibitors or ARBs are given even WITHOUT hypertension), and a ⭐ referral for a dilated eye exam - annual ophthalmology screening is the standard, and she needs one now.

③ Address the cardiovascular risk the exam uncovered: a ⭐ fasting lipid panel and an ECG, with her BP of 170/89 and a father who had an MI at 64.

⚠ A and D each name a real diagnostic test and stop there, leaving the retinopathy, the neuropathy, the kidneys and the lipids uninvestigated - ⭐ which is the actual error the question is testing. C investigates a lesion the examination argues against.

⭐ A TSH and a B12 are defensible additions - the first because her fatigue is unexplained, the second as a neuropathy baseline before metformin is started.

stem: You have just diagnosed a 24-year-old female patient with hyperthyroidism likely due to Graves' disease. You are discussing anti-thyroid therapy options in your office and she tells you the following pertinent information: she does not want surgery for cosmetic reasons; she does not want radiation therapy; and she is currently on a combined oral contraceptive pill. Which of the following anti-thyroid therapies will you recommend?

options.html: Methimazole
Propylthiouracil
Lithium
Radioactive iodine (I131)
Iodine supplementation
Thyroidectomy

answer:
The correct answer is B. Patient preference matters: surgery and radiation are appropriate treatments in general but are ruled out by this patient's wishes, leaving the two thioamides, methimazole and propylthiouracil. She is a woman of childbearing age on an OCP, so the workbook's reasoning is that PTU is safe in pregnancy should she conceive or stop the OCP - though it notes methimazole is more effective.

Iodine supplementation can have a transient anti-thyroid effect (Wolff-Chaikoff) but this is not sustained and is inappropriate here. Lithium has anti-thyroid properties but is not used to treat hyperthyroidism.

stem: Which of the following stages of thyroid gland development has the greatest clinical consequence?

options.html: Development starts at the foramen cecum, where the anterior 2/3 of the tongue meets the posterior 1/3
The developing gland travels through the tongue and anterior neck
As the gland travels, it may move through the hyoid bone, creating a space
As the gland grows in size, neural tissue becomes embedded in the gland
The gland may not develop properly, resulting in an agenic, ectopic or hypoplastic gland

answer:
The correct answer is E. The gland's development follows an interesting course (literally): it starts in the tongue at the foramen cecum and moves through the anterior neck - occasionally passing through the hyoid bone - to end up in the anterior neck, with neural tissue embedded within it that will later produce calcitonin.

Two clinical consequences to weigh:

  1. During its passage, the gland leaves behind a tract that can form a thyroglossal duct cyst; if a cyst forms, the entire tract must be removed.
  2. If the gland does not develop, or the individual has an ectopic thyroid, this causes congenital hypothyroidism - and abnormal thyroid gland development is the leading cause of CH in areas with adequate iodine. This is the greater consequence, hence E.

stem: You are seeing a patient for follow-up. Her hypothyroidism is currently being treated with levothyroxine, and she has done well over the past year. At this visit, she tells you that she is pleased to have lost 10lbs in 1 month, has a large appetite, but that she still feels fatigued. On physical exam, her skin is moist, her BP is higher than usual, her HR is 90 and regular, and she has a fine tremor of the hands. You are concerned that these are symptoms of hyperthyroidism. When you review her blood work, you find high free T3, low TSH, and high anti-TPO antibody titres. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's presentation:

options.html: The patient has increased the amount of medication she is taking
The dose of medication is appropriate but the patient may need some time to adjust
The dose of medication you have prescribed is too high
The patient has Graves' disease
The patient has Hashimoto's disease

answer:
The correct answer is E. Three pieces of information settle the etiology:

  1. Low TSH - confirms she is hyperthyroid.
  2. High free T3 - indicates the cause is NOT excessive levothyroxine (which is T4) but an endogenous source.
  3. High anti-TPO titres - with the known hypothyroidism, points to Hashimoto's thyroiditis as the etiology of both the hypo- and the hyperthyroidism. Hashimoto's can cause an acute thyroid hormone storm by damaging the gland and releasing preformed hormone.

Had the labs shown low free T4, that would point instead to overdose/overmedication as the cause.

stem: Which of the following is UNTRUE about Hashimoto's thyroiditis?

options.html: Patients with this condition will require supplementation with thyroid hormone
This is an autoimmune disorder with antibodies against TPO or thyroglobulin being the most common
This disorder results in the destruction of the thyroid gland by B cells
Hurthle cells are a pathologic finding
This disorder results in destruction of the thyroid gland by T cells

answer: The correct answer is C. Destruction is T cell-mediated, not B cell-mediated. Hashimoto's is a cause of hypothyroidism in which the body produces antibodies against thyroid components - namely TPO or thyroglobulin. Unlike Graves', these antibodies are not stimulatory; instead they signal T cell-mediated destruction of the gland. Pathologic features: lymphoid aggregates, Hurthle cells (follicular cells with increased pink cytoplasm) and fibrosis.

stem: Which of the statement/s is/are true regarding abnormalities of the endocrine system (could be multiple correct answers)?

options.html: An ACTH stimulation is used to screen for suspected Cushing’s syndrome
The most common cause of glucocorticoid excess is iatrogenic
The most common cause of thyrotoxicosis is iatrogenic
Hyperpigmentation and vitiligo are common presentations of Con’s disease

answer: The correct answer is B, C. A is false because ACTH stimulation is used to screen for suspected adrenal failure. D is false because hyperpigmentation and vitiligo are common presentations of Addison’s disease (primary adrenal insufficiency).

stem: The prescription of ergocalciferol should be avoided or prescribed with caution in which of the following patient/s (could be multiple correct answers)?

options.html: A patient with hyperparathyroidism due to renal insufficiency
A patient taking thiazide diuretics
A patient taking furosemide
A patient with hyperphosphatemia

answer: The correct answer is A, B, D. Furosemide promotes calcium excretion, thus it is helpful in preventing hypercalcemia when taking vitamin D. Ergocalciferol requires both hepatic and renal metabolism to become the active calcitriol. A patient with renal insufficiency can convert ergocalciferol into calcifediol (hepatic), but can’t effectively convert calcifediol into calcitriol (renal). Thiazide increases calcium reabsorption, thus it should be taken with caution in conjunction with vitamin D to prevent hypercalcemia. Vitamin D increases both calcium and phosphate absorption, thus can worsen hypophosphatemia.

stem: Which of the following warrant consideration of pharmacotherapy for osteoporosis in patients with moderate risk of fractures (could be multiple possible answers)?

options.html: Recurrent falls
Parental history of vertebral fractures
Aromatase therapy for breast cancer
Smoking
Androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer

answer:
The correct answer is A, C, E.

The key discriminator is whether the factor is already counted inside FRAX/CAROC. Osteoporosis Canada's moderate-risk "consider treatment" factors are the ones the calculators miss:

  • recurrent falls (A)
  • aromatase-inhibitor therapy (C) and androgen-deprivation therapy (E), which both cause rapid hypogonadal bone loss
  • vertebral fracture on imaging, and long-term glucocorticoids
  • B fails because parental fracture history is already an input to FRAX, so it has been counted once and should not push the patient up a second time. The standard FRAX input is also parental hip fracture, not vertebral.
  • D fails for the same reason: current smoking is a FRAX input.

Follicular cells in females produce hormones that upregulate the secretion of FSH
Seminiferous cells in males produce hormones that downregulate the secretion of FSH
The mechanism is not currently known

answer: The correct answer is C. Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules produce inhibin, which downregulates FSH, as LH is the main hormone of spermatogenesis.

stem: Which of the following is correct regarding oocyte development

options.html: The oocyte undergoes both mitosis and meiosis in a women of reproductive age
There is an even division of DNA and cellular content upon completion of meiosis I
Following ovulation, the oocyte rests in metaphase of meiosis I and transits through the fallopian tube, awaiting fertilization.
Nondisjunction in oocytes can occur upon fertilization with a sperm.

answer: The correct answer is D. Upon fertilization, the oocyte undergoes completion of meiosis II, where nondisjunction can occur. Oocytes only undergo mitosis during gestation, women are born with a set number of oocytes. There is an even division of DNA with meiosis I, but the first polar body contains very little oocyte cytoplasm. Following ovulation, the oocyte rests in metaphase of meiosis II.

stem: A patient comes to you with a problem. She has been tired, unable to concentrate, has put on a little weight, has a little trouble swallowing and feels like her neck is swollen. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms and the easiest solution to her problem?

options.html: These are classic symptoms of hypothyroidism. You suggest she be put on thyroid hormone therapy.
These are classic symptoms of hyperthyroidism and she should decrease her salt intake.

These are classic symptoms of hypothyroidism, most likely due to a lack of thyroid stimulating hormone secretion from the anterior pituitary. She should have a head/neck CT scan and follow-up with her doctor.

These are classic symptoms of hypothyroidism, most likely due to to thyroid hormone levels. Since she shows signs of a goiter, she should increase her intake of iodine and see if the symptoms disappear.

answer: The correct answer is D. This is a tricky question! The key to the answer was to realize what is the easiest solution (from a medical standpoint) for her problem. While this is definitely a case of hypothyroidism, answer A is incorrect as it would be premature to put the patient on thyroid hormone replacement therapy, without first trying to naturally boost T3/T4 production with increased dietary intake of salt (iodine). Answer C is also too drastic and premature. Therefore, Answer D is correct.

flags.title: Option D is garbled in the module

stem: A patient with hypocalcemia is prescribed a vitamin D supplement. They inquire about the effects of vitamin D on their bone health. How would you counsel the patient?

options.html: Since their serum calcium is currently low, vitamin D will promote bone resorption.
Since their serum calcium is currently low, vitamin D will promote bone formation.
Vitamin D will promote bone resorption regardless of their serum calcium levels.
Vitamin D will promote bone formation regardless of their serum calcium levels.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 01 - Thyroid and Parathyroid Gland Physiology and 02 - Drugs Affecting Calcium Homeostasis. Vitamin D's effect on bone flips with the serum calcium. When calcium is low, calcitriol drives osteoclastic resorption to release calcium into the blood, alongside ↑ gut absorption. Only when calcium is high does it favor mineralization by osteoblasts. This patient is hypocalcemic, so in the short term vitamin D will pull calcium out of bone.

  • B gets the direction backwards: formation and mineralization is the high-calcium response.
  • C, D fail on "regardless". The whole point is that the effect depends on the calcium level, and the notes flag "resorption regardless" as a classic trap.

stem: All of the following could possibly present in a patient with hypothyroidism except:

options.html: Decreased basal metabolic activity
Excessive lipolysis, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis
Defect in early neural development
Respiratory disorders concerning the lungs

answer: The correct answer is B. A lack of thyroid hormones will decrease lipolysis, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. Thyroid hormones are necessary for maintaining basal metabolic activity, permissive to GH action and necessary for induction of surfactant.

stem: The calcium-sensing receptors on the parathyroid chief cells stop detecting calcium. What would be a consequence?

options.html: Decreased levels of parathyroid hormones despite normal or low calcium levels.
Desensitization of parathyroid hormone receptors in the intestines.
Increased calcium absorption in the intestines despite normal or low calcium levels
Increased calcium reabsorption in the kidneys despite normal or high calcium levels.

answer: The correct answer is D. The chief cells are responsible for responding to high levels of calcium by shutting down parathyroid hormone release. If the chief cells malfunction, they will fail to detect hypercalcemia and the parathyroid hormone levels will remain high, which induces the kidneys to reabsorb even more calcium.

flags.title: Stem reworded
flags.html: The HippoNotes stem said "malfunctioning chief cells", which could mean cells that cannot sense calcium (D) or cells that cannot make PTH (A). It now says the calcium-sensing receptor is what fails. Readers reported this.

lecture: Case - Growth Failure in Hashimoto's Disease (Thyroid Physiology)
lectureMeta: Q69, the case illustration on the Hashimoto's slide of the `Thyroid Part 2 2023` deck. **Reasoned, not keyed** - the deck presents the case as an illustration and poses no question, so the stem and the answer are both written here, from [[01 - Thyroid and Parathyroid Gland Physiology]], which carries the same case.
stem: An 8-year-old with Hashimoto's disease is 3'6" with an immature body phenotype. One year after starting thyroid hormone replacement he is 4' tall with a normal body phenotype. What best explains the change? (originally a one-line case illustration with no question posed; written up as an MCQ)

options.html: Thyroid hormone is permissive to growth hormone action, so replacing it restored growth that had been arrested
Levothyroxine directly stimulates the epiphyseal growth plate independently of growth hormone
The anti-TPO antibodies were suppressing growth hormone secretion directly
The growth was unrelated to treatment and reflects normal pubertal timing

answer:
A. In Hashimoto's disease, anti-TPO antibodies block the iodination of thyroglobulin, so T3 and T4 cannot be made and the child becomes hypothyroid.

Thyroid hormone is required for growth hormone secretion and permissive to its action. Without it, GH cannot drive linear growth however much is present, so growth arrests and skeletal maturation is delayed - hence the immature body phenotype at 3'6". Replace the T4 and the permissive signal returns: ⭐ six inches in a single year is catch-up growth, and the phenotype normalises with it.

The teaching point is recoverability. Untreated childhood hypothyroidism stunts linear growth and delays development, and ⭐ both are largely recoverable once T4 is replaced - which is what makes the delay worth catching.

B inverts the mechanism: the effect is permissive, exerted through GH, not a direct action on the plate. C invents an antibody target - anti-TPO acts on the thyroid, not the pituitary. D is ruled out by the timing and by an 8-year-old being pre-pubertal.

flags.title: Contrast this with congenital hypothyroidism
flags.html: Here the neurological outcome is intact because the deficiency began after early neural development. In maternal or congenital deficiency the same hormone is missing during neural development itself, and that damage is not recoverable - which is why maternal iodine deficiency is the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide. Same hormone, same deficiency, different window, different reversibility.

lectureMeta: Source: both of this lecture's slide decks - `ThyroidGlandPathology_slides_nv` (Q86) and `Clinical Presentation Investigation of Thyroid Masses` (Q87-89), 4 questions. **All keyed and all carrying the lecturer's own written rationale**, transcribed here. stem: A patient of yours tells you that her sister recently underwent a hemithyroidectomy and was diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma. She asks you what the prognosis is. You tell her:

options.html: That it is a benign tumour and she should be cured
That it is an aggressive tumour with a poor prognosis
That it is malignant and generally has a very good prognosis
That it is malignant and generally has a very good prognosis if a completion thyroidectomy and lymph node dissection are done
That it is malignant and generally has a very good prognosis if radioactive iodine therapy is given

answer:
The correct answer is C. The session's own annotation: “Correct - can't say more about management as don't have details of report.”

  • A - “PTC is a malignant neoplasm; adenoma is a benign neoplasm.”
  • B - “PTC generally behaves indolently; anaplastic ca has a poor prognosis.”
  • D and E ⭐ attach a condition to the prognosis that you have no basis to state. They are not wrong that those treatments exist; they are wrong because ⭐ you do not have the pathology report, and the report is what decides whether completion thyroidectomy, nodal dissection or RAI is indicated at all.

The numbers behind C: PTC is the most common primary thyroid malignancy (85-90%) with 93% 10-year survival.

⭐ The teaching point is as much communication as pathology: give the prognosis you can support, and do not promise a management plan before the report is in.

stem: Akio has a 2 cm palpable enlarging thyroid nodule. TSH is normal. He has a family history of thyroid cancer in his father. Your next steps will be:

options.html: Re-examine in 2 months
Needle core biopsy
Ultrasound of nodule
Surgical removal
CT scan of neck

answer:
The correct answer is C. Transcribed from the session's explanation.

“This nodule needs investigation given enlargement and family history of cancer. Remember to choose the least invasive and most cost-effective test first for a mass. Ultrasound is an important first step for a thyroid nodule to determine risk of malignancy and need for nodule sampling.”

  • A is ruled out by two risk features already present: ⭐ enlargement and a ⭐ first-degree family history.
  • E - “A CT scan would not be indicated as a first line test here, since thyroid nodule sampling cannot be performed with the CT scan and it is an expensive test.”
  • B - “Needle core biopsy (NCB) is not used to sample neck nodules in general, and especially thyroid nodules. The needle is large bore, and there is a risk of tumour seeding and hematoma. One exception is for lymphoma in a neck lymph node, where NCB is first line sampling in some patients.”
  • D puts surgery before risk stratification, inverting the pathway.

⭐ A normal TSH is what sends you to ultrasound rather than to a radioactive iodine scan - a low TSH would have gone to RAI first.

preamble.title: The case - Akio
preamble.html: The case. Akio has a 2 cm palpable enlarging thyroid nodule. TSH is normal. He has a family history of thyroid cancer in his father.

stem: The imaging report indicates a TI-RADS score of 4. What type of nodule sampling would you choose for Akio?

options.html: Punch biopsy
Incisional biopsy
Fine needle aspiration biopsy
Excisional biopsy
Removal of thyroid

answer:
The correct answer is C. Transcribed from the lecture's explanation.

“For thyroid, which is a vascular organ, FNAB is the preferred biopsy type for sampling a nodule. As well, given the risk of tumour seeding and hematoma formation the large bore needles (needle core biopsy) would be avoided if possible.”

  • B and D - “Incisional biopsies are not performed for thyroid, due to the vascularity of the organ, such that surgery would either be a lobectomy or thyroidectomy.”
  • A - “Punch biopsy is used only for skin related lesions, not for deep lesions under the skin.”
  • E - “FNAB needs to be performed first for risk stratification before any decision about surgery usually.”

⭐ Vascularity is the reason for all of it. It is why a fine needle is right, why a large-bore core needle risks hematoma and seeding, and why there is no such thing as a partial cut into the thyroid.

stem: Kiaria has a 2.7 cm mildly symptomatic thyroid nodule and a normal TSH. The ultrasound report indicates a mixed cyst with a TI-RADS score of 2. You remove clear fluid with a fine needle aspiration biopsy and the cyst disappears. On follow-up the cyst does not reappear. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.html: Abscess
Benign cyst
Papillary carcinoma
Adenoma
Lymphoma

answer:
The correct answer is B. Transcribed from the module's explanation.

“With disappearance of the cyst with aspiration, a not suspicious TIRADs score and no reappearance of the cyst, this is in keeping with a benign cyst.”

  • A - “An abscess is unusual in the thyroid, and the aspirate should reveal pus. The clinical features do not indicate the classic signs of inflammation.” The fluid here was clear.
  • C - “Papillary carcinoma can be cystic, but would show increase in size on follow-up and some solid component.”
  • D - “An adenoma, which can be cystic would not disappear with aspiration in that there would be a solid component left.”
  • E - “Lymphoma is typically firm solid tissue, and not a cyst.”

⭐ Three findings have to line up, and all three are in the stem: clear fluid, complete disappearance, and no recurrence. A surviving solid component is what would have pushed this to C or D.

stem:
Ms. Smith is a 65-year-old lady who is being assessed for osteoporosis. The diagnosis of osteoporosis can be made if:

  1. Her BMD T-score is < −2.5
  2. She has had a skull fracture
  3. She has had a hip fracture as a result of a fall from standing height

options.html: All of the above
1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only

answer:
The correct answer is D. Two of the three statements are diagnostic, and the one that is not is the point of the question.

  • 1 is diagnostic. A T-score ≤ −2.5 makes the diagnosis on its own.
  • 3 is diagnostic. A hip fracture from a fall from standing height is a fragility fracture, and ⭐ a fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis irrespective of the BMD.
  • 2 is not. ⭐ The definition explicitly EXCLUDES fractures of the skull, hands, feet and ankles, and any fracture involving real trauma. A skull fracture tells you nothing about bone quality.

The third route to the diagnosis, not tested here, is a 10-year fracture risk above 20% with no fragility fracture and a T-score above −2.5.

⭐ The exclusion list is the examinable part. “Fragility fracture” is not “any fracture” - those sites are excluded precisely because they break for reasons other than low bone mass.

stem: Mrs. Jones is 65 years old and presents for assessment of osteoporosis. The presence of which of these factors would NOT warrant consideration of pharmacologic therapy?

options.html: History of vertebral fracture
BMD T-score > −2.5
Fracture risk being > 15%
History of hip fracture

answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ A T-score above −2.5 is, on its own, a reason NOT to treat - it is the threshold defining the no-treatment band when nothing else is present.

  • A and D - ⭐ a hip or vertebral fracture is a strong recommendation to treat, and carries more weight still if the fracture was within the last 2 years. A fragility fracture also makes the diagnosis outright, whatever the BMD shows.
  • C - a 10-year risk above 15% puts her at least in the moderate band, where treatment is suggested; above 20% it is recommended.

B is only a reason not to treat in isolation, and that is the trap: Mrs. Jones could have a T-score above −2.5 and still need treatment if she has had a fragility fracture or her calculated risk is high. ⭐ BMD is a surrogate for fracture, not the diagnosis itself, which is exactly why the fracture-based routes to treatment exist alongside it.

stem: Mrs. Davidson was on treatment with denosumab for 5 years, and has recently sustained a hip fracture. She received her injections on time, without any delays or missed treatments. She has no contraindications for any osteoporosis treatments. Which of the following would be the best treatment option for her?

options.html: Continue denosumab
Change to risedronate
Change to raloxifene
Start romosozumab

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Read the stem carefully: she took the drug correctly, on schedule, for 5 years, and fractured her hip anyway. That is ⭐ failure of antiresorptive therapy, one of the three named indications for bone-forming therapy - alongside a recent severe vertebral fracture and more than 2 vertebral fractures with a T-score below −2.5. Adherence is stated explicitly so that you cannot explain the fracture away as a missed dose.

  • A repeats a strategy that has already demonstrably failed in this patient.
  • B swaps one antiresorptive for another, which does not change the class that failed.
  • C is the worst option here: ⭐ raloxifene has no hip fracture data at all. It covers the spine only, so it is the wrong drug in a patient whose problem is a hip.
  • D moves her to an anabolic agent, and ⭐ romosozumab is the anabolic with hip fracture benefit (versus alendronate) - whereas teriparatide has no hip data either.

One thing not to forget after choosing D: ⭐ anabolic therapy must be followed by an antiresorptive, after 1 year for romosozumab. Also worth weighing first: romosozumab carries a cardiovascular signal (MI, stroke, death), and stopping denosumab without a follow-on antiresorptive risks rapid bone loss.

stem: Mrs. Smith is a 65-year-old lady who was on alendronate treatment for 10 years. She had aching pain in her thigh for 6 months and sustained an atypical femoral fracture as a result of no trauma, which required surgical repair. Her fracture risk remains high over the next 10 years. Her alendronate has been stopped. Which among these would be used for treatment of osteoporosis?

options.html: Denosumab
Risedronate
Teriparatide
Zoledronate

answer:
The correct answer is C.

She has had an atypical femoral fracture on long-term alendronate. ⭐ AFF is an adverse effect of BOTH the bisphosphonates AND denosumab, so every antiresorptive on this list is off the table:

  • B and D are more bisphosphonates - the same class that caused it, and bisphosphonates stay bound in bone, so the risk does not reset when you switch within the class.
  • A is a different class but shares the AFF risk.
  • C is anabolic, does not carry the AFF risk, and her fracture risk remains high, so she cannot be left on nothing.

⭐ The 6 months of aching thigh pain was the warning sign, present in 70% of AFF patients, and it is why that complaint in anyone on long-term therapy is taken seriously rather than treated as arthritis.

Also relevant: ⭐ teriparatide is not associated with ONJ and may even help treat it. Its own limits are no hip fracture data, it must be followed by an antiresorptive after 2 years, and it is contraindicated in hypercalcemia, eGFR under 30, and metabolic bone disease.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

  • ⭐ Zoledronate is the treatment, and IV zoledronate is better than an oral bisphosphonate in Paget's - which is what puts it ahead of B.
  • ⭐ A is actively contraindicated. Bone-forming agents must not be used in Paget's, because the disease already is disordered bone formation: increased osteoclastic resorption, followed by osteoblasts laying down structurally abnormal, fragile bone. Stimulating that further is the opposite of the goal.
  • D - denosumab has not been studied in Paget's.
  • Calcitonin is a real option the lecture lists, but it loses effectiveness after a few treatments, so it belongs early and only for pain.

The raised ALP is why this patient is treated at all. ⭐ Even an asymptomatic patient is treated when there is evidence of active disease - a raised ALP or scintigraphy showing active lesions - plus disease in the skull, long bones, spine, or bone abutting a joint. A femur is a long bone, so he qualifies on both counts.

The other two treatment triggers: ⭐ a surgical procedure planned in a pagetic site (the lesions are vascular and can hemorrhage) and ⭐ coexisting congestive heart failure, which Paget's vascularity can worsen. ALP also doubles as the monitoring marker on treatment.

stem: A 17-year-old woman with a history of osteogenesis imperfecta type 1 presents for a routine annual evaluation. She has had 5 fractures of various long bones in the last year, without any atypical fractures and without trauma. She is having regular menstrual periods and has normal vitamin D levels. What is the most appropriate treatment for her?

options.html: Teriparatide
Denosumab
Raloxifene
Zoledronate

answer:
The correct answer is D. ⭐ IV bisphosphonates are the mainstay of treatment for osteogenesis imperfecta, and zoledronate is the IV bisphosphonate.

She meets the criteria to be treated: the indications are long bone deformities, vertebral compression fractures, or ⭐ more than 3 fractures per year - and she has had 5.

The stem's negatives are doing deliberate work, ruling out the alternative explanations for fractures at her age:

  • no atypical fractures and no trauma - not drug-induced AFF, not simple injury
  • regular menstrual periods - not hypoestrogenic bone loss, which also removes the rationale for C
  • normal vitamin D - not osteomalacia on top of the OI

A is anabolic but is not the established treatment in OI, and the underlying defect is qualitative, not quantitative: ⭐ OI is a lack of, or poorly formed, type I collagen (COL1A1 and COL1A2, 85-90% of cases), so building more of the same defective matrix is not the fix. B is not the mainstay either.

The optimal duration of bisphosphonate therapy in OI has not been studied. Her type 1 disease carries a normal life span - type 2 is lethal in the perinatal period.

lecture: Case - The Worked Thyroid Nodule (Pathology of Thyroid Masses)
lectureMeta: Source: the worked case opening the `ThyroidGlandPathology_slides_nv` deck. **Reasoned, not keyed** - the deck walks the case through the diagnostic pathway to show what an appropriate workup looks like and poses no question, so the stem and the answer are both written from [[05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses]]. Banked as a case rather than a concept check because a patient is presented and reasoned through.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 42-year-old female with no risk factors and no family history has a lump in her neck, present and slowly enlarging over 6 months, causing some difficulty swallowing. She reports no symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. On examination there is a solitary, firm but not hard, 2-3 cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe, with no neck adenopathy and no signs of thyrotoxicosis. TSH is normal. Ultrasound confirms a solitary 3.2 cm nodule, TI-RADS 3. FNA is satisfactory and returns FLUS (follicular lesion of undetermined significance). After discussion she elected to undergo a hemithyroidectomy.

stem: Her ultrasound is low-risk (TI-RADS 3) and her cytology is FLUS. On the risk-adapted pathway, what makes hemithyroidectomy a defensible choice here rather than simple surveillance? (originally a worked case illustration with no question posed; written up as an MCQ)

options.html: FLUS is indeterminate, and the nodule is symptomatic and enlarging
A TI-RADS 3 nodule always requires excision regardless of cytology
FLUS is a malignant result, so completion thyroidectomy is mandated
Her normal TSH excludes a benign cause, leaving surgery as the only option

answer:
A. Two of the four risk-adapted management routes point at surgery, and neither of them is “the ultrasound said so”.

FLUS is an indeterminate Bethesda result, not benign and not malignant. The routes that apply are surgery (for malignancy, ⭐ some indeterminate cytology, or ⭐ benign but symptomatic) and repeat biopsy (insufficient or some indeterminate cytology). ⭐ She qualifies twice over: indeterminate cytology AND a symptomatic, enlarging nodule. Surveillance is the answer for low-risk ultrasound plus benign cytology, which is not what she has.

There is a deeper reason surgery resolves this and a repeat FNA might not. ⭐ FNA cannot distinguish a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma - their nuclei are identical, and only capsular or vascular invasion separates them, visible only in the resected specimen. Repeating the aspirate would sample the same cells and return the same uncertainty. This is the opposite of papillary carcinoma, whose nuclear features are diagnostic on FNA.

  • B inverts the pathway. TI-RADS decides whether to biopsy, not whether to operate; a TR3 with benign cytology gets clinical follow-up only.
  • C misreads the cytology. FLUS is indeterminate. Bethesda III and IV carry 12-30% and 23-34% risk of malignancy - real, but a long way from the 97-100% of a Bethesda VI.
  • D misuses the TSH. ⭐ A normal TSH excludes nothing malignant - it establishes she is euthyroid, and its role here is to send her to ultrasound rather than a radioactive iodine scan. A low TSH would have gone to RAI, where a hot nodule is benign.

What the operation then delivers, and why the session opens with this case: the surgical pathology report gives the definitive diagnosis, the elements needed for staging and prognosis, and the answer to whether further management is needed. ⭐ Cytology stratifies; only the specimen stages.

lecture: Case - Hypercalcemia Found on an Osteoporosis Workup (Hyperparathyroidism)
lectureMeta: Source: the case study in the `Hyper Hypo Parathyroidism and Calcemia Slides` deck. **Reasoned, not keyed** - the deck advances the case across four slides, asking “What next?” and “Diagnosis? Further studies?” without stating an answer, so the reasoning is written from [[04 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hyperparathyroidism and Hypoparathyroidism]] and the deck's own subsequent slides.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 65-year-old woman presents for assessment of osteoporosis. She complains of back pain, and has fractured her right radius and ulna at age 52 and her left ulna at 61. She had a hysterectomy at 35. Evaluation shows normal thyroid function and normal renal function, with Ca 2.95 mmol/L and albumin 45 g/L. Repeat testing gives Ca 2.73 mmol/L, phosphate 0.69 mmol/L, PTH 14 pmol/L (reference 1.6-6.9) and 25-OH vitamin D 70 nmol/L.

stem: Her repeat panel shows a high calcium with a clearly elevated PTH and a low phosphate. What is the diagnosis, and which single further test separates it from its main mimic? (originally a multi-part case study whose closing questions ask “Diagnosis? Further studies?” without stating an answer; written up as an MCQ)

options.html: Primary hyperparathyroidism; a 24-hour urine calcium to exclude FHH
Secondary hyperparathyroidism; a 25-OH vitamin D level
Hypercalcemia of malignancy; a PTHrP level
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism; an eGFR

answer:
A. The four-analyte pattern names the disease, and the urine names the mimic.

First, correct the calcium for albumin - her albumin is 45, so the correction is small and the calcium is genuinely high. Then: calcium 2.73 (high), PTH 14 against a ceiling of 6.9 (⭐ inappropriately high in the face of hypercalcemia), phosphate 0.69 (low, because ⭐ PTH is phosphaturic), and 25-OH-D 70, which rules out vitamin D deficiency as the driver.

⭐ A high calcium with a high PTH is the definition of primary hyperparathyroidism - a normal gland would have switched off. 80% are a single parathyroid adenoma.

Why the urine test. FHH produces the same picture, because an inactivating CaSR mutation shifts the calcium-PTH curve right. The urine separates them: ⭐ FECa < 0.01 means FHH, ⭐ > 0.02 means likely primary hyperparathyroidism, and 20% of FHH lands in the 0.01-0.02 overlap, where nothing is decided. The result only means something off thiazides for 3 months, with a normal magnesium and a 25-OH-D above 50 - hers is 70, so that condition is met.

  • B - secondary hyperparathyroidism runs a normal or low-normal calcium. Her renal function is normal and her vitamin D adequate, so there is nothing for the gland to be reacting to.
  • C - in hypercalcemia of malignancy the PTH is suppressed, because the driver is PTHrP or osteolysis. Her PTH is elevated, which excludes the whole PTH-independent branch. PTHrP would be the right test if PTH had come back low.
  • D - tertiary hyperparathyroidism arises on long-standing CKD and runs a high phosphate. ⭐ Her phosphate is LOW and her renal function normal, which is the cleanest way to tell primary from tertiary when both show a high calcium.

Why she was found at all. She came in for osteoporosis, with a fragility fracture history and back pain. ⭐ Chronic hypercalcemia from primary hyperPTH resorbs bone, and this is the presentation that catches it. She also meets surgical criteria on more than one count once confirmed. And while she is being worked up: ⭐ keep her hydrated and avoid thiazides and lithium.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with a history of celiac disease presents with a history of falls, muscle weakness, and the x-ray shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Atypical fractures due to bisphosphonate use
Pseudofractures due to vitamin D deficiency
Femoral neck fracture due to osteoporosis

answer:
The correct answer is B, keyed by the module, which asks this question identically. The lecture notes give it no answer, no bolded option and no highlight box, so on the notes alone it looked unkeyed. The module settles it. The reasoning below is written from the lecture note, since neither source gives a rationale.

Three features in the stem point the same way, and none of them fits the alternatives.

  • ⭐ Celiac disease is the lecture's named common cause of osteomalacia, because vitamin D is fat-soluble and malabsorbed.
  • ⭐ Proximal muscle weakness (myopathy) that contributes to falls is the osteomalacia feature that osteoporosis does not share. This is the most useful discriminator between the two, since they can look alike on x-ray and on BMD.
  • ⭐ Pseudofractures - healed microfractures - are the radiological hallmark of osteomalacia.

A requires a drug she is not on, and at 23 would be extraordinary. C names a single acute fracture, which explains neither the weakness nor the falls - and osteomalacia is routinely mistaken for osteoporosis, which is precisely the error this option offers. The tell is that osteomalacia has overt symptoms while osteoporosis is indolent.

Confirmatory labs: ↓ calcium, ↓ phosphate, ↑ ALP, ↑ PTH, ↓ 25-OH-D and ↓ urine calcium. ⭐ Both calcium and phosphate being low separates osteomalacia from Paget's, where both are normal.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with tremor and heat intolerance, but is otherwise well. No neck pain or tenderness. No family history of autoimmune disease. Thyroid is mildly enlarged, more on the right than left, with no definite nodule. There is no evidence of Graves' orbitopathy or dermopathy. TSH is <0.01 (0.3-4.5), FT4 is 28 (11-22), FT3 is 11.0 (3.5-6.5). What tests would you order?

options.html: Radioactive iodine uptake and scan
Thyroid ultrasound
Anti-TPO levels
Pituitary hormone assessment and pituitary MRI

answer:
The correct answer is A. The biochemistry has already made the diagnosis: TSH suppressed with both free hormones high is overt thyrotoxicosis. What is missing is why, and ⭐ RAI uptake and scan is the single best test for the etiology of thyrotoxicosis.

Read the negatives in the stem, because they are what remove the shortcut:

  • no family history of autoimmune disease, no orbitopathy or dermopathy, and an asymmetric goiter with no definite nodule. ⭐ Graves is symmetric and usually carries eye signs; asymmetry points at autonomous nodular tissue (TMNG or a toxic adenoma). Without the clinical picture of Graves you cannot diagnose it on signs alone, so imaging has to settle it
  • no neck pain or tenderness argues against subacute thyroiditis

C is the wrong antibody in the wrong direction: anti-TPO is a hypothyroid test, and even there it rarely changes management. B, ultrasound, tells you about structure, not about whether the gland is synthesizing. D would be for central disease, which is excluded here because ⭐ the TSH is suppressed in the presence of high hormone, which is exactly the appropriate pituitary response.

stem: A healthy 68-year-old man presents with dry skin, cold intolerance and mild fatigue. No clear cause is determined after appropriate investigations. Initial TSH is 7.5 (0.35-4.5), repeat TSH 8.4, FT4 14 (11-22). He requests a trial of levothyroxine. After 75 mcg for 3 months he feels no change and TSH is 2.5. What do you recommend?

options.html: Increase the dose to 100 mcg daily and repeat TSH in 6 weeks
Decrease the dose to 50 mcg and repeat the TSH in 6 weeks
Continue current levothyroxine and monitor TSH yearly
Stop levothyroxine and monitor for overt hypothyroidism

answer:
The correct answer is D. This is subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH raised, FT4 normal) treated as a therapeutic trial, and ⭐ the rule for a trial is that it ends if nothing changes.

He has now been biochemically euthyroid on treatment (TSH 2.5) for 3 months and feels no different. That is the trial answering its own question: his symptoms were not from his thyroid. ⭐ Stop after 3 months of no response and watch for progression to overt disease instead.

The other options all treat the number rather than the patient:

  • A chases a TSH that is already normal, which would push him toward iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis
  • B keeps him on a drug that has demonstrably done nothing
  • C commits a 68-year-old to lifelong therapy on no evidence of benefit

⭐ There is no evidence of benefit in treating subclinical hypothyroidism, with the exceptions being pregnancy, TSH > 10, anti-TPO positive, and exactly this kind of time-limited symptomatic trial. His TSH of 7.5-8.4 is below 10, so nothing else here argued for treating him indefinitely.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with obesity and hypothyroidism has adopted a healthier lifestyle and lost 10% of her body weight. She has developed a mild tremor and increased heat intolerance with worse and more frequent menopausal hot flashes. You measure TSH and it is <0.01 (0.3-4.5); the lab reflexively adds FT4, which is 27 (11-22). What do you suggest?

options.html: Stay on the same dose of levothyroxine and start HRT
Decrease the levothyroxine dose and repeat TSH in 2 weeks
Decrease the levothyroxine dose and repeat TSH in 6 weeks
Measure anti-TPO antibodies and order a thyroid ultrasound

answer:
The correct answer is C. She is over-replaced. ⭐ levothyroxine is weight-based at roughly 1.5 mcg/kg/day, so losing 10% of her body weight makes a dose that used to be right now excessive, and the tremor, heat intolerance and worsened flushes are iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis rather than menopause.

The discriminator between B and C is the interval, and it comes from one number: ⭐ levothyroxine's half-life is 1 week, so a level checked at 2 weeks has not reached steady state and will mislead you into another dose change. Recheck at 6 weeks, which is the same interval used for every other titration.

A treats the symptom as menopausal and leaves her thyrotoxic. D investigates a diagnosis she already has, and ⚠ anti-TPO and ultrasound almost never change management in hypothyroidism — they certainly do not explain a suppressed TSH in someone taking thyroid hormone.
