stem: A 38-year-old healthy woman presents with a tender thyroid and pain on swallowing 3 weeks after a mild respiratory infection. She is having heat intolerance, tremor and tachycardia with bothersome palpitations, but is hemodynamically stable. What treatment do you recommend?

options.html: Methimazole, beta blocker and NSAID
Beta blocker pending radioactive iodine ablation
Beta blocker and glucocorticoid (prednisone)
Beta blocker and NSAID
No treatment

answer:
The correct answer is D. The stem describes subacute (post-viral) thyroiditis: ⭐ a tender, painful thyroid with odynophagia, 3 weeks after a respiratory infection. Tenderness is the giveaway — post-partum and autoimmune thyroiditis are painless.

⭐ This is a LEAKAGE thyrotoxicosis, not a production one. The gland is not synthesizing hormone, it is releasing preformed hormone as it is damaged, which is why treatment is supportive only:

  • beta blocker for the palpitations, tachycardia and tremor
  • NSAID for the pain

A is the error the question is built around: ⭐ thionamides block synthesis, and synthesis is not the problem, so methimazole does nothing here. B is worse — RAI needs iodine uptake, and uptake in thyroiditis is low. E ignores treatable symptoms. C is not wrong so much as premature: ⭐ glucocorticoids are the second step, reserved for pain the NSAID does not control.

The thing to warn her about: watch for the hypothyroid phase as the gland recovers.

stem: A 24-year-old healthy man presents concerned that his Fitbit often reads his heart rate in the 50s. He read on the internet that this can be caused by hypothyroidism and is worried he might have it, because his mother has hypothyroidism. His TSH comes back 2.0 (0.3-4.5). What do you suggest?

options.html: Periodic TSH monitoring
Anti-TPO levels
Thyroid ultrasound
FT4 to rule out central hypothyroidism

answer:
The correct answer is A. ⭐ A normal TSH rules out thyroid dysfunction, and that is the end of the workup in someone with no reason to suspect pituitary disease. He has a family history, which is a legitimate reason to check a TSH periodically, and that is all this needs.

The distractors are three different ways of not accepting a normal result:

  • B — anti-TPO in a euthyroid man changes nothing. It is sensitive but not specific, and it almost never influences a clinical decision
  • C — ultrasound answers a structural question. He has no nodule and no mass
  • D — this is the one worth thinking about, because ⭐ central hypothyroidism is the single exception to "stop at a normal TSH". But it applies when there are other pituitary deficiencies or a known pituitary mass, and he has neither. A fit 24-year-old with a resting pulse in the 50s is describing athletic bradycardia, not pituitary failure

This is also a Choosing Wisely question: ⭐ only order tests that will change management, and none of B, C or D would.

stem: A 32-year-old healthy woman presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, 5 kg weight loss in the last month, normal appetite, tremor and anxiety. Thyroid is symmetrically moderately enlarged. TSH is <0.01 (0.35-4.5), FT4 is 44 (11-22), FT3 is 19.2 (3.5-6.5). Her mother and two sisters have Hashimoto's disease. You plan to prescribe methimazole. What is the next best step?

options.html: Check anti-TPO and TSH receptor antibody levels
Radioactive iodine uptake and scan
Thyroid ultrasound
Pregnancy test, liver enzymes and a complete blood count

answer:
The correct answer is D. Note what the stem has already settled: a young woman, symmetric goiter, strong family history of autoimmune thyroid disease, florid thyrotoxicosis. ⭐ When clinical suspicion of Graves disease is high enough you may diagnose it on signs and symptoms alone, and the question tells you the plan is already made. So the next step is not more diagnosis, it is the safety workup before starting the drug.

Each of the three tests maps onto a specific hazard of methimazole:

  • ⭐ Pregnancy test — thionamides can cause birth defects, and she is 32 with no contraception mentioned
  • ⭐ Liver enzymes — liver dysfunction is a recognised serious adverse effect
  • ⭐ Complete blood count — a baseline count before a drug whose feared complication is agranulocytosis

A and C would confirm what is already clinically clear. B is the sharper trap: RAI uptake would tell you the etiology, but it is ⛔ contraindicated in pregnancy, and you have not yet excluded pregnancy — which is precisely the test in option D.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents with peripheral vision loss and presyncope and is found to have a 2 cm pituitary adenoma and adrenal insufficiency. He is started on hydrocortisone and booked for surgery. He still feels fatigue and is developing constipation and cold intolerance. What tests would you order?

options.html: TSH
TSH and FT4
TSH, FT4 and anti-TPO
TSH and thyroid ultrasound

answer:
The correct answer is B. This is ⭐ the one situation where TSH alone is not enough. He has a known pituitary mass and an established second pituitary deficiency (adrenal insufficiency), and he is now describing hypothyroid symptoms. That is central hypothyroidism until proven otherwise.

⚠ ⭐ In central disease the TSH moves WITH the hormone, or not at all — it can be low or normal alongside a low FT4, because the pituitary making the TSH is the broken part. Ordering A, TSH alone, would return a normal-looking number and falsely reassure you.

C adds an antibody test for autoimmune thyroid destruction, which is not the mechanism here. D adds a structural test for a gland that is structurally fine.

⚠ One more thing the stem is quietly checking: he was started on hydrocortisone first. That is the correct order, because ⭐ giving levothyroxine in uncorrected adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis by increasing cortisol metabolism.

stem: A patient presents with decreased heart rate, cold intolerance, and weight gain despite decreased appetite. Their lab results demonstrate high TSH and low FT4. You inquire the patient about past thyroid diseases and thyroid treatments (radiation, surgery), which are negative. You also screened the patient for risk of pituitary disease, which is also negative. What is your next appropriate step?

options.html: Order FT3 level
Order anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibody levels
Order a radioactive iodine uptake test
Make the diagnosis of Hashimoto’s disease

answer: The correct answer is D. If you have excluded past thyroid disease and treatment and pituitary disease as causes of hypothyroidism, you can assume the diagnosis of Hashimoto’s disease based on the elevated FSH and low FT4 level. You do not need to order FT3 for assessing hypothyroidism. Radioactive iodine uptake test is ordered to assess causes for low TSH levels. Anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies are sensitive for Hashimoto’s disease, but they almost never influence clinical decisions in hypothyroidism, so they don’t need to be ordered.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of palpitations, unintentional weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, tremors, irritability, and difficulty sleeping. She reports no prior thyroid disease. On examination, her heart rate is 110 bpm and irregular, blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg, and she has a diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid with a bruit, as well as fine hand tremors and mild exophthalmos. Laboratory investigations reveal a suppressed TSH (<0.01 mIU/L), elevated free T4 (35 pmol/L) and T3 (10 nmol/L), and positive TSH receptor antibodies.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the appropriate initial management?

options.html: Subacute thyroiditis; start NSAIDs and beta-blockers for symptom control.
Graves’ disease; beta-blockers, then discuss antithyroid drugs, RAI or surgery.
Toxic multinodular goiter; proceed directly to immediate total thyroidectomy.
Primary hypothyroidism; start levothyroxine replacement therapy now.
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis; monitor only, as no treatment is required.

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck; reasoning ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis.

Suppressed TSH with high FT4/FT3 is thyrotoxicosis. A diffuse, symmetric, non-tender goiter, exophthalmos and positive TRAb make it Graves disease: TRAb is sensitive and specific for Graves, and proptosis is Graves-specific, while stare and lid lag occur in any thyrotoxicosis. Management is beta-blockers for adrenergic symptoms, then a risks-and-preference discussion of methimazole (often first line, because Graves can remit), RAI, or surgery (rarely). Subacute thyroiditis is tender (A); TMNG is asymmetric and surgery is not immediate (C); D and E are hypothyroid diagnoses.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman has had difficulty concentrating at work for the past month. She is constantly getting up and walking around to visit co-workers. She complains that the work area is too hot. She seems nervous and often spills her coffee. She has been eating more but has lost 5 kg in the past 2 months. On physical examination her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse 101/minute and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate 22/minute, and blood pressure 145/70 mm Hg. She has bilateral lid lag but no proptosis. Her thyroid gland is easy to feel and non-tender but is not obviously enlarged.

Which of the following lab findings is most likely to be present in this woman?

options.html: Increased FSH level
Decreased iodine uptake during a radioactive iodine uptake and scan
Decreased blood glucose level
Decreased TSH level
Increased ACTH level

answer:
The correct answer is D. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis.

From the review session. Heat intolerance, weight loss despite eating more and lid lag are hyperthyroidism, so the TSH is suppressed.

Heat intolerance, weight loss despite eating more, tremor, AF and a wide pulse pressure are thyrotoxicosis, and in primary thyroid disease TSH moves opposite the hormone, so it is low; TSH is the case-finding test. Lid lag is adrenergic and occurs in any thyrotoxicosis. RAI uptake (B) would be low only in thyroiditis or exogenous hormone; nothing here makes that the most likely finding.

stem:
A 49-year-old woman has had increasing cold intolerance, weight gain of 4 kg, and sluggishness over the past two years. Physical examination reveals dry, coarse skin and alopecia of the scalp. Her thyroid gland is not palpably enlarged. Her serum TSH is 11.7 mU/L with a free T4 of 9.2 pM (normal 11.0 – 22.0 pM). A year ago, anti-thyroglobulin and anti-microsomal antibodies were detected at high titer.

Which of the following thyroid diseases is she most likely to have?

options.html: DeQuervain’s disease
Papillary thyroid carcinoma
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
Multinodular goiter
Graves’ disease

answer:
The correct answer is C. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis.

From the review session. Primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low FT4) with high-titre antibodies is Hashimoto's. Of the two antibodies, anti-microsomal (anti-TPO) is the one to look for; anti-thyroglobulin matters less.

High TSH with low FT4 is primary hypothyroidism, and anti-thyroglobulin and anti-microsomal (anti-TPO) antibodies are the autoimmune markers of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the commonest cause. The gland can be small once it becomes fibrotic, so an impalpable thyroid fits. De Quervain's is painful and thyrotoxic first (A); Graves is thyrotoxic (E).

stem:
A 30-year-old woman, four months postpartum, has palpitations and anxiety. Her thyroid is slightly enlarged and non-tender, and she has no eye signs. TSH is < 0.01 mIU/L and free T4 is raised. A radioactive iodine uptake and scan shows low uptake throughout the gland.

What is the diagnosis and management?

options.html: Graves disease; start methimazole
Toxic adenoma; radioactive iodine ablation
Thyroiditis; beta-blocker, and watch for a hypothyroid phase
Toxic multinodular goiter; total thyroidectomy
TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma; order an MRI of the pituitary

answer: The correct answer is C. RAI uptake answers why: high uptake means the gland is synthesising (Graves, toxic adenoma, TMNG), low uptake means hormone is leaking out (thyroiditis, here postpartum) or coming from a bottle. Leakage is treated supportively (beta-blocker), while you monitor for the hypothyroid phase as the thyroiditis burns out. Antithyroid drugs, ablation and surgery (A, B, D) treat synthesis, which is not happening. A central cause would not have a suppressed TSH (E).

stem:
A 79-year-old man with stable angina and a previous MI is found to have primary hypothyroidism: TSH 24 mIU/L, free T4 low.

What is the most appropriate way to start treatment?

options.html: Full replacement at about 1.5 mcg/kg/day from the start
A low dose of levothyroxine, titrated up slowly
Liothyronine (T3) for a faster clinical response
No treatment until the TSH is above 50 mIU/L
Full replacement, with the TSH rechecked every week

answer: The correct answer is B. The usual requirement is about 1.5 mcg/kg/day, titrated to a normal TSH, but the lecture says to start low and titrate up in the elderly or in heart disease, because a sudden rise in metabolic demand can provoke ischaemia (A). Levothyroxine's half-life is a week, so the TSH is rechecked at 4-6 weeks, not weekly (E).

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with spotting and lower abdominal ache. She has not had her period for 5 weeks. Beta-hCG is elevated, confirming pregnancy. Ultrasound reveals an empty uterine cavity. Which of the following would most likely explain the condition?

options.html: An ectopic pregnancy, most commonly a mesenteric implantation
She is not pregnant and may have appendicitis
An ectopic pregnancy, most commonly a tubal implantation
A normal pregnancy

answer:
The correct answer is C. A positive hCG with an empty uterus is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise, and ⭐ 96-98% of them are tubal.

The full distribution: Fallopian tube 96-98% · ovary 4% · abdominal cavity 1% · internal cervical os 1% · endocervical canal 1%. ⚠ A is the trap — it names the right diagnosis with the wrong site; mesenteric implantation is vanishingly rare.

B contradicts the elevated hCG. D contradicts the empty cavity: by 5 weeks of amenorrhea with a positive test, an intrauterine gestation should be visible.

⭐ Why the tube: fertilization normally happens in the ampulla, so the conceptus starts there and only reaches the uterus if tubal transport works. Anything that damages the cilia or the tube lumen leaves it to implant where it already is. Worth pairing with the other hCG discriminator: ⚠ a LOW hCG also suggests ectopic.

stem: An infant is born with congenital anomalies of the special senses, including cataracts and sensorineural deafness. Which teratogen do you suspect?

options.html: Maternal rubella virus infection
Maternal consumption of alcohol
Maternal exposure to diagnostic radiation (e.g. x-ray)
Maternal undernutrition
Maternal exposure to nicotine

answer:
The correct answer is A. ⭐ Congenital rubella syndrome is the classic triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness and cardiac defects (typically patent ductus arteriosus). Two of the three are in the stem.

⭐ The risk of fetal rubella infection is greatest early, when the eye and the inner ear are forming — which is the same principle as the week-by-week teratogen windows.

The distractors each have their own signature, and none of it is this:

  • B, alcohol — fetal alcohol spectrum: midface hypoplasia, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, microcephaly, neurodevelopmental impairment
  • C, diagnostic radiation — diagnostic doses rarely reach a teratogenic threshold; the concerning data are from acute high-dose exposure
  • D, undernutrition — growth restriction, and neural tube defects with folate deficiency
  • E, nicotine — growth restriction, prematurity, placental complications

stem: A 22-year-old pregnant woman at 20 weeks of gestation has an ultrasound revealing spina bifida in the fetus. At what week of gestation did this defect most likely occur?

options.html: 1 to 2
4 to 6
9 to 11

answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ spina bifida is a failure of the CAUDAL neuropore to close, and that closure happens on day 26 — inside weeks 4 to 6. A defect cannot arise after the process it disrupts has finished.

The neural tube closes from the middle outward toward both ends:

  • ⭐ cranial neuropore closes day 24 → failure gives anencephaly
  • ⭐ caudal neuropore closes day 26 → failure gives spina bifida

A is excluded by the teratogen windows themselves: ⭐ weeks 1-2 are "all or nothing" — an insult either kills the conceptus or does nothing, because the cells are still totipotent and can replace losses. C, D and E all fall in the fetal period, where insults cause minor morphologic and functional defects rather than major structural ones.

⭐ Weeks 3-8 are the critical period, when organogenesis and morphogenesis peak and major congenital anomalies are made. This question is that principle applied to one date.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has consumed excessive quantities of alcohol almost every weekend for the last few years. Three weeks ago she missed her second consecutive period, and a pregnancy test is positive. Should you as her physician be concerned about the effects of her binge-drinking episodes on her baby?

options.html: You need not be concerned, as it is so early in development
You should be concerned, as early alcohol exposure can harm the fetus
She is not an alcoholic, so you have nothing to worry about
She has been eating well and exercising, so you need not be concerned

answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ Early is precisely when it matters most. Two missed periods puts her at roughly 8 weeks, so the binge episodes have spanned the embryonic period, weeks 3-8 — the critical period, when cell division, differentiation, organogenesis and morphogenesis are all at their peak and teratogens produce major congenital anomalies.

⚠ A inverts the "all or nothing" rule. That rule applies to weeks 1-2 only, and she is well past it.

C and D are the socially comfortable answers, and both are wrong for the same reason: ⭐ there is no established safe threshold, safe pattern, or safe drinker profile for alcohol in pregnancy. Binge drinking delivers high peak concentrations, which is if anything the more damaging pattern, and good nutrition does not offset a teratogen.

The clinical move is to say so plainly and without blame, and to arrange follow-up — she is still pregnant, and what she does from here still changes the outcome.

stem: How does GnRH regulate gonadotropin release?

options.html: The hypothalamus secretes GnRH into the general circulation and acts on the receptors of the posterior pituitary to induce the secretion of gonadotropins.
The hypothalamus secretes GnRH into the general circulation and acts on the receptors of the anterior pituitary to induce the secretion of gonadotropins.
The hypothalamus secretes GnRH through a portal system that directly reaches the receptors on the posterior pituitary and induces secretion of gonadotropins.
The hypothalamus secretes GnRH through a portal system that directly reaches the receptors on the anterior pituitary and induces the secretion of gonadotropins.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis. GnRH comes from parvicellular hypothalamic neurons, whose axons end in the median eminence. There it enters the primary capillary plexus, travels down the hypophysial portal veins, and reaches the secondary plexus of the anterior pituitary. It acts on GnRH receptors on gonadotropes, which release LH and FSH into the systemic circulation. The portal system keeps GnRH concentrated, which matters because it acts in pulses at very low amounts.

  • A, C name the posterior pituitary. That is where magnocellular axons end, releasing oxytocin and vasopressin directly into the blood. The posterior pituitary makes no gonadotropins.
  • B has the right target but the wrong route: GnRH does not go through the general circulation to reach the pituitary.

stem:
A 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and painful spinal metastases needs androgen deprivation.

Why might a GnRH antagonist be preferred over a GnRH agonist?

options.html: It is given as a pulsatile infusion
It avoids the initial testosterone surge
It works directly on the testicular Leydig cells
Agonists cannot lower testosterone to castrate levels
It permanently destroys the pituitary gonadotrophs

answer: The correct answer is B. A GnRH agonist first stimulates the axis, causing a surge in sex steroids, then desensitises the receptor and shuts production down. An antagonist acts immediately, with no surge, so there is no tumour flare, which matters with painful bone metastases. Agonists do eventually suppress testosterone (D); both act on the pituitary, not the testis (C).

stem: A 25-year-old woman with normal menstrual cycles wishes to become pregnant. In her monthly cycle, fertility is likely to be maximal when her:

options.html: basal body temperature has reached its highest value
plasma estradiol is at its lowest point
plasma progesterone is increasing toward its highest value
cervical mucus is thickest
plasma progesterone is rapidly decreasing

answer:
The correct answer is C. ⭐ Progesterone starts rising at ovulation, as the follicular remnants luteinize, so "increasing toward its highest value" marks the peri-ovulatory window — which is exactly when fertility peaks.

The distractors are all real events at the wrong point in the cycle:

  • A — the temperature rise is progesterone-mediated and ⚠ lags ovulation. By the time it has reached its highest value, the fertile window is closing. This is the classic limitation of temperature charting: it confirms ovulation retrospectively
  • B — oestradiol is lowest around menstruation, furthest from ovulation
  • D — ⚠ inverted. Around ovulation, oestrogen makes cervical mucus thin, clear and stretchy to let sperm through; thick mucus is the progesterone-dominant luteal pattern, which is hostile to sperm
  • E — falling progesterone is the end of the luteal phase, immediately before menstruation

⭐ B, D and E all describe times remote from ovulation; A describes the right event too late.

stem: For a 25 year old female who has a regular menstrual cycle, which of the following is correct

options.html: We can’t be certain of the duration of her luteal phase since it varies across women, but her follicular phase is likely 14 days.
Her FSH levels are the lowest after she ovulates.
Her estrogen levels will continuously decrease following ovulation
There is one developing follicle in her ovaries during each menstrual cycle

answer: The correct answer is B. FSH levels are at the lowest after ovulation due to negative feedback from estrogen and progesterone. The length of the follicular phase varies across women, but the luteal phase is usually consistently 14 days. The estrogen level has another surge in the luteal phase. There are multiple follicular waves in development during each cycle.

stem: What induces the mid-cycle LH-FSH surge

options.html: When estrogen reaches and maintains a high enough level
When estrogen levels drop and no longer exerts negative feedback on the HPO axis
When GnRH pulses are the strongest
When the corpus luteum begins to produce progesterone.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle. Estradiol is the one hormone that reverses the sign of its own feedback. Below threshold it suppresses FSH. Held above 300-500 pg/mL for about 48 hours, at the end of the follicular phase, it switches the GnRH response to feed-forward and triggers the mid-cycle LH and FSH surge. The surge needs both the level and the duration, which is exactly what "reaches and maintains" in A captures.

  • B inverts the mechanism: the surge follows a sustained rise in estrogen, not a fall that removes negative feedback.
  • C treats GnRH pulse strength as the cause, when it is only the consequence of estradiol's switch.
  • D gets the timing wrong: the corpus luteum forms after ovulation, so its progesterone comes after the surge.

stem: What are the hormones which granulosa cells and theca cells respond to, respectively?

options.html: Granulosa cells response to estrogen and theca cells respond to progesterone
Granulosa cells respond to FSH and theca cells respond to LH
Both granulosa cells and theca cells respond to GnRH
Granulosa cells respond to progesterone and theca cells respond to estrogen

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle and 09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis. This is the two-cell mechanism:

  • LH acts on theca cells, which convert cholesterol to androgen.
  • FSH acts on granulosa cells, which carry the aromatase that turns that androgen into estradiol.

Neither cell can make estradiol alone. The male mirror is LH on Leydig cells and FSH on Sertoli cells.

  • A, D name steroid products as the stimulating hormones. Estrogen and progesterone are what these cells make, not the hormones that drive them.
  • C fails because GnRH acts on anterior-pituitary gonadotropes. It never reaches the gonad.

stem: What is the difference between spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis

options.html: The two are synonymous
Spermatogenesis produces spermatogonia while spermiogenesis produces spermatozoa
Spermatogenesis produces spermatocytes while spermiogenesis produces spermatids
Spermatogenesis produces spermatids while spermiogenesis produces spermatozoa

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function. The two terms describe consecutive stages, each ending at a different cell:

  • Spermatogenesis runs from spermatogonia to spermatids. Spermatogonia renew themselves and make primary spermatocytes by mitosis, then the meiotic divisions end with early spermatids.
  • Spermiogenesis is the maturation of spermatids into spermatozoa, with no further division. Late spermatids shed their cytoplasm as residual bodies, grow a flagellum, and form the acrosome.

Both happen between Sertoli cells, moving from the basal side of the tubule to the lumen.

  • A fails because the two processes are distinct stages.
  • B fails because spermatogonia are the starting cells of spermatogenesis, not its product.
  • C stops spermatogenesis too early and misnames spermiogenesis's product: spermatids are its input, not its output.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 50-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of weight loss (~40 lbs) despite an increased appetite, frequent palpitations, and shakiness. She feels very hot and sweaty and can't get to sleep at night. She is on no medications. On exam: heart rate 120/min, BP 148/70, skin warm and moist, fine tremor in her hands. She has a noticeable stare and lid lag in both eyes but no chemosis, scleral injection, or diplopia on range of motion testing. Her thyroid is not tender but is diffusely enlarged and has a systolic bruit over both lobes. There is a Grade III/VI mid-systolic murmur heard best at the aortic area. TSH < 0.01 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 51 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 16.5 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: What diagnosis is most consistent with this history, physical exam, and lab tests? Justify your answer.

options.html: Subacute thyroiditis
toxic multinodular goiter
Graves disease
Factitious thyrotoxicosis

answer:
C. ⭐ Thyrotoxicosis is the lab picture from any cause; hyperthyroidism claims the gland is OVERPRODUCING. thyroiditis releases preformed hormone - thyrotoxic, but not hyperthyroid.

She is hyperthyroid, and Graves specifically:

  • ⭐ Diffusely enlarged gland - symmetric, not nodular
  • ⭐ Systolic bruit - increased vascularity, a driven gland
  • Eye findings, which are Graves-specific

Supported by weight loss despite increased appetite, tremor, heat intolerance, and the cardiovascular set: HR 120, ⭐ wide pulse pressure (148/70), palpitations.

A - subacute thyroiditis is ⭐ painful; hers is not tender. B - TMNG needs discrete nodules. D - she is on no medications.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 50-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of weight loss (~40 lbs) despite an increased appetite, frequent palpitations, and shakiness. She feels very hot and sweaty and can't get to sleep at night. She is on no medications. On exam: heart rate 120/min, BP 148/70, skin warm and moist, fine tremor in her hands. She has a noticeable stare and lid lag in both eyes but no chemosis, scleral injection, or diplopia on range of motion testing. Her thyroid is not tender but is diffusely enlarged and has a systolic bruit over both lobes. There is a Grade III/VI mid-systolic murmur heard best at the aortic area. TSH < 0.01 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 51 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 16.5 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: What is the relevance of her eye findings on the physical exam?

options.html: Adrenergic signs seen in any thyrotoxicosis, not specific to Graves
They point to Graves; the absent findings exclude active disease
A sign of imminent visual loss, so an ocular emergency needing referral
Unrelated to the thyroid, pointing to a separate neurological cause

answer:
A. 03 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis splits the eye signs in two:

  • ⭐ stare, lid retraction, lid lag → any thyrotoxicosis; they are adrenergic, not autoimmune
  • ⭐ proptosis, periorbital edema, inflammation, diplopia, visual loss → Graves orbitopathy specifically

She has a stare and lid lag, the non-specific pair. Her diffuse goiter with a bruit is what points to Graves disease. She has no chemosis, no scleral injection, no diplopia, so there is no sign of clinically active orbitopathy, but that does not exclude it, which is why B overstates.

⚠ The orbit runs on its own clock: eye disease can persist or progress after the gland is removed and the hyperthyroidism resolves.

C - she has no visual loss. D - wrong mechanism.

flags.title: The small-group session keys this B
flags.html: The small-group answer treated her stare and lid lag as Graves eye disease. The lecture calls those signs adrenergic and seen in any thyrotoxicosis, so the question is keyed A to match it. Readers reported this.

Her thyroid is not tender but is diffusely enlarged and has a systolic bruit over both lobes. There is a Grade III/VI mid-systolic murmur heard best at the aortic area. TSH < 0.01 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 51 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 16.5 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: What are other possible causes of elevated free T4 and free T3 levels and suppressed TSH levels

options.html: Primary hypothyroidism, or Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Central hypothyroidism, or failure of the anterior pituitary
Hypoparathyroidism, or vitamin D deficiency
Increased synthesis, or leakage of preformed hormone

answer:
D. ⭐ The split is synthesis versus leakage.

Overproduction - Graves disease · ⭐ toxic adenoma, one hot nodule with the rest of the gland quiet · TMNG, several nodules

Leakage (thyroiditis) - post-partum · subacute, where ⭐ pain is the discriminator · post-surgical · infectious

Exogenous - levothyroxine over-replacement · ⚠ ⭐ over-the-counter animal-thyroid supplements (porcine or bovine, unregulated, T3:T4 wrong for humans). ⭐ Take a supplement history - patients often do not know these contain hormone.

Iodine load, the substrate - ⭐ the Jod-Basedow effect: ⭐ iodinated contrast after a CT · ⭐ amiodarone, which ⚠ persists up to a year past the last dose, so ask what cardiac drugs they were on before

⭐ hCG resembles TSH: a first-trimester TSH of ~0.1 with normal free hormones is ⭐ physiological, not hyperthyroidism. Rarely, TSH-producing tumours.

A and B are hypothyroid states; C is a calcium disorder.

stem: Are further tests needed to confirm the diagnosis? If yes, what tests would you do and how could they help?

options.html: Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, to confirm Graves
A radioactive iodine uptake scan, read on its pattern of uptake
A thyroid ultrasound, which is definitive for the etiology
No further testing is needed; the clinical picture is diagnostic

answer:
B. ⭐ The pattern of uptake names the cause:

UptakeDiagnosis
One bright spotToxic adenoma
Multiple spotsTMNG
⭐ Diffuse⭐ Graves disease - expected in her
Decreasedthyroiditis

Radioactive iodine is swallowed and imaged at 24 hours. ⭐ The thyroid is the only organ that takes up iodine at that level, because it is the only one iodinating tyrosine to build T3 and T4.

⚠ Low uptake is not "Hashimoto's" - Hashimoto's is by definition hypothyroid. In a thyrotoxic patient, low uptake means thyroiditis.

A - anti-TPO is a Hashimoto's antibody; TRAb is the Graves-specific blood test. C - ultrasound is for a nodule, not etiology. D - the scan is what proves which cause.

stem: List the 4 main treatment options for this problem. For each, explain how they work and summarize the pros and cons (risks, side-effects).

options.html: Levothyroxine, calcitriol, thiazides and calcium
Beta-blockers, NSAIDs, steroids and watchful observation
Beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine, surgery
Methimazole, PTU, propranolol and iodine

answer:
C. Four aims:

AimTreatmentDetail
Supportivebeta-blockerspalpitations, tachycardia, tremor - ⚠ does not lower production
↓ production⭐ thionamides: methimazole > PTU⭐ 1st line for Graves, the one that can REMIT. 4-6 weeks. ⭐ agranulocytosis, liver dysfunction, ⚠ birth defects
↓ productionRAI⭐ 1st line for adenoma and TMNG. Permanent cure, but ⭐ permanent hypothyroidism; ⚠ worsens eye disease, especially in smokers; ⛔ not in pregnancy

⭐ Only Graves remits, which is why a thionamide goes first there and RAI first in nodular disease. ⚠ Her eye findings bear on the choice - RAI may worsen them.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 72-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his son. He has lived on his own since his wife died last year, and his son is concerned he has become more forgetful. Between them you get a further story of weight gain, poor appetite, cold intolerance, voice hoarseness, and leg puffiness. Past history: an inferior MI 5 years ago, for which he is on ASA, bisoprolol and atorvastatin; he also has SL NTG for angina though he can't remember the last time he needed it. On exam he is oriented, responsive (though slow), and not in distress. BP 140/90, heart rate 52 beats/min, RR 16, O2 saturation 94% on room air, T 36.2 C. Skin cool and dry. Non-pitting edema in both legs up to his knees. Heart sounds hard to hear, dullness at the right lung base with decreased tactile fremitus. You can't see his neck veins, nor see or feel his thyroid. ⭐ The relaxation phase of the DTRs at his knees is delayed.

stem: What diagnosis is consistent with this history and physical exam? Justify your answer.

options.html: Congestive heart failure from his previous MI
Primary hypothyroidism
Major depressive disorder following bereavement
Thyrotoxicosis, apathetic form

answer:
B. ⭐ The delayed relaxation phase (Woltman sign) is the most specific sign, and the rest follows the hypothyroid column: cold intolerance, ⭐ weight GAIN despite DECREASED appetite, slow mentation, bradycardia at 52, ⭐ diastolic hypertension with a narrow pulse pressure (140/90), cool dry skin.

⚠ An impalpable thyroid does not argue against it - the signs are not sensitive, and an atrophic gland is an ordinary end state of Hashimoto's.

A - ⚠ his neck veins are not visible, hard to square with congestive failure; heart failure sits under "both can do", so the edema does not discriminate. C - depression causes neither bradycardia nor a delayed relaxation phase. D is the opposite column.

⚠ Watch for myxedema coma - obtundation and hypothermia with hypotension and hyponatremia. He is bradycardic and cool but oriented and normothermic.

stem: What tests would you order?

A thyroid ultrasound
Free T4 and free T3, without a TSH
serum TSH first, with free T4 to confirm

answer:

stem: Based on your answer to Q1, and assuming the results of the lab tests you ordered in Q2 confirm your diagnosis, how would you treat him?

options.html: Oral levothyroxine, started low and titrated up
Oral levothyroxine at the full ~1.5 mcg/kg/day dose
Methimazole, titrated to a normal TSH
No treatment; replacement is of no proven benefit

answer:
A. Standard replacement is ⭐ ~1.5 mcg/kg/day titrated to a normal TSH, with the modifier ⭐ start low and titrate up if elderly or with heart disease. He is 72 with an inferior MI and angina.

⭐ Recheck TSH at 4-6 weeks, because ⭐ levothyroxine's half-life is 1 week - sooner reads a level short of steady state. ⚠ Do not monitor free T4 or T3 once you are the one replacing them.

Taken ≥ 1 h before or ≥ 2 h after eating, and ⭐ 4 h away from calcium, iron or magnesium.

B is the dose for a well young patient. C treats the opposite disease. D misapplies the subclinical rule - his free T4 is low, so this is overt.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 26-year-old female delivered a healthy baby 10 weeks ago and now presents complaining of palpitations that started 3 weeks ago, worse at night. She says the palpitations are getting better, but at first "my heart was going to jump out of my chest". She has had no chest pain, dyspnea, or lightheadedness. She has also been feeling warm and is tired, though she is up most nights at least once to breast feed. She is on no medications other than an iron supplement. On exam: BP 136/78, pulse 80 and regular, tremor in her hands. Her thyroid is immediately felt on palpation and might be a bit enlarged, but it is not tender and she has no nodules. TSH < 0.05 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 21.2 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 5.0 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: Intrepret her TFTs.

options.html: Overt thyrotoxicosis
Primary hypothyroidism, overt
Subclinical hyperthyroidism
Central hyperthyroidism

answer:
C. ⚠ Read the free hormones against their ranges before naming the pattern.

HersRange
TSH< 0.050.3-4.5⭐ suppressed
Free T421.29-22⚠ normal
Free T35.03.1-6.8normal

⭐ Suppressed TSH with normal free hormones is subclinical hyperthyroidism; overt disease needs free hormone above range. It carries a risk of bone loss and atrial fibrillation.

⚠ "Subclinical" describes the labs, not the patient - she is plainly symptomatic.

A needs a high free T4. B is the wrong direction. D would need ⭐ TSH normal or HIGH with a high free T4. > [!warning] Spelling in the source > The notes write "Intrepret". Quoted verbatim, flagged not corrected.

stem: What is the most likely cause of her thyroid problem?

options.html: Graves disease
Post-partum thyroiditis
Toxic adenoma
Factitious thyrotoxicosis

answer:
B. She is 10 weeks post-partum, and ⭐ post-partum is a listed thyroiditis trigger.

  • Goiter in thyroiditis may be ⭐ asymmetric, symmetric or absent - hers is barely enlarged
  • ⚠ Not tender: ⭐ pain belongs to the subacute, post-viral form
  • ⭐ Already improving, which is what burning out looks like

A - Graves disease is the main differential but expects a symmetric goiter, often eye signs, and ⭐ does not spontaneously improve at 3 weeks. C needs a nodule; she has none. D - iron is not thyroid hormone, though ⚠ it blocks levothyroxine absorption if she later needs replacement.

preamble.html: The case. A 26-year-old female delivered a healthy baby 10 weeks ago and now presents complaining of palpitations that started 3 weeks ago, worse at night. She says the palpitations are getting better, but at first "my heart was going to jump out of my chest". She has had no chest pain, dyspnea, or lightheadedness. She has also been feeling warm and is tired, though she is up most nights at least once to breast feed. She is on no medications other than an iron supplement. On exam: BP 136/78, pulse 80 and regular, tremor in her hands. Her thyroid is immediately felt on palpation and might be a bit enlarged, but it is not tender and she has no nodules. TSH < 0.05 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 21.2 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 5.0 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: Describe the natural history of this disorder according to its clinical and laboratory features.

options.html: Progressive worsening thyrotoxicosis, requiring definitive treatment
Permanent hypothyroidism, present from the outset
A single thyrotoxic episode with no later consequence
A thyrotoxic phase that burns out, then a hypothyroid phase

answer:
D. ⭐ Thyroiditis leaks preformed hormone, and that store is finite - which is why ⭐ it burns out.

  • Thyrotoxic phase - suppressed TSH with raised or high-normal free T4, while the gland leaks
  • Hypothyroid phase - TSH rises and free T4 falls, the damaged gland unable to synthesise

⭐ The hypothyroid phase is the one to watch for; low-uptake disease is treated supportively while you wait for it. Her improving symptoms and high-normal free T4 put her at the end of the thyrotoxic phase.

A describes Graves, which does not burn out. B skips the phase she is in. C is the dangerous version of the right answer - it drops the hypothyroid phase, which is the reason to keep monitoring.

She says the palpitations are getting better, but at first "my heart was going to jump out of my chest". She has had no chest pain, dyspnea, or lightheadedness. She has also been feeling warm and is tired, though she is up most nights at least once to breast feed. She is on no medications other than an iron supplement. On exam: BP 136/78, pulse 80 and regular, tremor in her hands. Her thyroid is immediately felt on palpation and might be a bit enlarged, but it is not tender and she has no nodules. TSH < 0.05 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 21.2 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 5.0 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: Do you need further tests to confirm the diagnosis? If yes, what test(s) would you do and how will they help?

options.html: An RAI uptake and scan; low uptake would mean leakage
Anti-TPO antibodies, which would establish Graves
A thyroid ultrasound, definitive for the etiology
No test can separate a thyroiditis from Graves disease

answer:
A. ⭐ RAI uptake is the best single test for the etiology of thyrotoxicosis:

  • ⭐ LOW uptake → leakage → thyroiditis → supportive care only
  • ⭐ HIGH uptake → synthesis → Graves, TMNG, adenoma → a thionamide, RAI or surgery

⚠ It is expensive, a 2-day test, and ⛔ contraindicated in pregnancy.

⭐ Whether she needs it is separate from what it would show. A painless small goiter 10 weeks post-partum, already improving, is typical enough that the result would not change management - which is supportive care either way. It becomes worth doing if she fails to improve or worsens.

B - anti-TPO is a Hashimoto's marker, often positive here too, so it separates nothing; ⭐ TRAb is the Graves-specific antibody. C - ultrasound is not required. D is false.

stem: Does she need to be treated?

options.html: Yes - methimazole, to bring the free T4 down
Supportive care only, with a beta-blocker if needed
Yes - levothyroxine, to pre-empt the hypothyroid phase
Yes - radioactive iodine ablation of the gland

answer:
B. ⭐ You cannot block a gland that is not synthesising - her hormone is leaked and preformed, so a thionamide has nothing to act on.

Supportive means beta-blockers for palpitations, tachycardia and tremor. Hers are mild and improving with a pulse of 80, so this is a judgement call rather than an obligation.

⚠ NSAIDs then steroids are for the PAIN of subacute thyroiditis - her gland is not tender.

A would do nothing for the leak and ⚠ deepen the hypothyroid phase. C treats a phase she is not in - she is currently thyrotoxic. D ablates a gland that is already burning out.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. A 68-year-old man is critically ill in the ICU. TSH 1.0 mU/L (0.3-4.5), Free T4 8.0 (9-22), Free T3 1.5 (3.5-6.5). Your resident tells you that the TFTs can be explained by Non-Thyroidal Illness (NTI) Syndrome.

stem: What is NTI syndrome? Outline the 3 main patterns in the TFTs in patients with NTI syndrome.

options.html: Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid in critical illness
Thyroid hormone resistance, unmasked by critical illness
Pituitary infarction occurring during critical illness
Abnormal thyroid tests in illness, with a normal thyroid

answer:
D. ⭐ The abnormality belongs to the illness, not the thyroid - the pattern seen in a critically ill patient whose thyroid is intrinsically normal.

⚠ The three TFT patterns are not covered anywhere in the Week 2 material, so they are left open here rather than filled in from elsewhere.

⭐ What his numbers DO support is in Q87, and it is the clinically important half: the same panel fits central hypothyroidism, which is a diagnosis rather than an adaptation.

A is an intrinsic thyroiditis - the opposite of "non-thyroidal". B is hormone resistance, which runs high free hormones. C names one specific pituitary event, not the syndrome.

stem: What is the other possible explanation for his abnormal thyroid function tests?

options.html: Central hypothyroidism
Primary hypothyroidism
Thyrotoxicosis
Subclinical hypothyroidism

TSHFree T4 / T3

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman noticed a lump on the left side of her neck when she was brushing her teeth. It moved up and down when she swallowed, and she has found that she experiences some pressure swallowing solids but not liquids. She has not noted any change in her voice or other discomfort. She is concerned that the mass seems to have enlarged since she first found it. She has been otherwise well and denies symptoms of hyper- or hypothyroidism. There is no family history of thyroid disease. On exam you confirm a palpable nodule on the left side of her neck in or near the thyroid gland. It is non-tender, moves with swallowing, and you do not feel any enlarged lymph nodes.

stem: Describe the four tests beyond the history and physical by which to investigate this nodule.

options.html: Anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin, thyroglobulin, calcitonin
Ultrasound, CT neck, MRI neck and a PET scan
TSH, an RAI scan, ultrasound with TI-RADS, and FNA
Needle core, punch, excisional biopsy and frozen section

answer:
C. ⭐ Biochemistry → imaging → pathology, with the imaging branch decided by the TSH:

StepTestDecides
1⭐ TSHwhich imaging comes next
2a. TSH LOWRAI scan⭐ a HOT nodule is NEVER cancer
2b. normal or HIGHultrasound + TI-RADSwhether to biopsy
3⭐ FNABcytology, by Bethesda category

⭐ TSH is first because a low result diverts the whole pathway - biopsying a hyperfunctioning nodule is the error the sequence prevents.

A tests thyroid function, not a structural nodule. B has no role in initial evaluation. D - ⚠ needle core biopsy is the wrong instrument for the neck and punch biopsy is for skin.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman noticed a lump on the left side of her neck when she was brushing her teeth. It moved up and down when she swallowed, and she has found that she experiences some pressure swallowing solids but not liquids. She has not noted any change in her voice or other discomfort. She is concerned that the mass seems to have enlarged since she first found it. She has been otherwise well and denies symptoms of hyper- or hypothyroidism. There is no family history of thyroid disease. On exam you confirm a palpable nodule on the left side of her neck in or near the thyroid gland. It is non-tender, moves with swallowing, and you do not feel any enlarged lymph nodes.

stem: The ultrasound report describes a "2.3 cm left-sided, solid hypoechoic nodule with normal borders and shape and no microcalcifications. American College of Radiology TI-RADS 4, American Thyroid Association - Intermediate Suspicion." What do you now recommend?

options.html: Clinical follow-up only, given the reassuring features
Fine needle aspiration biopsy
Total thyroidectomy, on the TI-RADS score
Ultrasound surveillance, repeated in 12 months

answer:
B. ⭐ TI-RADS decides whether to biopsy, on risk score AND size together:

TI-RADS⭐ FNA ifFollow if
TR3≥ 2.5 cm≥ 1.5 cm
⭐ TR4⭐ ≥ 1.5 cm≥ 1.0 cm
TR5≥ 1.0 cm≥ 0.5 cm

⭐ She is TR4 at 2.3 cm, past the threshold. Note the shape of the table: the higher the suspicion, the smaller the nodule needs to be.

⚠ The reassuring features are a distractor - normal borders and absent microcalcifications already fed into the TR4 score, so re-reading them double-counts them, which is what A does.

C - ⭐ TI-RADS decides whether to biopsy, not whether to operate. D applies the surveillance threshold when she has met the biopsy one, in a nodule that is already growing.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman noticed a lump on the left side of her neck when she was brushing her teeth. It moved up and down when she swallowed, and she has found that she experiences some pressure swallowing solids but not liquids. She has not noted any change in her voice or other discomfort. She is concerned that the mass seems to have enlarged since she first found it. She has been otherwise well and denies symptoms of hyper- or hypothyroidism. There is no family history of thyroid disease. On exam you confirm a palpable nodule on the left side of her neck in or near the thyroid gland. It is non-tender, moves with swallowing, and you do not feel any enlarged lymph nodes.

stem: You arrange a fine needle aspiration of the nodule that is read as "Bethesda 4 - Follicular Neoplasm (indeterminate)." What does this mean in terms of possible malignancy? What do you recommend?

options.html: 2-7% risk; reassure her and discharge
97-100% risk; total thyroidectomy and node dissection
5-20% risk; the sample was inadequate, so repeat it
23-34% risk; molecular analysis or hemithyroidectomy

answer:
D. ⭐ Bethesda IV is indeterminate, at 23-34%:

Bethesda⭐ Risk of malignancy
I non-diagnostic5-20%
II benign2-7%
III AUS12-30%
⭐ IV follicular neoplasm⭐ 23-34%
V suspicious67-83%
VI malignant97-100%

⭐ Repeating the aspirate cannot resolve it. A follicular adenoma and a follicular carcinoma have identical nuclei; only ⭐ capsular or vascular invasion separates them, and that is visible solely in the resected specimen. ⚠ A cytology sample contains no capsule. ⚠ The opposite of papillary carcinoma, where the nuclei are the diagnosis.

So: ⭐ molecular analysis or a diagnostic hemithyroidectomy, which is also the cure if it is an adenoma. Her enlarging, symptomatic nodule points the same way.

A is Bethesda II, B is VI, C is I.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 47-year-old woman has Graves disease with a large goitre and has opted for a total thyroidectomy. She is discharged three days post-op, but two days later is brought to hospital following a seizure. Her family notes that since she's been home she's been complaining of pins and needles in her fingers, toes, and around her lips. Labs: TSH 2.4 mU/L (0.3-4.5), Ca 1.71 mmol/L (2.12-2.62), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), Na 137, K 4.1, glucose 4.8.

stem: She has recovered from her seizure and is awake. What three clinical signs can you check for?

options.html: Trousseau's sign, Chvostek's sign, a prolonged QT
Hyporeflexia, a short QT interval, and an Osborn wave
Proptosis, lid lag and a systolic thyroid bruit
Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's sign and papilledema

answer:
A. ⭐ Hypocalcemia makes nerve and muscle hyper-excitable.

SignHow
⭐ Trousseau's signcuff above systolic for 3 min → carpopedal spasm. ⭐ More specific
Chvostek's signtap over the facial nerve → facial twitch
⭐ Prolonged QTon ECG - ⚠ risks torsades de pointes

Trousseau's and Chvostek's appear in MILD disease; convulsions, perioral paresthesias, carpopedal spasm and laryngeal spasm mark SEVERE. ⚠ She has already seized, and ⚠ laryngeal spasm is immediately life-threatening.

B is the ⭐ hyperCALCEMIA column - weakness, hyporeflexia, a short QT and an Osborn wave. C is thyroid, and she no longer has one. D is meningeal.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 47-year-old woman has Graves disease with a large goitre and has opted for a total thyroidectomy. She is discharged three days post-op, but two days later is brought to hospital following a seizure. Her family notes that since she's been home she's been complaining of pins and needles in her fingers, toes, and around her lips. Labs: TSH 2.4 mU/L (0.3-4.5), Ca 1.71 mmol/L (2.12-2.62), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), Na 137, K 4.1, glucose 4.8.

stem: What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

options.html: Hypoalbuminemia, giving a spuriously low total calcium
Dietary vitamin D deficiency
Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism
Pseudohypoparathyroidism

answer:
C. ⭐ Surgery causes 75% of primary hypoparathyroidism. The parathyroids sit on the thyroid and share its blood supply, so a total thyroidectomy for a large goitre is exactly the operation that risks them, and the timing here is textbook.

⭐ Correct for albumin first: every 1 g/L away from 40 shifts calcium by 0.02. ⚠ Hers is exactly 40, so 1.71 is genuine - which disposes of A.

⚠ It must persist 6 months post-surgery before it is called permanent; many post-surgical cases are transient.

B does not appear five days after a thyroidectomy, and ⭐ the phosphate separates them (Q93). D is failure to RESPOND to PTH - congenital, with a HIGH PTH.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 47-year-old woman has Graves disease with a large goitre and has opted for a total thyroidectomy. She is discharged three days post-op, but two days later is brought to hospital following a seizure. Her family notes that since she's been home she's been complaining of pins and needles in her fingers, toes, and around her lips. Labs: TSH 2.4 mU/L (0.3-4.5), Ca 1.71 mmol/L (2.12-2.62), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), Na 137, K 4.1, glucose 4.8.

stem: What other lab tests would confirm the cause of her hypocalcemia?

options.html: Calcitonin and thyroglobulin levels
PTH, phosphate and magnesium
A 24-hour urine calcium and creatinine
PTH alone, with no other test

answer:
B. ⭐ In hypocalcemia, phosphate is the branch point.

GroupCa⭐ PhosphatePTH
⭐ PTH deficient↓⭐ HIGHlow
PTH resistant↓HIGHhigh
Vitamin D↓⭐ LOWhigh

⭐ High phosphate is a PTH problem; low phosphate is vitamin D. PTH is phosphaturic, so losing it retains phosphate - expect a ⭐ low PTH with a high phosphate.

⭐ Magnesium is not optional: ⚠ the calcium will not correct until the magnesium does, and ⚠ magnesium at either extreme causes a functional hypoparathyroidism.

A are thyroid tumour markers. C is the ⭐ FHH versus primary hyperparathyroidism test - a hypercalcemia workup. D alone cannot place her on the table.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 47-year-old woman has Graves disease with a large goitre and has opted for a total thyroidectomy. She is discharged three days post-op, but two days later is brought to hospital following a seizure. Her family notes that since she's been home she's been complaining of pins and needles in her fingers, toes, and around her lips. Labs: TSH 2.4 mU/L (0.3-4.5), Ca 1.71 mmol/L (2.12-2.62), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), Na 137, K 4.1, glucose 4.8.

stem: How would you manage her acutely?

options.html: Oral calcium carbonate, with outpatient follow-up
Calcitriol alone, at 0.25 mcg b.i.d.
Observation; she has recovered from the seizure
IV calcium gluconate, with cardiac monitoring

answer:
D. ⭐ She meets the threshold on both limbs: a corrected calcium < 1.9 plus neurological or cardiac symptoms. Hers is 1.71, and she seized.

  1. ⭐ 1-2 g of 10% calcium gluconate in 50 mL of 5% dextrose over 15-20 min - ⚠ not a rapid push
  2. then ⭐ 1-3 mg/kg/h elemental calcium
  3. ⭐ cardiac monitoring and admission
  4. ⭐ treat coexisting hypomagnesemia - ⚠ the calcium will not correct until the magnesium does

A and C leave a patient who has seized with a calcium of 1.71 without IV treatment, exposed to ⚠ torsades de pointes and laryngeal spasm. B is the right chronic drug used alone - ⚠ calcitriol takes hours to days, far too slow here.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 47-year-old woman has Graves disease with a large goitre and has opted for a total thyroidectomy. She is discharged three days post-op, but two days later is brought to hospital following a seizure. Her family notes that since she's been home she's been complaining of pins and needles in her fingers, toes, and around her lips. Labs: TSH 2.4 mU/L (0.3-4.5), Ca 1.71 mmol/L (2.12-2.62), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), Na 137, K 4.1, glucose 4.8.

stem: How would you manage her long-term?

options.html: Calcitriol and oral calcium, with a thiazide
A loop diuretic, to bring her calcium up
Levothyroxine alone, having no thyroid
Recombinant PTH, as standard first-line therapy

answer:
A. ⭐ Treating chronic hypocalcemia and treating hypoparathyroidism are the same thing - you replace what the missing PTH used to do.

ComponentWhy
⭐ calcitriol 0.25 mcg b.i.d.⚠ PTH is what activates vitamin D - without it she cannot, so it must be given already activated
⭐ 1-2 g elemental calciumin divided doses
Monitor Ca and phosphate⚠ phosphate is already high
25-OH-D > 75 nmol/Lkeeps the substrate adequate
⭐ thiazides⭐ ↓ calcium excretion, lower stone risk

⭐ The thiazide inverts the hypercalcemia rule: ⚠ thiazides CAUSE hypercalcemia and loop diuretics TREAT it - and that same calcium-retaining effect is exactly what you want here.

⚠ She also needs levothyroxine, so C is incomplete rather than untrue. B would drive her calcium lower. D - rhPTH is approved in the US and Europe, not standard first line.

lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 1: The Puzzle)
lectureMeta: Q97-98, Case #1. Stems verbatim. **Keyed from the presenter's own answer slides** in `thyroid_nodules_live_sep_2025_p2_post_after_`.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. A 24-year-old male medical student had an incidentally noted ~2 cm thyroid nodule in Clinical Methods. No family history, no radiation, healthy, asymptomatic - though now aware of the stable nodule. TSH = 0.8.

The FNAB report. Satisfactory for evaluation. Follicular Neoplasm. Colloid: scant. Follicular cells: microfollicular predominant.

stem: What does this mean?

options.html: A benign colloid nodule, since the aspirate was satisfactory for evaluation
A papillary carcinoma, which the nuclear features on the aspirate establish
A non-diagnostic aspirate that has to be repeated before anything follows
It may be benign or it may be malignant, and FNAB alone cannot tell

answer:
D. ⭐ The lecture calls this the PEARL of the case:

  • Findings may represent a benign or malignant nodule.
  • May be benign or malignant. Can't tell by FNAB.

The case then asks what the histology behind a follicular neoplasm aspirate might turn out to be, and gives four answers:

Possible histologyWhat separates it
Nodular goiter / follicular nodular diseasebenign
Follicular adenoma⭐ intact capsule
Follicular carcinoma⭐ capsular invasion
⚠ Papillary carcinoma that forms folliclesthe nuclei, not the architecture

⭐ The aspirate has no capsule in it, which is why it cannot separate rows two and three. ⚠ The fourth row is the one that is easy to forget - a papillary carcinoma can present in a follicular pattern.

A reads the adequacy line as a diagnosis; ⚠ "satisfactory for evaluation" means a good aspirate, not a benign one. B would need nuclear features the report does not describe. C is Bethesda I, a different category.

lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 1: The Puzzle)
lectureMeta: Q97-98, Case #1. Stems verbatim. **Keyed from the presenter's own answer slides** in `thyroid_nodules_live_sep_2025_p2_post_after_`.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. A 24-year-old male medical student had an incidentally noted ~2 cm thyroid nodule in Clinical Methods. No family history, no radiation, healthy, asymptomatic - though now aware of the stable nodule. TSH = 0.8.

The FNAB report. Satisfactory for evaluation. Follicular Neoplasm. Colloid: scant. Follicular cells: microfollicular predominant.

stem: What do you recommend for further investigation or management?

options.html: Repeat the fine needle aspiration of the nodule in three to six months
Total thyroidectomy with a central neck lymph node dissection now
Weigh surgery against observation, using risk, imaging and cytology
A radioactive iodine scan, to establish whether the nodule is hot

answer:
C. The presenter frames it as ⭐ "Surgery vs Observation", then lists what the decision needs - the case's own heading is "Considerations - Need More Evidence":

ConsiderationNote from the case
Clinical risk factors for cancer
Comorbidities / life expectancy
Ultrasound features
Local cytology data
calcitonin⚠ rules IN rare MTC, does not rule OUT papillary
Molecular analysis of FNAB material⚠ expensive, not widely available
Sizeespecially if very small or very big

⭐ There is no single next test - which is the teaching point. The category is indeterminate, so the next move is a judgement built from several inputs at once.

A repeats a test whose limitation is the specimen type, not the sampling, so it returns the same category. B is the high-risk operation and nothing here establishes malignancy. D - ⭐ the RAI branch needs a LOW TSH; his is 0.8, normal, so that branch was already passed.

lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 2: To Treat or Not to Treat)
lectureMeta: Q99-100, Case #2. Stems verbatim. **Keyed.** ⚠ **This case is absent from the pre-session handout** and appears only in the post-session deck.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. A 57-year-old referred for assessment of thyroid nodules, incidentally discovered on a carotid Doppler ultrasound done for a TIA. History - no thyroid cancer family history, no radiation exposure. Physical - normal neck exam. Labs - TSH = 2.18.

The FNAB report. Satisfactory for evaluation. Positive for malignancy. Papillary carcinoma - nuclear criteria. The presenter's shorthand for those nuclei: "bubbles & coffee beans".

stem: What does this mean now?

options.html: An indeterminate result; only the resected capsule can settle it
A papillary carcinoma, diagnosed outright on its nuclear features
A medullary carcinoma, given the neuroendocrine-looking cells here
A benign follicular nodule that needs only an interval ultrasound

answer:
B. ⚠ This is the contrast the two cases exist to draw. Case 1's aspirate could not reach a diagnosis; this one does.

Case 1⭐ Case 2
ReportFollicular Neoplasm⭐ Positive for malignancy
Basisarchitecture⭐ nuclear criteria
Can FNAB call it?⚠ no⭐ yes

⭐ In papillary carcinoma the nuclei ARE the diagnosis - "bubbles and coffee beans" is the presenter's name for the pseudoinclusions and grooves, alongside nice papillae and nuclear atypia on the histology.

The case's own framing of the prognosis: ⭐ the most common type of thyroid cancer, 80-85% of cases, best overall prognosis, rarely fatal.

A is Case 1's answer, not this one. C would need nests, cords and amyloid. D contradicts a report that reads positive for malignancy.

lectureMeta: Q99-100, Case #2. Stems verbatim. **Keyed.** ⚠ **This case is absent from the pre-session handout** and appears only in the post-session deck.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. A 57-year-old referred for assessment of thyroid nodules, incidentally discovered on a carotid Doppler ultrasound done for a TIA. History - no thyroid cancer family history, no radiation exposure. Physical - normal neck exam. Labs - TSH = 2.18.

The FNAB report. Satisfactory for evaluation. Positive for malignancy. Papillary carcinoma - nuclear criteria. The presenter's shorthand for those nuclei: "bubbles & coffee beans".

stem: She goes on to have a total thyroidectomy. What, if any, further treatment would be recommended?

options.html: External beam radiotherapy directed at the whole of the thyroid bed
No further treatment at all, since papillary carcinoma is low risk
Lifelong suppressive levothyroxine, whatever the surgery showed
Radioactive iodine, decided by her ATA recurrence risk category

answer:
D. ⭐ The notes answer this entirely through risk stratification - the question is not whether RAI works but which patients it is for:

ATA riskThe notes' wording
⭐ LOW⭐ "RAI Not Recommended"unifocal or multifocal < 1 cm; 1-4 cm "not routine"; > 4 cm "consider"
INTERMEDIATE"Generally Favoured"any size + ETE; central or lateral neck nodes; aggressive histology
HIGH"RAI Recommended"⭐ gross extrathyroidal extension, incomplete resection, distant mets

What puts a patient in each band: low is no local or distant mets, no extrathyroidal extension, no vascular invasion, no aggressive histology; high adds gross ETE, incomplete resection, distant mets or a high post-op thyroglobulin.

⭐ RAI has three distinct uses in the notes - remnant ablation (making later Tg and ultrasound easier to read), adjuvant therapy for suspected microscopic disease, and treatment of metastatic disease in lung and bone.

B is true only for the low-risk band, so it answers a third of the question. A belongs to extensive ETE and anaplastic disease. C is not how the notes follow a resected papillary carcinoma.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 68-year-old male with a slowly enlarging right-sided neck mass over 6 months. Exam shows a firm ~3 cm right thyroid mass and no palpable lymph nodes. TSH normal. The FNAB comes back positive for malignancy - medullary carcinoma: not papillary, cells that look neuroendocrine, 2-4% of all thyroid cancers, arising from parafollicular C cells that produce calcitonin.

stem: What Heritable Syndromes Include MTC?

options.html: Familial adenomatous polyposis, and also the Cowden syndrome
Von Hippel-Lindau disease, and neurofibromatosis type 1 as well
MEN2A, MEN2B, and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma (FMTC)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, and also the Carney complex

answer:
C. ⚠ Three syndromes, not two - the notes' table puts FMTC alongside MEN2A and MEN2B, and it is the one most often left off:

MEN2AMEN2B⭐ FMTC
⭐ MTCpeak 3rd decade⚠ childhoodpeak 3rd decade
⭐ Pheo⭐ ~50%⭐ ~50%⭐ 0
HPTH⭐ 10-25%00
CLArare00
HD~7%neuromas, etc0

⭐ Read the table down the MTC row: every one of the three includes it - that is what makes it the answer to this question. ⚠ Then read across: only FMTC is MTC alone, which is exactly what its name says.

⭐ MEN2B is the childhood one, and the one with mucosal neuromas. The notes reach the table from a heading reading "RET Mutation Positive - MEN2a" - ⭐ MTC is a RET POINT mutation, while papillary carcinoma is a RET-PTC translocation.

A, B and D are all real tumour syndromes, and none of them includes medullary thyroid carcinoma.

lectureMeta: Q101-104, Case #3. Stems verbatim. Q101-102 keyed from the deck's MEN table; Q103-104 were taken live and have no answer slide.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 68-year-old male with a slowly enlarging right-sided neck mass over 6 months. Exam shows a firm ~3 cm right thyroid mass and no palpable lymph nodes. TSH normal. The FNAB comes back positive for malignancy - medullary carcinoma: not papillary, cells that look neuroendocrine, 2-4% of all thyroid cancers, arising from parafollicular C cells that produce calcitonin.

stem: What tests should be ordered to rule out associated diseases before surgery?

options.html: A thyroid autoantibody panel, with anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin
An ACTH stimulation test, a morning cortisol and a plasma renin
Serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen, as tumour markers
Plasma metanephrines, plus a serum calcium with a PTH alongside

answer:
D. ⭐ Read the case's MEN table as a pre-operative checklist and it answers itself:

Associated diseaseFrequency⭐ The testWhy it matters before surgery
⭐ Pheo⭐ ~50% in MEN2A and 2B⭐ serum metanephrines⚠ an unrecognised pheo can turn induction into a hypertensive crisis
HPTH10-25% in MEN2Acalcium + PTHit changes the neck operation

⚠ The pheo figure is the one that drives this. At ~50% it is close to a coin toss in a syndromic patient, and it is the one associated disease that can kill on the table rather than later.

C is the right pair of markers for the tumour itself - ⭐ calcitonin is what you monitor for recurrence - but the stem asks about associated disease. A tests thyroid function, which is not what travels with MTC. B screens the adrenal cortex; the MEN2 tumour is in the medulla.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 3: Caught in the NET)
lectureMeta: Q101-104, Case #3. Stems verbatim. Q101-102 keyed from the deck's MEN table; Q103-104 were taken live and have no answer slide.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 68-year-old male with a slowly enlarging right-sided neck mass over 6 months. Exam shows a firm ~3 cm right thyroid mass and no palpable lymph nodes. TSH normal. The FNAB comes back positive for malignancy - medullary carcinoma: not papillary, cells that look neuroendocrine, 2-4% of all thyroid cancers, arising from parafollicular C cells that produce calcitonin.

stem: What tests should be ordered for surgical planning?

options.html: A neck ultrasound mapping the cervical nodes, plus a calcitonin
A radioactive iodine uptake scan of the thyroid and of the neck
A repeat fine needle aspiration of the opposite thyroid lobe now
A positron emission tomography scan of the head and of the neck

answer:
A. ⭐ The operation's extent is decided by the nodes, and medullary carcinoma metastasises frequently, so the neck is mapped before the incision - lymph node dissection is indicated by evidence of nodal disease, and ⚠ "no palpable lymph nodes" on exam is not the same as no nodal disease. The case makes the same point twice over in Case 4: ⭐ "Don't forget neck ultrasound to look for lymph nodes."

A baseline calcitonin is drawn pre-operatively because ⭐ serum calcitonin is what you monitor for recurrence - a post-op value means little without one to compare against.

⚠ B is the tempting wrong answer. RAI belongs to follicular-cell disease and a low TSH; MTC arises from ⭐ parafollicular C cells, which do not take up iodine, and his TSH is normal regardless.

C biopsies the wrong lobe for a question about extent. D has no role the block gives it in initial planning.

lectureMeta: Q101-104, Case #3. Stems verbatim. Q101-102 keyed from the deck's MEN table; Q103-104 were taken live and have no answer slide.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 68-year-old male with a slowly enlarging right-sided neck mass over 6 months. Exam shows a firm ~3 cm right thyroid mass and no palpable lymph nodes. TSH normal. The FNAB comes back positive for malignancy - medullary carcinoma: not papillary, cells that look neuroendocrine, 2-4% of all thyroid cancers, arising from parafollicular C cells that produce calcitonin.

stem: What tests are needed for post operative monitoring/screening?

options.html: Thyroglobulin and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, checked serially
Serial serum calcitonin, with genetic testing of first-degree kin
An annual radioactive iodine whole body scan for many years after
Annual thyroid function tests alone, since the gland is now gone

answer:
B. Two separate jobs, and the stem names both - ⭐ monitoring the patient, and screening the family:

JobTestWhy
⭐ Monitor him⭐ serum calcitonin⭐ what the block has you follow for recurrence in MTC
⭐ Screen the familyRET testing⚠ 25% of MTC is syndromic, and the case's own route in was "RET Mutation Positive - MEN2a"

⚠ A is the trap, and it is a good one. ⭐ Thyroglobulin is the follow-up marker for DIFFERENTIATED thyroid cancer, which is what Case 2 was. Medullary carcinoma is ⚠ negative for thyroid markers - it makes calcitonin, not thyroglobulin - so a thyroglobulin here follows nothing.

C fails for the same reason RAI is not treatment here: ⭐ C cells do not take up iodine. D monitors the replacement, not the cancer.

This question was taken live and the session holds no answer for it, so the emphasis above is mine.

lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 4: The Rapidly Growing Mass)
lectureMeta: Q105-110, Case #4. Stems verbatim. Q105-109 keyed; Q110 was taken live.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A patient in her late 50s presented with a rapidly growing neck mass. Previously well, no family history, no radiation. TSH normal.

stem: What are your next steps?

options.html: Start levothyroxine suppression and review her again in three months' time
A radioactive iodine scan first, since the thyroid mass is the concern here
A thyroid and neck ultrasound, then consider CT and a metastatic workup
Reassure her, since a normal TSH makes a thyroid malignancy quite unlikely

answer:
C. The session's own words, verbatim:

  • Thyroid ultrasound
  • Don't forget neck ultrasound to look for lymph nodes
  • Consider CT scan, w/u for mets

⭐ The neck ultrasound is the part that gets forgotten, which is why the session says so in those words. The thyroid ultrasound scores the mass; ⭐ the neck ultrasound looks for the nodal disease that may be the initial presentation.

⚠ CT and a metastatic workup are on this list and were not on Case 1's, because rapid growth is an urgent presentation rather than a routine nodule.

B - ⭐ the RAI branch needs a LOW TSH, and hers is normal. A and D both treat an urgent presentation as a routine one.

lectureMeta: Q105-110, Case #4. Stems verbatim. Q105-109 keyed; Q110 was taken live.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A patient in her late 50s presented with a rapidly growing neck mass. Previously well, no family history, no radiation. TSH normal.

stem: What are some common urgent presentations of thyroid cancer?

options.html: Weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation and a slowed ankle relaxation
Shortness of breath, dysphagia, unexplained pain, symptoms of metastases
Palpitations, heat intolerance, a fine tremor and a widened pulse pressure
Muscle cramping, perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek or Trousseau

answer:
B. The case's own four:

Urgent presentation
⭐ Short of breath, unable to breatheairway narrowing / obstruction
Difficulty swallowing
⭐ Unexplained continued pain
⭐ Systemic symptoms of metastaseslung, bone

⭐ Notice what the list is made of: mechanical and systemic findings, not hormonal ones. A thyroid cancer is usually euthyroid, so ⚠ the urgency is structural or metastatic - the mass closing an airway, or disease already gone elsewhere.

A is hypothyroidism and C is thyrotoxicosis - ⚠ both are the wrong axis entirely. D is hypocalcemia, a post-thyroidectomy complication rather than a presentation.

flags.title: The case's list and the lecture note's list are not the same list
flags.html: 05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses tabulates urgent presentations as rapid growth, progressive dysphagia, stridor, a large solid fixed firm mass, diffuse enlargement and thyrotoxicosis alongside the mass - which is what the clinician finds. This case lists what the patient reports. ⭐ Dysphagia and airway compromise appear on both; unexplained continued pain and systemic symptoms of mets appear only here. Worth knowing both, since they are two views of one thing rather than a disagreement.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 4: The Rapidly Growing Mass)
lectureMeta: Q105-110, Case #4. Stems verbatim. Q105-109 keyed; Q110 was taken live.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A patient in her late 50s presented with a rapidly growing neck mass. Previously well, no family history, no radiation. TSH normal.

stem: What is your differential diagnosis for this thyroid mass?

options.html: Lymphoma, anaplastic carcinoma, and poorly differentiated carcinoma
A colloid nodule or a simple thyroid cyst, given that her TSH is normal
Hashimoto's thyroiditis, producing real nodules and also pseudonodules
Graves disease with a diffusely enlarged and highly vascular thyroid

answer:
A. The notes give exactly three, and ⚠ poorly differentiated carcinoma is the one most often dropped from the list:

The notes' differential
⭐ Lymphomawhy flow cytometry appears in the next answer
⭐ Anaplastic carcinomaaka undifferentiated carcinoma
⭐ Poorly differentiated carcinomasits between differentiated and anaplastic

⭐ All three are on the lecture note's URGENT column, and all three fit a rapidly growing mass in an older patient. ⭐ Anaplastic carcinoma is what a well-differentiated carcinoma becomes - sheets of malignant cells with no follicle formation, extending into the neck soft tissue.

⚠ A normal TSH argues nothing here - most thyroid cancers are euthyroid - which is what sinks B. C and D are both in the common column and neither grows this fast; D is a diffuse gland, not a mass.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 4: The Rapidly Growing Mass)
lectureMeta: Q105-110, Case #4. Stems verbatim. Q105-109 keyed; Q110 was taken live.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A patient in her late 50s presented with a rapidly growing neck mass. Previously well, no family history, no radiation. TSH normal.

stem: What are your next steps?

options.html: Start empirical external beam radiotherapy without waiting for tissue
Repeat the ultrasound in six weeks to confirm the growth is genuine
Fine needle aspiration alone, which is always preferred in the neck
Tissue sampling with flow cytometry, and ask the lab to rush the case

answer:
D. The session, verbatim: ⭐ "Talk to your pathologist", tissue sampling, could do fine needle aspiration biopsy or needle core biopsy, ⭐ flow cytometry (since could be lymphoma), ⭐ "Ask for rush on case".

⭐ Flow cytometry is on the list because lymphoma is on the differential - it is the test that separates row one of Q107 from rows two and three, and it needs the sample collected with that in mind.

⭐ "Ask for rush on case" is not a courtesy. Case 4 shows why: the tumour outran the 2-4 week molecular turnaround.

A treats before there is a diagnosis, and the treatment differs by row. B waits on a mass already declaring itself urgent. C is addressed below.

flags.title: The session contradicts the lecture note on needle core biopsy
flags.html:
05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses states that ⚠ "needle core biopsy is the wrong instrument for the neck" and routes neck → FNA. This session says the opposite for this presentation: ⭐ "Needle core biopsy preferred here over FNAB" in suspected anaplastic carcinoma, because it ⭐ needs a wide panel of markers, hence lots of tissue, and ⚠ FNAB may be limited - may not have material for markers.

⭐ Both are right about different questions. FNA wins for diagnosing a nodule, where it is safer and seeds no tumour. Needle core wins when the diagnosis needs immunohistochemistry and molecular markers off the same specimen, which is anaplastic carcinoma and lymphoma. The lecture note has been corrected to carry this exception.
