lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 4: The Rapidly Growing Mass)
lectureMeta: Q105-110, Case #4. Stems verbatim. Q105-109 keyed; Q110 was taken live.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A patient in her late 50s presented with a rapidly growing neck mass. Previously well, no family history, no radiation. TSH normal.

stem: Her tumour keeps growing, she needs intubation to protect her airway, and imaging finds lung metastases. What are the next steps?

options.html: Debulking surgery, to relieve the airway before anything else begins
Molecular testing for a BRAF mutation, to open up targeted therapy
Standard cytotoxic chemotherapy, started the same day she presents
A tracheostomy first, then radioactive iodine to the lung metastases

answer:
B. The case reasons by elimination, and it is worth following its order:

Option⚠ Why not
Tracheostomy⚠ not possible - the tumour is in the way
Standard chemotherapy⚠ would not act quickly enough
⭐ Targeted therapy⭐ the only option - but requires a BRAF mutation

So NGS testing is initiated, with a ⚠ 2-4 week turnaround - and that clock is the rest of the story. She deteriorated, MAiD was scheduled for 08:00, the molecular result returned at 18:30 the evening before, an emergency family meeting was held at 23:00, MAiD was cancelled and targeted therapy started. She responded, left the ICU, relapsed at a year, and gained another year with her family.

⭐ This is why the case says, just before this, "ask for rush on case."

D - ⚠ anaplastic carcinoma does not take up iodine, so RAI does nothing, and the tracheostomy was not available. A and C are the two the case rules out by name.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lecture: Approach to Thyroid Nodules (Case 4: The Rapidly Growing Mass)
lectureMeta: Q105-110, Case #4. Stems verbatim. Q105-109 keyed; Q110 was taken live.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A patient in her late 50s presented with a rapidly growing neck mass. Previously well, no family history, no radiation. TSH normal.

stem: Why not surgery?

options.html: Because she was not fit enough for any general anaesthetic at all
Because surgery is never offered once distant metastases are found
Because the airway had already been secured, so it added nothing
Because anaplastic disease infiltrates and cannot be fully removed

answer:
D. ⭐ Anaplastic carcinoma's growth pattern is the answer. It forms sheets of malignant cells with no follicle formation, shows angioinvasion, and extends into the neck soft tissue - and ⭐ that infiltration often prevents adequate surgical removal. There is no plane to take it out along.

⚠ The same fact explains the tracheostomy. The case says one was not possible; a tumour that has infiltrated the soft tissue of the neck is a tumour you cannot cut a safe airway through either. The two refusals have one cause.

⭐ It also explains the treatment that IS offered: external beam radiotherapy is the lecture note's answer for extensive extrathyroidal extension and anaplastic carcinoma, precisely because surgery is not.

B overstates it - metastatic disease alone does not rule surgery out in every tumour. A is never stated. C inverts the sequence: the airway was secured because the disease could not be resected.

The session poses this question and takes it live, so the reasoning above is mine, from 05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses.

lecture: Osteoporosis and Calcium Cases (Patient A, aged 69 to 78)
lectureMeta: Q111-121, one case followed across nine years. Stems verbatim from "Osteoporosis and Calcium Cases" (`approach_to_abnormal_calcium_osteoporosis_cases_post_after_`). **Keyed from the deck's own answer slides**, except Q114.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: Does patient A have osteoporosis?

options.html: No, because she has never sustained any fragility fracture at all
No, because her femoral neck T score of -2.4 sits above the cutoff
Yes, because her lumbar spine T score of -2.7 is lower than -2.5
Only if her calculated ten-year fracture risk also exceeds 20 per cent

answer:
C. ⭐ The case's definition gives three independent routes in, and meeting ANY one of them is the diagnosis:

RouteThreshold
⭐ A fragility fracture⚠ excluding skull, hands, feet and ankles, and any fracture with trauma
⭐ BMD T score⭐ < -2.5
High fracture risk> 20% over 10 years

⭐ Her lumbar spine is -2.7, so she is diagnosed on the second route and the other two never need to be reached.

⚠ B is the trap, and it is the common error: it reads only the femoral neck. ⭐ The lowest site counts - a normal hip does not undo an osteoporotic spine.

A and D both treat one route as though it were mandatory. ⭐ They are alternatives, not requirements - which is exactly why a fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis whatever the BMD says.

lectureMeta: Q111-121, one case followed across nine years. Stems verbatim from "Osteoporosis and Calcium Cases" (`approach_to_abnormal_calcium_osteoporosis_cases_post_after_`). **Keyed from the deck's own answer slides**, except Q114.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: How do you calculate fracture risk?

options.html: FRAX Canada, or the Canadian Radiologists and Osteoporosis Canada score
The T score on its own, read directly off the bone mineral density report
The Z score, which compares her against others of the same age and sex
The ratio of her lumbar spine T score to her femoral neck T score value

answer:
A. The case names two tools: ⭐ FRAX Canada and the ⭐ Canadian Radiologists and Osteoporosis Canada score (CaROC).

⭐ Risk is not the T score. The tools take the femoral neck T score combined with age and return a ten-year probability, which is a different quantity and the one treatment decisions are made on:

Ten-year riskCategory
< 10%low
⭐ 10-20%⭐ moderate
> 20%high

The lecture note adds the modifiers: a ⭐ prior fragility fracture after 40 moves her up one category, and ⭐ a prior hip or vertebral fracture, or more than one non-vertebral fragility fracture, puts her straight into high risk.

⚠ C is the one to be sure about. ⭐ The T score compares to a young adult and the Z score to age-matched peers - and ⭐ only the T score diagnoses. B confuses the input with the output. D is not a measure that exists.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: FRAX risk is 12% for major osteoporosis fractures and 2.9% for hip fractures. To treat or not to treat?

options.html: Suggest treatment, as her spine T score is below -2.5 and she is under 70
Do not treat, as 12% is below 15% and she has had no fragility fracture
Treat only after a hip or vertebral fracture, or more than two others
Defer treatment until her ten-year major fracture risk is beyond 20%

answer:
A. ⭐ Her lumbar spine T score of -2.7 is below -2.5, and she is 69. The lecture's decision to treat:

10-year risk or T scoreDecision
< 15% and T score > -2.5do NOT recommend pharmacotherapy
⭐ 15-19.9%, or T score ≤ -2.5 and age < 70⭐ SUGGEST pharmacotherapy (intermediate benefit)
≥ 20%, or T score ≤ -2.5 and age ≥ 70RECOMMEND pharmacotherapy (largest benefit)

⚠ B reads only the percentage. 12% alone would not reach treatment, but her T score puts her in the suggest row whatever FRAX says.

⭐ C is the lecture's strong recommendation to treat (hip, vertebral or more than 2 osteoporosis-related fractures, with greater consideration when the fracture was within 2 years). It is a reason to treat, not the only one. D waits for the high-risk band.

preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: What would be some treatment options for Patient A?

options.html: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone, which she already takes
An antiresorptive or a bone formation agent, chosen by fracture site
Hormone therapy with estrogen, which is first line at any age at all
Bone formation therapy first, then an antiresorptive agent afterwards

answer:
B. The case answers with a grid of agent against fracture site:

AntiresorptiveBone formation
Agents⭐ bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, [[zoledronatezoledronic acid]]) · denosumab · raloxifene · hormone therapy (estrogen)teriparatide · romosozumab

⭐ The columns of that grid are the fracture sites - vertebral, hip and non-vertebral - and not every agent has evidence at every site. The lecture note states the discriminator directly: ⭐ raloxifene and teriparatide have no hip fracture data, so ⚠ when the hip is the concern, reach for a bisphosphonate, denosumab or estrogen.

⭐ That is why the case lays this out as a table rather than a list. The question is never just which drug but which fracture are you trying to prevent.

A is what she is already doing, and it is not treatment. C names one option as though it were the only one. D inverts the sequence - ⭐ anabolic therapy is not where you start in a patient who has failed nothing yet.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: Patient A is started on oral alendronate. She takes it for 3 months, but develops intolerable abdominal pain due to it. What could be some other treatment options?

options.html: Halve the alendronate dose and continue with the same oral tablet
Stop all treatment, since she has now failed bisphosphonate therapy
Switch her to teriparatide or to romosozumab as the next agent used
Denosumab or zoledronate, neither of which is taken by mouth at all

answer:
D. The session's answer, in its own words: ⭐ "Both Denosumab and zoledronate can be used in patients who are unable to tolerate oral bisphosphonates."

⭐ The problem is the route, not the drug class. Her intolerance is abdominal - an upper GI effect of a tablet sitting in the esophagus and stomach - so the fix is to leave the oral route:

OptionRoute
⭐ denosumabsubcutaneous, 6-monthly
⭐ **[[zoledronateZoledronate]]**intravenous, yearly

⚠ Note that zoledronate is still a bisphosphonate. She has not failed the class; she has failed a formulation, and the same class given intravenously bypasses the problem entirely.

B makes exactly that error. A keeps the route that caused it. C escalates to anabolic therapy for an adverse effect rather than for treatment failure - ⭐ an intolerance is not a failure of efficacy.

preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: Patient A was transitioned to denosumab. She takes it for 5 years. However, she develops a hip fracture despite adherence to treatment. What treatment options are available now?

options.html: Bone formation therapy, since an antiresorptive agent has now failed
Continue the denosumab, since five years is not yet an adequate trial
Switch her to oral alendronate, which she has not completed properly
Add raloxifene alongside the denosumab she is already receiving now

answer:
A. ⚠ This is what treatment failure looks like - a fracture despite adherence - and it is one of the case's three indications for anabolic therapy:

⭐ Indications for bone formation therapy
Recent severe vertebral fractures
> 2 vertebral fractures and a T score < -2.5
⭐ Failure of anti-resorptive therapy

⭐ The rule that follows it is the one most often dropped, and the case states it explicitly: anabolic courses must be followed by an antiresorptive - at ⭐ 1 year for romosozumab and ⭐ 2 years for teriparatide.

⚠ Bone built by an anabolic is lost again if nothing holds it, which is why the sequence is anabolic then antiresorptive, never anabolic alone.

B ignores a fracture on treatment. C returns her to the drug she could not tolerate. D adds a second antiresorptive - ⭐ and raloxifene has no hip fracture data, which is the fracture she just had.

stem: You are considering bone formation therapies for her. What are some of the serious side effects of anabolic therapies?

options.html: Atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw, from both agents
Severe hypocalcemia and tetany, seen with each of the two anabolic drugs
Romosozumab raises cardiovascular risk; teriparatide has its cautions
Both agents commonly cause an upper gastrointestinal intolerance instead

answer:
C. The notes split them by agent, and they are not the same concern:

Agent⚠ The notes' entry
⭐ romosozumab⭐ increased risk of cardiovascular disease - ⚠ versus alendronate, NOT versus placebo
teriparatidePaget's disease · radiation treatment · bone malignancies · undiagnosed hypercalcemia

⭐ The comparator qualification on romosozumab is the whole point of that line. A risk that appears against an active comparator and not against placebo is a different claim from a drug simply causing harm, and the notes write it out precisely so the distinction is not lost.

A describes the antiresorptive class hazards. B is not the anabolic profile. D is the oral bisphosphonate problem from Q116.

flags.title: The case asks for side effects and lists contraindications
flags.html: The stem says "serious side effects", but the teriparatide entry - Paget's disease, radiation treatment, bone malignancies, undiagnosed hypercalcemia - is a list of settings in which the drug should not be used, not of effects it produces. Only the romosozumab line is an adverse effect. Flagged rather than corrected.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: You treat patient A with romosozumab for one year, followed by one dose of zoledronate. She is now 78 and received zoledronate one year ago. Her corrected calcium is 3.06, phosphate 0.65, magnesium 0.92, PTH 10.9 and 25-OH-D 80. What is the most important next step in management?

options.html: Start oral prednisone at 40 to 60 mg daily and then taper the dose
Give intravenous furosemide immediately to bring the calcium down
Repeat the calcium in three months, since she is asymptomatic right now
Admit her, and begin volume repletion with intravenous normal saline

answer:
D. ⭐ A corrected calcium of 3.06 is over the admission threshold, and the notes' sequence for acute hypercalcemia begins with fluid:

Step⭐ The notes' own wording
Admit⭐ usually if corrected Ca > 3 mmol/L
⭐ 1. Volume repletionassume a ⭐ 4 to 6 L deficit, replace with normal saline
2. Forced diuresis4-10 L NS + furosemide + K - ⚠ only after the patient is well hydrated
3. BisphosphonateIV zoledronate
4. calcitonin
5. prednisone40-60 mg/day then taper - for myeloma, vitamin D intoxication

⚠ B is the single most important distractor here. ⭐ A loop diuretic given before the patient is volume repleted makes the hypercalcemia worse, because it deepens the very dehydration that is concentrating the calcium. The notes write "only after patient well hydrated" for exactly this reason.

⭐ Her labs also name the mechanism. A PTH of 10.9 alongside a calcium of 3.06 is ⚠ inappropriately high, so this is PTH-dependent hypercalcemia, and the low phosphate of 0.65 fits - which is what sets up the next question.

A is reserved for myeloma and vitamin D toxicity. C defers a calcium that warrants admission.

lectureMeta: Q111-121, one case followed across nine years. Stems verbatim from "Osteoporosis and Calcium Cases" (`approach_to_abnormal_calcium_osteoporosis_cases_post_after_`). **Keyed from the deck's own answer slides**, except Q114.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: In addition to the above, what other investigations would you request, and in what order?

options.html: A parathyroid scan first, then a serum PTH level to confirm the source
A serum protein electrophoresis, then a skeletal survey looking for myeloma
A 24-hour urine for calcium and creatinine, for fractional excretion
Repeat the 25-OH vitamin D and magnesium before anything else is done

answer:
C. ⭐ The PTH has already told you this is PTH-dependent, so the remaining question is which PTH-dependent cause - and the urine is what separates them:

⭐ Fractional excretion of calcium = (Urine Ca × Serum Cr / 1000) / (Serum Ca × Urine Cr)

ResultPoints to
⭐ < 0.01⭐ FHH
⚠ 0.01 - 0.02⚠ overlap zone - 20% of FHH sits here
⭐ > 0.02⭐ likely primary hyperPTH

⚠ The result is only interpretable under three conditions, which the case lists: ⭐ off thiazides for 3 months, a normal magnesium, and a 25-OH-D above 50 nmol/L. Her 25-OH-D is 80 and her magnesium 0.92, so two are already satisfied.

⭐ This is why the stem asks "in what order". Imaging a parathyroid before establishing that the biochemistry is hyperPTH risks operating on an incidental adenoma in a patient who actually has FHH - and ⚠ FHH is not treated with surgery. That is what makes A the wrong order rather than merely a wrong test.

B investigates a PTH-independent cause the PTH has already excluded. D repeats two values that are already adequate.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Patient A is a 69-year-old lady, 166 cm, 72 kg, with a BMD showing lumbar spine T score -2.7 and femoral neck T score -2.4. She has been otherwise healthy, takes 4 servings of dairy and 2000 IU vitamin D3, and is on no medications.

stem: Patient A has received iv hydration and another dose of zoledronate. Her corrected calcium is now 2.69 mmol/L. (ULN <2.6 mmol/L). Her 24 hour urine calcium/creatinine ratio was 3.9%. A parathyroid scan identified a 2 cm left inferior parathyroid adenoma. What are indications for surgery for asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism?

options.html: A calcium more than 0.25 above the upper limit, or a T score under -2.5
A visible adenoma on imaging, which is on its own sufficient to operate
Any calcium above the upper limit of normal, at any age and any density
Age over 50, together with a calcium persistently above the normal range

answer:
A. ⭐ Her fractional excretion of 3.9% is well above 0.02, so this is primary hyperparathyroidism, not FHH - and the session then lists seven indications, any one of which is enough:

⭐ Indications for surgery in asymptomatic primary hyperPTHPatient A
Serum calcium > 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit⚠ no - 2.69 against an ULN of 2.6 is 0.09
⭐ BMD T score < -2.5 at LS, femoral neck, total hip or ⅓ radius⭐ YES - her spine was -2.9
Vertebral fractureno
Creatinine clearance < 60 mL/minnot stated
24-hour urine calcium > 10 mmol/day with increased stone risknot stated
Nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosisno
⚠ Age < 50no - she is 78

⭐ She qualifies, and on exactly one criterion. ⚠ Her calcium is nowhere near the threshold, which is the trap in reading only the first line - it is her bone density that earns the operation.

⚠ Age cuts both ways. ⭐ Under 50 is a reason to operate; over 50 and asymptomatic is a reason to watch. D inverts this and would operate on her because she is 78.

B treats the scan as the indication - ⭐ imaging localises the adenoma, it does not decide the operation. C drops the 0.25 margin, which would send nearly every mild case to surgery.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Tim Andrews is a 57-year-old Caucasian male, ⭐ two weeks post laparoscopic lysis of adhesions for a partial bowel obstruction. His wife brings him in with three days of diarrhea, fevers and palpitations, and ⚠ found him confused and hallucinating this morning. HPI - surgery uncomplicated, discharged day 1; loose watery stools 3-4 times a day from 3-4 days post-op, no blood or mucus; ⭐ daily fevers to ~39 °C since 6-7 days post-discharge, taking Tylenol; a week of upper abdominal discomfort of uncertain quality; palpitations, intermittent breathlessness, and a pulse his wife found very fast. ⭐ His wife reports a SIX-MONTH history of aggressive behaviour and decreased sleep, with ⭐ a 10 kg weight loss DESPITE an increased appetite. Medical history - depression; open appendectomy 5 years ago. Medications - citalopram 20 mg od; no allergies. Family history - ⚠ both parents died in a car accident in his early teens, so it is unobtainable. Social - raised on a farm in Northern Ontario, construction worker, very demanding job and a major source of stress, off work since surgery; smokes 1/2 pack/day for 30 years; ⭐ does not drink alcohol.

stem: Based on the limited information you have, what differential diagnoses (DDx) are you considering?

options.html: Post-operative sepsis alone, with the weight loss explained by his recent surgery
Delirium tremens from alcohol withdrawal, given the confusion and the tachycardia
Thyrotoxicosis tipping into storm, alongside post-operative sepsis and colitis
Serotonin syndrome from his citalopram, accounting for the fever and agitation

answer:
C. ⭐ The six-month history is the half of the case that the acute presentation keeps hiding. Read on its own, the last three days are a post-operative patient with fever and diarrhea. ⚠ Read with the six months in front of it, the acute illness becomes a decompensation of something that has been running since before the operation.

From the six monthsthyrotoxicosis feature
⭐ 10 kg lost DESPITE increased appetite⭐ the block's single most specific pairing
aggressive behaviour, decreased sleepemotional lability, insomnia
From the three daysthyrotoxicosis feature
palpitations, a very fast pulsetachycardia
loose stools 3-4x daily, no blood or mucus⭐ hyperdefecation - "patients call it diarrhea"
fevers, breathlessness, confusion⚠ the urgent form: thyroid storm

⭐ The block names the precipitant explicitly. Storm is "usually precipitated by a homeostatically stressful event" - and an abdominal operation two weeks ago is exactly that.

⚠ This is a differential, not a diagnosis, and the post-operative causes stay on it. Intra-abdominal sepsis and ⭐ Clostridioides difficile colitis both fit a post-op patient with fever and watery diarrhea, and ⭐ either could be the thing that tipped him into storm. They are co-listed, not displaced.

A is on the list but cannot account for six months of weight loss with a rising appetite. B is the trap the social history is there to close: ⚠ his wife states he does not drink. D is worth a thought on a serotonergic drug, but he is on citalopram monotherapy, unchanged, and it explains none of the six-month history.

flags.title: The case notes carry no answers, and says nothing about why
flags.html: ⚠ This is a different situation from the Week 1 in-class session at Q122-127. Those notes stated that written answers are never provided; this one makes no such claim - it simply contains none. The document is the case, its questions, and nothing else. ⚠ Part 2's investigation results are absent too, so the labs the whole case is building toward were only ever shown in the room. Every answer below is therefore reasoned from the Week 2 notes and labelled as mine. ⭐ The session's take is the authority, not this.

flags.title: The case's word for the stools is transcribed, not corrected
flags.html: It says "diarrhea" throughout. ⭐ The block is explicit that thyrotoxic hyperdefecation is what "patients call diarrhea" - which is the point of the finding, and why it is not evidence for a primary bowel cause. ⭐ Transcribed as the case writes it.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Examination findings. ⭐ Temperature 39.5 °C, ⭐ pulse 132 regular, ⭐ blood pressure 110/52, SaO₂ 88% on room air and 95% on 2 L NP. ⚠ Patient somnolent, rouses to voice, unable to give history due to confusion, but able to identify himself and his partner. Head and neck - dry mucous membranes; ⭐ thyroid non-tender with apparent GLOBAL enlargement; no lymphadenopathy. CVS - tachycardic sinus rhythm, normal S1 and S2, no murmurs or rubs, peripheral pulses palpable. Resp - chest clear, no wheezing or crackles. Abdomen - diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound; incision sites clean and dry; liver and spleen not palpable. Extremities - ⭐ +2 pitting edema to mid-shins bilaterally, ⭐ warm, with normal capillary refill. Neuro - cranial nerves unremarkable, power normal, ⭐ reflexes +3 and symmetric, sensory exam unremarkable, gait deferred. Skin - dry, no rashes, no obvious nail issues.

stem: Does the above information expand or refine your DDx?

options.html: It refines it, with a symmetric goiter, a wide pulse pressure and brisk reflexes
It expands it, since the pitting edema points to a new and separate cardiac disease
Neither, since these findings are non-specific two weeks after an abdominal operation
It refines it toward hypothyroidism, given his somnolence and the pitting edema

answer:
A. ⭐ Every free discriminator the block offers was available at the bedside, and all of them point the same way.

FindingReads as
⭐ thyroid "apparent GLOBAL enlargement", non-tender⭐ a SYMMETRIC goiter - the block's pointer to Graves disease, and non-tender excludes subacute thyroiditis
⭐ BP 110/52 - a pulse pressure of 58⭐ WIDE - thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroidism
⭐ reflexes +3brisk - ⚠ the opposite of the Woltman sign
⭐ warm extremitiessoft, warm skin of thyrotoxicosis
pulse 132, temperature 39.5 °Ctachycardia, and a fever beyond his post-op baseline
⚠ somnolent and confused⚠ the "mental health crisis" the block lists under the urgent form
+2 pitting edema, SaO₂ 88%⭐ heart failure - which the block lists under BOTH columns, and specifically as HIGH-OUTPUT failure in thyrotoxicosis

⭐ The edema is the finding most likely to send you the wrong way, which is why B and D are both built on it. ⚠ Thyrotoxicosis causes heart failure with edema and orthopnea in the block's own table - it is not evidence against the diagnosis, and it is not a second unrelated illness.

⭐ What it does not do is settle the cause. Symmetric goiter favours Graves, but the block puts RAI uptake as "the best single test for the ETIOLOGY", and ⚠ a two-day test is not what you do to a confused, febrile, tachycardic patient.

B promotes a consequence to a separate diagnosis. C would be defensible for the fever and the abdominal tenderness alone, but ⚠ not for a goiter, a wide pulse pressure and +3 reflexes together. D inverts every thyroid sign on the list: hypothyroidism runs a narrow pulse pressure, slow-relaxing reflexes and cool skin.

flags.title: The pulse pressure is not given, only the blood pressure
flags.html: ⭐ The case notes record "Blood pressure 110/52" without comment. That is a pulse pressure of 58, and the block makes the width the discriminator, not the systolic. ⚠ Transcribed as written - the arithmetic is left to the reader, as the source leaves it.

stem: What investigations would you like to order and why?

options.html: A radioactive iodine uptake scan first, to establish the cause before treating
Anti-TPO and thyroid ultrasound first, as the highest-yield initial thyroid tests
TSH with free T4 and T3, plus septic workup, electrolytes, ECG and cultures
TSH alone, stopping there if it returns within the normal reference interval

answer:
C. ⭐ The block's rule is one line: "TSH case-finds, free hormone confirms" - and in suspected thyrotoxicosis you order FT4 and FT3 together, because ⭐ FT3 grades severity, which is the question in a patient this sick.

TestWhy here
⭐ serum TSHcase-finding; expected LOW
⭐ free T4 + free T3⭐ confirms, and FT3 grades how severe
TRAbsensitive and specific for Graves, a simple blood test - ⚠ but not covered by OHIP
CBC, electrolytes, glucose, renal and liverthe diarrhea, the vomiting, the drugs
⭐ blood cultures, C. difficile toxin, CXR⭐ find the precipitant - it is a separate question from the thyroid
ECGregular at 132, but ⚠ atrial fibrillation is what the block links to thyrotoxicosis

⭐ Many labs add FT4 and FT3 reflexively once TSH returns abnormal, so the confirmatory step may already be running.

A is the right test for the wrong moment: the block calls RAI uptake the best test for etiology, and also ⚠ "a 2-day test" - the cause can wait, the treatment cannot. B names the two tests the block specifically says to leave alone: "anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin, and ultrasound are the tests to leave alone." D is the correct algorithm applied to the wrong patient - ⚠ the block's one stated exception to stopping at a normal TSH is suspected central disease, and in any case a normal TSH in a patient this unwell warrants FT4 alongside it.

stem: What would you do for this patient in the ER while awaiting the lab results?

options.html: Levothyroxine replacement started promptly, alongside intravenous fluids and oxygen
Oxygen, fluids, cooling and a beta-blocker, while also treating the precipitant
Observation on the ward with antipyretics alone until the thyroid results return
Immediate total thyroidectomy, since storm is the standard indication for surgery

answer:
B. ⭐ You do not wait for the TSH. He is febrile to 39.5, tachycardic at 132, hypoxic at 88% on room air, dehydrated and confused - and the block's supportive treatment is available now:

DoWhy
⭐ beta-blockers⭐ the block's named treatment for storm, and its supportive treatment for thyrotoxicosis generally: "palpitations, tachycardia, tremor"
oxygen88% on room air, corrected to 95% on 2 L
IV fluidsdry mucous membranes, days of losses
cooling and antipyretics39.5 °C
⭐ cultures, then treat the precipitant⭐ the storm does not settle while the thing that caused it runs
a monitored bedconfusion, hypoxia, rate of 132

A is the treatment for the opposite disease. C is the error the case is built to punish - ⚠ the block calls storm an "urgent form" and lists it alongside myxedema coma, and his confusion is already an organ manifestation. D misreads the one surgical indication the block gives: total thyroidectomy is reserved for ⚠ storm "refractory to medical treatment" - which cannot be said of a patient who has not yet had any.

stem: WHich of the following is true regarding bone diseases?

options.html: Paget’s disease involves a defect in bone mineralization while osteomalacia involve a defect in bone remodeling
Cotton wool appearance is a clinical presentation of osteogenesis imperfecta
Teriparatide can be used to treat Paget’s disease.
Hearing loss can be a clinical presentation for both Paget’s disease and osteogenesis imperfecta.

answer: The correct answer is D. Skull abnormalities in Paget’s disease and osteogenesis imperfecta can lead to compression and damage of cranial nerves, resulting in hearing loss. Osteomalacia involves a defect in bone mineralization while Paget’s disease involves a defect in bone remodeling. Cotton wool appearance is seen in Paget’s disease, representing increased and abnormal bone remodeling. Bone formation therapies, such as teriparatide, should be avoided in Paget’s disease since there is already increased bone formation.

stem: A patient presents with decreased serum calcium and phosphates, with increased alkaline phosphatase. Upon physical exam, you also discover proximal muscle weaknessYou observe pseudofractures in the left femoral neck on radiography. Which of the following bone diseases does this patient most likely have.

options.html: Paget’s disease
Osteoporosis
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Osteomalacia

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 07 - Overview of Metabolic Bone Disease. The lecture says the lab panel separates the three metabolic bone diseases before imaging, and this panel is osteomalacia's signature. Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect from vitamin D deficiency:

  • calcium AND phosphate are both low, with a high ALP
  • it causes proximal myopathy, which osteoporosis never does
  • the x-ray shows pseudofractures (Looser zones)
  • A Paget's has normal calcium and phosphate with a very high ALP, and a cotton-wool, expanded, dense bone picture.
  • B osteoporosis has a normal panel and is indolent until a fragility fracture, with no myopathy.
  • C osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen defect with a normal panel, blue sclerae and fractures from birth.

Which laboratory pattern is expected?

Calcium normal, phosphate normal, ALP normal
Calcium low, phosphate high, ALP normal

answer: The correct answer is C. Malabsorption causes vitamin D deficiency, and the result is osteomalacia: a mineralisation defect. Labs: low calcium and phosphate, raised ALP, low urine calcium; the proximal myopathy is what separates it from osteoporosis. Normal calcium and phosphate with a very high ALP is Paget's (B); a normal panel fits osteogenesis imperfecta (D); low calcium with high phosphate is hypoparathyroidism (E).

stem:
A 74-year-old man says his hat no longer fits and he is going deaf. His right tibia is bowed and warm to touch. ALP is markedly raised; calcium and phosphate are normal. Skull x-ray shows a cotton-wool appearance.

What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.html: Daily teriparatide
High-dose vitamin D
Observation only
IV zoledronate
Subcutaneous denosumab

answer: The correct answer is D. This is Paget's disease: very high ALP with normal calcium and phosphate, increased hat size, deafness, warmth over bone. Skull involvement is an indication to treat even without symptoms (C). Treatment is analgesia and bisphosphonates, with IV zoledronate better than oral. Bone-forming agents such as teriparatide are contraindicated, since formation is already disordered (A), and denosumab has not been studied (E).

Perform a radioactive iodine uptake test

Perform a fine needle aspiration biopsy

stem:
A 46-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm thyroid nodule found on examination. She has mild heat intolerance. Her TSH is 0.05 mIU/L.

What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.html: Radioactive iodine uptake and scan
Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration
Referral for hemithyroidectomy
Serum calcitonin level
Repeat TSH in six months

answer: The correct answer is A. The first test for a nodule is the TSH, and a low TSH sends you to a radioactive iodine scan before any ultrasound. A hot nodule is benign: treat the hyperthyroidism and stop there. A cold nodule goes back to ultrasound and TI-RADS scoring, and only then to FNA if it meets the size cut-off (B).

stem:
A 52-year-old man's thyroid nodule is aspirated. The cytology report reads "follicular neoplasm" (Bethesda IV).

Why can the aspirate not say whether this is an adenoma or a carcinoma?

options.html: Follicular carcinoma has nuclear grooves that aspirates miss
Most follicular aspirates are too scant to be diagnostic
Follicular lesions can only be typed with calcitonin staining
Carcinoma is defined by invasion, which cytology cannot show
Only needle core biopsy can show the nuclear atypia involved

answer: The correct answer is D. Follicular carcinoma is like a follicular adenoma but with invasion: capsular, lymphatic or angioinvasion. It lacks nuclear atypia, and the lecture puts it plainly: no difference in nuclei, so FNA cannot distinguish them. Contrast papillary carcinoma, whose nuclear features are diagnostic on FNA. Calcitonin is the medullary marker (C).

stem:
A 34-year-old woman who had a pheochromocytoma removed last year now has a thyroid nodule. The resected nodule shows nests of cells with amyloid deposition, negative for thyroid markers.

Which serum test is used to monitor her for recurrence?

options.html: Thyroglobulin
TSH
PTH
Anti-TPO antibodies
Calcitonin

answer: The correct answer is E. Pheochromocytoma plus a C-cell tumour is MEN 2 (25% of medullary carcinoma). Medullary carcinoma arises from calcitonin-producing parafollicular C-cells, its amyloid is calcitonin, and it stains negative for thyroid (follicular) markers such as thyroglobulin, which is why thyroglobulin (A) is useless here. The lecture: monitor serum calcitonin for recurrence.

stem: A patient presents acutely with perioral paresthesia, carpo-pedal spasm and palpitations. Their correct serum calcium is 1.8 mmol/l. Which of the following would be the most appropriate to administer in this acute setting.

options.html: Calcitriol
Furosemide
Thiazide diuretic
Calcium gluconate

answer: The correct answer is D. Calcium gluconate should be used to treat acute hypocalcemia. Calcitriol and thiazide diuretics are used to manage chronic hypocalcemia. Furosemide promotes the excretion of calcium, thus should be avoided in hypocalcemia.

stem:
A 50-year-old man has a lump on his neck found at physical examination. A fine needle aspirate of this lump shows a follicular neoplasm of the thyroid. He undergoes a total thyroidectomy. Within a day following surgery, he is noted to have tingling sensations and neuromuscular irritability.

Which of the following lab tests should be ordered immediately to determine further therapy for this man?

options.html: TSH level
PTH level
T4  and T3 levels
Serum calcium and albumin levels
Calcitonin level

answer:
The correct answer is D. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hyperparathyroidism and Hypoparathyroidism.

From the review session. The class read the calcium as low, from iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism after the thyroidectomy, and the presenter agreed.

Tingling and neuromuscular irritability a day after total thyroidectomy is hypocalcaemia from post-surgical hypoparathyroidism, the commonest cause (75%). What decides treatment now is the albumin-corrected calcium: IV calcium gluconate if it is < 1.9 mmol/L with neurological or cardiac signs. A PTH (B) confirms the cause but does not decide the next dose; thyroid hormones and calcitonin (A, C, E) are irrelevant to the symptoms.

stem:
A 67-year-old woman with cirrhosis has a total serum calcium of 2.10 mmol/L and an albumin of 25 g/L.

What is her corrected calcium?

options.html: 1.8 mmol/L
2.1 mmol/L
2.25 mmol/L
2.4 mmol/L
2.7 mmol/L

answer: The correct answer is D. Each 1 g/L fall in albumin below 40 lowers the measured calcium by 0.02 mmol/L. Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin) = 2.10 + 0.02 × 15 = 2.10 + 0.30 = 2.40 mmol/L, which is normal. Her apparent hypocalcaemia is the low albumin.

stem:
A 66-year-old smoker with a lung mass is confused, thirsty and dry. His corrected calcium is 3.4 mmol/L and PTH is suppressed.

What is the first step in treatment?

options.html: IV normal saline
IV furosemide
Oral hydrochlorothiazide
Subcutaneous calcitonin
Oral prednisone 40-60 mg

answer: The correct answer is A. Admit anyone with corrected calcium > 3 mmol/L. Hypercalcaemia causes a large water deficit, so step 1 is volume repletion with normal saline (assume a 4-6 L deficit). Furosemide (B) only comes once he is well hydrated, and thiazides are never used, since they raise calcium (C). IV zoledronate is step 3; calcitonin (D) is only a bridge; prednisone (E) is for myeloma, lymphoma, sarcoid or vitamin D toxicity.

stem:
A day after a total thyroidectomy, a 48-year-old woman has perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm. Her corrected calcium is 1.72 mmol/L and her ECG shows a prolonged QT interval.

What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.html: Oral calcium carbonate
IV calcium gluconate
Oral calcitriol alone
Hydrochlorothiazide
Observation, since it is expected after surgery

answer: The correct answer is B. Acute treatment is indicated when the corrected calcium is < 1.9 mmol/L with neurological (tetany, carpopedal spasm) or cardiac (prolonged QT) signs: IV 10% calcium gluconate, with cardiac monitoring and correction of magnesium. Oral calcium, calcitriol and thiazides (A, C, D) are for the chronic phase.

stem: Your patient with osteoporosis and a previous hip fracture has been treated with romosozumab for 6 months. Their bone mineral density has been stable and they experienced no fracture events so far. How would you continue the management?

options.html: Romosozumab seem to be working well for the patient, so you will keep them on romosozumab until their osteoporosis progress or they experience a fracture
Add teriparatide to the treatment
Follow up with zoledronic acid after 1 year of romosozumab therapy.
Follow up with raloxifene after 1 year of romosozumab therapy.

answer: The correct answer is C. Romosozumab, a bone formation therapy, should be followed with anti-resorptive therapy after 1 year. Both zoledronic acid and raloxifene are anti-resorptive therapies, but raloxifene is not effective for hip fractures.

stem:
A 70-year-old postmenopausal woman presents for routine follow-up. She has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. She does not smoke, drinks alcohol occasionally, and has a diet low in calcium. She has no history of fragility fractures. A routine DEXA scan shows a T-score of −2.7 at the femoral neck, and her 10-year FRAX score is >20%.

What is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient?

options.html: Reassure her and repeat the DEXA scan in 1 year
Lifestyle measures only: calcium, vitamin D, exercise, fall prevention
Start hormone replacement therapy to improve bone density
Refer to orthopedics to assess for vertebral fracture
Start an oral bisphosphonate alongside those lifestyle measures

answer:
The correct answer is E. No written rationale in the deck; reasoning ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis.

A T-score ≤ −2.5 diagnoses osteoporosis, and a 10-year fracture risk > 20% is high risk, which means treat with a drug (the SR slide: < 10% lifestyle, moderate individualise, > 20% treat). Calcium and vitamin D alone do not raise BMD enough (B), so lifestyle measures go alongside a bisphosphonate, not instead of it. HRT alone (C) drops the lifestyle measures, and there is no fracture to refer (D).

stem:
A 78-year old female presented with back pain that was precipitated by lifting her 25 pound grandson. She has generally been in good health and is on no medications. Her menopause occurred at age 51 years and she received hormone replacement therapy for 2 years. She does not currently smoke but has a 20 pack year history of smoking. She drinks two cups of coffee a day and is lactose intolerant. Physical examination is normal except for a mild thoracic kyphosis. Lab tests including a CBC, TSH, serum calcium, albumin, and serum 25-OHD are normal. Thoraco-lumbar spine x-rays revealed two thoracic vertebral compression fractures.

I) The most likely diagnosis in this patient is:

options.html: Paget’s disease of bone
Metastatic disease
Postmenopausal osteoporosis
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Cushing’s syndrome

answer:
The correct answer is C. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis.

From the review session. Low-trauma vertebral fractures in a postmenopausal woman with normal labs are osteoporosis until proven otherwise.

A vertebral compression fracture from lifting a child is a fragility fracture, which diagnoses osteoporosis on its own, whatever the BMD. Normal calcium excludes primary hyperparathyroidism (D); normal labs and a low-trauma mechanism make Paget's (A), metastases (B) and Cushing's (E) unlikely.

stem:
A 78-year old white female presented with back pain that was precipitated by lifting her 25 pound grandson. She has generally been in good health and is on no medications. Her menopause occurred at age 51 years and she received hormone replacement therapy for 2 years. She does not currently smoke but has a 20 pack year history of smoking. She drinks two cups of coffee a day and is lactose intolerant. Physical examination is normal except for a mild thoracic kyphosis. Lab tests including a CBC, TSH, serum calcium, albumin, and serum 25-OHD are normal. Thoraco-lumbar spine x-rays revealed two thoracic vertebral compression fractures.

II) Which of the following treatments would be most effective in preventing future fractures:

options.html: Hormone replacement therapy
Nasal calcitonin
A bisphosphonate
Sodium fluoride
Increased dietary calcium and vitamin D intake

answer:
The correct answer is C. No written rationale in the deck; reasoning ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis.

Two vertebral fractures put her at high risk, and a bisphosphonate prevents vertebral, hip and non-vertebral fractures. Calcium and vitamin D (E) are needed alongside, but are not enough on their own. Estrogen also has fracture data in the lecture's table (A), but it is not the choice for a 78-year-old.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman breaks her distal radius falling from standing height. A DEXA scan shows a femoral neck T-score of −1.9.

What is the correct diagnosis?

options.html: Osteopenia, with a repeat DEXA scan in five years
No diagnosis until the T-score reaches −2.5
Osteomalacia until vitamin D is checked
Osteoporosis only if the Z-score is also low
Osteoporosis, on the fragility fracture alone

answer: The correct answer is E. Osteoporosis is diagnosed by any one of: a fragility fracture (whatever the BMD), a T-score ≤ −2.5, or a 10-year fracture risk > 20%. A wrist fracture from standing height counts; fractures of the skull, hands, feet and ankles, and genuinely traumatic ones, do not. The T-score (against a young adult) is the one used for diagnosis, not the Z-score (D).

stem: A baby was born with anencephaly. During which week of embryogenesis did this defect most likely occur.

options.html: Week 1
Week 2
Week 3
Week 4

answer: The correct answer is D. Neurulation is completed in week 4, during which the caudal and rostral ends. Failure of the caudal end to close results in anencephaly.

But the explanation says "failure of the caudal end to close results in anencephaly". 08 - Embryology & Histology says it is the cranial neuropore (closing on day 24) that fails in anencephaly; failure of the caudal neuropore (day 26) gives spina bifida. stem: If a teratogen is introduced during week 6 of embryogenesis, which of the following will be the most likely effect on the developing embryo.

options.html: The teratogen either kills the embryo or has no effect on it
The teratogen could induce major congenital heart abnormalities
The teratogen could induce minor morphological abnormalities
The teratogen could induce minor functional abnormalities.

answer: The correct answer is B. Week 3-8 is the most critical period for cell differentiation, organogenesis, and morphogenesis, thus a teratogen exposure at week 6 can potentially introduce a major congenital abnormality. Teratogens have an all or nothing effect during the first 2 weeks of development. Teratogens introduced during the fetal period (week 9 onwards) could potentially introduce minor morphological and functional abnormalities.

stem: Which of the following is untrue about thyroid hormone production?

options.html: The Na+/I- symporter (NIS) transports sodium and iodine into follicular cells
Transporting iodine into the colloid space allows the thyroid gland to trap iodine
Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) transports iodine out of the cell and then oxidatively couples iodine to thyroglobulin
TSH increases the action of NIS and TPO, and increases thyroglobulin production
Pinocytosis transports iodinated thyroglobulin into the cell, where it is broken into T3 and T4 by lysosomal enzymes and then secreted

answer:
The correct answer is C. TPO does not transport iodine - pendrin does. The basics of thyroid hormone production:

  • NIS transports sodium and iodine into follicular cells
  • Pendrin transports iodine from the follicular cell into the colloid
  • In doing so, pendrin allows the gland to store iodine without an insurmountable iodine concentration inside the follicular cells
  • TPO oxidatively couples iodine to thyroglobulin
  • TPO couples MIT/DIT to make T3/T4
  • Pinocytosis brings iodinated thyroglobulin back into the cell in lysosomes, where enzymes break the thyroglobulin down into T3 and T4 for secretion

See 01 - Thyroid and Parathyroid Gland Physiology.

stem: Which of the following is untrue of circulating thyroid hormone?

options.html: 90% of secreted thyroid hormone is T4
Peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 occurs primarily via deiodinase 3
1% of T3 and 0.1% of T4 is free in plasma
Thyroid binding globulin is the most important transporter of thyroid hormone
Thyroid hormone binds nuclear receptors

answer:
The correct answer is B. Peripheral conversion of T4 → T3 is by deiodinases 1 and 2 - D1 and D2 are the activators. D3 inactivates thyroid hormone, converting T4 → rT3 and T3 → T2.

Thyroid hormone is tyrosine-based and contains an aromatic ring, which lets it enter cells to bind nuclear receptors. TBG binds 75% of circulating thyroid hormone. 90% of hormone produced by the gland is T4.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a cause of hyperthyroidism?

options.html: Taking dessicated thyroid hormone supplements
Graves' disease
Post-partum thyroiditis
Post-traumatic thyroiditis
Hot nodule
Endemic goitre
Pregnancy
Radiation-induced thyroiditis

answer:
The correct answer is F. All the listed answers except endemic goitre can cause hyperthyroidism. Endemic goitre by definition arises from iodine deficiency: the gland enlarges (hence goitre) but there is no hormone production. Hypertrophy occurs because the lack of T3/T4 negative feedback on the pituitary drives high TSH.

Of the others: C, D and H cause thyroid irritation, inducing release of the thyroid's preformed reserve; A is exogenous hormone; in B (Graves disease) antibodies cause inappropriate TSH-receptor activation; in G beta-HCG, structurally homologous to TSH, stimulates the gland; E is signalling-independent synthesis of thyroid hormone, not an autoimmune process.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Vitamin D intoxication

answer: The correct answer is C. Because PTH is normal (i.e. inappropriately unsuppressed in the face of hypercalcemia) and phosphate is low, we can rule out vitamin D intoxication and hypercalcemia of malignancy - in both of those, PTH should be suppressed by the high calcium. In multiple myeloma you would expect increased phosphate. Thus this is primary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: Which of the following is untrue about Graves's disease?

options.html: The constellation of signs of this disorder includes pre-tibial myxedema
Pathologic features include scalloping of the thyroid gland and a gland that weighs more than 100g
The antibodies that cause this disorder cause hyperthyroidism by blocking the TSH receptor
RAI uptake and scan will show diffuse iodine uptake within the gland
Patients with this condition can fluctuate between hyper- and hypothyroidism

answer:
The correct answer is C. In Graves disease, thyroid-stimulating antibodies bind the TSH receptor and either stimulate it (causing hyperthyroidism) or, less commonly, block it (causing hypothyroidism) - which is why patients may fluctuate between hyper- and hypothyroid states. Stimulation, not blockade, is the mechanism of the hyperthyroidism, so C is untrue as written.

The TSH-receptor antibodies do not destroy the gland. The entire gland is affected, hence diffuse uptake on RAI scan. Pathologic features include scalloping of the colloid, finger-like projections in the follicles, and an enlarged gland (>100 g).

stem: Which of the following is NOT a cause of hypothyroidism:

options.html: Hashimoto's disease
Lithium
Removal of the thyroid gland
Iodine deficiency
Iodine supplementation
Human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG)

answer: The correct answer is F. All the listed items except F cause hypothyroidism. Iodine deficiency causes goiter and decreased hormone production; excess iodine suppresses hormone production via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect. HCG, however, is a cause of hyperthyroidism - it shares structural homology with TSH.

stem: You have recently diagnosed a 52-year-old patient with hypothyroidism. She comes to see you to discuss treatment and next steps. Select 3 of the following to discuss with this patient regarding the management of her hypothyroidism:

options.html: You advise her to stop taking lithium because it is exacerbating or causing her hypothyroidism
You recommend that she take levothyroxine to supplement her T4
You warn her about the signs of excessive thyroid hormone supplementation, including sweating, fast heartbeat, tremor, anxiety, and diarrhea
You impress upon her the importance of taking hormone supplementation to reduce the risk of mental retardation
You tell her to increase the dose of all of her other medications by 1.5x to compensate for an expected increase in BMR
You tell her that she will have to repeat blood work so that you can be sure supplementation is adequate

answer:
The correct answers are B, C, F. Management involves replacing thyroid hormone with levothyroxine or liothyronine, or "natural supplement" desiccated thyroid (B). The goal is to titrate to a normal TSH, which requires follow-up blood work (F). Side effects of supplementation are extension effects of the hormone, and patients should be alert to the sympathetic and cardiovascular risks of excess (C).

A is wrong: you should not tell her to stop lithium solely because she has hypothyroidism. E is wrong: do not adjust other drug doses until you know the supplementation is working, at which point it may become necessary. D is wrong: hypothyroidism in adults does not cause mental retardation (that is congenital hypothyroidism), although it may cause decreased mentation and concentration.

stem: Which of the following is untrue regarding RAI uptake and scan?

options.html: A normal test shows 25% of administered iodine is taken up by the thyroid gland
The scan can identify hot nodules, cold nodules, or diffuse pathology
Hot nodules can be identified because they function autonomously from the rest of the gland
The scan is safe for use in pregnancy
Cold nodules are more worrisome for cancer than hot nodules

answer:
The correct answer is D. The scan is contraindicated in pregnancy because it uses radioactive iodine.

The RAI uptake and scan administers 123-I and evaluates uptake (how much iodine enters the gland) then scans the distribution within it. Normally the gland takes up 25% of the administered dose. Distribution should be uniform in a normal test, or in pathology affecting the entire gland such as Graves' or Hashimoto's. Hot nodules are identifiable because they function autonomously - they do not need TSH to drive iodine uptake, whereas the rest of the gland does and therefore takes up nothing (cold gland). Hot nodules are generally not worrisome for cancer; cold nodules are.

stem: A 39-year-old woman comes to your office complaining of a 2-month history of 10lb unintentional weight loss, heat intolerance, and sweating. She is worried that she may be experiencing premature menopause, although her periods continue to be regular. On physical exam, her HR is 88 and pulse is irregular; her RR is 16; her BP is 144/65 sitting; you hear a grade II systolic ejection murmur in the aortic area; her skin is warm and moist; and she has a noticeable stare. On palpation of the thyroid gland, you find that it is slightly large. What is the most likely cause for this patient's presentation?

options.html: Acute storm from Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Graves' Disease
Post-viral thyroiditis
Pregnancy
She may have premature menopause, but more tests are required to be sure

answer:
The correct answer is B. The question asks for the most likely etiology. All the options are possible, but Graves disease is most likely given the patient's age and sex.

An acute storm would not produce 2 months of symptoms - the same objection applies to post-viral thyroiditis, and she gives no history of a preceding viral infection. Pregnancy is possible but unlikely given continued regular periods. Finally, thyroid disease is more likely than pregnancy given the physical exam findings.

stem: Which of the following is untrue about calcitonin?

options.html: It is a 34 amino acid peptide
It is produced by C cells of the thyroid gland
It is produced by cells of neural developmental origin
It functions in bone by preventing osteoblast activity
It functions in kidney by preventing reabsorption of calcium in the DCT

answer:
The correct answer is D. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast resorption of bone, not osteoblast activity. It is a hormone of unknown clinical importance, but we do know:

  • Calcitonin is 34 amino acids
  • Produced by C cells (neural origin)
  • Overall function appears to be to decrease circulating calcium
  • Inhibits osteoclast resorption of bone
  • Inhibits calcium resorption at the DCT

stem: \* All of the following would be appropriate treatments for hypercalcemia EXCEPT:

options.html: Fluid hydration
Thiazide diuretics
Use of iv bisphosphonates
Loop diuretics after fluid hydration

answer: The correct answer is B. This is the only option that would make the hypercalcemia worse, by increasing calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule. (Thiazides block the apical Na/Cl cotransporter, which lowers intracellular Na and thereby drives the basolateral Na/Ca exchanger harder - more calcium into the blood.) IV bisphosphonates and loop diuretics after volume repletion both lower calcium. See 02 - Drugs Affecting Calcium Homeostasis.

stem: Ms. Smith is a 70 year old female who sustained two fragility fractures including a hip fracture and a wrist fracture. Secondary causes of osteoporosis have been ruled out. Which of the following treatments have been shown to reduce the risk of hip fractures?

options.html: Risedronate
Denosumab
Raloxifene
Zoledronate
A, B, D

answer: The correct answer is E (A, B, D). Raloxifene has not been shown to reduce the risk of hip fractures (it reduces vertebral fracture risk only). risedronate, denosumab and zoledronate all have hip-fracture data. See 06 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis.

stem: Which of the following is not a characteristic of Leydig cells:

options.html: Produce testosterone
Line seminiferous tubule epithelium
Synthesize pregnenolone from a precursor
Have LH receptors

answer: The correct answer is B. Leydig cells are located between the seminiferous tubules — it is the Sertoli cells that line the tubule epithelium. Their major function is production of testosterone, via conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone. LH, secreted by the anterior pituitary, stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone; testosterone in turn exerts negative feedback on hypothalamic GnRH (the stimulus for both LH and FSH). See 11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Ovarian Function
lectureMeta: Workbook Q2-Q5, Q67-Q68, Q135. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis]], [[11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function]].
stem: Which of the following is a physiological effect of androgens in the male.

options.html: Catabolism in muscle
Maintenance of spermatogenesis
Positive feedback on LH
Inhibition of chondrocytes

answer: The correct answer is B. Androgens are crucial for spermatogenesis and differentiation of the male reproductive tract. Non-reproductive effects: muscle anabolism (so A is the wrong direction), proliferation of chondrocytes and eventual closure of the epiphyseal plate (so D is the wrong direction), and activation of sebaceous glands in the skin. Testosterone exerts a negative effect on LH release from the anterior pituitary and on GnRH from the hypothalamus (so C is the wrong direction).

stem: What hormone receptor plays a major role in follicular dominance and atresia?

options.html: LH
Estrogen
FSH
GnRH

answer: The correct answer is C. Early in the cycle a surge of estrogen causes negative feedback on FSH, so FSH drops. Follicles without enough FSH receptors cannot respond to the lower hormone level and undergo atresia. The dominant follicle expresses more FSH receptors and keeps responding — this follicle then responds to the LH surge and is ovulated. See 10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle.

stem: Fill in the blanks regarding breast tissue development. Estrogen ____________ and progesterone ___________:

options.html: Stimulates fat deposition; stimulates growth of the duct systems
Stimulates growth of the duct systems; promotes lobule development of the mammary glands
Promotes alveoli development of the mammary glands; promotes lobule development of the mammary glands
Promotes lobule development; stimulates fat deposition

answer:
The correct answer is B. estrogen stimulates fat deposition and growth of the duct system of the breast; progesterone promotes development of the lobules and alveoli of the mammary glands.

Note that estrogen does both listed jobs, so A and B each capture half of estrogen's role — B wins because it pairs a true estrogen effect with the correct progesterone effect.

stem: Which cell of the ovary is the primary producer of estradiol, the major female sex steroid?

options.html: Theca interna cells
Granulosa cells
Corpus Luteum cells
Sertoli cells

answer: The correct answer is B. LH stimulates theca interna cells, which produce androgen for aromatization. Aromatization to estrone occurs in the granulosa cells of the follicle when stimulated by FSH. Both processes are cAMP-mediated. Estrone is immediately converted to estradiol. Both theca interna and granulosa cells are part of the follicle, which becomes the corpus luteum.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q2-Q5, Q67-Q68, Q135. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis]], [[11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the ovaries?

options.html: Production of estrogen (estradiol)
Production of progesterone after ovulation
Production of small amounts of testosterone
Production of follicle-stimulating hormone

answer:
The correct answer is D. The ovaries produce estrogen and progesterone — regulating the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and secondary sex characteristics — plus small amounts of testosterone.

FSH is produced by the anterior pituitary, not the ovary. FSH acts on the ovary, stimulating growth and development of the ovarian follicles.

stem: _____ causes growth of the endometrium and is considered the "fertilizer" and _____ causes stabilization and shedding and is considered the "lawn mower".

options.html: Progesterone, estrogen
Testosterone, progesterone
Estrogen, progesterone
Estrogen, testosterone

answer: The correct answer is C. estrogen = the "fertilizer" (grows the endometrium); progesterone = the "lawn mower" (stabilizes it, and its withdrawal triggers shedding).

lectureMeta: Workbook Q7-Q9, Q28. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle]].
stem: Maureen is a 25-year-old female who presents to your clinic complaining of periods that come anywhere from 20-40 days apart and are very unpredictable. This has been a problem since she started her period at the age of 14 and has become very frustrating. She is also concerned about possible fertility problems. She wants to understand what is happening. In your discussions with her which part of her cycle would you focus on as the most likely culprit?

options.html: The follicular phase
The ovulatory phase
The luteal phase
Menstruation

answer:
The correct answer is A. The follicular (proliferative) phase is dominated by FSH and estrogens and involves growth of the primordial follicle to a tertiary follicle, while the uterine lining grows in preparation for implantation. The follicular phase is usually the cause of cycle-length differences between women — for women with irregular cycles, the follicular phase is often the culprit. Problems in this phase can also cause pregnancy loss and infertility.

The ovulatory phase is preceded by the LH surge and is the release of an oocyte. The luteal (secretory) phase is usually fairly consistent between cycles and between women; it is dominated by LH and progesterone, and implantation can occur during it if fertilization has happened.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Ovarian Function
lectureMeta: Workbook Q7-Q9, Q28. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle]].
stem: Which of the following is matched incorrectly?

options.html: Estrogen causes thickening of the vaginal epithelium
The basalis layer of the uterine endometrium is shed during a menstrual cycle
Abnormal uterine bleeding is an indication for an endometrial biopsy
The endometrial lining becomes receptive to implantation during the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle.

answer: The correct answer is B. It is the functionalis layer of the endometrium that is shed during menses. The basalis layer is retained — it is the regenerative reserve from which the functionalis regrows each cycle.

stem: What is the difference between premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)?

options.html: PMDD includes both physical and behavioural symptoms while PMS is purely behavioural
PMS occurs prior to the onset of PMDD
PMDD is more disruptive to daily functioning than PMS
The two are synonymous

answer: The correct answer is C. Both PMS and PMDD can have behavioural and physical symptoms. PMS may predicate PMDD but this is not required. PMDD is a much more disabling condition than PMS.

options.html: The onset of menarche does not necessarily mean the full reproduction capacity has been reached
Adrenarche is the onset of axillary and pubic hair due to increased androgen production by the gonads
Gonadarche is the activation of gonads by FSH and LH
Thelarche is the appearance of breast tissue due to estrogen production by the ovaries

answer: The correct answer is B. Adrenarche is due to the production of adrenal androgens, not from the gonads.

stem: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: In girls delayed puberty is defined by no pubertal signs by 13 years of age
Boys are taller than girls because they have an accelerated growth rate during puberty
In early to mid-puberty, LH secretion increases at night
Familial short stature and constitutional delay of growth and puberty are normal variations causing short stature

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck; reasoning ours, checked against Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty and Disorders of Puberty.

Boys end up taller because they start later, with their growth spurt at Tanner 3-4 rather than 2-3, not because they grow faster. The others are true: delayed puberty in girls is no signs by 13 (14 in boys); the earliest change is a nocturnal rise in LH; familial short stature and CDGP are normal variants.

stem:
A 51-year-old woman's last menstrual period was eight months ago, and she has hot flushes.

By the definition taught, when is she menopausal?

options.html: Already, after 6 months of amenorrhoea
When a single estradiol level comes back low
At 53, the average age of menopause
When one FSH level is above 10 IU/L
After 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea

answer: The correct answer is E. Menopause is 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea and/or an FSH consistently over 30, from depletion of ovarian follicles and the fall in estrogen and progesterone. The average age in North American women is 53 (C), but that is an average, not a definition.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q60-Q62. Tests [[10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle]], [[11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function]].
stem: What statement most accurately describes the hormone abnormalities found in PCOS?

options.html: FSH is constantly overproduced, leading to the development of multiple cystic follicles.
Only androgens produced by the ovaries are found in high concentrations in PCOS; not adrenal sources.
A higher than normal LH surge and LH levels are often found in PCOS.
Most women with PCOS do not yet have any measurable insulin resistance.

answer:
The correct answer is C. In PCOS, LH is relatively overproduced, and LH receptors in thecal and granulosa cells are also overproduced.

A is wrong: FSH is underproduced but at constant levels - the loss of cyclical variation is what forms the cystic follicles. B is wrong: both adrenal and ovarian androgen sources may be overproduced. D is wrong: at least half of women with PCOS already have measurable insulin resistance.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q60-Q62. Tests [[10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle]], [[11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function]].
stem: A 32 year old woman presents with complaints of irregular periods over the past 2 years after a long history of regular menses. On physical exam you notice she has some acne present on her face and slightly thinning hair on the top of her head. Her BMI is 29. She tells you she has started having to remove hair on her upper lip frequently. She is "sick of these constant pregnancy scares" and wants something to fix it. You recommend:

options.html: Oral BCP
Metformin
Clomiphene
Spironolactone
Exercise, diet, and weight loss will be sufficient.

answer:
The correct answer is A. She has two complaints - hirsutism and oligomenorrhea - plus an explicit wish not to conceive. Oral BCPs treat both symptoms and provide the contraception she is asking for, which is why they are the common choice here.

  • Metformin helps oligomenorrhea and may aid fertility - which is not what she wants - and does not address the hirsutism.
  • Clomiphene, a SERM/fertility agent, treats infertility - none of her symptoms.
  • Spironolactone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, has anti-androgen effects that help hirsutism but not the irregular cycles.
  • E: weight loss may help, but PCOS itself creates a propensity to gain weight, so it may not be sufficient.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q59, Q128. Tests [[10 - PCOS]].
stem: You are seeing a new, 33-year old female patient. She tells you that she has always had irregular periods but that this has only recently become a concern as she wishes to conceive. Below is a list of your findings from the history and physical exam. Which of the following options would suggest a cause for her oligomenorrhea?

options.html: Cushingoid features
No nipple discharges
Multiparity
Use of spermicide and male condoms
Anteverted/retroflexed uterus
Normal body weight

answer:
The correct answer is A. Cushingoid features would point to an adrenal or medication cause at the root of her oligomenorrhea — the best of the listed options.

Note how the distractors are all negative or neutral findings: nipple discharge, if present, would suggest raised prolactin — but its absence tells you little (B). Multiparity (C) actually argues against a problem, since it shows she previously ovulated and conceived. Non-hormonal contraception (D), uterine position (E) and normal body weight (F) should not affect cycles.

stem: Which of the following conditions mimic PCOS?

options.html: Exogenous testosterone intake
Pregnancy
Ovarian Tumor
CAH
All of the above

answer: The correct answer is E. Exogenous testosterone, CAH, and ovarian tumor lead to hyperandrogenism; while pregnancy causes oligomenorrhea. Hyperandrogenism & Oligomenorrhea are common features of PCOS.

lectureMeta: HippoNotes (Meds 2025 Academic Resources Team, May 2023) - the question bank at the back of the block's HippoNotes document. The source groups its questions by week only, with no per-lecture attribution, so the week is as fine as the provenance goes.
stem: Select common features found in patients with PCOS

options.html: Acanthosis
Hirsutism
Acne
Female alopecia
All of the above

answer:
The correct answer is E.

All four are on the examination list, so E is right. The lecture groups them by what they are actually showing you, which is more useful than the list itself:

  • Acanthosis nigricans (A), over the back of the neck and in the axilla, usually with skin tags beside it. These are the insulin resistance signs.
  • Hirsutism (B) — terminal hair in a male pattern: face, chin, chest, upper arms.
  • Acne (C) and frontal alopecia (D), which sit with hirsutism as the androgen signs.

One caution the lecture attaches to the same list: rate of onset, ethnicity and parental appearance all have to be weighed before hair growth is called abnormal, and a rapid onset is the androgen-secreting tumour question rather than the PCOS one.

Note this material is taught in the endocrinology block, under the name PMOS, not in reproduction.

stem: Which of these women would NOT be diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.html: Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound with no other relevant physical exam or history findings
Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound and hirsutism
Oligomenorrhea for 6 months and hirsutism
Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound and irregular menses for 6 months
Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, irregular menses for 6 months, and severe acne

answer:
The correct answer is A, D. This year's lecture, 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), diagnoses PCOS by a triad, all three needed:

  1. Hyperandrogenism, on exam or on labs
  2. Ovulatory dysfunction: oligomenorrhea or cystic ovaries on ultrasound
  3. Exclusion of other disorders

Cystic ovaries and irregular menses are the same criterion, so neither A (ultrasound alone) nor D (ultrasound plus irregular menses) shows hyperandrogenism. B (hirsutism), C (hirsutism) and E (severe acne) each add it.

flags.html: The workbook keyed A only, using the Rotterdam "2 of 3" rule, where cystic ovaries and irregular menses count as two separate criteria and D qualifies. Adapted to the lecture's triad at a reader's request.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: When is serum cortisol level greatest?

options.html: 8 AM
1 PM
8 PM
1 AM
Cortisol level is unrelated to time

answer:
The correct answer is A. Cortisol release is pulsatile and follows a diurnal rhythm, rising to a maximum at 8 AM then slowly declining through the day. The 8 AM concentration is usually 2-4x the evening concentration.

Why it matters: an 8 AM serum cortisol is useful to test for adrenal insufficiency - if the daily maximum is too low (<100 nmol/L), you can be confident levels are too low all day. That inference cannot safely be made from a PM measurement.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: What would be the best test for diagnosing Cushing's syndrome?

options.html: 250 mcg ACTH stimulation test
1 mg overnight Dexamethasone Suppression Test
8 AM serum cortisol
PM serum cortisol
24-hour urinary free cortisol

answer:
The correct answer is E. With most endocrine disorders the investigative algorithm is the same: first a test to diagnose the disturbance in the axis, then a test to determine etiology (primary vs. secondary vs. tertiary). If the problem is hormone insufficiency, you stimulate; if the problem is overproduction, you suppress.

Cushing syndrome is a syndrome of excessive glucocorticoid activity, so we need a test showing overproduction of cortisol.

  • A (ACTH stimulation) - tests adrenal responsiveness to exogenous ACTH; an etiology test, used to distinguish primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency.
  • B (dexamethasone suppression test) - tests HPA-axis negative feedback; also an etiology test, the hypercortisolism analogue of the ACTH stimulation test. It is the ideal follow-up once Cushing's is diagnosed.
  • C (8 AM serum cortisol) - most useful for adrenal insufficiency, being cortisol at its maximum.
  • D (PM serum cortisol) - can diagnose Cushing's but is a poor test both analytically (single point measurement at a time of fluctuation) and practically (drawing blood in the evening).
  • E (24-hour urinary free cortisol) - best choice: no blood draw, and a 24-hour integrated measure rather than a point value. Diagnostic if >3x the upper limit of normal.

stem:
A 61-year-old female patient was referred to your clinic from the Cardiology outpatient clinic due to hypokalemic hypertension, for which the cardiologist suspected Primary Hyperaldosteronism. Due to budget cuts by the Ontario government, your hospital is underfunded and you can only perform 1 test. Which of the following tests can be used to diagnose Primary Hyperaldosteronism?

i. Aldosterone/Renin Ratio ii. Furosemide Stimulation test iii. 24-hour urine aldosterone iv. Saline Infusion/Fludrocortisone Suppression Test

options.html: i only
ii only
iii only
i and iv
i, iii, and iv

answer:
The correct answer is D (i and iv). The cardiologist has already established hypokalemia and hypertension; we are testing for etiology, so per the algorithm in Q31 we need a suppression test for aldosterone.

  • Aldosterone/Renin Ratio works because it reflects both the hormone and its stimulatory signal, which is what lets it separate primary from secondary hyperaldosteronism. An elevated ratio means far more aldosterone is produced than the prevailing renin justifies - i.e. aldosterone elevation is independent of its regulatory signal, equivalent to aldosterone staying up after mineralocorticoid or IV salt loading.
  • Saline infusion / fludrocortisone suppression is a good choice for the same reason any suppression test would be.
  • Furosemide stimulation tests responsiveness to stimulatory signals - used for insufficiency, not this.
  • 24-hour urine aldosterone adds nothing: we already know she is hyperaldosteronemic, and urine aldosterone is a poor diagnostic test in isolation.

See primary aldosteronism and 01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.
