stem: Which of the following descriptions is most likely to be a malignant pheochromocytoma?

options.html: Well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm mass in the adrenal cortex with low density of cells of clear adrenal origin with low nuclear pleomorphism
Well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm mass in the adrenal cortex with high cellularity but normal nuclei and normal mitoses
3 well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm masses, all in the adrenal cortex, with capsular invasion but normal nuclei, low cellularity, and normal mitoses
3 well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm masses, 1 in the adrenal cortex, 1 in the liver, and 1 in the thyroid gland, with vascular invasion, high cellularity and mitotic activity, but normal nuclei
1 poorly-circumscribed (i.e. diffuse growth), 1.5 cm mass in the adrenal medulla with profound nuclear pleomorphism, low cellularity, low mitotic rate, and no vascular or capsular invasion.

answer:
The correct answer is D. The point is the criteria for benign vs. malignant pheochromocytoma, formalised as the PASS criteria - which you are unlikely to be expected to memorise for this course.

The one key feature to remember: the only absolute criterion for malignancy is the presence of distant metastases. D is the only option with distant metastases (liver, thyroid). It is also the only mass fulfilling the PASS criteria (score ≥ 4), if confirmation is needed.

stem:
A 51-year-old woman presents to your general endocrine clinic complaining of generalized weakness, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting over the last two months. Also over that time, she reports a weight loss of 30 pounds. Appetite is unchanged from before, but she mentions that she has been adding increasingly large amounts of salt to all food, as she has been craving salt. She is not on any medications. On physical exam, her blood pressure was measured to be 90/60 sitting, in both arms. Upon standing, she became lightheaded and could not maintain balance.

Her blood work shows the following:

MeasurementValueNormal
Hemoglobin (g/L)156120-160
Na (mmol/L)120135-145
K (mmol/L)6.03.5-5.1
8 AM cortisol (nmol/L)200170-635
8 AM ACTH (pmol/L)1402.2-13.3

Based on this information, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Exogenous Cortisol Intake
Primary Adrenal Insufficiency
Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency
A disease in other organ systems
A psychogenic condition

answer:
The correct answer is B. Lab values are not meaningful without clinical context - do not fixate on the numbers; let them complement the clinical picture.

She is clearly showing signs of adrenal insufficiency. Generalized weakness, fatigue and weight loss are non-specific, but salt craving and orthostatic hypotension point strongly to adrenal insufficiency. From history and physical alone the differential could still include anemia from GI bleeding, and dehydration from malnutrition (given nausea/vomiting).

The bloodwork excludes those and reinforces an endocrine cause:

  • Hemoglobin at the upper end of normal - excludes GI bleeding.
  • Hyperkalemic hyponatremia on no medications - indicates dysregulated mineralocorticoid activity.
  • The 8 AM cortisol is "normal" - but this is not normal at all. In a situation this stressful, where her body cannot even maintain her vitals, cortisol should be much higher.
  • What confirms diagnosis and etiology is the ACTH: 10x the reference range while cortisol sits at the low end of normal. That is a failure to respond to the ACTH signal - equivalent to failing an ACTH stimulation test - so the lesion is at the adrenal: primary adrenal insufficiency.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT an action of cortisol?

options.html: Increased renal Na+ reabsorption
Increased renal H+ excretion
Increased liver glycogenolysis
Increased peripheral glucose uptake
Atrophy (thinning) of the skin

answer:
The correct answer is D. Cortisol is a stress hormone generating three categories of action:

  1. Increases serum glucose and amino acids
  2. Increases lipid and bone catabolism
  3. Increases mineralocorticoid activity

A and B are mineralocorticoid functions. C is correct - hepatic glucose-liberating activity is upregulated. E is correct - lipid catabolism increases, best illustrated by the skin thinning in Cushing syndrome.

D is the exception: increased peripheral glucose uptake would deplete serum glucose. If a person were hypoglycemic, the body needs what little glucose there is to go to vital organs, not peripheral tissues.

stem: A 48-year-old man has recently been diagnosed with pheochromocytoma and has come to you to be evaluated before surgical resection in one week. He does not take any medications. On physical examination, he appears anxious but otherwise well. BMI is 22. Temperature is 37.0°C, heart rate is 112/min, respiration rate is 16/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Fundoscopic, neurologic, and cardiovascular exams show normal findings. Which of the following would be the next best step in management?

options.html: No therapy; continue monitoring.
Add hydrochlorothiazide
Add metoprolol
Add prazosin
Hospitalize and give intravenous sodium nitroprusside.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Patients with pheochromocytoma must be pre-treated to stabilize blood pressure before surgery, because both anesthesia and the operation can trigger catecholamine release. The next step is a short-acting alpha-blocker - prazosin, doxazosin or terazosin - targeting a BP of 140/90 to 150/90 mm Hg. Skipping this step can produce a fatal acute hypertensive crisis before or during the operation.

It is critical that beta-blockers are never used before alpha-blockade. Beta-blockade alone leaves unopposed alpha stimulation, giving overwhelming vasoconstriction that can exacerbate or even cause a hypertensive crisis - so C (metoprolol) can be fatal here.

A is wrong for the reason above. B is wrong: even if hydrochlorothiazide lowers BP, it does not address the inappropriate sympathetic activation, and most pheo patients are already vasoconstricted and volume depleted, so a diuretic worsens things. E is wrong: sodium nitroprusside is first-line for acute hypertensive crisis, but this patient is not currently in crisis.

stem: A 41-year-old female presents to your clinic with fatigue, weakness, and lethargy over the last 12 months. She also reports spontaneous, unexplained bruising and weight gain of 40 lbs over the last two months. On physical examination, you notice mild acne, hirsutism, pink striae over the abdomen, moon facies, and a dorsal fat pad. All vital signs were unremarkable. The rest of the physical examination was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Conn Syndrome
Cushing's Syndrome
Diabetes Mellitus type 2
Hypothyroidism
Pheochromocytoma

answer:
The correct answer is B. Cushing syndrome is a syndrome of excessive glucocorticoid activity, so look for signs of excess circulating cortisol:

  • Cortisol elevates serum glucose → weight gain from central fat accumulation in a "Cushingoid" distribution (moon facies, dorsal fat pad).
  • Cortisol catabolizes peripheral lipid and protein → skin thinning (digestion of collagen and subcutaneous fat), leaving skin weak and prone to hemorrhage. The likelihood ratio of ecchymoses for Cushing's is 10-11.3. Striae appear from rapid fat expansion plus weakened skin. Muscle weakness develops as muscle is catabolized for amino acids. Osteopenia/osteoporosis follow from osteoblast inhibition plus collagen catabolism.

A (Conn) - no hypokalemic hypertension, so primary aldosteronism does not fit. E - no sympathetic features. D - shares weight gain, fatigue, weakness, lethargy, but the absence of cold intolerance, diminished reflexes, low pulse pressure and bradycardia, plus the presence of steroid-excess signs (acne, hirsutism), makes it unlikely. C - overlaps heavily since hypercortisolism induces insulin resistance, but again the hirsutism and acne favour Cushing's.

stem: In the previous case, what would you order to confirm your diagnosis? Choose one answer.

options.html: Fractionated urinary catecholamines and metanephrines
Fasting serum glucose and/or HbA1C, followed by 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) if indicated
Plasma Aldosterone/Renin Ratio
24 urinary free cortisol, followed by 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) if indicated
Serum TSH, T3, and T4

The correct answer is D. This is essentially a matching exercise against Q43's options:

  • B → type 2 diabetes workup

  • E → hypothyroidism workup

stem: A 37-year-old woman presents with a 6 month history of 40 pound weight loss, and a 1 month history of anorexia, recurrent nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, pain, and lightheadedness upon standing. She was diagnosed with Type I diabetes at the age of 9 years; she is currently well-managed with insulin pump therapy. She also was diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis at age 19; she is currently taking a stable dose of 100 mcg levothyroxine. Family history is significant for hypothyroidism (mother), systemic lupus erythematosus (mother, father), and type I diabetes (brother). Physical examination only reveals orthostatic hypotension and hyperpigmentation of her skin. Which of the following provides the most comprehensive, most likely explanation for her situation?

options.html: Myxedema coma
Cushing's Disease
Panhypopituitarism
Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndrome type I
Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome

answer: The correct answer is D. She currently has adrenal insufficiency - orthostatic hypotension plus skin hyperpigmentation (i.e. primary, ACTH-driven) - but in the context of several signs pointing to a global autoimmune condition: she personally has two autoimmune diseases (DM1, Hashimoto's thyroiditis), and her family history is positive for DM1, presumably Hashimoto's, and SLE. The single unifying diagnosis is Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndrome.

flags.title: The syndrome's type label is likely wrong
flags.html: The key, D, is the only unifying diagnosis offered, so it stands as the answer. But type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto's thyroiditis and primary adrenal insufficiency together are classically polyglandular autoimmune syndrome type II (Schmidt), not type I. ⚠ The block's notes do not distinguish the types, so that correction comes from outside them. Flagged, not corrected.

stem: Mutations in which of the following genes is responsible for most (90%) of cases of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia?

options.html: 11-beta-HSD
17-alpha-hydroxylase
21-hydroxylase
5-alpha reductase
aromatase

answer:
The correct answer is C. CAH is a disorder of defective adrenal steroid biosynthesis; all genetic causes are autosomal recessive. 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for more than 90% of cases - which is why 17-hydroxyprogesterone (the substrate for the 21-hydroxylase reaction) is elevated, and why serum 17-OHP is the standard investigation.

A catalyzes cortisol ↔ cortisone interconversion; does not cause CAH. B can cause CAH but is very rare (and produces an unusual subtype with low androgens and high aldosterone). D converts testosterone → DHT; mutation causes 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, not CAH. E converts testosterone/androstenedione → estrogens; not CAH.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: A 3-week-old male infant was found to be homozygous for a mutation in 21-hydroxylase. Which of the following would NOT be expected in his clinical presentation?

options.html: Hypoglycemia in salt-losing crisis
Ambiguous genitalia
Elevated serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Hyperkalemia
Metabolic acidosis

answer:
The correct answer is B. Group the features of 21-hydroxylase CAH by hormone abnormality:

  • Substrate buildup: 17-OHP is not consumed, so levels rise → C expected.
  • Cortisol deficiency (precursors need 21-hydroxylase) → hypoglycemia, especially under stress/illness → A expected.
  • Aldosterone deficiency → impaired Na reabsorption, K excretion and H+ excretion → hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis → D and E expected.
  • Androgen excess (excess 17-OHP shunted into androgen synthesis) → in females, virilization (clitoral hypertrophy, labial fusion); in males, inappropriate penile enlargement and scrotal pigmentation.

Because this is a male patient, the expected genital findings are penile enlargement and scrotal pigmentation - not ambiguous genitalia. Hence B is not expected.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Testosterone produced by the Leydig cells promotes Wolffian duct development and Mullerian duct regression
Hypothetically, if a developing male fetus lacked MIS production, they would develop a Mullerian duct instead of a Wolffian duct.
A XY patient with complete androgen insensitivity would be phenotypically female both internally and externally.
Dihydrotestosterone induces the development of external male genitalia

answer:
The correct answer is D. DHT does induce differentiation of the male external genitalia.

A is incorrect - testosterone only stimulates Wolffian duct development; MIS is needed to cause Mullerian duct regression. B is incorrect - without MIS the fetus would develop both a Mullerian and a Wolffian duct, since testosterone production is intact. C is incorrect - an XY patient with CAIS (androgen insensitivity syndrome) has a normal external female phenotype but not a normal internal female phenotype, because SRY is still expressed, MIS is still released from Sertoli cells, and the Mullerian ducts still regress.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (3 questions).
stem: You are asked to assess a 1-week old infant due to a disorder of sexual development. On examination, the child has a 2 cm phallus with fused labio-scrotal folds and a single uro-genital opening. Gonads are not palpable. The remainder of the physical examination is normal. If the karyotype is 46XY, which of the following is the most likely cause of this clinical presentation?

options.html: 21-hydroxylase deficiency congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
Leydig cell hypoplasia
5-alpha reductase deficiency
11-beta hydroxylase deficiency congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Androgen secreting tumour

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation. D. A 46,XY infant with an under-virilised 2 cm phallus, fused labio-scrotal folds and a single urogenital opening has testes that made testosterone but external genitalia that never saw enough DHT - the lecture's starred cause, 5-α reductase deficiency. DHT builds the external genitalia and testosterone the internal ducts, so it is ambiguous outside, male inside, and the testes may lie abdominally or inguinally, which fits the impalpable gonads.

  • A, E - in a 46,XY infant CAH adds androgen: boys look normal (penile enlargement, scrotal pigmentation) and present in salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks, not with ambiguity.
  • B - complete androgen insensitivity gives female external genitalia, not a phallus.
  • C - Leydig cell hypoplasia is on the 46,XY list, but with no testosterone the internal ducts fail too; the notes list it without a phenotype, so this split is reasoned from the testosterone/DHT division of labour.
  • F - an androgen-secreting tumour virilises a 46,XX fetus; it cannot under-virilise an XY one.

Confirm with a raised T:DHT ratio after hCG stimulation.

stem:
A patient presents with ambiguous external genitalia at birth but is genetically male (46,XY). Later, during puberty, there is a significant virilization.

This clinical picture is most consistent with:

options.html: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
McCune Albright syndrome
5-alpha reductase deficiency
Klinefelter syndrome

answer: The correct answer is C. From the deck's summary slide: 5-alpha reductase deficiency impairs conversion of testosterone to DHT, so the testes are internal and the external genitalia ambiguous; at puberty virilisation occurs, though incompletely; diagnosis is an elevated T:DHT ratio after hCG stimulation. The lecture agrees: it virilises at puberty because testosterone itself is normal. CAH virilises a 46,XX infant (A); McCune-Albright is peripheral precocious puberty (B); Klinefelter is 47,XXY (D).

stem:
A 2-week-old boy with normal-looking genitalia and a hyperpigmented scrotum presents with vomiting and poor feeding. Sodium is 124 mmol/L, potassium 7.1 mmol/L, and glucose 2.8 mmol/L.

Which test confirms the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Karyotype alone
Testosterone:DHT ratio after hCG
Serum TSH and free T4
Plasma renin alone

answer: The correct answer is A. This is salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency: cortisol and aldosterone are both lost, giving hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia, with ACTH excess causing hyperpigmentation. The 46,XY infant looks normal and presents in a salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks, while the 46,XX infant is caught at birth by ambiguous genitalia. The diagnostic marker is a markedly raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone. T:DHT after hCG is the test for 5-alpha reductase deficiency (C).

stem:
\* A 59-year old man presents with abdominal pain. A CT scan of the abdomen makes an incidental finding of 1.9 cm left adrenal cortex mass with 20 Hounsfield units. His only past medical history is significant for hypertension and he takes ramipril. What screening tests would you order?

I. 24 hour urine for metanephrines, catecholamines and creatinine II. 1 mg dex suppression test, and ACTH III. Serum aldosterone/renin ratio

options.html: I only
I and II only
I and III only
All of the above
None of the above

answer:
The correct answer is D (all of the above). Because the mass is over 1 cm, any zone of the adrenal gland could be involved. All three investigations are therefore needed to rule in/out:

  • a glucocorticoid issue (Addison's / Cushing's) → 1 mg DST + ACTH
  • a mineralocorticoid issue (hyper/hypoaldosteronism) → aldosterone/renin ratio
  • a catecholamine issue (pheochromocytoma) → 24 h urine metanephrines/catecholamines

lectureMeta: Workbook Q3-Q5. Tests [[02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease]].
stem: A male patient with a history of traumatic brain injury presents at your office with anorexia, weight loss, decreased libido, hypoglycemia, constipation, dry skin, low bone mineral density. After ruling out malignancy and reaching a diagnosis, which of the following would not be prescribed?

options.html: Hydrocortisone or prednisone
Fluticasone
Levothyroxine
Testosterone

answer: The correct answer is B. This patient has symptoms of overall hypofunction of the pituitary gland (hypopituitarism), likely secondary to past traumatic brain injury. The key with any hormone deficiency is to replace it, but with a few exceptions. Adrenal insufficiency needs to be replaced with a corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone or prednisone. However, mineralocorticoid replacement is generally only required for primary adrenal insufficiency (such as Addison's disease), and not in this case - in secondary/central disease the aldosterone axis is intact because it is driven by renin-angiotensin, not ACTH. Levothyroxine and testosterone support the thyroid and gonadal axes respectively.

flags.title: Workbook error
flags.html: The key gives the example of mineralocorticoid replacement as "fluticasone". Fluticasone is an inhaled/topical glucocorticoid for asthma and rhinitis, with no mineralocorticoid role at all. The mineralocorticoid used for replacement is fludrocortisone. The letter answer is still B, but for the simpler reason that fluticasone has no place in this patient's regimen.

review.t: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease

lectureMeta: Workbook Q3-Q5. Tests [[02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease]].
stem: A 40-year-old female was referred to your endocrine office by her family physician. She was recently diagnosed with hypertension. She complains of enlargement of her jaw, nose, and hands. Her heels from 3 years ago no longer fit her and she reports easier flossing. Which one of the following would not be an appropriate finding or primary treatment option for the presenting case?

options.html: Her serum IGF-1 or fasting GH are elevated
She has impaired glucose tolerance
A dose of glucose fails to suppress GH
You prescribe her a somatostatin analogue

answer:
The correct answer is D. GH overproduction in an adult is usually the result of a GH-producing adenoma (acromegaly). Patients typically present with increased acral growth (macrognathia, increased space between teeth, enlargement of nose and frontal bones, enlarged hands and feet), hypertrophic arthropathies of joints, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, increased soft tissue (skin thickening, increased polyps, deeper voice, sleep apnea), hypogonadism, and insulin resistance (thus impaired glucose tolerance). Screening findings include increased IGF-1 (produced by the liver under GH), or a failed glucose suppression test (normally glucose should suppress GH to <1 µg/L).

While somatostatin analogues are a possible treatment for GH-producing adenomas, the first-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery. Hence D is incorrect.

A somatostatin analogue is a treatment for acromegaly, which is why the question reads "primary treatment": in the lecture it comes after transsphenoidal surgery, not instead of it.

flags.title: Option C corrected to GH
flags.html: The source wrote option C as "a dose of glucose fails to suppress IGF-1". The lecture's confirmatory test is failure of GH to suppress below 1 µg/L on a 75 g OGTT, so C now says GH. As written, C was also a false statement, which gave the question two answers. A reader reported this.

stem: A 25-year-old female comes to your office complaining of irregular periods, galactorrhea, headaches and visual disturbances for the past 3 months. You determined that she has a prolactinoma. Which of the following is false?

options.html: She needs to be referred to a surgeon for removal of tumour
Visual disturbances could result from optic chiasm compression by the tumour
Oligomenorrhea is the result of PRL suppressing LH and FSH
Her serum prolactin would unlikely be elevated to > 200 ng/mL

answer: The correct answer is A. Surgery is not first-line treatment for prolactinomas. Dopamine agonists - such as bromocriptine or cabergoline - would be used before considering an operative approach.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q7. Tests [[05 - Disorders of Growth]].
stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought in because her parents are worried due to her slow growth. Records show that she had a normal birth weight and length, and normal growth within the first year of birth. You suspect growth hormone insufficiency. As part of her assessment, you would:

options.html: Order random growth hormone levels
Order a serum IGF-1 test
Perform provocative testing using arginine, clonidine, or glucagon.
A and C
B and C

answer:
The correct answer is E. The key to this question is that random growth hormone values are NOT useful, due to the pulsatile nature of GH release - hence A and D are incorrect. E is correct because the IGF-1 level is the screening test and provocative testing is diagnostic.

The complete diagnostic criteria for GH deficiency:

  • Short stature - height below 3rd percentile
  • Growth velocity < 25th percentile
  • Bone age delayed by more than 2 SD below chronologic age
  • Inadequate serum GH response to 2 provocative tests (<8 µg/L)

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: In girls delayed puberty is defined by no pubertal signs by 13 years of age
Boys are taller than girls because they have an accelerated growth rate during puberty
In early to mid-puberty, LH secretion increased at night
Pulsatile GnRH release is stimulated by Kisspeptin at puberty

answer:
The correct answer is B. B is incorrect - the peak height velocity and total growth during puberty are largely similar between boys and girls. The main reason boys end up taller is that they spend more time growing before the onset of puberty.

A is correct: delayed puberty is defined as the absence or incomplete development of puberty at an age 2.5 SD above the population mean - no pubertal signs by 13 in girls, 14 in boys.

review.t: Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: GABA and neuropeptide Y have an inhibitory effect on the hypothalamus GnHR production in females and males respectively
The first sign of puberty in girls is breast enlargement and penile growth in boys
The effect of estrogen during puberty leads to breast tenderness, mood swings, and vaginal discharge
Delayed puberty is defined as a lack of signs of puberty by 13 in girls, and 14 in boys

answer:
The correct answer is B. GABA and NPY are inhibitory and glutamate is stimulatory. Know the Tanner staging of pubic hair, breast and genital development. The order of pubertal staging:

  • Girls: thelarche → growth spurt → pubarche → menarche
  • Boys: testicular enlargement → penile growth → pubarche → growth

So the first sign in boys is testicular enlargement, not penile growth.

Mnemonic from the key: "Estrogen effects are moody, androgen effects are gross."

flags.title: Workbook typo
flags.html: The key writes "glutamine is stimulatory" - it means glutamate. (The stem's own typo, "GnHR", is GnRH.)

stem: A 14-year-old female patient presents in your office. She has breast development and pubic hair but has not started menses. There are no other symptom complaints. She has always been short for her age, although her parents are of reasonable heights. Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Likely constitutional growth delay. Reassure the patient and parents
Order a MRI of head to rule out secondary causes of hypogonadism
Order a karyotype to rule out Turner's syndrome
None of the above

answer: The correct answer is C. Although constitutional growth delay and secondary hypogonadism are both possible causes of delayed puberty, the most appropriate action is to rule in/out Turner syndrome, which presents with short stature and primary hypogonadism. The patient fits the picture: Turner syndrome patients usually have pubarche, and about 10-15% have breast development as well.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought in. He recently developed strong body odour, grew pubic hair and rapid growth in height and weight in the last 6 months. On physical examination his height and weight are at >95% percentiles, bilaterally enlarged testes. Pubic hair T3, penis T5. Which of the following would NOT be consistent or appropriate with this presentation?

options.html: Serum testosterone levels elevated
LH, FSH below normal
Give depot LHRH analog
Bone age elevated

answer: The correct answer is B. First determine whether this is a central (gonadotropin-dependent) or peripheral cause of precocious puberty. Because the patient has bilateral testicular enlargement, it is unlikely that the testes are an autonomous source of testosterone - bilateral enlargement means they are being driven by gonadotropins. This is therefore gonadotropin-dependent precocious puberty, so serum LH/FSH would be elevated, not below normal. Treatment is a continuous LHRH analogue, which suppresses pubertal development.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q46-Q47. Tests [[09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation]].
stem: What is the expected phenotype of a patient who is 46XY but has a complete defect in the androgen receptor?

options.html: Completely female external and internal genitalia, with normal female puberty and menses
Completely female external and internal genitalia, with no menses but otherwise normal female puberty
Completely female external genitalia, both testes and ovaries, and no menses but otherwise normal puberty
Ambiguous external genitalia, female internal genitalia, and normal female puberty
Completely female external genitalia, only testes internally, and absent menses but otherwise normal female puberty.

answer:
The correct answer is E. This is Complete Androgen Insensitivity.

Internally there will be testes only. Recall that creation of the internal genitalia is sex steroid-independent: testes form under the influence of SRY, and Sertoli cells then generate Mullerian Inhibiting Substance (MIS), which prevents development of the ovaries, fallopian tubes and upper ⅓ of the vagina.

Externally, the lack of androgen signalling at the receptor produces female external genitalia, and at puberty female secondary sex characteristics develop. But because the female internal genitalia are absent, menses does not occur.

See 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q46-Q47. Tests [[09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation]].
stem: While conducting a physical examination for an infant with ambiguous external genitalia, you notice a palpable gonad in the inguinal canal. Which of the following is NOT a possibility for the identity of this gonad?

options.html: testis
dysgenic testis
ovotestis
ovary

answer: The correct answer is D. The key point, and the whole purpose of palpating for gonads on physical exam: "A PALPABLE GONAD IS NOT AN OVARY." This holds generally even in adults - only extremely thin patients and patients with ovarian pathology have palpable ovaries.

preamble.title: The case - adrenal insufficiency, 19-year-old woman
preamble.html:
The case. A 19-year-old woman. PMH: hypothyroidism (well-controlled), infiltrative keratitis, mononucleosis, occasional headaches. Medications: levothyroxine 75 µg OD, ibuprofen 200 mg PRN, never steroids. FH: hypothyroidism (mother, aunt), type 1 diabetes (cousin).

Over 3-4 years: weight loss (dress size 7 to 0, non-intentionally), weakness, fatigability, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, orthostatic presyncope, and multiple infections.

Over the last 3 months: two infections resulting in hospitalisation, one progressing to a 5-day ICU stay for a urinary tract infection and acute kidney injury secondary to Group-B Streptococcus, with low blood pressure that was hard to treat. More recently an upper respiratory tract infection, at which point she was started on hydrocortisone.

stem: Four years of unintentional weight loss, weakness, nausea, abdominal pain and orthostatic presyncope, and now two admissions in three months - one a five-day ICU stay for Group-B streptococcal urosepsis in which her hypotension was hard to treat. What is the diagnosis?

options.html: Secondary adrenal insufficiency from a pituitary lesion compressing the corticotrophs
Primary adrenal insufficiency, undiagnosed for years and now presenting in crisis
Undertreated hypothyroidism, her levothyroxine dose having fallen behind her requirement
Occult gastrointestinal blood loss from her regular ibuprofen, with secondary anaemia

answer:
B. The case summary says it outright: "a young woman with primary adrenal insufficiency", ⚠ "unfortunately not diagnosed until repeated adrenal crises."

⭐ "Hard to treat" is the diagnostic phrase, not "septic". Cortisol is permissive for the vascular response to catecholamines, so without it fluids and pressors underperform. ⭐ A septic patient who will not come up is the commonest way an undiagnosed adrenal insufficiency announces itself, and it is the one line in this history that a competent ICU team would have found inexplicable at the time.

The chronic picture had been there for years and maps onto the case's own list: unintentional weight loss, weakness, fatigability, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, orthostatic presyncope. ⭐ The recurrent infections are a consequence of the cortisol deficit, not a competing diagnosis.

Why primary rather than secondary. She already has autoimmune hypothyroidism, her mother and aunt have it, and a cousin has type 1 diabetes. ⭐ Autoimmune adrenalitis travels in company, which is why the notes list "other auto-immune features" among the signs of the disease.

A is the wrong level: secondary insufficiency spares aldosterone, so the salt-losing, pressor-resistant hypotension fits poorly, and nothing points at a sellar mass. C cannot produce shock, and her hypothyroidism is stated to be well-controlled. D would give anaemia, not a four-year multisystem decline, and 200 mg PRN is not the dose that causes it.

flags.title: What "never steroids" is doing in the medication list
flags.html: It removes exogenous glucocorticoid as both cause and confounder, which matters because steroid use is the commonest reason a cortisol axis looks suppressed. ⭐ It also means the hydrocortisone started for her most recent infection was the first she had ever received - and is very likely why that admission went better than the one before it.

preamble.title: The case - adrenal insufficiency, 19-year-old woman
preamble.html:
The case. A 19-year-old woman. PMH: hypothyroidism (well-controlled), infiltrative keratitis, mononucleosis, occasional headaches. Medications: levothyroxine 75 µg OD, ibuprofen 200 mg PRN, never steroids. FH: hypothyroidism (mother, aunt), type 1 diabetes (cousin).

Over 3-4 years: weight loss (dress size 7 to 0, non-intentionally), weakness, fatigability, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, orthostatic presyncope, and multiple infections.

Over the last 3 months: two infections resulting in hospitalisation, one progressing to a 5-day ICU stay for a urinary tract infection and acute kidney injury secondary to Group-B Streptococcus, with low blood pressure that was hard to treat. More recently an upper respiratory tract infection, at which point she was started on hydrocortisone.

stem: She is stabilised and you now want to establish the diagnosis properly. Her AM cortisol comes back low. Which single further result tells you whether the failure is in her adrenal or in her pituitary?

options.html: A 24-hour urine free cortisol, collected with a paired creatinine for completeness
An overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, read against a 50 nmol/L threshold
A renin and aldosterone pair, to establish whether the mineralocorticoid axis is intact
A simultaneous ACTH, high in adrenal failure and low or normal in pituitary failure

answer:
D. The lecture's diagnostic summary for chronic adrenal insufficiency gives two lines only: ⭐ "AM cortisol (+ACTH)" and "ACTH stimulation test". The bracketed +ACTH is the whole answer to this question.

⭐ A low cortisol tells you the axis has failed. Only the ACTH tells you where. In primary failure the adrenal cannot respond, so the pituitary shouts louder and ACTH is high. In secondary failure the pituitary is the problem, so ACTH is low or inappropriately normal beside the low cortisol. ⭐ Same cortisol, opposite ACTH, and the two diseases are managed differently - the primary patient needs a mineralocorticoid as well.

Why the sample has to be a morning one. Cortisol runs a diurnal rhythm and peaks in the morning, so ⭐ a low AM value is interpretable in a way that a low afternoon value simply is not.

A and B are tests for cortisol excess, not deficiency; B asks whether cortisol suppresses, which is the opposite question. C describes a real consequence of primary failure but is not how the level is localised, and it would leave a secondary case unexplained.

flags.title: The cut-off is deliberately not the examinable part
flags.html: The lecture flags that ⚠ thresholds vary between studies - "some use 450, others 500, others 550" - and then states the instruction in its own words: ⭐ "TIP: know main principle for approach." The principle is morning timing, a paired ACTH, and a stimulation test if the result sits on the fence.

preamble.title: The case - adrenal insufficiency, 19-year-old woman
preamble.html:
The case. A 19-year-old woman. PMH: hypothyroidism (well-controlled), infiltrative keratitis, mononucleosis, occasional headaches. Medications: levothyroxine 75 µg OD, ibuprofen 200 mg PRN, never steroids. FH: hypothyroidism (mother, aunt), type 1 diabetes (cousin).

Over 3-4 years: weight loss (dress size 7 to 0, non-intentionally), weakness, fatigability, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, orthostatic presyncope, and multiple infections.

Over the last 3 months: two infections resulting in hospitalisation, one progressing to a 5-day ICU stay for a urinary tract infection and acute kidney injury secondary to Group-B Streptococcus, with low blood pressure that was hard to treat. More recently an upper respiratory tract infection, at which point she was started on hydrocortisone.

stem: Return to her ICU admission. She was hypotensive with Group-B streptococcal urosepsis and responding poorly to fluids and pressors. Had adrenal insufficiency been suspected at that moment, what should have happened?

options.html: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV given at once, with the diagnostic samples drawn alongside it
A cortisol and ACTH drawn and the steroid withheld until the results were available
Fludrocortisone started first, since the mineralocorticoid deficit drives the hypotension
The hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia corrected before any steroid was introduced

answer:
A. The lecture's acute management is explicit: ⭐ "Treatment is critical - do not delay waiting for test results." Its order is ABCs · get electrolytes and glucose · IV fluids, 2-3 L normal saline or dextrose, as fast as possible through two large-bore IVs · hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, then 50-100 mg Q6-8h.

⭐ Notice where the samples sit: second, not last. They are drawn and the treatment does not wait on them. That is what "do not delay" means in practice - investigate and treat in parallel.

⭐ The asymmetry of harm is the whole argument. A dose of hydrocortisone given to someone who turns out not to need it is very nearly harmless. An hour's delay in someone who does can be fatal, and a cortisol assay takes hours. ⭐ This is the one endocrine emergency where you treat on suspicion. The lecture's own summary: "although not a frequent condition, it is certainly one not to miss, as outcomes may be fatal."

Her case is the cost of getting this wrong. She survived five days in ICU with the diagnosis unmade, and the lecture's verdict is that she went undiagnosed "until repeated adrenal crises".

B is precisely the error that rule exists to prevent. C is both the wrong agent and the wrong moment - ⭐ mineralocorticoid is a subacute step once the patient is stabilised, and at 100 mg IV hydrocortisone carries substantial mineralocorticoid activity anyway. D treats the electrolytes as the disease; they correct as the volume and the cortisol are restored.

stem:
A 45-year-old man with a history of primary adrenal insufficiency due to autoimmune Addison’s disease presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe fatigue, dizziness, and vomiting. He reports a recent gastroenteritis with poor oral intake. On examination:

  • Blood pressure: 85/50 mmHg
  • Heart rate: 120 bpm
  • Temperature: 38.3°C
  • Skin: diffuse hyperpigmentation
  • Mucous membranes: dry
  • Patient appears confused and lethargic

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?

options.html: Wait for cortisol and ACTH results before starting any treatment.
Give IV fluids only, then monitor vital signs and urine output closely.
IV hydrocortisone now, aggressive dextrose-saline fluids, and correct electrolytes.
Give oral fludrocortisone and schedule endocrine follow-up in 1 week.
Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics only, as hypotension is likely septic shock.

answer: The correct answer is C. From the deck's next slide (adrenal crisis): the trigger is a stressor (infection, surgery, trauma) in known adrenal insufficiency; features are refractory hypotension, shock, GI symptoms, altered mental status and hyperpigmentation; labs show hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia. Immediate management: 1. IV hydrocortisone · 2. aggressive IV fluids, 0.9% saline + dextrose · 3. correct electrolytes · 4. treat the trigger. The lecture is the same, and explicit that you do not wait for results (A).

stem:
A 54-year old female presents with a 3-week history of progressive weakness, nausea, and vomiting. She has lost approximately 15 pounds. She is on no medications. Although she is alert, she is slow to respond to your questions. Her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg and heart rate 115 bpm when lying and on standing, her blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg with a heart rate of 150 bpm. She is afebrile. Her weight is 50 kg and BMI of 23. She has hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa.

What are the initial steps in her management – select up to 4 as points are deducted if more than 4 are chosen.

options.html: Intravenous normal saline
Intravenous dextrose
Check serum electrolytes and creatinine
Check serum calcium and albumin
Check serum TSH, FT4, FT3
Check serum glucose
Check serum ACTH and cortisol
Check 24 hour urine for cortisol

answer:
The correct answers are A, C, F and G. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. Orthostatic shock with buccal hyperpigmentation points to primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's). ACTH runs very high, and POMC, the precursor it is cut from, also yields melanocyte-stimulating hormone, which darkens the buccal mucosa. Resuscitate with IV fluids, check electrolytes and glucose, draw ACTH and cortisol straight away, then give high-dose hydrocortisone without waiting for the results. A 24-hour urine cortisol (H) has no role: it takes too long while she may become unstable, and it is a test for cortisol excess, not deficiency.

Weight loss, vomiting, marked orthostatic hypotension and buccal hyperpigmentation are primary adrenal insufficiency heading into crisis. Resuscitate with IV normal saline, and draw the bloods that answer the immediate questions: electrolytes and creatinine (Na↓, K↑, azotemia), glucose (hypoglycemia), and a paired cortisol and ACTH before steroids are given, without waiting for the results to treat. Dextrose (B) is added if she is hypoglycemic; calcium, thyroid tests and a 24-h urine cortisol (D, E, H) do not change the first hour.

stem:
For each scenario below, choose the single BEST screening test:

i. A 31 year-old female has a 3-month history of proximal muscle weakness, worsening diabetes, easy bruising, and hirsutism. Her only medication is the oral contraceptive.

options.html: Am serum cortisol
Serum ACTH level
Plasma aldosterone/renin ratio
24 hour urine for cortisol
1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test
24 hour urine for catecholamines and metanephrines
24 hour urine for VMA
Serum DHEA and androstenedione
CT (adrenals)

answer:
The correct answer is D. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. The room split between A, D and E, and the presenter keyed D. Estrogen in the oral contraceptive raises hepatic cortisol-binding globulin, so total serum cortisol reads falsely high. That spoils the morning cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone (E) and a plain AM cortisol (A), while the 24-hour urine measures only free cortisol and is unaffected. ⭐ Look in the stem for a drug that raises CBG; if there is one, pick the 24-hour urine. Without one, the presenter opens with both the 24-hour urine and the 1 mg DST, because Cushing's needs more than one positive test and a high pretest probability. Late-night salivary cortisol is the third test, but most community labs cannot run it. An AM cortisol on its own is mainly a test for adrenal insufficiency: a low value tells you something, a high one does not.

Proximal weakness and easy bruising are the highest-likelihood-ratio Cushing signs, so screen for cortisol excess. Of the screens, the lecture says the 1 mg DST is not useful in women on an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive (estrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin, so total cortisol looks unsuppressed), which leaves the 24-hour urine free cortisol. A single AM cortisol (A) cannot diagnose excess, and ACTH (B) comes after cortisol excess is proven.

stem:
A 19-year-old previously healthy man is brought to the emergency department with a history of a mild pharyngitis and then a high fever over the past 24 hours. In the emergency room, he is confused, hard to arouse, and has extensive areas of purpura. Vital signs include temperature 39°C, pulse rate 102/minute, respiratory rate 21/minute, and blood pressure 80/55 mm Hg. Lab studies show a serum sodium of 115 mM, potassium 5.3 mM, chloride 92 mM, CO2 22 mM, glucose 3.2 mM, and serum creatinine 156 uM.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Disseminated tuberculosis
Primary Adrenal Insufficiency
Thyrotoxicosis
Pheochromocytoma

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. The cause is meningococcemia (pharyngitis, fever, purpura), which can bleed into both adrenals: Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome, giving shock with low sodium, high potassium and low glucose. A student asked about thyroid storm, since fever, pharyngitis and tachycardia fit it too. The labs separate them, because storm does not cause hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypoglycemia. So does the presentation: a storm patient is agitated or combative, tremulous and warm, not obtunded on arrival. His confusion can come from the hypoglycemia and the shock.

Fever, purpura and shock after a pharyngitis suggest meningococcal sepsis, and adrenal haemorrhage is one of the lecture's causes of primary insufficiency. The labs are the primary pattern: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia and azotemia, because the whole cortex is lost, aldosterone as well as cortisol. TB (A) is a cause of Addison's, but not over 24 hours.

stem:
A 48-year-old man has experienced constant back pain exacerbated by movement over the past month. He also reports increasing difficulty climbing stairs over the past 4 months. He is no medications but has a 45 pack year history of cigarette smoking. On physical exam his blood pressure is 165/110 mm Hg. He is overweight with a BMI of 28. A radiograph of the spine reveals a compression fracture at T10. Lab findings include a random plasma glucose 18.5 mM, serum sodium 134 mM, and serum potassium 2.9 mM.

I) Which one of the following test results would be most likely in this man?

options.html: An 8:00 AM serum cortisol of 45.9 nM after 1 mg dexamethasone PO the night before (Nl <50 nmol/L)
A 24 hour urine free cortisol level of 439 nmol/d (normal 120 – 384 nmol/d)
An AM plasma ACTH level 232 pM (normal < 14 pM)
A 1.3 cm pituitary mass consistent with an adenoma on an MRI
A hemoglobin A1c level of 6.0%

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. The fragility fracture, hypertension, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia and proximal myopathy all point to Cushing's, so expect a raised urine free cortisol.

Proximal weakness, a vertebral fracture, hypertension, hyperglycemia and hypokalemia add up to cortisol excess, and the high-LR signs (fracture, proximal weakness) are present. A raised 24-h urine free cortisol fits. A post-dexamethasone cortisol of 45.9 is suppressed, i.e. normal (A); an A1c of 6.0% does not fit a random glucose of 18.5 (E).

stem:
A 36-year-old woman with Addison's disease takes hydrocortisone 15 mg in the morning and 5 mg in the afternoon, with fludrocortisone. She phones with influenza and a fever of 38.6°C. She is eating and drinking and has not vomited.

What should she do?

options.html: Keep taking her usual doses
Triple her hydrocortisone for three days
Double her dose for one day only
Stop the fludrocortisone until she recovers
Go to the emergency department for IV hydrocortisone

answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture's rule of 3s: with flu and similar illness, increase the dose 3-fold for 3 days. She needs an injection or IV hydrocortisone (E) only if she cannot take or absorb oral doses, e.g. vomiting or severe diarrhoea. Failing to stress-dose is how chronic insufficiency becomes an adrenal crisis.

stem:
A patient has a low 8 AM cortisol and symptoms of adrenal insufficiency.

Which finding points to primary rather than secondary adrenal insufficiency?

options.html: Hyponatraemia
Hypoglycaemia
Hyperkalaemia
Fatigue and weight loss
Hypotension

answer: The correct answer is C. Primary insufficiency destroys the whole cortex, so aldosterone is lost as well as cortisol: potassium rises, ACTH is high (hence hyperpigmentation), and fludrocortisone is needed. In secondary insufficiency the aldosterone axis is preserved and K⁺ is normal. Hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, fatigue and hypotension (A, B, D, E) occur in both.

stem:
A CT done for abdominal pain shows a 3.5 cm left adrenal mass in a 61-year-old man. His blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg. The radiologist offers a CT-guided biopsy.

What must be done before any biopsy?

options.html: Plasma free metanephrines
MRI of the pituitary
Adrenal vein sampling
Cosyntropin stimulation test
Repeat CT in six months

answer: The correct answer is A. Never biopsy an adrenal mass until pheochromocytoma has been excluded: in the lecture's series 14 of 20 biopsied patients (70%) had a complication. Every incidentaloma is screened for all three excess states anyway: cortisol, aldosterone (he is hypertensive), and catecholamines, for which plasma free metanephrines are the best single test.

stem:
You are seeing a 45-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and wondering about Cushing's syndrome.

Which finding would most increase the likelihood that she has it?

options.html: Her general obesity and weight gain
Frequent headaches
Her hypertension
Easy bruising (ecchymoses)
Mild hirsutism

answer: The correct answer is D. The signs with the highest likelihood ratios are ecchymoses (10-11.3), osteopenia or fracture, and proximal muscle weakness. Hypertension (C), hirsutism (E) and especially general obesity (A), the weakest, are too common in ordinary metabolic disease to discriminate. That is the SR slide's point: more than HTN and oedema.

stem:
Scenario: In your clinic you see a 38 year old male patient referred for a pituitary adenoma discovered incidentally on MRI scan. Further testing demonstrates classic bitemporal visual field defects. Please select the laboratory result that would make you decide NOT to refer the patient for pituitary surgery:

OptionParameterResultReference range
1Cortisol (24-hour urine)800<275 nmol/day
2TSH
Free T4		6
32		0.5-4 mIU/L
10-22 pmol/L
3Testosterone38-30 nmol/L
4Prolactin800<23 µg/L
5Insulin-like growth factor 180068-222 µg/L

options.html: 1: urine cortisol 800 nmol/day
2: TSH 6 with free T4 32
3: testosterone 3 nmol/L
4: prolactin 800 µg/L
5: IGF-1 800 µg/L

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease. D (prolactin 800). A prolactin of 800 µg/L is far above the macroadenoma threshold of ~200, so this is a prolactinoma - and the prolactinoma is the one pituitary macroadenoma treated medically first: a dopamine agonist (cabergoline, bromocriptine) shrinks it and the field defect lifts. A visual field defect is not an indication for surgery here.

  • A (urine cortisol 800) - Cushing disease → transsphenoidal surgery.
  • B (TSH 6 with free T4 32) - a non-suppressed TSH beside a high free T4 suggests a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, also surgical; the notes do not cover it, so this is reasoned from general principles.
  • C (testosterone 3) - hypogonadism from compression of the normal gland; it needs replacing but does not argue against operating.
  • E (IGF-1 800) - acromegaly → transsphenoidal surgery first.

stem:
A 48-year-old man has experienced constant back pain exacerbated by movement over the past month. He also reports increasing difficulty climbing stairs over the past 4 months. He is no medications but has a 45 pack year history of cigarette smoking. On physical exam his blood pressure is 165/110 mm Hg. He is overweight with a BMI of 28. A radiograph of the spine reveals a compression fracture at T10. Lab findings include a random plasma glucose 18.5 mM, serum sodium 134 mM, and serum potassium 2.9 mM.

II) Based on the information you have to this point, which of the following pathologic lesions is most likely to explain his findings?

options.html: Adrenal cortical carcinoma
Small cell lung cancer
Pituitary adenoma
Pheochromocytoma

answer:
The correct answer, as keyed by the deck, is C. No written rationale. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. Common things being common: an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma causes about 70% of endogenous Cushing's. Several students picked adrenocortical carcinoma (A) for the short history and the spinal fracture. It would suppress ACTH, and the fracture is osteoporotic from cortisol excess, which can happen at any vertebral level, not a metastasis from the adrenal. Small cell lung cancer (B) fits the smoking history, but ectopic ACTH is rare. Pheochromocytoma (D) gives adrenaline-type symptoms instead. Students also read the hypertension and low potassium as aldosterone excess. ⭐ Cortisol at very high levels acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor itself, so any cause of hypercortisolism gives both, with or without aldosterone.

Once exogenous steroid is excluded (he takes no medications), the commonest cause of endogenous Cushing's is an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease), and the review session confirmed that is the logic behind "the information you have to this point". The lecture separates the causes by ACTH (dependent: pituitary, ectopic ACTH or CRH; independent: adrenal adenoma, hyperplasia, carcinoma), then localises.

flags.title: Small cell lung cancer is a strong alternative
flags.html: A 45 pack-year smoker with a fast course, marked hypokalemia (2.9) and hypertension is the classic picture of ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer (B). The lecture lists ectopic ACTH as an ACTH-dependent cause and says its ACTH is "usually higher", but does not give hypokalemia or smoking as discriminators. The deck keys C.

preamble.title: The case - acromegaly, 45-year-old man
preamble.html:
The case. A 45-year-old married gentleman, presenting with classical acromegaly. IGF-1: 393 µg/L (reference 57-197). Oral glucose tolerance test:

Time (min)GlucoseGH
05.34.7
309.52.8
6011.12.5
908.32.4
1205.42.4

stem: His IGF-1 is 393 µg/L against an upper limit of 197. Across the glucose tolerance test his glucose climbs from 5.3 to 11.1 mmol/L, while his GH falls only from 4.7 to a floor of 2.4 µg/L. What has this established?

options.html: Nothing yet, since a GH of 2.4 is within the range seen in healthy pulsatile secretion
Impaired glucose tolerance, which must be treated before the GH axis can be assessed
Acromegaly, since the glucose load failed to suppress his GH below 1 µg/L
That the test was invalid, because the glucose rise shows he was not fasting at baseline

answer:
C. The case states the rule beside the table: ⭐ "For diagnosis of acromegaly, lack of GH suppression. Cut-off 1 µg/L."

⭐ Read the two columns against each other, because the glucose column is the control. His glucose more than doubles, which proves the load was given and absorbed. In an intact axis that rise switches GH off. ⭐ His GH bottoms out at 2.4 and never approaches 1. The failure to suppress is the diagnosis.

⭐ Why IGF-1 screens and a random GH does not. GH is secreted in pulses, so one level can be high in a healthy person and low in an acromegalic one. IGF-1 is made by the liver in response to GH and has a long half-life, so it integrates GH exposure over days. His is roughly double the upper limit.

⭐ The logic mirrors Q129 exactly, in reverse. Suspected excess: try to suppress it and show you cannot. Suspected deficiency: try to stimulate it and show you cannot. Same test architecture, opposite direction.

A would be true of a random GH but not of one drawn during a glucose load, which is the entire point of doing the load. B inverts cause and effect - ⭐ the glucose intolerance is caused by the GH excess, and treating it would not make the axis assessable. D misreads the table: a rise from a fasting 5.3 is what the test is designed to produce.

flags.html: The case opens with "45-year old married gentleman"; the continuation is headed ⚠ "Case 1 52M - continued". Flagged, not corrected - neither question turns on his age.

preamble.title: The case - acromegaly, 45-year-old man
preamble.html:
The case. A 45-year-old married gentleman, presenting with classical acromegaly. IGF-1: 393 µg/L (reference 57-197). Oral glucose tolerance test:

Time (min)GlucoseGH
05.34.7

6011.12.5

stem: His acromegaly is now biochemically confirmed. What comes next?

options.html: MRI of the pituitary to locate the adenoma, then transsphenoidal resection
A trial of a somatostatin analogue, with imaging reserved for those who fail to respond
Repeat the glucose tolerance test in six months to establish the rate of progression
Screen the anterior pituitary axes and treat any deficiency before addressing the adenoma

answer:
A. The case's next two steps are exactly this sequence: an MRI of the pituitary, then pituitary surgery - ⭐ "most common approach transsphenoidal using endoscope."

⭐ The biochemistry says there is a GH excess; only the imaging says where it is. And in acromegaly, unlike the prolactinoma two cases later, ⭐ the definitive treatment is surgical - which is the contrast worth holding onto across the two cases.

⭐ The approach is transsphenoidal because the route already exists. The pituitary sits in the sella directly above the sphenoid sinus, so an endoscope through the nose reaches it without opening the skull or retracting brain.

B is the wrong order and the wrong default; medical therapy has a role, but it does not precede locating the tumour. C delays treatment in a disease whose morbidity accrues silently. D describes a reasonable adjunct - a macroadenoma can cause hypopituitarism - but it is not what follows confirmation, and the case does not do it here.

flags.title: What this case does not cover
flags.html: The case asks only for symptoms and testing, so it says nothing about the systemic consequences of acromegaly - the cardiomyopathy, sleep apnoea, colonic polyps, arthropathy and excess mortality. ⚠ They are why the diagnosis matters, but they are not in this case; if they are wanted they come from 02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease, not from this review.

preamble.title: The case - macroprolactinoma, 29-year-old man
preamble.html:
The case. A 29-year-old gas-fitter, married, two children aged 2 and 6. Referred for a pituitary macroadenoma discovered on a CT head done for headaches. PMH unremarkable. No smoking, 12 beers/week.

Since about one year: headaches, 15 lb weight increase, decreased muscle strength and stamina, decreased libido and morning erections, shaves every 2nd day.

Physical exam: 114.5 kg, height 194.5 cm, BMI 30 kg/m². BP supine 118/80, standing 114/78 mmHg. Visual field: right supratemporal field defect.

stem: He has a macroadenoma found incidentally, a year of lost libido and morning erections, now shaves only every second day, and has a right supratemporal field defect. What should you measure?

options.html: Prolactin alone, since an incidental macroadenoma is a prolactinoma until proven otherwise
The posterior pituitary axes, since a mass this size threatens ADH before anything else
Visual fields formally, deferring all biochemistry until the mass effect is documented
Both what the tumour may be secreting and what its mass may be suppressing

answer:
D. The case's answer gives the framework in two lines: ⭐ "Test for - Overproduction - Insufficiency due to mass effect of macroadenoma."

⭐ A macroadenoma is two diseases in one lesion. It secretes whatever its cell of origin secretes, and by exceeding 1 cm it compresses the normal gland beside it and the chiasm above it. Test only for the hormone it makes and you miss the hypopituitarism; test only for deficiency and you miss the tumour's product.

His results show both halves at once:

ResultWhich half
Prolactin 1357 µg/L (N < 20)⭐ overproduction - roughly 68× the upper limit
Testosterone 2.7 nmol/L (N 9-55)⭐ both at once - the mass compresses, and the hyperprolactinaemia independently suppresses GnRH
Cortisol PM 170 nmol/L, TSH 2.3, free T4 14normal - corticotroph and thyrotroph axes so far spared

⭐ The highest-yield clue in the history is the most mundane sentence in it. "Shaves every 2nd day" in a 29-year-old man, next to lost libido and absent morning erections, is hypogonadism described without the word. Every symptom he has is now accounted for, and the field defect is the mass effect made visible.

A is a reasonable instinct that stops at half the framework and would leave his hypogonadism undocumented. B is the wrong axis - adenomas threaten the anterior gland and the chiasm, and diabetes insipidus is characteristically absent in an untreated adenoma. C inverts the order for no gain; the imaging is already done and it is the biochemistry that picks the treatment.

preamble.title: The case - macroprolactinoma, 29-year-old man
preamble.html:
The case. A 29-year-old gas-fitter, married, two children aged 2 and 6. Referred for a pituitary macroadenoma discovered on a CT head done for headaches. PMH unremarkable. No smoking, 12 beers/week.

Since about one year: headaches, 15 lb weight increase, decreased muscle strength and stamina, decreased libido and morning erections, shaves every 2nd day.

Physical exam: 114.5 kg, height 194.5 cm, BMI 30 kg/m². BP supine 118/80, standing 114/78 mmHg. Visual field: right supratemporal field defect.

stem: His prolactin returns at 1357 µg/L (normal < 20) and his testosterone at 2.7 nmol/L (9-55), with normal cortisol and thyroid function. He has a visual field defect from chiasmal compression. What is the first-line treatment?

options.html: Transsphenoidal resection, since the tumour is already compressing his optic chiasm
A dopamine agonist such as cabergoline, which shrinks the tumour and lifts pressure
Testosterone replacement first, to correct the hypogonadism while the tumour is observed
Radiotherapy, reserving surgery for a tumour that regrows once the field defect resolves

answer:
B. The case states the principle in one line and then proves it: ⚠ ⭐ "Surgery is not first option for macroprolactinoma."

⭐ This is the single most examinable fact in the case, because it is the exception. Every other pituitary macroadenoma with chiasmal compression goes to theatre - the acromegaly case two questions earlier does exactly that. ⭐ The prolactinoma is the one that is treated medically first, because it is the one that shrinks on a drug. Dopamine is the physiological brake on prolactin, so a dopamine agonist both switches off the secretion and reduces the tumour bulk.

His course proves it worked. Started on cabergoline at a gradually increasing dose: by August 08 his prolactin had fallen from 1357 to 196, and ⭐ his vision improved - the compression lifted without an operation. ⚠ His hypogonadal symptoms had not yet changed, which is the honest part of the case: the gonadal axis recovers more slowly than the prolactin falls.

A is the right operation for the wrong tumour, and would expose him to surgical risk for a lesion that melts on a tablet. C treats the consequence and leaves the cause growing against his chiasm - ⭐ and it is unnecessary, since lowering the prolactin releases his own gonadal axis. D is a late-line option for refractory disease, not an opening move.

preamble.title: The case - vertebral fracture, 41-year-old man
preamble.html: The case. In 2001, a then 41-year-old man, director of a smaller NGO, university educated, presented with back pain (thoracic spine). X-ray showed some vertebral collapse. There was no trauma.

stem: A 41-year-old man has thoracic back pain, and his X-ray shows vertebral collapse. There was no injury. What does this finding oblige you to do?

options.html: Nothing beyond analgesia, since single-level collapse at this age is usually mechanical
Begin calcium, vitamin D and a bisphosphonate, since the fracture itself makes the diagnosis
Measure his bone mineral density, since a fracture without trauma is not normal at 41
Investigate for malignancy first, since myeloma and metastasis outrank every other cause

answer:
C. The case next lists what vertebral fractures are - they may follow trauma (explicitly "not in this patient"), they are a common site for osteoporotic fracture, they are more common with increasing age, and more common in women - and closes with the action: ⭐ "Indication to measure bone mineral density."

⭐ The force of the case is in the mismatch. He is the wrong age, the wrong sex, and there is no mechanism. ⭐ Three of the case's four risk statements point away from him, and he fractured anyway - that is the finding. The identical X-ray in an 80-year-old woman would be unremarkable; in him it demands an explanation, and the case spends most of its length getting one.

His density confirms the suspicion: ⭐ lumbar T-score -2.6, femoral -1.7, against a normal range of +1.5 to -1.5.

A is false and would have cost him the diagnosis. B is the trap worth naming: ⭐ it treats the bone and stops there, which is exactly what the case's close shows going wrong in this man's life. D is clinically defensible and not the case's route; the case's whole point is that the cause was endocrine and reachable by asking why the bone was thin.

preamble.title: The case - vertebral fracture, 41-year-old man
preamble.html: The case. In 2001, a then 41-year-old man, director of a smaller NGO, university educated, presented with back pain (thoracic spine). X-ray showed some vertebral collapse. There was no trauma.

stem: His lumbar T-score is -2.6. He reports easy fatiguability and low sex drive, with no heat or cold intolerance, and shaves daily. His testosterone measures 5 and 7.8 nmol/L against a normal range of 10.5-34.5. Why is his bone density low?

options.html: Hypogonadism, the one risk factor his history and his biochemistry both point at
Hyperthyroidism, given the fatiguability, though his thyroid symptoms are equivocal
Vitamin D deficiency, given that his only dairy intake is the milk in his coffee
Low peak bone mass, since nothing acquired in his history accounts for a T-score this low

answer:
A. The case lists every factor associated with low BMD in men - low body weight, vitamin D deficiency, smoking, excess alcohol, hyperthyroidism, hypogonadism, glucocorticoids, gastrointestinal disease, low peak BMD or genetic factors, reduced physical activity, anticonvulsants - and then walks this patient against the list line by line.

⭐ The history is built to eliminate, not to confirm. Read it as a checklist being crossed off: "no heat/cold intolerance" strikes out thyroid disease. What survives is low sex drive, and the biochemistry settles it - ⭐ two testosterone measurements, 5 and 7.8, against a lower limit of 10.5. Measured twice, low both times.

⭐ Testosterone is what maintains male bone, directly and through aromatisation to estradiol. A man hypogonadal for years loses density the way a postmenopausal woman does, which is how a 41-year-old arrives at a T-score of -2.6.

B is excluded on the case's own words. C is a genuine risk factor and his dairy intake is poor, but no vitamin D level is given and it would not explain the low libido. D cannot be sustained once the testosterone is back.

flags.title: Why "shaves daily" is in the stem
flags.html: ⭐ It argues against the answer, and it is still true. Terminal facial hair, once established at puberty, persists on relatively little androgen, so ⚠ a normal shaving frequency does not exclude hypogonadism in an adult man. Contrast the 29-year-old in Q133, who shaves every second day. ⭐ Same disease, same gland, and the razor tells you different things in different patients - which is why the case measured the testosterone twice rather than trusting the history.

preamble.title: The case - vertebral fracture, 41-year-old man
preamble.html: The case. In 2001, a then 41-year-old man, director of a smaller NGO, university educated, presented with back pain (thoracic spine). X-ray showed some vertebral collapse. There was no trauma. His lumbar T-score is -2.6. He reports easy fatiguability and low sex drive, with no heat or cold intolerance, and shaves daily. His testosterone measures 5 and 7.8 nmol/L against a normal range of 10.5-34.5.

stem: His LH is 1 IU/L and his FSH 1 IU/L. His prolactin returns at 3145.8 µg/L (normal 2-28). He then recalls that twenty years ago, living elsewhere, he had symptoms of low testosterone, a prolactin over 200, and was prescribed bromocriptine - which he stopped, because he never understood why he should take it. What does this explain?

options.html: That his gonadotrophins are low because bromocriptine withdrawal suppressed them directly
That the original prolactin of 200 was a laboratory error, given the level measured now
That his hypogonadism is primary, the testis having failed over the intervening decades
That an untreated prolactinoma cost him twenty years of testosterone, and his bone

answer:
D. ⭐ He had the right diagnosis and the right drug two decades before the fracture, and none of it helped, because nobody made him understand why he was taking it. The exclamation marks in the notes are the lecture's own.

The chain the case has been building, complete: ⭐ macroprolactinoma → prolactin ↑ → LH and FSH ↓ → hypogonadism → bone density ↓ → vertebral fracture. He presented at the far end of it with back pain.

⭐ Read the gonadotrophins the way the case does: the finding is not that LH and FSH are low, it is that they are not HIGH. With a testosterone of 5, an intact axis should be driving them up. They sit at 1 and 1. ⭐ That inappropriate normality puts the lesion above the gonad - secondary, not primary. And the history picks the column: normal puberty, married, no surgery, no head injury, no medications means acquired, not congenital. The notes' acquired causes are drugs, high prolactin, systemic illness, pituitary tumours, infection and irradiation - and the prolactin comes back at 3145.8, which it calls "usually a macroprolactinoma". MRI then finds an eccentric left sellar lesion, 2.4 × 1.7 × 1.6 cm, not extending suprasellarly, which is why his vision was never affected as the 29-year-old's was.

⭐ A prolactinoma is where non-adherence bites hardest: an indefinite tablet, for a condition that feels like nothing, preventing consequences that arrive silently years later. A patient who does not know it is protecting his bones and his fertility has no reason to keep taking it.

A inverts the pharmacology - a dopamine agonist lowers prolactin and thereby raises gonadotrophins. B misreads the number: 200 was already far above the reference range and entirely consistent with the disease. C is excluded by the low LH and FSH, which would be high if the testis had failed.

flags.title: Treatment attacks every link
flags.html: The case's final summary sets each treatment against the step it repairs: ⭐ bisphosphonate, vitamin D and calcium for the bone · testosterone for the hypogonadism · dopamine agonist and pituitary surgery for the tumour. ⚠ Treating only the bone, which is where he presented, would have left the chain intact - the point option B in Q135 is there to test.

stem:
A 55-year-old man with a known non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma has fatigue and cold intolerance. His TSH is 3.1 mIU/L (normal 0.3-4.2) and his free T4 is low.

How should these results be interpreted?

options.html: Euthyroid, because the TSH is within the normal range
Primary hypothyroidism, needing a repeat TSH in about six weeks
Subclinical hypothyroidism, to be monitored
Assay interference; repeat only the TSH
Central hypothyroidism; the TSH is inappropriately normal

answer: The correct answer is E. TSH is an excellent screen for primary disease and unreliable in secondary. With a pituitary lesion, a normal TSH beside a low free T4 is "inappropriately normal" and is the diagnosis of central hypothyroidism. Replace on the free T4, never the TSH, and treat any adrenal insufficiency before starting thyroxine. Primary hypothyroidism would have a high TSH (B).

stem: You are asked to see a 7 yr old girl for growth assessment.Her height is 110 cm ( 1st percentile) and weight is 25 kg ( 75th percentile). Mother measures 160 cm and father measures 180 cm. What is the mid-parental height for this child?

options.html: 176.5 cm (97th percentile)
160.5 cm (26th percentile)
163.5 cm ( 50th percentile)
170 cm (80th percentile)

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 05 - Disorders of Growth. C. Mid-parental height is (mother + father ± 13 cm) / 2, with +13 for boys and −13 for girls. For this girl: (160 + 180 − 13) / 2 = 327 / 2 = 163.5 cm, the 50th percentile. Her genetic target is average, which makes her 1st-percentile height a real departure from it.

  • A (176.5) is the boy's formula: (160 + 180 + 13) / 2.
  • B (160.5) matches no version of the formula.
  • D (170) is the plain parental average with the sex correction left out.

stem: You are asked to see a 7 yr old girl for growth assessment.Her height is 110 cm ( 1st percentile) and weight is 25 kg ( 75th percentile). Mother measures 160 cm and father measures 180 cm. In further assessment, you notice that her height was 109 cm (10th percentile) one year ago at age 5.5 yrs. She had a normal birth weight and length. Mother reported a normal pregnancy with no complications. She had "low sugar" in the neonatal period but resolved in 48-72 hrs. CBC, ferritin, renal function were normal. The likely cause for these findings is :

options.html: Familial short stature (FSS)
Suboptimal growth likely related to endocrine/hormonal abnormality
Short stature due to under-nutrition/mal-absorption or chronic illness
Normal growth. There is no short stature.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 05 - Disorders of Growth. B. The lecture's first question - did the weight fall before the height? - settles it. Weight is at the 75th percentile while height has slid from the 10th to the 1st: a short, relatively chubby child, which is the endocrine pattern. She grew about 1 cm over the interval, far under the 4.5 cm/yr trigger, and she is crossing percentiles after 18 months. Normal birth size plus neonatal hypoglycaemia is the lecture's signature of congenital growth hormone deficiency.

  • A - familial short stature has a normal velocity and a low parental target; her target is 163.5 cm, the 50th percentile.
  • C - illness and undernutrition drop weight first; her weight is preserved, and CBC, ferritin and renal function are normal.
  • D - a height under the 3rd percentile is short stature by definition.

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida who received no prenatal care had marked vaginal bleeding after the onset of labor at 38 weeks gestation. Cesarean section was done and a lacerated low-lying placenta was removed. She remained hypotensive for 6 hours and required transfusion of 12 packed RBC units. She was discharged home but was not able to breast-feed. Over the next 2 months, she also noted increasing fatigue, anorexia, and lightheadness especially when she stands up. Despite not breastfeeding, her periods have not resumed.

Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her current symptoms?

options.html: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage
Pituitary necrosis
Post-partum thyroiditis
Insulitis

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease.

From the review session. Postpartum hemorrhage and hypotension infarct the pituitary, which is enlarged in pregnancy: no lactation (prolactin), no menses (LH and FSH), fatigue and orthostasis (ACTH). A student asked about treatment. She is acutely unwell, so replace what is missing, hydrocortisone first, then levothyroxine if she has central hypothyroidism. Lactation cannot be restored, and most patients do not recover gonadal function, so they need long-term estrogen and progesterone, which also affects future pregnancies.

Postpartum haemorrhage with prolonged hypotension, then failure of lactation (prolactin), amenorrhoea (gonadotropins) and orthostatic fatigue (ACTH), is several anterior pituitary axes failing together: pituitary infarction after postpartum haemorrhage (Sheehan syndrome). Infarction is one of the lecture's causes of hypopituitarism. Adrenal haemorrhage (A) would not stop lactation or menses.
