preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. A patient seen by her family doctor. Three years ago, gestational hypertension and gestational diabetes, both resolved post-partum. For the last 18 months: on an ACE inhibitor and levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, and metformin for diabetes. No other medications.

On examination: BP 156/92 · BMI 37, against a pre-pregnancy BMI of 29 three years ago · her face seems rounder than at the last visit, though the weight is not otherwise centrally concentrated · the skin on the back of her hands is thin compared with the examiner's · a couple of bruises on her shins · a few abdominal striae, but not violaceous · proximal muscle strength: asked to stand from a chair with arms folded and repeat over 30 seconds, ⭐ she manages five and has to stop and rest.

Labs: A1c 9.8% · creatinine 119 · potassium 3.8 (normal) · normal CBC.

The typed key's clue list for this case: hypertension · diabetes · weight gain · amenorrhea · easy bruising · thin skin · proximal muscle weakness · rounded face.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Polycystic ovary syndrome, with the obesity, the diabetes and the amenorrhea
Cushing syndrome, from the myopathy and thin skin alongside the metabolic picture
Poorly controlled type 2 diabetes with obesity, which explains all of the findings
Hypothyroidism that is under-replaced, giving the weight gain and the rounded face

answer:
B. The typed key: "These are classic features of hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome)." And it maps each finding onto a mechanism:

FindingMechanism
HypertensionCortisol enhances vasoconstriction and mineralocorticoid activity
Diabetes⭐ Cortisol causes insulin resistance
Weight gainFat redistribution and increased appetite
AmenorrheaSuppression of gonadotropins
Thin skin, bruising⭐ Protein catabolism
Proximal myopathy⭐ Muscle protein breakdown
Round faceFat redistribution

⭐ Two findings do the work, and the session says so: the proximal muscle weakness and the thin skin with easy bruising are "more specific physical findings that are suggestive of cortisol excess of some sort rather than just the obesity, hypertension et cetera."

⭐ That is the whole discrimination. Obesity, hypertension and diabetes are the common picture and point nowhere. A catabolic sign in someone who is gaining weight is the contradiction that names the disease - she is laying down fat and breaking down protein at the same time, and only cortisol does both at once.

⚠ She does not have the postcard version, and the key says so: "Not every patient has all the classic signs (purple striae, buffalo hump, central obesity)." Her striae are not violaceous, her weight is not centrally concentrated. ⭐ Waiting for the textbook picture is how this diagnosis gets missed.

A is the trap the session itself raises - a woman with obesity and irregular periods - and the session allows it as a real alternative before noting that irregular cycles are a general marker of endocrine dysfunction rather than a specific one. It does not explain the myopathy or the thin skin. C is what everything looks like until you do the chair-stand test. D gives weight gain and a puffy face, but she is on levothyroxine and hypothyroidism does not cause a proximal myopathy with bruising.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. A patient seen by her family doctor. Three years ago, gestational hypertension and gestational diabetes, both resolved post-partum. For the last 18 months: on an ACE inhibitor and levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, and metformin for diabetes. No other medications.

On examination: BP 156/92 · BMI 37, against a pre-pregnancy BMI of 29 three years ago · her face seems rounder than at the last visit, though the weight is not otherwise centrally concentrated · the skin on the back of her hands is thin compared with the examiner's · a couple of bruises on her shins · a few abdominal striae, but not violaceous · proximal muscle strength: asked to stand from a chair with arms folded and repeat over 30 seconds, ⭐ she manages five and has to stop and rest.

Labs: A1c 9.8% · creatinine 119 · potassium 3.8 (normal) · normal CBC.

The typed key's clue list for this case: hypertension · diabetes · weight gain · amenorrhea · easy bruising · thin skin · proximal muscle weakness · rounded face.

stem: What would you do next?

options.html: Start a trial of treatment and judge the diagnosis by whether she responds to it
A random serum cortisol, which if elevated establishes the cortisol excess
An MRI of the pituitary, to find the adenoma before committing to biochemistry
Screen for Cushing syndrome with one of the three accepted first-line tests

answer:
D. The typed key lists them, and the session walks through all three:

Screening testWhat it asks
⭐ 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test ("frequently used first")Does cortisol suppress when it is told to? Target is under 50
Late-night salivary cortisolIs cortisol low when it should be lowest?
24-hour urinary free cortisolHow much free cortisol is made across a whole day

⭐ B is the answer the session explicitly demolishes, and it is worth the detour. Asked whether a random cortisol helps, the session is blunt: a random cortisol "that's elevated doesn't tell you anything." ⭐ Cortisol has a diurnal rhythm, so a high value is normal in the morning and a single number has no reference point. A low one is a different matter and matters later, for a case where you are worried about deficiency rather than excess - which is exactly Tom Joad.

⭐ The three tests are three different questions, not three ways of asking one. Two probe the rhythm (does it suppress, is it low at night); one probes the total (24-hour output). That is why a shift worker breaks the first two and not the third - see Q165.

Why the urine test measures FREE cortisol. The session draws this out: in blood, cortisol is bound to cortisol-binding globulin, so a blood measurement is confounded by how much binding protein there is; ⭐ in urine you are measuring only the free fraction, which is why it survives a patient on estrogen.

A treats a trial of therapy as a diagnostic test in a condition that needs a cause found. C images before the biochemistry has established there is anything to image, and before ACTH has said whether the source is even pituitary.

stem: False positives (select all that apply)

options.html: An incomplete 24-hour urine collection, and a suppression test taken at the wrong hour
Phenytoin, carbamazepine and rifampin, which speed up dexamethasone metabolism
Cyclic Cushing syndrome, in which cortisol is normal between the active phases
Depression, alcohol use disorder, severe obesity, acute illness and stress

answer:
B and D. The typed key's list for a falsely positive screen - "conditions causing elevated cortisol without true Cushing syndrome" - is depression · alcohol use disorder · severe obesity · acute illness · stress.

⭐ The session gives these a name: pseudo-Cushing. The session: "alcohol abuse and depression... and obesity in general, called pseudo Cushings." ⭐ Stress raises cortisol, and being in hospital is stressful - so the very setting in which you order the test can produce the result.

⭐ The shift worker is the most useful one to hold on to, because it tells you which test to reach for. Someone working nights has a genuinely abnormal diurnal rhythm, so ⚠ a late-night salivary cortisol and a dexamethasone suppression test will both mislead - but the session's point is that "the twenty four hour urine cortisol should be the same." ⭐ When the rhythm is the thing that is disturbed, measure the total instead of the rhythm.

B is a false positive too. The test gives dexamethasone and expects cortisol to fall. ⭐ An enzyme inducer (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin) clears the dexamethasone before it can act, so cortisol is not suppressed and the test reads positive in someone without Cushing syndrome. The lecture lists P450 inducers among the dexamethasone test's caveats (02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease).

A and C are false negatives, the other column (Q166): a short collection or a test at the wrong hour, and cyclic disease caught between its active phases, both make real Cushing syndrome look normal.

flags.title: The session's key files the drugs under false negatives
flags.html: The small-group session's typed key lists phenytoin, carbamazepine and rifampin as false negatives. They speed dexamethasone clearance, so cortisol fails to suppress and the test reads positive: a false positive. B is now a correct answer, alongside D. Readers reported this.

flags.title: One more false positive, from the session only
flags.html: An over-collected 24-hour urine. The session: upper limit of normal urine volume is "up to three litres", so ⚠ four or five litres suggests the collection ran past 24 hours, or that someone else contributed to it - and the elevated result is an artefact. Not in the typed key.

stem: False negatives

options.html: Severe obesity, depression and alcohol use, which raise cortisol without the disease
An acutely ill inpatient, in whom the stress of admission suppresses the axis
Mild or cyclic Cushing syndrome, and a test done at the wrong time
A patient on estrogen, whose cortisol-binding globulin is raised by the estrogen

answer:
C. The typed key: mild or cyclic Cushing syndrome · improper test timing. It also lists drugs that increase dexamethasone metabolism (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin), but those make the test falsely positive, so they are in Q165 instead.

⚠ The session adds the one that is not a drug and not the disease: exogenous steroid. Asked for a cause of a failure to suppress, the group answers "steroids" - someone already on glucocorticoid has an axis you cannot interpret.

⭐ And the commonest false negative of all is human. For the 24-hour urine the session identifies it immediately: ⭐ an incomplete collection. "Probably the most common thing that we see is that the patient hasn't collected all the urine for twenty four hours." The safeguard is to measure the volume and the creatinine alongside it - a 24-hour creatinine has a known normal range, so ⚠ a low volume with a low creatinine means the collection was short, not that the cortisol was normal.

A is the false-positive column from Q165. B inverts the direction: acute illness raises cortisol, which is why it is a false positive. D is a real confounder but it acts on the blood measurement, not the urine - and it is the reason the session sends an estrogen-exposed patient to the 24-hour urine free cortisol, which sees only the unbound fraction.

On examination: BP 156/92 · BMI 37, against a pre-pregnancy BMI of 29 three years ago · her face seems rounder than at the last visit, though the weight is not otherwise centrally concentrated · the skin on the back of her hands is thin compared with the examiner's · a couple of bruises on her shins · a few abdominal striae, but not violaceous · proximal muscle strength: asked to stand from a chair with arms folded and repeat over 30 seconds, ⭐ she manages five and has to stop and rest.

stem: If the test is normal?

options.html: The diagnosis is excluded, since these are sensitive tests and the screen was negative
Repeat it, use a different screening test, refer, consider cyclic disease
Proceed straight to pituitary imaging, since the biochemistry has been unhelpful
Treat empirically for Cushing syndrome and review whether the features improve

answer:
B. The typed key is emphatic: "Don't dismiss the diagnosis", because "her clinical picture is very convincing" - repeat testing · use a different screening test · refer to endocrinology · consider cyclic Cushing syndrome. And then the line to carry away: ⭐ "High clinical suspicion overrides one normal screening result."

⭐ This is a statement about what a screening test is for, not about this patient. The session frames it generally: "whenever we're talking about diagnostic or screening tests, no test is over a hundred percent right, so we talk about false positives and false negatives and we have to keep those in mind when we're interpreting the results."

⭐ A normal result updates your suspicion; it does not replace it. Q165 and Q166 exist precisely so that a normal result can be interrogated: was she acutely unwell, is she a shift worker, is she on carbamazepine, was the collection complete? ⭐ Each of those is a reason the test could be normal in someone who has the disease.

⭐ And cyclic Cushing syndrome is the reason a repeat is not just a re-run. If cortisol is normal between active phases, a single test lands wherever it lands - so the answer to a normal test in a convincing patient is another test, at another time, of another kind.

A is the error the whole question exists to prevent. C images before the biochemistry has established anything. D commits a patient to treatment for a disease that has not been shown, on a test that was negative.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. "You are an emergency physician and are working on New Year's Day when you see Tom Joad, a 42-year-old man who came to the ER complaining of severe weakness. He has lost 20 pounds in the last six months, with anorexia, and abdominal pain in the last week. He can barely stand up."

Vitals. Supine BP 100/60, HR 88. ⭐ On sitting up, BP 70 systolic and HR 120. The internal jugular veins are not visible. He has an apparently good tan.

Labs, sent after treatment was started immediately: creatinine 110 · ⭐ sodium 125 · ⭐ potassium 6.7 · chloride low · bicarbonate 24.8 · ⭐ glucose 3.1 · ⭐ TSH 7.3. CBC normal. Chest X-ray normal. ⭐ ECG: sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves.

stem: What is this diagnosis?

options.html: Primary adrenal insufficiency, an adrenal crisis presenting on New Year's Day
Secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary failure, with the low TSH to match
Gastrointestinal losses from the abdominal pain, with dehydration and prerenal failure
An occult malignancy, given six months of weight loss, anorexia and abdominal pain

answer:
A. The typed key: ⭐ "Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)", and "this is almost the textbook picture." Its clue list is his case verbatim: weight loss · anorexia · abdominal pain · severe postural hypotension · hyponatremia · hyperkalemia · hypoglycemia · hyperpigmentation ("good tan") · elevated TSH.

⭐ The word "primary" is carried by two findings, and the session makes you find them. Asked what points to primary rather than secondary, the group offers the peaked T waves, and the session accepts it: peaked T waves, the potassium of 6.7 and the hyponatremia are one finding in three forms. ⭐ Only primary failure loses aldosterone, because only primary failure destroys the whole gland - secondary insufficiency is an ACTH problem and the zona glomerulosa answers to renin, not ACTH.

⭐ The second is the tan, which is Q169.

⚠ A caution the session adds, worth more than the rule: the autoimmunity "isn't like one day it's here, the next day it's not" - it is ⭐ "a bit of a grumbling process", and the glucocorticoid can go first with the aldosterone following later. ⭐ So you will not always see the hyperkalemia, and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. The exception the session names is checkpoint-inhibitor immunotherapy, which can take the gland out abruptly.

B is excluded by the labs pointing the other way: his TSH is high, not low, and secondary insufficiency spares aldosterone, so the hyperkalemia and salt-losing hypotension would be absent. C would not give hyperkalemia with hypoglycemia and a tan. D is the right instinct for six months of weight loss in isolation, but does not explain a potassium of 6.7 or a glucose of 3.1.

preamble.html:
The case. "You are an emergency physician and are working on New Year's Day when you see Tom Joad, a 42-year-old man who came to the ER complaining of severe weakness. He has lost 20 pounds in the last six months, with anorexia, and abdominal pain in the last week. He can barely stand up."

Vitals. Supine BP 100/60, HR 88. ⭐ On sitting up, BP 70 systolic and HR 120. The internal jugular veins are not visible. He has an apparently good tan.

Labs, sent after treatment was started immediately: creatinine 110 · ⭐ sodium 125 · ⭐ potassium 6.7 · chloride low · bicarbonate 24.8 · ⭐ glucose 3.1 · ⭐ TSH 7.3. CBC normal. Chest X-ray normal. ⭐ ECG: sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves.

stem: Explain the abnormalities: f) apparently good tan

options.html: Chronic illness and weight loss give a sallow discolouration mistaken for a tan
Cortisol deficiency removes the restraint on melanocytes in sun-exposed skin
High ACTH stimulates melanocytes, sharing the POMC precursor with MSH
Aldosterone deficiency concentrates pigment as the extracellular volume falls

answer:
C. The typed key: "High ACTH stimulates melanocytes. In primary adrenal failure: cortisol low, ACTH high. ⭐ ACTH shares a precursor (POMC) with melanocyte-stimulating peptides."

A student gives the full chain in the session and it is worth reading as spoken: ⭐ "ACTH is produced... there's like a pro hormone, is a POMC, that is then cleaved to make ACTH and melanocyte stimulating hormone MSH. So when you've got the negative feedback loop thing isn't happening because you don't have cortisol, your hypothalamus is first going to secrete CRH, which is going to stimulate pituitary to secrete more ACTH, but you get that precursor with it, and so then you get that increased production of the MSH, which causes hyperpigmentation."

⭐ This is why the tan means PRIMARY. The pigment is a by-product of the pituitary shouting. In secondary insufficiency the pituitary is the thing that has failed, so there is no shouting and ⚠ no hyperpigmentation - the same cortisol deficiency, the opposite skin.

⭐ Where to look, which is the examinable part. The session presses the group on this, and notes first that ⭐ skin colour varies and a "tan" is not a reliable thing to eyeball. So look where pigment concentrates regardless of baseline colour: ⭐ palmar creases · skin folds · buccal mucosa · scars. "It won't necessarily just be skin, it'll be your palmar creases, buccal mucosa, sometimes looking at scars can be helpful."

A is the competing read of a tan in a wasted patient, and the reason you go to the creases rather than the face. B inverts the mechanism - the driver is excess ACTH, not absent cortisol acting locally. D is not a mechanism of pigmentation.

stem: Explain the abnormalities: g) elevated TSH

options.html: Volume depletion concentrates TSH, as it concentrates the other measured solutes
Two reasons: glucocorticoid restrains TSH, and autoimmune disease clusters
The high ACTH cross-reacts with the TSH assay, both being pituitary glycoproteins
Hyponatremia interferes with the immunoassay and falsely raises the reported TSH

answer:
B. ⭐ The session calls this one out before asking it: "What about the TSH level? That one's the tricky one, an important one." And then: "Quick, would be two reasons."

Reason one is physiological. The typed key: "cortisol deficiency itself can modestly increase TSH levels." The session corrects a student who has the arrow backwards: ⭐ "it's more that glucocorticoids tend to inhibit the release of TSH rather than the other way around... so then when you lose the glucocorticoids you sort of lose a little bit of that mechanism of restraint, and the TSH can often be a little bit higher." ⭐ So it may be that there is no thyroid disease at all.

Reason two is that there may be a second disease. The typed key: "Autoimmune Addison disease often coexists with autoimmune thyroid disease." The session: ⭐ "autoimmune diseases often cluster together... in one particular type of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, APS type two", historically Schmidt syndrome. ⚠ Thyroid disease is far commoner than adrenal disease, so the pairing is much more often found from the thyroid end.

⭐ Holding both at once is the point of the question. One reading says the TSH is an artefact of the adrenal failure and needs no action; the other says he has a second autoimmune disease. You cannot tell from this number, and the honest answer is that both are live until he is replaced and retested.

A is raised by a student in the session and the session rejects it directly: "it's not like electrolytes." C and D are assay artefacts that are not described anywhere in the material.

preamble.html:
The case. "You are an emergency physician and are working on New Year's Day when you see Tom Joad, a 42-year-old man who came to the ER complaining of severe weakness. He has lost 20 pounds in the last six months, with anorexia, and abdominal pain in the last week. He can barely stand up."

Labs, sent after treatment was started immediately: creatinine 110 · ⭐ sodium 125 · ⭐ potassium 6.7 · chloride low · bicarbonate 24.8 · ⭐ glucose 3.1 · ⭐ TSH 7.3. CBC normal. Chest X-ray normal. ⭐ ECG: sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves.

stem: Explain the abnormalities: c) hyponatremia

options.html: Dilution from the intravenous fluid given before the bloods were drawn
Sodium wasting from aldosterone deficiency, plus ADH release from low cortisol
A syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, driven by the abdominal pain and nausea
Pseudohyponatremia, the measured sodium falling because of the high potassium

answer:
B. The typed key gives two contributors: "sodium loss from aldosterone deficiency" and "increased ADH release because of cortisol deficiency."

⭐ The two arrive from opposite directions and that is why the sodium falls so far. Without aldosterone the kidney wastes sodium - so there is genuinely less salt. Without cortisol the restraint on ADH is lost - so there is more water retained. ⭐ Less salt and more water, and 125 follows.

⭐ Which half is which decides the treatment, and the session turns on exactly this. Asked whether to use hypertonic saline, the session draws the line: ⭐ "hypertonic saline is for when the problem is not with not enough salt, it's with too much water." Tom Joad is missing salt, so he gets 0.9% normal saline, not 3%, and not the 0.45% that is hypotonic to his blood. See Q174.

⭐ And the fluid fixes it without being aimed at it. The session notes that the sodium "will still correct a little bit in this case because he's missing salt" - restore the volume and the inappropriate ADH switches off, because the stimulus was the volume depletion.

C describes the SIADH pattern the session explicitly contrasts with this one - a water problem, not a salt problem. A is excluded by the case: the labs were ordered as treatment began. D is not a mechanism; pseudohyponatremia comes from extreme lipids or protein.

Labs, sent after treatment was started immediately: creatinine 110 · ⭐ sodium 125 · ⭐ potassium 6.7 · chloride low · bicarbonate 24.8 · ⭐ glucose 3.1 · ⭐ TSH 7.3. CBC normal. Chest X-ray normal. ⭐ ECG: sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves.

stem: Explain the abnormalities: d) hypoglycemia

options.html: The anorexia and six months of weight loss, with nothing left in the glycogen stores
Increased insulin sensitivity once the counter-regulatory catecholamines are exhausted
Cortisol normally promotes gluconeogenesis and maintains fasting glucose
The abdominal pain has stopped him eating, and this is a simple starvation hypoglycemia

answer:
C. The typed key: "Cortisol normally promotes gluconeogenesis and maintains fasting glucose. Without cortisol, glucose falls."

⭐ Cortisol is a counter-regulatory hormone, and this is that fact presented from the deficiency side. Everywhere else in the block cortisol appears as the thing that causes hyperglycemia - it is why Case 1 has an A1c of 9.8%, and why the key there lists "cortisol causes insulin resistance." ⭐ Same hormone, same action, opposite direction: too much gives diabetes, too little gives hypoglycemia. Reading the two cases against each other is the cheapest way to make either stick.

⭐ It also explains why his glucose has to be corrected before anything else settles, and the treatment list in Q174 has it second.

A and D are the same answer and both are plausible on their own, which is what makes them the useful distractors: a man who has lost 20 pounds and stopped eating would be prone to hypoglycemia. ⚠ But starvation alone does not give a glucose of 3.1 in a 42-year-old with intact counter-regulation - the liver keeps making glucose. What is missing here is the hormone that tells it to. B inverts the physiology and is not described anywhere in the material.

preamble.html:
The case. "You are an emergency physician and are working on New Year's Day when you see Tom Joad, a 42-year-old man who came to the ER complaining of severe weakness. He has lost 20 pounds in the last six months, with anorexia, and abdominal pain in the last week. He can barely stand up."

Vitals. Supine BP 100/60, HR 88. ⭐ On sitting up, BP 70 systolic and HR 120. The internal jugular veins are not visible. He has an apparently good tan.

Labs, sent after treatment was started immediately: creatinine 110 · ⭐ sodium 125 · ⭐ potassium 6.7 · chloride low · bicarbonate 24.8 · ⭐ glucose 3.1 · ⭐ TSH 7.3. CBC normal. Chest X-ray normal. ⭐ ECG: sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves.

stem: How to confirm?

options.html: A cosyntropin stimulation test, done now, before any steroid is given
A random serum cortisol alone, which if under 80 is effectively diagnostic
Morning cortisol with a paired ACTH, and cosyntropin once he is stable
Adrenal imaging, to show the small atrophic glands of autoimmune adrenalitis

answer:
C. The typed key separates the two: ⭐ initial labs are "morning cortisol" and "ACTH", expecting low cortisol with high ACTH; the ⭐ definitive test is cosyntropin (ACTH stimulation), in which primary failure shows "cortisol fails to rise appropriately."

⭐ A is what the group answers first, and the session's reply is the lesson of the case. Asked whether a stimulation test is feasible here: "an ACTH stimulation test takes hours to do; in my experience it takes days or weeks to arrange. ⭐ There's no bottle of ACTH sitting on the crash cart. You've got to measure the level at ninety minutes, at sixty minutes, a whole bunch of different minutes." ⚠ It is the right test and the wrong moment - this man is about to die.

⭐ Why the ACTH must be drawn WITH the cortisol, not after it. A low cortisol says the axis has failed; ⭐ only the paired ACTH says where. High ACTH means the adrenal cannot answer - primary. Low or inappropriately normal means the pituitary never asked - secondary.

⚠ ⭐ And the timing point that is the real trap: both must be drawn BEFORE the hydrocortisone goes in. The session is emphatic: "it's very important that you would draw the cortisol and ACTH blood before you give the hydrocortisone... if we don't get those levels drawn off before we start treatment then it can be very challenging to confirm the diagnosis, because you can't really hold it in this situation to measure it later." ⭐ The treatment destroys the evidence - exogenous hydrocortisone is read by the cortisol assay, and it suppresses ACTH.

⭐ Note what C does not say: it does not say wait. Asked whether to wait for the results, the session: "I'll give you a hint, they don't come back quickly... and ACTH doesn't even come back the same week." Draw, then treat. That is Q174.

B has the right threshold - the session names under 80 as potentially diagnostic - but drops the ACTH, which is the half that localises. D is not how the diagnosis is made.

preamble.html:
The case. "You are an emergency physician and are working on New Year's Day when you see Tom Joad, a 42-year-old man who came to the ER complaining of severe weakness. He has lost 20 pounds in the last six months, with anorexia, and abdominal pain in the last week. He can barely stand up."

Vitals. Supine BP 100/60, HR 88. ⭐ On sitting up, BP 70 systolic and HR 120. The internal jugular veins are not visible. He has an apparently good tan.

Labs, sent after treatment was started immediately: creatinine 110 · ⭐ sodium 125 · ⭐ potassium 6.7 · chloride low · bicarbonate 24.8 · ⭐ glucose 3.1 · ⭐ TSH 7.3. CBC normal. Chest X-ray normal. ⭐ ECG: sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves.

stem: Immediate treatment

options.html: Draw cortisol and ACTH, then saline, glucose, the potassium, hydrocortisone
IV hydrocortisone at once, with the confirmatory bloods drawn afterwards once he is stable
Hypertonic saline first to correct the sodium of 125, then steroid once it is above 130
Fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone together, since both adrenal hormones are deficient

answer:
A. The typed key: "This patient is critically ill. Start immediately: 1. IV normal saline · 2. correct glucose if needed · 3. treat dangerous hyperkalemia (calcium gluconate, insulin + glucose) · 4. IV hydrocortisone. ⭐ Do not delay treatment while waiting for confirmation." And from Q173, the bloods come off before the steroid.

Which fluid, and the session works it out in real time. ⭐ 0.9% normal saline - "because we know he's already volume deplete and he's missing salt." Not 0.45%, "because that's hypotonic to his blood." Not hypertonic, for the reason in Q171. With D5 alongside, for the glucose of 3.1.

How much: "a thousand millilitres... there's no limit in this case. Forty-two-year-old guy, he has no heart disease, he's got no blood pressure - you're gonna just fill him up."

⭐ Why hydrocortisone specifically, which is the bit worth keeping. The group gets there: it is shorter acting, has a faster onset, can be given IV - and, crucially, ⭐ at high doses it has mineralocorticoid action as well. "So that plus the saline is going to be what we need in this case." That single fact is also the answer to Q175.

⭐ On the potassium of 6.7, the session is reassuring rather than alarming: calcium gluconate would likely already have been given on the ECG, but "the potassium will correct quite quickly with the fluid as well" - because the volume and the cortisol are the disease and the potassium is a symptom of it.

B is right about urgency and wrong about order - and it is the specific error Q173 exists to prevent, because it costs the diagnosis. C delays the one treatment that works, for a sodium that will correct on its own. D is Q175's question, answered too early.

stem: When add fludrocortisone?

options.html: Immediately, alongside the hydrocortisone, since aldosterone is deficient from the outset
Never in primary adrenal insufficiency, where hydrocortisone replaces both hormones
Only if the hyperkalemia fails to correct with saline within the first 24 hours
Once he is diagnosed and stable, and the hydrocortisone comes down off crisis dosing

answer:
D. The typed key: "Fludrocortisone replaces aldosterone. Usually started after: diagnosis established · patient stabilized · hydrocortisone dose reduced from crisis-level dosing."

⭐ And the reason is the single fact from Q174: "High-dose hydrocortisone initially provides enough mineralocorticoid activity on its own." At crisis doses the hydrocortisone is already doing the aldosterone's job, so adding fludrocortisone changes nothing. ⭐ It becomes necessary only as the hydrocortisone comes down and that incidental mineralocorticoid effect goes with it.

⭐ This is a dose-dependent property, not a property of the drug, which is the thing to hold: the same molecule that needs a mineralocorticoid partner at replacement doses does not need one at 100 mg IV.

A is the intuitive answer - both hormones are missing, replace both - and it is wrong for a reason worth knowing rather than a technicality. B is true only at crisis dosing and becomes dangerous as a general rule: ⚠ a patient maintained on hydrocortisone alone will salt-waste. C makes it a rescue for a lab value; the hyperkalemia corrects with fluid, and fludrocortisone is long-term replacement, not an acute potassium treatment.

preamble.title: Case 3 - Fiona Anderson
preamble.html: Case 3 - Fiona Anderson. Recurrent spells of palpitations, headaches and sweating.

stem: Laboratory assessment

options.html: Plasma free metanephrines, or 24-hour urine metanephrines and catecholamines
Plasma catecholamines drawn during an attack, when the tumour is actively secreting
A clonidine suppression test first, as the most specific of the available options
CT of the adrenals, since imaging is what ultimately locates a secreting tumour

answer:
A. The typed key: "Best screening tests: plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine metanephrines/catecholamines. ⭐ These are more sensitive than measuring episodic catecholamine levels."

⭐ That last clause is the entire question, and B is the answer it is aimed at. Catecholamines are released in bursts, so a level between spells can be normal and a level during one is hard to catch. ⭐ Metanephrines are the METABOLITES, and they are produced continuously inside the tumour regardless of whether it is having a moment - so they integrate secretion the way IGF-1 integrates growth hormone.

⭐ The same pattern has now appeared three times in this block, which is why it is worth naming: a pulsatile or episodic hormone is never measured directly. Growth hormone is measured through IGF-1; LH is measured under stimulation; catecholamines are measured through metanephrines. Measure the steady thing downstream of the unsteady thing.

B is the intuitive answer and the one the key explicitly ranks lower. C is a confirmatory test for an equivocal result, not a screen. D images before the biochemistry says there is anything to find - and an adrenal mass found this way is Case 5's problem, not a diagnosis.

preamble.title: Case 4 - Tom Bombadil
preamble.html: Case 4 - Tom Bombadil. A 36-year-old with new hypertension, potassium 2.3 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 32 - a metabolic alkalosis.

stem: Differential of hypertension + hypokalemia

options.html: Renovascular hypertension first, hyperaldosteronism being far rarer at this age
Diuretic use is the commonest cause and should be assumed until excluded by history
Coarctation of the aorta, which produces both the hypertension and the potassium loss
Primary hyperaldosteronism, then renovascular, Cushing, AME, Liddle and diuretics

answer:
D. The typed key's order is the answer: ⭐ 1. primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) · 2. renovascular hypertension · 3. Cushing syndrome · 4. apparent mineralocorticoid excess · 5. Liddle syndrome · 6. diuretic use - and then, flatly: ⭐ "Primary hyperaldosteronism is the leading diagnosis."

⭐ Adding the potassium to the hypertension is what collapses the eight-item list to this one. The key's own framing of his case: new hypertension · severe hypokalemia (2.3) · metabolic alkalosis (HCO₃ 32) "should immediately make you think of hyperaldosteronism."

⭐ The three findings are one mechanism seen three ways. Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to retain sodium and excrete potassium and hydrogen ion. Sodium retention gives the hypertension; potassium excretion gives the 2.3; hydrogen ion excretion gives the bicarbonate of 32. ⚠ A hypertensive patient whose potassium is low and whose bicarbonate is high has told you the mechanism before any test is sent.

⭐ Severity matters as much as direction. A potassium of 2.3 is not a mild thiazide effect; it is profound, and it is the thing that makes a secondary cause likely rather than possible.

B is on the list and is genuinely common, but a drug history settles it in one question and nothing suggests he takes one. A inverts the key's own ranking. C gives hypertension, but by mechanical obstruction, and does not waste potassium.

preamble.title: Case 4 - Tom Bombadil
preamble.html: Case 4 - Tom Bombadil. A 36-year-old with new hypertension, potassium 2.3 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 32 - a metabolic alkalosis.

stem: Screening test?

options.html: A 24-hour urine potassium, to prove the loss is renal rather than gastrointestinal
An adrenal CT, to find the aldosterone-producing adenoma before any biochemistry
Plasma aldosterone and plasma renin, read as the aldosterone-to-renin ratio
A saline suppression test, since a ratio alone cannot confirm autonomous secretion

answer:
C. The typed key: measure ⭐ plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) and ⭐ plasma renin activity (PRA), and calculate the ⭐ aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR). Expected: high aldosterone · suppressed renin · elevated ARR. "This is the standard screening test for primary aldosteronism."

⭐ The ratio exists because either number alone is ambiguous, and the renin is the half that does the work. A high aldosterone can be perfectly appropriate - it is what a volume-depleted or renovascular patient should have, driven by high renin. ⭐ What makes it PRIMARY is that the adrenal is making it without being asked, so the renin is suppressed by the resulting volume expansion. ⭐ High aldosterone with high renin is secondary; high aldosterone with LOW renin is Conn.

⭐ The same shape as every other axis in this block. A hormone measured beside its own trophic signal, and the pair localises what neither can alone - cortisol beside ACTH, testosterone beside LH and FSH, aldosterone beside renin.

D is a fair objection and a real test, but it is confirmatory, run after a positive ratio - the question asks for the screen. B images before the biochemistry, and adrenal nodules are common enough that a scan can mislead before a hormone has been shown to be autonomous. A establishes renal potassium wasting but does not name the cause.

preamble.html: Case 5 - Max Havelaar. An ⭐ adrenal incidentaloma - the typed key's definition: "an adrenal mass found unexpectedly during imaging done for another reason." The lesion is 3.2 cm.

stem: History and exam

options.html: Look for evidence of hormone excess, and for constitutional features of malignancy
Establish why the original imaging was ordered, which usually explains the finding
A careful family history, since most incidentalomas are part of a hereditary syndrome
Nothing specific, since an incidentaloma is by definition asymptomatic at presentation

answer:
A. The typed key: "Look for evidence of hormone excess." And it lists what each syndrome would show, which is a compact revision of the whole session:

If it is makingLook for
Cushing syndromeweight gain · easy bruising · diabetes · muscle weakness
Pheochromocytomaheadaches · sweating · palpitations
Hyperaldosteronismhypertension · hypokalemic symptoms
Cancerweight loss · pain · constitutional symptoms

⭐ Read that table against the earlier cases and it is the same four presentations arriving from the other end. Cushing's row is Case 1; the pheochromocytoma row is Fiona's triad exactly; the hyperaldosteronism row is Tom Bombadil. ⭐ There the patient came with symptoms and you looked for the lesion. Here the lesion came first and you go looking for the symptoms.

D is the trap in the word "incidental", and the key answers it directly in Q183: ⚠ "even if asymptomatic, evaluate for hormone production." ⭐ Incidental means nobody was looking, not that there is nothing to find - mild autonomous cortisol secretion in particular is often clinically silent.

B is worth knowing for context but does not assess the mass. C overstates it: most incidentalomas are sporadic adenomas, and a family history matters chiefly for the pheochromocytoma column.

preamble.title: Case 5 - Max Havelaar
preamble.html: Case 5 - Max Havelaar. An ⭐ adrenal incidentaloma - the typed key's definition: "an adrenal mass found unexpectedly during imaging done for another reason." The lesion is 3.2 cm.

stem: What labs?

options.html: A full pituitary panel, since the adrenal is downstream of the pituitary in every axis
An overnight dexamethasone suppression test, metanephrines, ARR if hypertensive
A random cortisol, a random catecholamine level and an aldosterone, all drawn together
None unless he is symptomatic, with imaging alone repeated to watch for growth

answer:
B. The typed key: "Even if asymptomatic, evaluate for hormone production." Its three tests map one-to-one onto the three secreting possibilities:

Looking forTest
Cortisol excess⭐ overnight dexamethasone suppression test
Pheochromocytoma⭐ plasma free metanephrines, or urine metanephrines
Hyperaldosteronism⭐ aldosterone-to-renin ratio - ⚠ if hypertensive

⭐ Each of these has already been arrived at once in this session, for its own reason, and this is where they collect: the suppression test from Case 1, the metanephrines from Case 3, the ARR from Case 4. ⭐ Three tests, three axes, and the incidentaloma is the case that asks all three at once because it has no symptoms to narrow them.

⭐ The conditional on the last one is deliberate. The key qualifies only the ARR with "if hypertensive" - ⚠ primary aldosteronism without hypertension is not a thing you screen for, whereas silent cortisol excess is, which is why the other two are unconditional.

C is the wrong version of the right instinct and is the error Q164 already dismantled: ⭐ a random cortisol is uninterpretable because of the diurnal rhythm, and a random catecholamine is uninterpretable because secretion is episodic. Each of these hormones has a test designed around the reason the raw level fails. A tests the wrong organ. D is what the key's opening words exist to forbid.

preamble.title: Case 5 - Max Havelaar
preamble.html: Case 5 - Max Havelaar. An ⭐ adrenal incidentaloma - the typed key's definition: "an adrenal mass found unexpectedly during imaging done for another reason." The lesion is 3.2 cm.

stem: Follow-up

options.html: Discharge from follow-up, a 3.2 cm lesion being below the size threshold for concern
Immediate adrenalectomy, since at over 3 cm the risk of carcinoma is unacceptable
It depends on size, imaging appearance and hormonal status, surgery if indicated
A biopsy of the lesion, which settles benign against malignant before anything else

answer:
C. The typed key: follow-up "depends on: size · imaging characteristics · hormonal status." For a 3.2 cm lesion specifically: ⭐ "repeat imaging may be recommended" and ⭐ "repeat hormonal evaluation may be recommended", with surgery considered if ⭐ hormonally active · enlarging · suspicious for malignancy · a large lesion.

⭐ Three axes, and the same three from Q182 and Q183. How big, what it looks like, what it makes. ⚠ No single one of them decides - which is why the key's four surgical triggers are a list of any, not a threshold.

⭐ Why repeat, rather than decide now. Both the imaging and the hormones are snapshots, and the two things that would change the plan - growth and the onset of autonomous secretion - are only visible over time. ⭐ An incidentaloma is a diagnosis you keep making, not one you make once.

A and B are the two ways of treating 3.2 cm as a threshold, and the key deliberately gives neither - its language is "may be recommended" and "considered if". ⭐ Size is one input among three, and this lesion sits where it is neither reassuringly small nor decisively large, which is precisely why it gets watched rather than dismissed or resected.

D is the answer to avoid hardest. ⚠ Biopsy is not part of the key's pathway at all, and the reason is Q183: a pheochromocytoma must be excluded biochemically first, because needling one is dangerous. The hormones come before the needle.

stem: How is short stature defined?

options.html: Height below that expected for age and sex and below that expected for parental height
Height and weight below that expected for age and sex AND height below that expected for parental height
Height below that expected for age and sex and plots below the 10th percentile on growth chart
Height and weight below the 3rd percentile and below what is expected for age and sex and parental height

answer:
[!success]- Answer

A. The block defines short stature as ≥2 SD below the mean, i.e. height below the 3rd percentile, and lists ">2 SD below mid-parental height" separately as a trigger to investigate. ⭐ So the definition measures height twice - against the population, and against the family - and A is the only option that does both and nothing else.

⭐ Weight has no place in the definition, and B and D both smuggle it in. The block does use weight, but for a completely different job: weight relative to height is the question that splits chronic illness from endocrine disease. That is a differential question, asked after short stature has already been established.

C fails on the number - 10th percentile, not 3rd. That is roughly a 1.3 SD cut-off rather than 2, and it would call about one child in ten short.

⚠ A is the weakest-worded correct answer in the set, because it names no percentile at all. The number the block wants is the 3rd.

stem: Jason and Joanne are fraternal twins. Their mother is 160cm tall and their father is 177cm. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: Given that they are twins, they will be close in height and each approximately 168cm
Joanne's approximate adult height will be 160 cm and Jason will be approximately 177cm
Joanne's approximate adult height will be 162 cm and Jason will be approximately 175cm
Joanne's approximate adult height will be 168 cm and Jason will be approximately 175cm

answer:
[!success]- Answer

C. Mid-parental height is (mother + father ± 13) / 2, ⭐ +13 cm for a boy and −13 cm for a girl.

  • Joanne: (160 + 177 − 13) / 2 = 162 cm
  • Jason: (160 + 177 + 13) / 2 = 175 cm

⭐ The 13 cm is the average adult height difference between the sexes, and it is the whole content of the question. Every distractor is the same arithmetic with the correction mishandled.

A takes the plain midpoint, 168.5, and gives it to both - which is what you get by forgetting the correction exists. ⚠ It also invites the wrong idea that fraternal twins should be similar in height; they are no more alike than any other siblings. B assigns each child the same-sex parent's height, which is not how the target is built. D applies the correction to Jason but not to Joanne.

preamble.title: The case - Samantha
preamble.html: The case - Samantha (Q140-Q142). "You are seeing 6-year-old Samantha in your clinic. She has been referred for short stature. She was born at 30 weeks gestation, and spent 12 weeks in the NICU. She walked at 18 months, and said her first words at 16 months. She now plays soccer and sees a speech language therapist at school. The remainder of the history is non-contributory. Her growth chart is as shown on the next page and the remainder of the physical exam is unremarkable"

stem: What is the most important first step?

options.html: Obtain previous growth charts
Obtain a bone age and karyotype
Obtain details of NICU admission
Calculate mid-parental height

answer:
[!success]- Answer

A. The block frames the workup as four questions: genetic potential, height-age, growth velocity and growth potential. ⭐ Growth velocity needs two measurements a full year apart, so it cannot be computed from today's visit - and it is the number that decides whether this is a child who has always been small or one who has stopped growing. Previous charts give it at no cost and no radiation.

D is the closest competitor and the source itself answers it: ⚠ her parents' heights are not in this stem. They arrive in the next question, which is the giveaway that mid-parental height is not yet available to calculate.

B is premature. A bone age and a karyotype are both in the workup - the block says "karyotype every short girl" - but ordering tests before characterising the growth pattern means ordering them without a question to answer.

C is real history. 30 weeks, 12 weeks in the NICU and a speech therapist at school are all relevant, and prematurity is on the block's list of causes. But it does not change the first move, and ⭐ a child who is small because she was born early should still be growing at a normal velocity - which is exactly what the previous charts will tell you.

stem: Referring to the growth chart on the next page, what is Samantha's height age?

options.html: Approximately 115 cm
Approximately 6 years
Approximately 5.5  years
Approximately 4.5 years

answer:
[!success]- Answer

D. The block's definition: ⭐ height age is the age at which a child's height would be the 50th percentile. So it is read off the chart in one move - find her height, slide across to the 50th percentile line, and read the age underneath.

She plots at ~105 cm at 6 years, which is below the 3rd percentile for her age. 105 cm is the 50th percentile at about 4½.

⭐ A height age two years behind a chronological age is the number that makes "short" quantitative, and it is why the block puts height-age alongside bone age: height age says how far behind she has fallen, bone age says how much runway is left to catch up in.

A is a category error - a height age is an age, not a height, and 115 cm is not even her height. B is her chronological age, which by definition is what a height age differs from when a child is short. C is the same idea read too generously off the chart.

stem: On further history, Samantha has no known medical co-morbidities, is on no medications and has no known allergies. Her previous growth charts show that at 5 years of age height was 104 cm and weight was 14.5 kg. Bone age and karyotype are ordered. Her mother's height is 160cm and her father's height is 185cm. With the information available, which of the following is the top diagnosis on your differential?

options.html: familial short stature
Hypothyroidism
Constitutional delay
Ulcerative colitis

answer:
[!success]- Answer

B. Put the two visits side by side and the answer is arithmetic:

Age 5Age 6 (chart)Change
Height104 cm~105 cm⚠ +1 cm in a year
Weight14.5 kg~20 kg⭐ +5.5 kg in a year

⭐ Her height has arrested while her weight has climbed, and that is the block's single splitting question. It puts it as one line: "did the weight fall before the height, or is the child short and relatively chubby?" Illness starves growth; ⭐ endocrine disease arrests it and leaves the weight behind. She is the second pattern.

1 cm/yr against a trigger of <4.5 cm/yr is not borderline - it is growth failure, and the block's endocrine column for slow growth with weight gain is hypothyroidism. ⭐ TSH is "the test that must not be missed in any short child."

Her mid-parental height settles A. (160 + 185 − 13) / 2 = ⭐ 166 cm, which is a perfectly ordinary target. She is nowhere near it, so this is not a short child in a short family.

C requires a normal growth velocity - the block's CDGP is a child who tracks along a low percentile at a normal rate and is late to puberty. 1 cm/yr is not tracking. D is the pattern in reverse: ⭐ inflammatory bowel disease takes the weight first, and hers went up.

stem: Ella is 13 year old female referred for delayed puberty. She is quite distraught that she has not developed as fast as some of her classmates. She was born 34 weeks gestational age and was admitted to the NICU for 4 weeks for issues around feeding. She hit her developmental milestones approximately and is currently a B student in grade 7. Her height is 143 cm and her weight is 45kg. On exam, she is well looking. She has a II/VI systolic ejection murmur at the LLSB. She is Tanner stage II for breast development and stage I for pubic hair. What is the most important first step in approaching the diagnosis?

options.html: Determination of bone age
Pituitary hormone testing
Determine growth velocity
Determine growth velocity

answer:
[!success]- Answer

C. ⭐ The course keys this one, and the answer is "Determine growth velocity" - highlighted on option C in Noor's annotated copy. ⚠ Option D is the same text again, so the paper prints the right answer twice; the duplicate is a typographical fault in the source, not a second answer. ⚠ The stem carries her own uncertainty marker in the margin - (unsure)** - so the room found it hard too.

⭐ The whole session turns on this move, and this is the third time it is asked. Samantha, James and Ella all open with "what is the most important first step", and in every case the answer is to characterise the growth pattern before ordering anything. ⭐ Growth velocity is the number that separates a child who has always been small from one who has stopped growing, and no test replaces it.

What the case is pointing at. Short (143 cm at 13 is below the 3rd percentile), stalled puberty (Tanner II breast, Tanner I pubic hair), and ⭐ a systolic ejection murmur. The block says a Turner girl is screened lifelong for congenital heart disease, and that short stature is the commonest feature of Turner at 95-100%. ⭐ The one test the block says is done in every short girl is a karyotype - and it is not among the four options, which is part of why the question reads oddly.

⭐ One finding cuts the other way and is worth sitting with. The block says pubarche occurs in 100% of Turner girls, because the adrenal glands are normal. Ella is Tanner I for pubic hair. At 13 that is not impossible, but it is the detail that would keep the differential open.

A is the test that makes the CDGP diagnosis, and it is defensible - but it is a test, and the velocity comes before the test. B is the workup for low gonadotropins, which have not been measured.

stem: What is the normal pubertal sequence in females?

options.html: Pubarche → thelarche → growth spurt → menarche
Thelarche → menarche → pubarche → growth spurt
Thelarche → growth spurt → pubarche → menarche
Growth spurt → thelarche → pubarche → menarche

answer:
[!success]- Answer

C. The block gives the sequence with its average ages attached:

OrderEventAverage age
①⭐ Thelarche - the first sign in most girls10.3 ± 1.0 y
②⭐ Growth spurt, at Tanner 2-3-
③Pubarche11.2 ± 1.1 y
④Menarche, at Tanner 4-512.7 ± 1.0 y, ~2.5 y after thelarche

⭐ The growth spurt's position is the whole discriminator, and it is the one thing all four options move around. In girls it comes early, at Tanner 2-3; in boys it comes late, at Tanner 3-4 - ⭐ which is why boys grow for longer first and finish taller.

A is a real variant, not nonsense: the block notes that ⚠ 15% of girls have pubarche as the first sign instead of thelarche. It is just not the normal sequence, and ⭐ pubarche is adrenal - the block says it is "not a marker of puberty at all." B puts menarche second, two years too early and before the growth spurt. D starts with the growth spurt, which no one does.

stem: You are seeing John, a 7 year old boy, brought in by mom for concerns regarding pubertal development. He has Tanner stage III pubic hair, testicular volume of 2ml on the right and 6mls on the left. There is moderate acne and his voice is deep. The next most important step is:

options.html: Ultrasound of the testes
MRI of the head
Measure serum FSH and LH
GnRH stimulation test

answer:
[!success]- Answer

A. ⭐ The course's answer is the ultrasound, and Noor's annotated copy gives the reason in the margin: ⭐ "Ultrasound of the testes (Correct) > concerned about a malignancy, can do it right away."

⚠ This overturns the reasoning that was banked here first, which argued for C. That argument ran: gonadotropins are the branch point, so measure LH and FSH before imaging anything - and it cited the puberty and growth session, whose answer to "what investigations would you propose" for a nearly identical boy is LH/FSH, testosterone, bone age. ⭐ The two questions are not the same question, which is where that went wrong: that session asks what panel to send, and this one asks what the single next step is with an asymmetric testis in front of you.

⭐ What makes the ultrasound first is that the finding is already localising. The block says asymmetric testis suggests a Leydig tumour, and his are 2 mL on the right and 6 mL on the left. ⭐ A mass in a gonad is a malignancy question, and the annotation says so - it is answered immediately, with a test that is quick, available and non-invasive. The gonadotropins are still going to be sent; they are just not what the asymmetry demands first.

Noor's note on D is the one to carry: ⭐ "GnRH stimulation test > need to know FSH, LH first, but does not tell you what the diagnosis is." That is the general point about the stimulation test - it establishes central or peripheral, not what the lesion is.

⭐ C was the group's answer too - it is the option marked green, "think right w grp" - which is worth knowing, because it means the reasoning behind it is defensible and still lost. B images the head, and the next question is about to establish that the axis is switched off, so the head is the wrong organ.

preamble.title: The case - John
preamble.html: The case. You are seeing John, a 7 year old boy, brought in by mom for concerns regarding pubertal development. He has Tanner stage III pubic hair, testicular volume of 2ml on the right and 6mls on the left. There is moderate acne and his voice is deep.

stem: John has precocious puberty. Based on the likely diagnosis, how would you classify it?

options.html: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Premature adrenarche
Gonadotropin independent
Gonadotropin dependent

answer:
[!success]- Answer

C. The block reduces this to one sentence: ⭐ "In a virilised boy, bilaterally enlarged testes mean CENTRAL and small testes mean PERIPHERAL, because only LH grows the testis."

⭐ Read "bilaterally" carefully - it is doing all the work. Central activation sends LH into the bloodstream, so it reaches both gonads and enlarges both to ≥4 mL. John has 2 mL on the right and 6 mL on the left. ⚠ One testis over 4 mL is not bilateral enlargement; it is one testis that has grown for a local reason - and the block names that reason: asymmetric testis = Leydig tumour, a gonadal cause of peripheral precocity.

Peripheral precocity is GnRH-independent: the androgen is made without the pituitary's instruction, which is C. D is the same disease one level up.

A and B are causes, not classifications - and neither fits anyway. ⭐ CAH is adrenal, so it virilises with BOTH testes small (<3 mL); his left is 6 mL. Premature adrenarche is the block's benign variant: pubic hair alone, from a physiological rise in adrenal hormones, with no other sign of androgen action. John has moderate acne, a deep voice and an enlarged testis.

preamble.title: The case - Anita
preamble.html: The case - Anita (Q147). "You are seeing Anita, a 6-year-old girl, regarding concerns about growth. She was born at term. She was admitted to hospital at 2 months of age, for 5 days, with respiratory syncytial virus infection (RSV) and again at 3 years of age with pneumonia. There is a family history of asthma and a maternal cousin has Down Syndrome. Anita has otherwise been healthy and is on no medications. Anita's mother recalls that at the 4 year check-up Anita was 3'1" and weighed 32 lbs. Anita's mother's height is 155 cm and father's height is 158 cm. The physical exam reveals a single palmar crease on the left hand. Anita's current height and weight are shown on the growth chart on the next page."

stem: In this scenario, the most likely cause of Anita's growth pattern is:

options.html: inadequately treated asthma
familial short stature
constitutional growth delay
Down Syndrome

answer:
[!success]- Answer

B. Two numbers decide it, and they are the same two the block always asks for.

⭐ Her target is low. (155 + 158 − 13) / 2 = ⭐ 150 cm - itself near the 3rd percentile for an adult woman. She is not below her family's target; she is on it.

⭐ Her velocity is normal. 3'1" is 94 cm at age 4; the chart puts her at ~105 cm at 6. That is ~5.5 cm/yr, which is the block's normal childhood rate (5-6 cm/yr) and well above the <4.5 cm/yr trigger. ⭐ A child growing at a normal rate along a low percentile, in a short family, is the definition of familial short stature - and the block's row for it reads: height ≤3rd percentile, normal puberty timing, low parental target, bone age matching chronological age, treatment reassurance.

C is the one to argue with, and the block gives two ways to separate them. CDGP has a ⭐ DELAYED bone age where familial has a normal one - and CDGP carries pubertal delay, which a 6-year-old cannot yet demonstrate. Her normal velocity fits either; the parental target does not.

A confuses a family history with a diagnosis: ⚠ Anita does not have asthma. RSV at 2 months and one pneumonia at 3 years are ordinary childhood illness, and the block is explicit that chronic illness takes the weight first - hers is tracking with her height.

D is a distractor built from two red herrings. ⚠ A maternal cousin with Down syndrome confers no meaningful risk, and Anita's development is normal.

flags.title: The single palmar crease is not in this block
flags.html: The exam finding is clearly placed to point at option D, but ⚠ nothing in the endocrinology block discusses palmar creases. It is not reasoned from here. The block's Down-syndrome content is one line - it appears on the list of genetic causes of short stature, and on the list of indications to screen a TSH. Worth raising in the session.

preamble.title: The case - James
preamble.html:
The case - James (Q148-Q151). "James is a 3.5-year-old male referred for short stature. He was born at 34+3, and spent 3 weeks in the NICU for jaundice, hypoglycemia, and poor feeding. He has met his developmental milestones appropriately but seems to lag behind other children in growth. His growth chart is shown on the next page."

Given at Q150: "You obtain previous growth parameters. At age 3 years James' height was 89 cm and weight was 12 kg."

stem: The most important next step is to

options.html: Obtain further history
Obtain previous growth charts
Calculate growth velocity
Calculate mid-parental height

answer:
[!success]- Answer

A. ⭐ Red in Noor's annotated copy, whose legend says red is the right answer - Obtain further history ** (initially have stuff).

⚠ This overturns the reasoning banked here first, which argued for B. That argument leaned on the document answering itself two questions later ("You obtain previous growth parameters") and on the fact that a velocity needs two points. ⭐ But the stem carries its own annotation - "(but should have all of them)" - and that reframes the question: all four are things you will do, and it is asking which comes first.

⭐ "Initially have stuff" is the argument. You already hold a history: 34+3 weeks, three weeks in the NICU for jaundice, hypoglycemia and poor feeding. ⭐ Every one of those is a thread, and taking them further is free - Noor's margin note on the stem reads "probably nutrition prob", which is a hypothesis generated from the history alone and which Q150 goes on to confirm as celiac disease.

⭐ And B collapses into A on its own annotation: "Obtain previous growth charts (if they didn't come in with them, would get hx beforehand)". The charts may simply not be in the room. The history always is.

⭐ Worth reading against Q140, where the official answer IS "obtain previous growth charts". Same question, different case, opposite answer - because Samantha's history is explicitly "non-contributory" and there is nothing further to take, while James's neonatal history is loaded. ⚠ So the rule is not "always get the charts" or "always take a history"; it is take whichever one the case has left on the table.

C needs two measurements a year apart and cannot be done today. D needs parental heights, which this case never gives.

preamble.html:
The case - James (Q148-Q151). "James is a 3.5-year-old male referred for short stature. He was born at 34+3, and spent 3 weeks in the NICU for jaundice, hypoglycemia, and poor feeding. He has met his developmental milestones appropriately but seems to lag behind other children in growth. His growth chart is shown on the next page."

Given at Q150: "You obtain previous growth parameters. At age 3 years James' height was 89 cm and weight was 12 kg."

stem: How do you classify his growth problem(s)?

options.html: Short stature with increased weight-for-height
Disproportionate short stature with prematurity
Short stature with decreased weight for age
Deceleration of growth with normal weight for height

answer:
[!success]- Answer

C. Read the chart first, then the previous parameters against it:

Age 3.0Age 3.5 (chart)Change
Height89 cm~90 cm, at about the 3rd percentile+1 cm in six months
Weight12 kg~11 kg, ⚠ below the 3rd percentile⚠ −1 kg

⭐ He has lost weight while barely growing, and the weight is the more affected of the two. That is the block's chronic-illness pattern verbatim: "usually weight loss (or at least a lack of weight gain) precedes the changes in linear growth."

A is the endocrine pattern and the exact opposite - the block's "short and relatively chubby" child, which is Samantha. ⭐ The two small-group cases are deliberately built as a matched pair, and getting this row right is the whole session.

B requires disproportion - the block means limb length against trunk, which is skeletal dysplasia and FGFR3. Nothing here is described as disproportionate, and prematurity is not a classification of a growth pattern. ⭐ Noor's note on it is the useful objection: "was a premature baby, but disproportionate could refer to limbs / weight - not sure what disproportionate means", which is exactly why the word has to be pinned to limb against trunk and not to weight.

⭐ D is what the group chose, and her note on why it is wrong is better than the option is. Marked green - "group decides" - with the reasoning: ⚠ "not enough to conclude deceleration, there is no definition of deceleration, would be going from NORMAL growth velocity to deceleration, basically a created term". ⭐ Deceleration is a claim about a trajectory and you need two points to make it; at this moment you have one chart and one earlier reading, and the weight is what has actually moved.

He has met his developmental milestones appropriately but seems to lag behind other children in growth. His growth chart is shown on the next page."

Given at Q150: "You obtain previous growth parameters. At age 3 years James' height was 89 cm and weight was 12 kg."

stem: What diagnostic test be most helpful in determining the diagnosis?

options.html: MRI head
Tissue Transglutaminase (TTG) / IgA
No testing needed
Bone Age

answer:
[!success]- Answer

B. Q149 has already placed him in the weight-fell-first column, and that column is chronic illness or undernutrition. The block lists celiac disease first under impaired absorption, puts celiac serology in the standard screen for a short child ("CBC, ferritin, renal function, TSH, celiac serology"), and gives a gluten-free diet as the treatment that fixes the growth.

⭐ Celiac is the diagnosis that rewards testing more than any other on that list, because a cheap serology finds a cause that a diet reverses completely - and it is the one whose growth pattern is exactly his.

A is the workup for a pituitary cause, which belongs to the other arm of the split - the short, chubby child. D is in every short-stature workup, and his would be delayed, but ⚠ bone age does not name a disease. The block uses it to separate familial (on time) from constitutional delay (behind), and it is delayed in celiac, chronic disease and GH deficiency alike. C is ruled out by a child who has crossed percentiles and lost a kilogram.

stem: What lab finding is most likely?

options.html: Hemoglobin = 90 g/L, MCV = 50
Free T4 = 2 nmol/L, TSH = 20 U/mL
Bone mineral density < 3 Z scores
Hemoglobin = 90 g/L, MCV = 90

answer:
[!success]- Answer

A. ⭐ A and D are the same haemoglobin and differ only in the MCV, so the question is entirely about the size of the red cell. Celiac disease damages the proximal small bowel, which is where iron is absorbed, so the anaemia it causes is iron-deficient and therefore microcytic - a low MCV. D's MCV of 90 is normal, and would point somewhere else entirely.

B is hypothyroidism, which is the endocrine arm - the block's "slow growth with weight gain". James lost weight. C would be a late consequence of long-standing malabsorption rather than the first thing to turn up at 3½.

flags.title: The session supplies the step the block does not
flags.html:
⚠ Grep the endocrinology block for "microcytic", "MCV" or "iron deficiency" and there is nothing - it gives only the screen, "CBC, ferritin, renal function, TSH, celiac serology", where ferritin beside the CBC is the hook. ⭐ The session closes that gap itself: Noor's annotated copy marks the answer "(microcytic) (bc iron deficiency)", so the chain from celiac to iron deficiency to a low MCV was taught in the room even though it is not written in the block. ⭐ Flagged here because it is worth knowing which of your sources a fact came from.

Two more notes she took on this question: ⭐ "Celiacs may present with isolated short stature", and, on option B, "(high TSH, normal FT4) >> BMI tends to increase with endocrine reaction" - which she then writes out as the line of the session: ⭐ "KEY: BMI increases with endocrine causes!!!!!!" That is the same discriminator as Samantha's, stated from the other side.

lecture: Case - Andrew, 4y8m: Precocity with Asymmetric Testes (Puberty and Growth After-Class Cases)
lectureMeta: Q152-Q154, the first case of `ph_cases_puberty_and_growth_aferclass_` (pp. 2-9). ⭐ **Keyed by the lecturer's own worked slides** - the deck poses each question and then answers it on the following slide. Q154's stem and its six options are verbatim from the deck; Q152 and Q153 are posed as open prompts in the deck, so their options are written here and the key taken from the answer slide. Banked here rather than in [[Module Questions - Endocrinology]] because it is a patient case.

preamble.title: The case - Andrew, 4 years 8 months
preamble.html:
The case. Andrew, 4 years 8 months, referred for assessment of precocious puberty. Body odour for 6 months (using deodorant) · pubic hair 4 months · increased penile size 4 months · rapid growth for 6 to 12 months - +20 lb and +6-8 inches in a year · no previous heights available · a year ago he was shorter than his 6-year-old sister and is now a few inches taller. Mother 171 cm (menarche 16), father 183 cm, normal puberty.

Physical. Height 122.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 7 years (CA 4 y 8 m) · weight 26.5 kg, >97th · "muscular" appearance and deep voice · pubic hair Tanner II, penile length Tanner IV · ⭐ testicular volume: right 2 mL soft, left 8 mL firm.

stem: What investigations would you propose for Andrew?

options.html: An MRI of the head, on the grounds that under half of precocious boys are idiopathic
A 17-hydroxyprogesterone and adrenal imaging, to find the source of the androgen
LH and FSH, a serum testosterone, and a bone age taken at the left wrist
A GnRH stimulation test, since a single random gonadotropin is pulsatile and insensitive

answer:
C. The case answers itself in the next step: ⭐ LH/FSH · Testosterone · Bone age. The block's first-line panel is the same list - "random LH (>0.3 mIU/L suggests CPP) · FSH · estradiol or testosterone · bone age".

⭐ Three tests, three different questions. The gonadotropins say whether the brain is driving it. The testosterone says how much androgen is actually there. The bone age says what it has already cost him in final height - and his comes back at 11.5 years against a chronological 4.8.

D is the gold standard, for the wrong question. A GnRH stimulation test confirms central precocity; you do not run it before the random pair tells you which way to look. The cases do run one - on Sarah, after her LH came back borderline.

A is mandatory in a boy whose precocity is central, and that fact is the trap: it is true, it is high-yield, and it is not yet applicable. ⚠ The case never images Andrew's head at all. B names a real peripheral source - CAH or a virilising tumour - but ⭐ an adrenal source virilises without touching the testis, and his left testis is 8 mL and firm.

preamble.title: The case - Andrew, 4 years 8 months
preamble.html:
The case. Andrew, 4 years 8 months, referred for assessment of precocious puberty. Body odour for 6 months (using deodorant) · pubic hair 4 months · increased penile size 4 months · rapid growth for 6 to 12 months - +20 lb and +6-8 inches in a year · no previous heights available · a year ago he was shorter than his 6-year-old sister and is now a few inches taller. Mother 171 cm (menarche 16), father 183 cm, normal puberty.

Physical. Height 122.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 7 years (CA 4 y 8 m) · weight 26.5 kg, >97th · "muscular" appearance and deep voice · pubic hair Tanner II, penile length Tanner IV · ⭐ testicular volume: right 2 mL soft, left 8 mL firm.

Results: FSH <1 (low, suppressed) · LH <0.3 (low, suppressed) · Testosterone 25.3 nmol/L (ref. prepubertal <1.0, adult 10.5-35) · Bone age 11.5 yrs (CA 4.8 yrs).

stem: Is this Precocious puberty? If so, central or peripheral?

options.html: Central precocity: the bone age is advanced, which only an activated axis can produce
Peripheral precocity: the androgen is high while both gonadotropins are suppressed
Premature adrenarche: body odour and pubic hair without true pubertal axis activation
Not precocity: a testosterone within the quoted adult range is normal at any age

answer:
B. The case's own summary: "Low LH and FSH · Very high Testosterone · Bone age is too advanced for CA" ⭐ "= Consistent with GnRH Independent PP or Peripheral PP."

The block reduces the whole distinction to which direction the two move: ⭐ central = gonadotropins HIGH and steroid HIGH; peripheral = gonadotropins LOW and steroid HIGH.

⭐ Suppressed gonadotropins beside a testosterone of 25.3 is negative feedback working perfectly, on a source it cannot switch off. The pituitary sees an adult testosterone in a four-year-old and shuts down - and shutting down changes nothing, because the androgen was never coming from its instruction.

A treats the bone age as if it were specific. It is not: ⭐ bone age is advanced by androgen exposure from any source, which is why the block lists precocious puberty and hyperthyroidism together under advanced bone age. It tells you how long this has been going on, not where it comes from.

C is the block's benign variant - pubic hair alone, adrenal, with no growth spurt and no bone-age advance. He has a deep voice, Tanner IV penile length, a height-age of 7 and a bone age of 11.5. D misuses a reference range: quoting an adult interval for a 4-year-old is the abnormality, not the reassurance - his prepubertal ceiling is 1.0.

stem: What is the most likely cause for Andrew's precocious puberty?

options.html: Idiopathic
Adrenal tumour
Testicular tumour
Exogenous source of androgen
CNS pathology
This is a normal variation and I am not worried about his pubertal development

answer:
C. The case's management: ⭐ left orchidectomy · histology confirmed a benign Leydig cell tumour · post-op testosterone <0.3 nmol/L.

⭐ The asymmetry was the finding all along - 2 mL on the right, 8 mL firm on the left. The block puts it twice: "asymmetric testis suggests a Leydig tumour", and the Leydig cell tumour sits at the head of its gonadal causes of peripheral precocity.

⭐ Why the asymmetry has to mean a local cause. LH travels in the blood and reaches both gonads, so central activation enlarges both. A source inside one testis enlarges that one, and the contralateral testis stays where it was - his is still 2 mL and soft, which is prepubertal.

B and D would virilise him with BOTH testes small. The block: androgen arriving from a peripheral source elsewhere gives acne, pubic hair, increased penile length and accelerated growth ⚠ "with NO change in testicular volume (<3 mL)". His left is 8 mL.

E causes central precocity, which his suppressed LH and FSH exclude - and it is the tempting wrong answer, because the block's own line about boys ("<50% idiopathic, image the CNS") is exactly the fact a well-prepared reader reaches for. ⭐ It applies only once the gonadotropins have said "central", which is why they are measured first. A and F are excluded by the same numbers; a post-operative testosterone of <0.3 settles it retrospectively.

preamble.title: The case - Sarah, 3 years 6 months
preamble.html:
The case. Sarah, 3 years 6 months. Breast bud noticed since 18 months, with ⭐ rapid progression in the last 6 months · vaginal discharge for 6 months · pubic hair 6 months ago · always tall, but a recent growth spurt in the last 6 months. Family history: mother 157 cm, ⚠ menarche age 9-10 yrs; father 180 cm, normal puberty.

Physical. Height 118.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 6 y 10 m (CA 3.6 y) · mid-parental height on the 50th percentile · weight 24.5 kg, >97th · breasts Tanner III · pubic hair Tanner III · no clitoromegaly · leukorrhea and estrogenisation of the vaginal mucosa.

Results: Random LH 0.32 IU/L (pre-pubertal <0.31) · FSH 5.3 IU/L (high) · Estradiol 70 pmol/L (ref <30) · TSH 1.34 mIU/L (0.45-4.8) · fT4 15 (11-18) · Prolactin 15 µg/L (<20) · Bone age 7.9 yrs (CA 3.6 yrs).

stem: Is Sarah in Puberty? If so, is it Central or peripheral?

options.html: Not puberty: an estradiol of 70 is too low to account for Tanner III breast development
Premature thelarche: isolated breast tissue, which regresses without any treatment
Peripheral: a random LH of 0.32 is pre-pubertal and cannot be driving this picture
Central: the LH is over the pre-pubertal cut-off, with a high FSH and estradiol

answer:
D. The session's reading of its own panel: "Borderline LH of 0.32 · High estradiol level · Normal thyroid function and prolactin · Advanced bone maturation" → ⭐ "In puberty = likely GnRH dependent PP or CPP."

The block gives the threshold: ⭐ a random LH >0.3 mIU/L is consistent with the onset of central puberty. Hers is 0.32 against a stated pre-pubertal ceiling of 0.31 - ⚠ the thinnest margin the number can have, which is why the session calls it borderline and goes on to a stimulation test in Q156.

⭐ The asymmetry of that threshold is the thing to hold onto. The block warns that an undetectable random LH has low sensitivity, because secretion is pulsatile - so ⭐ a LOW random LH proves very little, while a value over the cut-off, beside a high FSH and a high estradiol, points central. One direction of this test is informative and the other is not.

C reads 0.32 as low. It is over the line - and in peripheral precocity the gonadotropins are suppressed, not borderline, as Andrew's <0.3 and <1 were.

A misreads the reference: 70 against <30 is more than double, and the tissue has already responded - leukorrhea and an estrogenised mucosa are estrogen effect you can see. B is excluded by the block's own definition: premature thelarche is breast only, ⚠ with NO growth spurt and NO bone-age advance. She has a growth spurt, pubarche, and a bone age of 7.9 at 3.6.
