stem: How to confirm Central PP?

options.html: A GnRH stimulation test, taking a peak LH above 5 mIU/L as confirmation
A repeat random LH drawn in the early morning, when secretion is highest
An MRI of the head, since a structural lesion is what defines central precocity
A pelvic ultrasound, to show a uterus that has responded to circulating estrogen

answer:
A. The case runs the test and prints the table:

min0306090
LH0.3⭐ 15149
FSH3.571013

"Diagnosis: LH Peak > 5 mIU/L · Confirmed: GnRH dependent precocious puberty (CPP)." The block says the same: ⭐ "the GnRH stimulation test is the gold standard - an exaggerated LH response with a peak LH >5 confirms CPP." Hers peaks at 15.

⭐ The architecture is worth memorising once and reusing. To prove an axis is switched ON, stimulate it and show it over-responds. To prove one is switched OFF, stimulate it and show it barely moves. ⭐ The same test appears again in this case set on the 14-year-old Andrew, where the peak is 0.7 and the verdict is the exact opposite.

B repeats a test the block calls insensitive - a random LH screens, and its low values are uninformative because secretion comes in pulses. Repeating it earlier in the day does not change that.

C is the next step, not this one - and the case takes it, finding a normal hypothalamic/pituitary MRI. ⭐ A normal MRI does not unmake central precocity, which is precisely why the confirmation comes before the imaging. D demonstrates an estrogen effect that her mucosa has already demonstrated.

preamble.title: The case - Sarah, 3 years 6 months
preamble.html:
The case. Sarah, 3 years 6 months. Breast bud noticed since 18 months, with ⭐ rapid progression in the last 6 months · vaginal discharge for 6 months · pubic hair 6 months ago · always tall, but a recent growth spurt in the last 6 months. Family history: mother 157 cm, ⚠ menarche age 9-10 yrs; father 180 cm, normal puberty.

Physical. Height 118.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 6 y 10 m (CA 3.6 y) · mid-parental height on the 50th percentile · weight 24.5 kg, >97th · breasts Tanner III · pubic hair Tanner III · no clitoromegaly · leukorrhea and estrogenisation of the vaginal mucosa.

Results: Random LH 0.32 IU/L (pre-pubertal <0.31) · FSH 5.3 IU/L (high) · Estradiol 70 pmol/L (ref <30) · TSH 1.34 mIU/L (0.45-4.8) · fT4 15 (11-18) · Prolactin 15 µg/L (<20) · Bone age 7.9 yrs (CA 3.6 yrs).

stem: What is the most likely cause of Sarah's precocious puberty?

options.html: Idiopathic
Benign premature thelarche
Adrenal tumour
Ovarian tumour
Exogenous source of estrogen
CNS pathology

answer:
A. The case's MRI report: "Normal description of hypothalamic/pituitary regions; no evidence of tumor or any other [vascular] abnormalities" - and it goes straight on to management with an LHRH analogue.

The block gives the epidemiology that makes idiopathic the answer rather than a shrug: ⭐ in girls, central precocious puberty is mostly idiopathic; in boys, under 50% is - which is why the head MRI is mandatory in a boy and confirmatory in a girl.

F is what the MRI was done to exclude, and it came back clean. C, D and E are the whole peripheral column, and a stimulation test that confirmed GnRH-dependent precocity rules the column out in one move - peripheral steroid is made independently of GnRH. B is excluded by her growth spurt and her bone age.

⭐ "Idiopathic" is a positive finding here, not an absence of one. It is what is left after a borderline LH was pushed to a peak of 15 and a head MRI came back normal - and it is what makes the LHRH analogue the entire management. The case's three aims for it are worth keeping: ⭐ suppress LH to pre-pubertal and arrest progression · drop growth velocity back to pre-pubertal · avoid further bone acceleration so final height is less compromised. ⚠ Untreated idiopathic CPP costs an average 5-6 cm of adult height.

lecture: Case - Denise, 15.5y: Short Stature with Primary Amenorrhea (Puberty and Growth After-Class Cases)
lectureMeta: Q158-Q159, the third case of the same deck (pp. 19-23). ⭐ **Keyed by the lecturer's own worked slides.** Both prompts are open in the deck (*"INVESTIGATIONS?"*, then a stated diagnosis), so the options are written here and the keys taken from the answer slides.

preamble.title: The case - Denise, 15.5 years
preamble.html:
The case. Denise, 15.5 years, referred for assessment of short stature and amenorrhea. ⭐ Shortest girl in the class since grade 3 · breast bud started at age 13 yrs; not much progression · no menses · surgery for a cleft mitral valve at age 5 · history of multiple ear infections, myringotomy tubes. Mother 172 cm, menarche 14; father 176 cm.

Physical. Height 146 cm, <3rd · weight 50 kg, 25-50th · multiple pigmented nevi face and body · ⭐ cubitus valgus · ⭐ breast development Tanner II · pubic hair Tanner V.

stem: Investigations?

options.html: An MRI of the head, on the basis that absent puberty points at the hypothalamus
LH, FSH and estradiol, thyroid function, bone age, pelvic ultrasound, a karyotype
IGF-1 and two provocative growth hormone tests, since she is below the 3rd percentile
A GnRH stimulation test first, to establish whether the axis can be driven at all

answer:
B. The case's list, in its own order: ⭐ CBC and ferritin · LH/FSH and estradiol · thyroid function · bone age · pelvic / abdomen US · karyotype.

⭐ The gonadotropins are the branch point for every hypogonadism - the block: high means the gonad failed, low means the brain did. Hers come back LH 59.4 and FSH 156.9, which sends you to the gonad.

⭐ And the karyotype is not optional here. The block says it flat: "karyotype every short girl" - which is the single line that makes this case, and the reason the case closes with with "the only feature of Turner syndrome may be short stature."

A and D are both downstream of the gonadotropins. You image the head or stimulate the axis once you know which way the pair points, and hers point away from the brain. C is the growth-hormone workup, and the block reserves it for a child who is short with otherwise normal puberty and no other explanation. Hers is not isolated short stature - it comes with primary amenorrhea, a stalled thelarche and a dysmorphic feature.

Mother 172 cm, menarche 14; father 176 cm.

Physical. Height 146 cm, <3rd · weight 50 kg, 25-50th · multiple pigmented nevi face and body · ⭐ cubitus valgus · ⭐ breast development Tanner II · pubic hair Tanner V.

stem: Results: LH 59.4 IU/L (high) · FSH 156.9 IU/L (high) · Estradiol <40 pmol/L · IGF-1 243 (237-996) · Bone age 15 yrs · Karyotype 45,XO · Pelvic US: small pre-pubertal uterus and small (? streak) ovaries, normal kidneys. What is the diagnosis?

options.html: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty, the commonest cause of delayed puberty
Growth hormone deficiency, her IGF-1 sitting at the bottom of the reference range
Secondary hypogonadism from a hypothalamic lesion, with a low estradiol to match
Turner syndrome - primary ovarian failure, with the karyotype and the phenotype

answer:
D. The case states it: ⭐ "Diagnosis: Primary Ovarian Failure (Primary hypogonadism); Turner syndrome" - and then spends a whole section on three lines worth memorising: ⭐ "The only feature of Turner syndrome may be short stature" · "Consider Turner syndrome in short slowly growing girls" · "Early diagnosis and referral important to optimize growth and final height."

The block's Turner column reads back through her almost item by item:

Block saysDenise
⭐ Short stature in 95-100% - the commonest feature146 cm, <3rd since grade 3
45,X in 60%karyotype 45,XO
Gonadal failure complete in 90% - "streak ovaries"small (? streak) ovaries, pre-pubertal uterus
Thelarche 10-15%, menarche only 1%breast bud at 13, stalled at Tanner II; no menses
⭐ Pubarche 100%, because the adrenal glands are normal⭐ pubic hair Tanner V
Cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpals, webbed neckcubitus valgus

⭐ The split between Tanner V pubic hair and Tanner II breast is the most useful thing in the case. It looks self-contradictory until you know the two come from different glands: ⭐ pubarche is adrenal and her adrenals are normal; thelarche is ovarian and her ovaries are streaks. A girl fully developed for pubic hair and barely developed for breast is that dissociation made visible.

A requires low-normal gonadotropins and a delayed bone age. Hers are enormous and her bone age is 15 at 15.5. C inverts the level entirely - secondary hypogonadism has LOW LH and FSH; hers are the loudest possible evidence of a failed gonad. B misreads a number inside its range, and the block requires an inadequate response to two provocative tests, which was never done.

flags.title: What the case records that the block does not
flags.html: Her cleft mitral valve repair and recurrent ear infections both belong to Turner's associated burden - the block says to screen a Turner girl lifelong for congenital heart disease, renal anomaly, autoimmune thyroid disease, celiac, T1DM and hearing loss. ⚠ The multiple pigmented nevi the case records are not mentioned anywhere in the block, and are not reasoned from here.

preamble.title: The case - Andrew, 14 years
preamble.html:
The case. Andrew, 14 years, referred for assessment of delayed puberty. ⭐ Puberty - no changes noted · undescended testis noted at birth, orchidopexy at 18 months · ⭐ shortening of the metacarpals · no family history of delayed puberty - mother menarche 12, father completed growth by 16. Mother 160 cm, father 180 cm, ⭐ mid-parental target 176.5 cm (50th percentile).

Physical. Height 168 cm (50-75th) - ⭐ at his parental target · weight 62 kg, 85th · stretched penile length Tanner I (4 cm) · pubic hair Tanner I · ⭐ testicular volume 2-3 mL bilaterally.

Results: LH <0.1 IU/L and FSH <0.1 IU/L · Testosterone <0.4 nmol/L · Karyotype 46,XY · ⭐ Bone age 14 yrs (CA 14 yrs) · normal CBC and ferritin · TSH 1.23, fT4 16 (11-18) · Prolactin 15 (<20).

stem: Andrew - unifying diagnosis?

options.html: Central hypogonadism: gonadotropins and testosterone low, with a bone age on time
Klinefelter syndrome, the commonest cause of testicular failure in boys by some way
Constitutional delay, the commonest cause of delayed puberty in boys, needing no more
Primary hypogonadism: the undescended testis and 2 mL volumes mean the gonad failed

answer:
A. The case's own unifying summary: "Absent signs of puberty · Cryptorchidism and small penile length · Mild dysmorphic features: short metacarpals · Pre-pubertal LH, FSH, Testosterone · Bone age consistent with chronologic age" → ⭐ "Diagnosis: Central hypogonadism."

The block gives the rule in one line: ⭐ LOW LH and FSH with a low sex steroid is SECONDARY (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism - "the brain never sent the signal."

⭐ The bone age is what excludes the normal variant, and it is the single most useful number in the case. The block says CDGP is diagnosed on a DELAYED bone age - "the test that makes the diagnosis". His is ⭐ 14 at 14. A boy whose skeleton is exactly on time but whose puberty has not started is not running late; ⚠ he is not starting. His height sitting at his mid-parental target says the same thing from the other direction - CDGP tracks at or below the 3rd percentile, and he is 50-75th.

C is the commonest cause of delayed puberty in boys, which is exactly what makes it the dangerous answer - ⚠ it is the diagnosis of a normal variant, and treating this boy as a normal variant means never replacing his testosterone.

B and D both require HIGH gonadotropins. A failed gonad removes the feedback and the pituitary shouts; his are <0.1, which is the opposite of shouting. B is further excluded by a 46,XY karyotype - the block puts Klinefelter at 47,XXY in 80%.

stem: GnRH test - LH 0 / 30 / 60 / 90 min: <0.1 → 0.7 → 0.4 → 0.4. FSH over the same points: 0.3 → 3.0 → 3.1 → 3.2. How do you read it?

options.html: Constitutional delay: the gonadotropins did rise, so the axis is intact and merely late
Primary gonadal failure, the flat LH reflecting a gonad that cannot make testosterone
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: the pituitary barely responds, LH peaking at 0.7
A normal pubertal response, the FSH having risen tenfold from its baseline value

answer:
C. The notes label the table exactly that: ⭐ "Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism."

⭐ The number to read it against is Sarah's, from the earlier case. Her peak LH was 15 against a threshold of 5. ⭐ His is 0.7. Same test, same units, opposite verdict - and that symmetry is why the session runs it on both patients.

Stimulated peak LHReading
Sarah, 3.6 y15⭐ axis switched ON early - CPP confirmed
Andrew, 14 y⚠ 0.7⭐ axis will not switch ON at all

A misreads a move from <0.1 to 0.7 as a response. In CDGP the axis is intact and merely late, so a stimulated pituitary responds when asked. ⚠ A pituitary that cannot get its LH past 1 on direct stimulation is not late.

D is true about the FSH - 0.3 to 3.2 is a real rise - but ⭐ LH is the informative gonadotropin for pubertal onset, which the block states outright: "LH is more useful than FSH for assessing the onset of puberty." A normal pubertal response is an LH-dominant one.

B inverts the level, for the same reason it did in Q160: a failed gonad leaves the pituitary unrestrained, so LH and FSH would already be high before any stimulation was given.

stem: Further information: he reports "no sense of smell". MRI: "underdevelopment of olfactory bulbs". What is the diagnosis?

options.html: A craniopharyngioma compressing the pituitary stalk, found on the same MRI scan
Prader-Willi syndrome, in which hypogonadism accompanies hyperphagia and obesity
Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome, a congenital cause of the hypogonadotropic picture
Kallmann syndrome - hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia and absent bulbs

answer:
D. The case: "He reports 'no sense of smell' · MRI: 'Underdevelopment of olfactory bulbs'" → ⭐ "Diagnosis: Kallmann Syndrome." The block carries it in six words: ⭐ Kallmann = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism + anosmia.

⭐ The point of the case is that nobody asked about the smell until the end. It is one line of history, it costs nothing, and it converts an unexplained hypogonadotropic hypogonadism into a named diagnosis with a known inheritance and a known set of associations. ⭐ That is why "anosmia" sits in the history skeleton of both Week 3 puberty notes - it is only ever found if it is asked for.

B is the block's Prader-Willi: failure to thrive in infancy, then ⚠ hyperphagia and severe obesity in early childhood, with a chromosome 15 microdeletion. His weight is 85th and nothing else fits. C is on the block's list of congenital causes of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, but it is defined by retinal dystrophy, polydactyly and obesity, none of which is described. A would be an acquired cause, and the MRI found no mass - his other pituitary axes (TSH, fT4, prolactin) are all normal too.

flags.title: The case's Kallmann associations are broader than the block's
flags.html: Its closing summary lists cleft palate and lip · kidney malformations · metacarpal malformations and pes cavus · sensorineural deafness · cerebellar ataxia and epilepsy · colour blindness, nystagmus · mirror motions. ⚠ The block names only the anosmia. So his shortened metacarpals - flagged in the case's own unifying summary - are the case's association, not the block's: the block links short metacarpals to pseudohypoparathyroidism ("knuckle-knuckle-dimple-dimple", Archibald's sign) and to Turner, and does not list them under Kallmann.

lecture: Case - Baby Tyler, 3 weeks: Salt-Losing Crisis (DSD Review Session)
lectureMeta: Q191-196, the worked case running through `dsd_review_afterclass_` (Pediatric Endocrinology), slides 5-16. ⭐ **Stems verbatim - the deck poses all six as its own questions.** ⭐ **Keyed from the deck's own answer slides**, which follow each question directly. The `_afterclass_` suffix is the same convention as the earlier after-class cases at [[#152|Q152-162]]. Built against [[09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation]], whose CAH section came from the same lecturer's earlier decks.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. ⭐ Baby Tyler is 3 weeks old, assigned male at birth. Vomiting intermittently for 7 days, ⭐ loose frequent stools 6-8 per day, poor feeding, irritable, and ⚠ failing to gain weight. History - birth weight 3.7 kg, birth length 55 cm, normal pregnancy, labour and delivery; no other pregnancies; ⭐ parents unrelated and non-consanguineous. Examination - dehydrated, cold, ⭐ hyperpigmented, ⭐ NORMAL appearance of the male genitalia, ⚠ HR 150, BP 50.

stem: You see Tyler in the emergency Department. Before doing any investigations, is there anything else that you want to know about him on history or physical examination?

options.html: A detailed feeding and formula-preparation history, with an abdominal examination
A developmental and immunisation history, with a full neurological examination
A maternal medication history alone, since drugs are the commonest cause here
Birth and family history, plus genitalia, hydration and pigmentation on exam

answer:
D. ⭐ The case answers its own question straight after it, and both are in the note's workup skeleton already:

The case asks forIt reports
birth measurements3.7 kg, 55 cm - ⭐ normally grown, so this is acute, not antenatal
pregnancy, labour, deliverynormal
other pregnancies⭐ none - ⚠ so there is no earlier neonatal death to have raised the alarm
⭐ consanguinityparents unrelated - ⚠ asked because CAH is autosomal recessive, and a negative answer does not exclude it
hydration and perfusiondehydrated, cold, HR 150, BP 50
⭐ hyperpigmentation⭐ present - this is the ACTH excess, visible on the skin
⭐ the genitalia⭐ NORMAL male appearance

⭐ Two of those findings are the whole case. ⚠ Hyperpigmentation in a collapsing neonate is ACTH excess, and ⭐ normal-looking genitalia is not reassurance - it is the expected finding in a 46,XY infant with CAH. The note puts it as the block's highest-yield point: ⭐ "the 46,XX infant looks ambiguous and is caught at birth; the 46,XY infant looks normal and presents in crisis a fortnight later."

⚠ The note's PEx line would also have you palpate for gonads - "a palpable gonad is almost always a testis" - which is how the same examination serves an ambiguous-genitalia presentation.

A and B are the reasonable general-paediatric work-ups for vomiting and failure to thrive, and ⚠ both would miss this, because neither looks at the skin or the genitalia. C asks a question the note does list - maternal medications and maternal virilisation - but ⭐ as one line of a history, not instead of one, and transplacental androgen is not the commonest cause.

stem: What investigations will help determine the cause of his symptoms?

options.html: Electrolytes, glucose and cortisol, then 17-hydroxyprogesterone and a karyotype
A septic workup with blood cultures and a lumbar puncture as the first-line tests
An abdominal ultrasound and contrast study to exclude malrotation with volvulus
A sweat chloride test and stool studies, given the diarrhoea and failure to thrive

answer:
A. ⭐ The case's next step is exactly this list, and it matches the note's Ix line:

TestWhat it is for
⭐ sodium, potassium⭐ Na↓ and K↑ are the mineralocorticoid failure
⭐ glucosehypoglycaemia in a salt-losing crisis
⭐ cortisolthe glucocorticoid failure
⭐ 17-hydroxyprogesterone⭐ the diagnostic marker - markedly raised in 21-OHD
karyotype and pelvic ultrasound⭐ the note asks for these in every case

⭐ The order is not arbitrary. The electrolytes and glucose are the ones that change what you do in the next ten minutes; the 17-OHP and the karyotype name the disease but will not come back in time to treat him.

⚠ A septic workup is not a wrong instinct - a 3-week-old who is vomiting, irritable and shocked gets cultures, and B would often be started in parallel. ⭐ It is wrong as the answer to "what will determine the cause", because it would not find this one. C and D are each the right test for a different cause of the same presentation - volvulus and cystic fibrosis both belong on the differential - but neither explains the hyperpigmentation.

stem: What is your interpretation of these lab results? Na 110 mmol/l (135-145) · K 8.4 mmol/l (3.5-5.0) · Glu 2.5 mmol/l (3.4-7.0) · Cortisol 40 nmol/l (119-618)

options.html: Cortisol deficiency alone, with the sodium and potassium explained by the diarrhoea
Isolated mineralocorticoid deficiency, with the cortisol inside its normal range
Aldosterone deficiency and cortisol deficiency, present together in this child
Gastrointestinal losses alone, since vomiting and diarrhoea account for all of these

answer:
C. ⭐ The session's answer names both deficiencies, in those words - and the panel separates into two halves that fail for two different reasons:

ResultReads as
⭐ Na 110, ⭐ K 8.4⭐ ALDOSTERONE deficiency - sodium not retained, potassium not excreted
⭐ Cortisol 40 (119-618)⭐ CORTISOL deficiency - ⚠ and this is a shocked child, in whom it should be at the top of the range, not below it
Glucose 2.5hypoglycaemia - the consequence of the cortisol deficiency

⭐ Losing both at once is what localises the lesion. The adrenal note makes this the discriminator between primary and secondary disease: ⭐ "Primary insufficiency loses aldosterone as well as cortisol - so K⁺ is high, ACTH is high, and fludrocortisone is required; secondary spares all three." ⚠ A potassium of 8.4 is therefore not an incidental abnormality - it is the finding that says the problem is at the adrenal.

⭐ It also fits the hyperpigmentation, which is ACTH driven, and which secondary insufficiency does not produce.

A and B each take half the panel. D is the one worth taking seriously, because ⚠ he genuinely has been vomiting and stooling for a week - but ⭐ GI losses do not drive potassium UP, and they do not suppress cortisol in a shocked infant. The direction of the potassium is what rules it out.

preamble.html: The case. ⭐ Baby Tyler is 3 weeks old, assigned male at birth. Vomiting intermittently for 7 days, ⭐ loose frequent stools 6-8 per day, poor feeding, irritable, and ⚠ failing to gain weight. History - birth weight 3.7 kg, birth length 55 cm, normal pregnancy, labour and delivery; no other pregnancies; ⭐ parents unrelated and non-consanguineous. Examination - dehydrated, cold, ⭐ hyperpigmented, ⭐ NORMAL appearance of the male genitalia, ⚠ HR 150, BP 50.

stem: What is your diagnosis? Be as specific as possible Testosterone 10.5 nmol/l (<0.03) · 17OHP 1365 nmol/l (<7.8)

options.html: Simple virilising congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia presenting in the neonatal period
Primary autoimmune adrenal insufficiency presenting in the neonatal period
Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency

answer:
D. ⭐ "As specific as possible" is the whole instruction - and the diagnosis has three parts, each earned by a different result:

PartEarned by
⭐ CAH⭐ 17-OHP 1365 against a normal <7.8 - over 170x, with testosterone 10.5 where it should be undetectable
⭐ 21-hydroxylase deficiency⭐ the 17-OHP is the substrate immediately above the block, and the note puts 21-OHD at ≈95% of CAH
⭐ SALT-WASTING form⭐ Na 110, K 8.4, and a crisis at 3 weeks

⭐ The mechanism runs in one chain, as the note has it: cortisol blocked → ACTH excess → adrenal hyperplasia → blocked precursors shunted into androgen → virilisation, with ⭐ aldosterone lost as well because the same enzyme sits on the mineralocorticoid limb.

⚠ His testosterone of 10.5 is an adult male level in a 3-week-old, and it has produced no visible sign, because there is nothing left to virilise in a 46,XY infant.

A is the same enzyme with 1-5% residual activity - ⚠ cortisol deficiency and androgen excess WITHOUT significant salt loss, which a sodium of 110 excludes. B is the mild end, which the note says presents as ⭐ premature pubarche and later hirsutism and oligomenorrhoea, not as neonatal collapse. C would give low cortisol and high potassium, but ⚠ not a 17-OHP of 1365 - and the note lists autoimmune disease as 80-90% of primary insufficiency in the West while naming CAH separately as its own cause.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. ⭐ Baby Tyler is 3 weeks old, assigned male at birth. Vomiting intermittently for 7 days, ⭐ loose frequent stools 6-8 per day, poor feeding, irritable, and ⚠ failing to gain weight. History - birth weight 3.7 kg, birth length 55 cm, normal pregnancy, labour and delivery; no other pregnancies; ⭐ parents unrelated and non-consanguineous. Examination - dehydrated, cold, ⭐ hyperpigmented, ⭐ NORMAL appearance of the male genitalia, ⚠ HR 150, BP 50.

stem: How would you manage this acute presentation of CAH?

options.html: Potassium-containing maintenance fluid with oral hydrocortisone started next day
Dextrose-saline without potassium, intravenous hydrocortisone, and fludrocortisone
Insulin and dextrose to lower the potassium, deferring steroids until results return
Normal saline alone, with steroid replacement withheld until the karyotype returns

answer:
B. ⭐ The session's answer gives the crisis protocol in three parts, and each doses against a problem already on the panel:

ComponentThe session's numbersAgainst
⭐ Fluid⭐ 5% dextrose / normal saline (D5/NS), NO potassium, resuscitate at 20 ml/kg, continue at 1.5-2x maintenance⚠ Na 110 and Glu 2.5 in one bag; the potassium is omitted because his is 8.4
⭐ hydrocortisone IV⭐ bolus 2 mg/kg, then an infusion of 100 mg/m²/daythe cortisol of 40
⭐ fludrocortisone0.1-0.3 mg/daythe aldosterone deficiency

⭐ Leaving the potassium out of the fluid is the detail most easily lost, and it is the one that would do immediate harm: ⚠ adding potassium to a child at 8.4 is the opposite of the treatment.

⭐ Hydrocortisone is the glucocorticoid of choice here rather than dexamethasone, and the adrenal note's potency table is why: ⭐ hydrocortisone carries mineralocorticoid activity, dexamethasone carries none.

⭐ The adrenal note's crisis line is the same instinct in one phrase - "Crisis: saline + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, do not await results."

A gets the potassium exactly wrong and defers steroid in a shocked child. C treats the hyperkalaemia as the diagnosis: ⚠ it is real and it is dangerous, but the potassium falls when the missing hormones are replaced, and deferring steroid is what kills. D misses the dextrose in a hypoglycaemic infant, omits both hormones, and ⭐ waits on a test that will take days and change nothing about tonight.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. ⭐ Baby Tyler is 3 weeks old, assigned male at birth. Vomiting intermittently for 7 days, ⭐ loose frequent stools 6-8 per day, poor feeding, irritable, and ⚠ failing to gain weight. History - birth weight 3.7 kg, birth length 55 cm, normal pregnancy, labour and delivery; no other pregnancies; ⭐ parents unrelated and non-consanguineous. Examination - dehydrated, cold, ⭐ hyperpigmented, ⭐ NORMAL appearance of the male genitalia, ⚠ HR 150, BP 50.

stem: What would be the presentation of a female patient (46XX) with the same diagnosis?

options.html: Normal female genitalia, with the diagnosis made only at puberty on investigation
Undervirilised genitalia with palpable gonads in the inguinal canals on examination
Virilised genitalia, clitoral enlargement, fused folds and one urogenital opening
Normal female genitalia and an identical salt-losing crisis at one to three weeks

answer:
C. ⭐ The case answers with a second baby, A.H., and the findings are the answer:

Baby A.H.
⭐ 3 cm phallusthe clitoral hypertrophy
⭐ hyperpigmented, FUSED, rugated labio-scrotal folds⚠ the fusion is the virilisation
⭐ single uro-genital sinus at the base of the phallusthe note's "single urogenital opening", its most severe form
⭐ NO gonads palpable⭐ consistent with 46,XX - there are ovaries, and they are intra-abdominal

⭐ This is the asymmetry the block calls its highest-yield point, and it is the reason the case asks the question at all: ⭐ "The 46,XX CAH infant looks ambiguous and is caught at birth; the 46,XY CAH infant looks normal and presents in salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks." ⚠ Same enzyme, same severity, same salt loss - the only difference is whether anyone noticed before the crisis.

⭐ The note's own examination language applies here: describe and diagram the gonads, phallus and labio-scrotal folds in neutral terms, ⚠ delay assignment of the sex of rearing, do not assign a name, and do not register the birth until the investigations are complete.

A and D both keep the genitalia normal, which is the 46,XY picture. ⚠ D is the sharpest distractor, because the salt-losing crisis half of it is true - the girl is at the same risk - ⭐ but she does not look normal at birth, which is exactly what buys her the earlier diagnosis. B is undervirilisation with palpable gonads, which is the 46,XY differential - 5α-reductase deficiency or androgen insensitivity - and ⭐ a palpable gonad is almost always a testis.

stem: What difference would there be in a patient presenting with 11-beta hydroxylase deficiency CAH compared to 21-OH deficiency CAH?

options.html: Hypertension with low potassium, rather than salt wasting with high potassium
An identical salt-losing crisis, since both block the mineralocorticoid pathway
No virilisation, since androgen precursors are not shunted in this enzyme block
A milder course presenting only at puberty, never in the neonatal period at all

answer:
⚠ The session poses this question and never answers it. It asks three questions in a row; ⭐ only the last gets a written answer, so this one was taken live in the room and is not recoverable from the notes.

⚠ And the endocrinology block does not close the gap. A search across the whole 01 - Endocrinology folder returns 11β-hydroxylase exactly once - ⭐ a single row in the CAH enzyme table giving its share of CAH as 5% - with no phenotype, no mechanism and no comparison to 21-OHD anywhere.

⭐ So this ships unkeyed rather than answered from outside the block, in the same way Q86 leaves the NTI patterns open. The session's answer is the one to write in.

⭐ What the block DOES put within reach, for what it is worth: the adrenal note's steroid potency table lists ⭐ deoxycorticosterone with a mineralocorticoid activity of 20 against hydrocortisone's 1 - ⚠ which is a fact about a steroid, not a statement about 11β-hydroxylase CAH, and it is left as that rather than assembled into an answer that would then read as taught material.

⚠ 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation needs a short 11β-hydroxylase section. Logged under Outstanding at the foot of this note.

lectureMeta: Q197-199, the three closing questions of the same deck, slides 17-21. ⭐ **Stems verbatim, including a typo.** Q198 and Q199 are keyed - Q199 from the deck's own answer slide, Q198 from [[09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation|the note's long-term management callout]], which came from the same lecturer's earlier decks. ⚠ **Q197 ships UNKEYED** - see the warning below.
stem: What are the long-term considerations in gthe management of a patient with CAH?

options.html: Glucocorticoid for the first two years only, then weaning once growth is complete
Mineralocorticoid alone lifelong, since cortisol recovers once hyperplasia resolves
No ongoing treatment once the acute crisis resolves, with annual electrolytes only
Lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid with stress dosing and surveillance

answer:
D. ⭐ The note's long-term management callout is the lecture's own earlier point, and it answers this directly:

ComponentDose
⭐ hydrocortisone⭐ 10-15 mg/m²/day divided bid or tid - set against a normal cortisol secretion rate of 12.5 ± 3 mg/m²/day; prednisone or dexamethasone in older adolescents
⭐ fludrocortisone (Florinef)⭐ 0.05-0.20 mg daily, with ⭐ additional oral saline in infants
⚠ Stress dosing⭐ increase the glucocorticoid during illness or stress, to prevent a salt-losing crisis
Plusgenital surgery where indicated, education, and surveillance

⭐ Stress dosing is the part that has to be taught to the family rather than prescribed, and it is what the education is for: ⚠ the child's next crisis will begin at home, during an ordinary childhood illness.

⭐ The dose is deliberately physiological, not pharmacological. It is pegged to what the adrenal would have made - which is why ⚠ it is replacement for life rather than a course that finishes.

A and C both treat the crisis as the illness. ⚠ The enzyme defect does not resolve, and stopping replacement returns the child to the state they presented in. B keeps the half that fixes the sodium and drops the half that prevents hypoglycaemia and ⭐ allows the ACTH drive - and so the androgen excess - to continue unopposed.

stem: When examining a 14 year old boy, which of the following findings would make you most concerned about abnormal growth?

options.html: His height is >2 SD below the average for his age and sex
An X ray of wrists shows delayed bone age despite his short stature
His puberty has been delayed despite his short stature
He is currently significantly below his genetic potential

answer: The correct answer is D. While having a height >2 SD below the average could be an indicator for abnormal growth, having short stature alone is not enough to indicate abnormal growth; he could just be on the shorter end of normal. Delayed bone age and delayed puberty indicate normal growth variants in individuals with shorter stature.

stem: Anh is a 13 year old Vietnamese male who presents to your clinic with concerns of short stature. His mother’s height is 155cm and his father’s height is 171cm. What is his genetic height potential?

options.html: 168cm
170cm
171cm

answer: The correct answer is B. The equation for the genetic potential of males is (height of mother + height of father + 13)/2, so (155 + 171 + 13)/2 = 339/2 = 169.5 cm.

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is below the 3rd percentile for height, growing 3.5 cm per year, with a delayed bone age. A random GH level taken in clinic is low.

What is needed to diagnose GH deficiency?

options.html: The low random GH level is already diagnostic
A single GH level drawn overnight during deep sleep
An inadequate GH response to two provocative tests
A karyotype showing a normal 46,XY pattern
A trial of GH with a rise in growth velocity

answer: The correct answer is C. GH is secreted in pulses, so a random GH is worthless (A). The diagnosis needs an inadequate GH response to two provocative tests (currently < 8 µg/L), alongside short stature, low growth velocity and a delayed bone age. IGF-1/IGFBP-3 screen; treatment is recombinant GH.

stem:
A 14-year-old boy is below the 3rd percentile for height and has no signs of puberty. He has grown at a normal rate along his curve for years. His father was a "late bloomer" who reached average adult height. Bone age is 11 years.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Familial short stature
Isolated growth hormone deficiency
Primary hypothyroidism
Constitutional growth delay
Klinefelter syndrome

answer: The correct answer is D. Normal growth velocity with a delayed bone age, late puberty and a family history of late puberty is constitutional delay, a normal variant with a normal adult height, so reassurance is the treatment. In familial short stature the bone age matches chronological age and puberty is on time (A). GH deficiency and hypothyroidism slow the growth velocity (B, C).

preamble.html: Darlene is an 18 year old woman who is completing a victory lap at one of the local high schools. She attends clinic with her mother, who is concerned because she is not menstruating. With her mother present, it is difficult to get a history from Darlene.

stem: What physical characteristics might you find in someone presenting with a genetic cause of amenorrhea?

options.html: Low body weight and a heavy exercise load, as in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea
Hirsutism, acne and obesity, as in polycystic ovary syndrome
Short stature, a webbed neck and a shield chest, as in Turner syndrome
Galactorrhoea and bitemporal field loss, as in a prolactinoma

answer:
C. Reasoned from In-Class - Amenorrhea and 05 - Disorders of Growth.

  • ⭐ Turner syndrome is the commonest primary cause (27%), and its clues are "short stature, webbed neck, shield chest". Short stature is "the commonest feature" (95-100%), along with "cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpals".
  • The other two genetic causes are told apart by the uterus and the pubic hair. "MRKH (46,XX, female range, hair present)" has complete absence of the uterus and cervix. "AIS (46,XY, male range, hair absent)" has breast development but no pubic hair.
  • A, B and D are all real clues from the same table, but for hypothalamic, PCOS and pituitary causes, none of which is genetic.

stem: A 48 year old woman has been diagnosed with cervical cancer. Her physician is concerned that it has spread to her lymph nodes. Which of the following collection of lymph nodes should be investigated first?

options.html: Deep Inguinal Lymph Nodes
Internal Iliac Lymph Nodes
Sacral Lymph Nodes
Lumbar Lymph Nodes

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. B. Lymph follows the lecture's nodal watershed: the cervix and uterine body drain to the internal and external iliac nodes, so the iliac basin on the lateral pelvic wall is the first to investigate in cervical cancer.

  • A - Deep inguinal nodes drain the clitoris and vestibular bulb (erectile tissue).
  • C - sacral nodes drain the inferior vagina.
  • D - lumbar (para-aortic) nodes drain the ovary, tubes and fundus, which is why the lecture calls the uterus "one organ, two basins". For the cervix they are a later site, not the first.

stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in active labor requests an epidural anesthetic to relieve pain from her uterine contractions and cervical dilation. Pain derived from uterine contractions from the fundus of the uterus would be conveyed along which of the following routes?

options.html: Via the parasympathetic pathway to the dorsal root ganglia of S2-S4
Via the parasympathetic pathway to the dorsal root ganglia of T12-L2
Via the sympathetic pathway to the dorsal root ganglia of S2-S4
Via the sympathetic pathway to the dorsal root ganglia of T12-L2
Via pudendal nerves to the dorsal root ganglia of S2-S4

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. D. The fundus lies above the pelvic pain line (the lower limit of the peritoneum). Visceral afferents above that line travel back along the sympathetics to the T11/12-L2 dorsal root ganglia. That is why contraction pain is felt in the back, flank and mid-trunk, and why it takes a lumbar epidural (L3/4) to block it.

  • A - the parasympathetic route to S2-S4 serves structures below the line (cervix, upper vagina). It carries cervical dilation pain, not fundal contraction pain.
  • B, C - these mismatch the outflows: parasympathetics leave at S2-S4, never T12-L2, and sympathetics leave at T11/12-L2, never S2-S4.
  • E - the pudendal nerve is somatic, supplying the perineum and lower vagina, so a pudendal nerve block never reaches the fundus. A caudal epidural block (S2-S4) also spares the fundus, and that is why the mother still feels her contractions.

stem: Is an estrogen block required for female-to-male transition?

options.html: Yes, so that the effects of testosterone is not counteracted
Yes, so that the feminizing effects of estrogen is downregulated
No, because testosterone will automatically downregulate estrogen
No, because the effects of testosterone supercedes the effect of estrogen

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 08 - Introduction to Transgender Medicine and 09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis. Gender-affirming hormones have two goals: suppress the endogenous hormone and replace as for a hypogonadal patient. The regimens are asymmetric:

  • Trans women need an anti-androgen (spironolactone, cyproterone acetate) or a GnRH agonist alongside estrogen.
  • Trans men are listed with exogenous testosterone alone, because testosterone suppresses the ovary itself. At therapeutic levels (target 14-24 nmol/L) it exerts negative feedback on the HPG axis, ↓ LH/FSH, and so ↓ ovarian estradiol.
  • A, B fail because a separate estrogen block is unnecessary: the suppression comes free with the testosterone.
  • D reaches the right "no" for the wrong reason. Testosterone does not overpower circulating estrogen at the receptor; it removes the estrogen upstream by shutting down gonadotropins.

stem: Which of the following regarding transgender medicine is false?

options.html: Criteria for puberty blockers includes having achieved Tanner 2 and informed consent
Hormone therapy can be initiated at any age as long as informed consent can be established
Parental consent is not required to initiate hormone therapy, but encouraged
Bottom surgery can be done after reaching age of majority, top surgery can be done earlier, if >16

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck; checked against Introduction to Transgender Medicine.

The lecture's criteria for gender-affirming hormones: confirmed persistence, able to consent, preferably with parental consent/support, usually around age 16, so not "any age". stem:
A 16-year-old transgender boy on puberty blockers meets the criteria to start testosterone, and he and his parents are keen to begin.

What must be discussed before testosterone is started?

options.html: A date for top surgery
Fertility preservation
Genital surgery options
Stopping the blockers for a year
His sexual orientation

answer: The correct answer is B. Fertility preservation is discussed before hormonal therapy, not after. The lecture notes that oocyte preservation is expensive, not covered, and requires time off hormones with 1-2 normal periods. Surgery comes later and is irreversible (A, C), and orientation is a separate axis from gender identity (E).

stem: You are asked to assess a 7 yr old girl for growth and pubertal development. Your assessment reveals the presence of single breast mound, single contour. Her growth velocity is 12 cm/yr over the past 12 months. What is the pubertal Tanner staging that better corresponds to these findings?

options.html: She is pre-pubertal with a Tanner stage 1
She has completed her puberty with a Tanner stage 5
She is just starting pubertal development with a Tanner stage 2
She is in the middle stages of pubertal development with a Tanner stage 3

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 04 - Disorders of Puberty and 06 - Adolescent Development. D. A breast that has grown beyond the areola but still forms one smooth contour with it is Tanner III; in Tanner IV the areola and papilla lift into a secondary mound, and Tanner II is only a bud. The 12 cm/yr velocity agrees: girls hit their growth spurt between Tanner 2 and 3.

  • A - Tanner I has no glandular tissue, and a prepubertal child does not grow 12 cm/yr.
  • B - Tanner V is the adult breast, with the areola back in the breast contour and a projecting papilla.
  • C - Tanner II is a breast bud with surrounding glandular tissue only; a full mound is further along.

Mid-puberty at 7 is precocious (girls < 8) - the thread Q199-200 pick up.

stem: In a case of a 7yr old boy with findings consistent with Tanner stage 3 for testicular volume (between 8-10 mL), LH of 6 (Reference for Tanner 1 < 1.3) and FSH of 9 (Reference for Tanner 1 < 3.1); testosterone level of 8 nmol/L (Reference for Tanner 1 < 0.4). What would be your next step?

options.html: Clinical findings and investigations are consistent with normal pubertal development and no need for further assessment
I would request a head MRI for further assessment of CNS changes as a possible cause for precocious puberty
This child has idiopathic central precocious puberty and does not require further assessment. I would only recommend LHRH analog for therapy
This child has peripheral precocious puberty driven by peripheral exposure to testosterone.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. B. This is central precocious puberty in a boy: onset before 9, testes 8-10 mL (bilaterally ≥ 4 mL means LH is driving the Leydig cells), and LH, FSH and testosterone all far above Tanner 1 ranges. In boys fewer than 50% of CPP cases are idiopathic - hypothalamic or pineal tumour, hamartoma, hydrocephalus, trauma and radiation must be sought - so MRI head is mandatory.

  • A - puberty at 7 is precocious by definition in a boy.
  • C - calling it idiopathic without imaging is the error; the idiopathic default belongs to girls. The LHRH analogue comes after the MRI.
  • D - peripheral testosterone would suppress LH/FSH and leave the testes small (< 3 mL); both are the opposite here.

stem: Correctly order the following pubertal milestones for girls from earliest to latest onset:

options.html: Growth spurt
Menarche
Thelarche
Pubarche

answer:
The correct answer is C, A, D, B.

From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. The lecture gives the girls' sequence as thelarche → growth spurt → pubarche → menarche:

  • Thelarche (C) is the first sign in most girls, at about 10.3 years. Ovarian estradiol drives breast development.
  • The growth spurt (A) comes early in girls, at Tanner 2-3 (in boys it comes later, at Tanner 3-4, which is why boys finish taller).
  • Pubarche (D) follows.
  • Menarche (B) comes last, at about 12.7 years, roughly 2.5 years after thelarche.

Two traps:

  • 15% of girls have pubarche first, because it is adrenal rather than gonadal, so the order is typical, not invariant.
  • Menarche is never early in the sequence: it needs enough estradiol and progesterone to build and shed endometrium, which comes after peak height velocity.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an accepted definition of delayed puberty?

options.html: Absence of puberty >13 years old for females
Absence of puberty >15 years old for males
Absence of puberty > 2.5 SD of the average age for either sex
Incomplete puberty > 2.5 SD of the average age for either sex

answer:
The correct answer is B. The standard definition for males is >14 years old.

From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. Delayed puberty is defined statistically as the absence or incomplete development of puberty at an age 2.5 SD above the population mean. That works out to 13 years for girls and 14 years for boys. So B's 15-year cut-off is not the accepted definition, and waiting until 15 would delay the workup (karyotype, LH/FSH, bone age) by a year. The other three are accepted:

  • A matches the girls' cut-off of 13.
  • C (absent puberty at >2.5 SD) is the definition itself.
  • D is also accepted, because the definition covers incomplete puberty as well as absent puberty. Arrested puberty counts.

stem: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: Central precocious puberty in boys are usually idiopathic and does not need Ix
The first sign of puberty in girls is breast enlargement and testicular growth in boys
The effect of estrogen during puberty leads to breast tenderness, mood swings, and vaginal discharge
Precocious puberty is defined as onset before the age of 8 in girls, and 9 in boys

answer: The correct answer is A. From the deck's summary slide on central precocious puberty: males are pathologic (need MRI), think tumour, trauma, radiation; females are idiopathic. The lecture: under 50% of boys with CPP are idiopathic, so an MRI head is mandatory. B, C and D are true (thelarche and testicular volume > 3 mL are the first signs; estrogen gives breast development, mood swings and vaginal discharge; precocity is before 8 in girls, 9 in boys).

stem:
A 7-year-old boy has pubic hair, acne, body odour and a growth spurt over six months. Both testes are 2 mL. His LH is suppressed.

What kind of precocious puberty is this?

options.html: Peripheral, from androgen outside the testes
Central, from early GnRH activation
Premature adrenarche, a normal variant
Central, from a hypothalamic hamartoma
Constitutional advance of an otherwise normal puberty

answer: The correct answer is A. Only LH grows the testes. Bilaterally enlarged testes (≥ 4 mL) mean central; virilisation with small testes (< 3 mL) and low LH mean peripheral, with androgen coming from elsewhere (CAH, an adrenal tumour, exogenous testosterone). An asymmetric testis would suggest a Leydig cell tumour. Central causes (B, D) would enlarge the testes and raise LH.

stem: The uterine artery can be found embedded in which endopelvic ligament?

options.html: Transverse cervical (cardinal) ligament
Uterosacral ligament
Broad ligament
Suspensory ligament of the ovary

answer: The correct answer is A. The transverse cervical ligament, aka the cardinal ligament, contains both the uterine vessels and the ureters. The suspensory ligament of the ovary is not an endopelvic ligament, and contains the ovarian vessels.

stem: Which of the following best describes polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)?

options.html: A diagnosis of PCOS can be made entirely based on evidence of cystic ovaries on ultrasound.
PCOS can be diagnosed entirely based on history and physical examination.
PCOS is rare compared to other endocrinopathies.
Excess estradiol is a common finding in PCOS.

answer:
The correct answer is B. PCOS is a symptom complex with multiple definitions; a commonly used one requires 2 of 3:

  • Presence of cysts on ovarian imaging
  • Evidence of androgen excess (e.g. acne, hirsutism)
  • Disrupted menstruation (amenorrhea)

Since both androgen excess and disrupted menstruation can be established from history and physical exam alone, B can be correct. A is wrong - cystic ovaries are extremely common and never sufficient alone under any definition. C is wrong - PCOS is common. D is wrong - excess androgens and estrone are found in PCOS; estradiol levels are usually normal.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: Which of the following does NOT increase serum cortisol levels?

options.html: Intense or prolonged physical exertion immediately prior to test
Hypoglycemia
Hyperglycemia
Pregnancy
Oral contraceptive pills

answer:
The correct answer is C. Anything affecting either the total amount of cortisol or the amount of cortisol-binding globulin (CBG) can interfere with a serum cortisol measurement.

  • A does interfere - intense or prolonged exertion induces cortisol release.
  • B does - cortisol antagonizes insulin and raises serum glucose, so in hypoglycemia cortisol rises.
  • D and E do - pregnancy and OCP use elevate CBG, and to maintain free cortisol the body synthesizes more, raising the total concentration.
  • C does not: it is unreasonable to release cortisol and raise glucose when glucose is already high.

stem: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding pheochromocytomas?

options.html: 10% arise in childhood
10% are extra-adrenal
10% are benign
10% are associated with familial syndromes
10% are bilateral

answer:
The correct answer is C. Built around the lecture's "Rule of 10s":

  • ~10% arise in association with familial syndromes (MEN2A, MEN2B, VHL, NF1, NF2)
  • ~10% are extra-adrenal
  • ~10% are bilateral
  • ~10% are malignant ← so ~90% are benign, making C the incorrect statement
  • ~10% arise in childhood

The key also walks through reasoning it out if you forget which items the 10% attaches to: tumours are generally rare in children and almost never environmental when they do occur, so "10% childhood" and "10% familial" support each other and are unlikely to be the wrong one. "10% bilateral" is reasonable because it implies 90% unilateral, far more plausible than the inverse - bilateral disease would require either two independent de novo neoplastic events or undetected metastasis to the other gland.

lecture: Development of the female reproductive tract
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1. Taught in the **Endocrinology** block. Tests [[07 - Development of the Female Reproductive System]].
stem: Which of the following structures gives rise to the female external genitalia?

options.html: Paramesonephric ducts
Mesonephric ducts
Urogenital sinus
Wolffian ducts

answer:
The correct answer is C. Urogenital sinus.

From Development of the Female Reproductive System. C wins by elimination: it is the only option that is not an internal duct. Female external genitalia develop in weeks 9-14, driven by estrogen and the absence of DHT, from the swellings around the urogenital sinus's opening: genital tubercle → clitoris, urethral folds → labia minora, labioscrotal swellings → labia majora, all three staying unfused. The sinus itself gives the lower 2/3 of the vagina via the sinovaginal bulbs.

  • A fails: the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts form the tubes, uterus, cervix and upper 1/3 of the vagina - all internal.
  • B, D fail: one structure under two names (mesonephric = Wolffian), which degenerates without testosterone and leaves only remnants such as Gartner's duct.

flags.title: Off-curriculum
flags.html: This year's lectures do not teach this. Checked against 07 - Development of the Female Reproductive System, the nearest lecture, which says: “genital tubercle → clitoris, urethral folds → labia minora, labioscrotal swellings → labia majora”.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter and the phrase only. For context: the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts give the uterus, fallopian tubes and upper vagina; the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts are the male internal tract and regress in females — note that B and D are the same structure under two names, which is itself a clue.

flags.title: The key is loosely worded
flags.html: Development of the Female Reproductive System derives the external genitalia from the genital tubercle, urethral folds and labioscrotal swellings, not from the urogenital sinus, which gives the lower 2/3 of the vagina. C is still the best of the four (the others are internal ducts), so the key stands - but learn the tubercle / folds / swellings mapping, not "sinus → external genitalia".

options.html: Exogenous cortisol
Pituitary adenoma
Adrenal adenoma
